Reliability is evaluated via both int32 bit-flip injection (as a conservative proxy) and direct CKKS encrypted fault injection across 40 full-model and 108 per-layer experiments spanning two architectures, two datasets, two numerical representations, and five bit-error rates.
AI.result: PSAP-pruned models limit catastrophic layers (>10 pp accuracy drop) to ≤2, versus 5–14 for magnitude-pruned baselines, reducing worst-case vulnerability by up to 29× under int32 faults. Direct CKKS fault injection identifies a safe operating boundary near BER ≈ 10⁻⁵. Fault-critical structural layers comprise only 1.1% of total parameters, enabling selective hardening at minimal overhead. On efficiency, PSAP reduces Halevi–Shoup rotations by up to 45.2% on ResNet-32, and the mixed-degree allocation scheme lowers multiplicative depth from 66 to 56 levels, enabling leveled inference without bootstrapping.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware structured pruning (PSAP) is a viable and effective strategy for deploying neural networks under CKKS homomorphic encryption, achieving both competitive computational efficiency and significantly improved fault resilience. The finding that only ~1% of parameters are fault-critical opens the door to cost-effective selective hardening for secure encrypted inference.

title: BatchDAG: LLM-Planned Execution Graphs for Scalable Ad-Hoc Analysis Over Enterprise Data
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at analyzing individual documents but break down on exhaustive, cross-entity analytical questions over enterprise-scale datasets due to context overflow, loss of per-entity attribution, and linear latency from sequential tool calls. We present BatchDAG, a system in which an LLM generates a typed directed acyclic graph (DAG) of operations -- SQL queries, semantic searches, in-memory transforms, parallel fan-outs, and single-shot analyses -- which a deterministic engine evaluates with topological-wave parallelism and structured JSON data flow. A key optimization, entity-aware batching, groups rows by logical entity before fan-out, reducing LLM calls by up to 47x. BatchDAG is not primarily an accuracy improvement over hand-optimized pipelines; rather, it is a general-purpose orchestration layer that replaces multiple hand-engineered workflows with a single system that generates the appropriate execution strategy from natural language. In controlled experiments on 12 transcript-heavy queries, BatchDAG (3.74/5) achieves quality comparable to an expert-designed pipeline (3.25/5) and significantly outperforms a ReAct agent (3.09/5, p<0.01), with superior provenance (77% transcript evidence rate vs. 46-60% for baselines). A controlled ablation shows structured JSON intermediates reduce hallucinations by 27% versus prose summaries (paired t-test, p=0.107, n=12). The planner achieves 98.8% valid-DAG rate across 300 planning calls. In production at Brevian.ai, BatchDAG processes queries over 50,000+ meetings in under 60 seconds, with measured per-query costs of $0.02-$0.24 at published GPT-5.1 pricing.

AI.tldr: BatchDAG is an LLM-powered system that generates a typed DAG of operations (SQL, semantic search, parallel fan-outs) to answer cross-entity analytical queries over enterprise-scale datasets. It replaces multiple hand-engineered workflows with a single natural-language-driven orchestration layer, achieving quality comparable to expert pipelines while reducing LLM calls via entity-aware batching and cutting hallucinations through structured JSON intermediates.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with exhaustive cross-entity analytical queries over large enterprise datasets due to three failure modes: (1) context overflow when attempting to process all entities at once, (2) loss of per-entity attribution in aggregated analyses, and (3) linear latency from sequential tool calls. Existing solutions require hand-optimized, brittle pipelines for each query type.
AI.method: BatchDAG uses an LLM planner to generate a typed directed acyclic graph (DAG) of operations — including SQL queries, semantic searches, in-memory transforms, parallel fan-outs, and single-shot analyses. A deterministic engine executes this DAG with topological-wave parallelism, flowing structured JSON between nodes. The key optimization is entity-aware batching, which groups rows by logical entity before fan-out to minimize redundant LLM invocations (up to 47x reduction).
AI.result: On 12 transcript-heavy queries, BatchDAG scored 3.74/5 vs. 3.25/5 for expert-designed pipelines and 3.09/5 for ReAct agents (p<0.01 vs. ReAct). It achieved 77% transcript evidence rate vs. 46–60% for baselines. Structured JSON intermediates reduced hallucinations by 27% compared to prose summaries (p=0.107, n=12). The planner produced valid DAGs in 98.8% of 300 calls. In production over 50,000+ meetings, queries complete in under 60 seconds at $0.02–$0.24 per query (GPT-5.1 pricing).
AI.conclusion: BatchDAG demonstrates that an LLM-driven DAG orchestration layer can match expert-crafted pipeline quality while generalizing across query types, with structured data flow and entity-aware batching being critical design choices for scalability, provenance, and cost efficiency in enterprise-scale document analytics.

title: EduPanel: A Three-Agent LLM Judge for Teaching Videos -- Reliability, Complementarity, and Human Trust Calibration
summary: Teaching videos are becoming a major medium for education, creating a growing need for scalable evaluation of their pedagogical quality. Existing automatic judges do not fully address this setting because teaching quality depends on multimodal evidence and should be evaluated with respect to the intended learner rather than as a universal property. We present EduPanel, a rubric-grounded, learner-conditioned LLM judge that decomposes evaluation across specialized agents to produce interpretable assessments for different aspects of teaching quality. Across expert studies, architecture ablations, and learner-persona analyses, EduPanel achieves reliability comparable to a median human expert. In expert evaluation, its feedback improves scoring accuracy (MAE 0.87 to 0.73), while experts remain able to detect unreliable outputs (AUC = 0.77) instead of accepting them blindly. These results suggest that EduPanel can serve as effective assistants for educational evaluation rather than replacements for human experts.

AI.tldr: EduPanel is a rubric-grounded, learner-conditioned LLM judge that decomposes teaching video evaluation across specialized agents, achieving reliability comparable to human experts while improving expert scoring accuracy when used as an assistive tool.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic evaluation methods for teaching videos are inadequate because they fail to account for two key factors: (1) teaching quality is inherently multimodal (requiring integration of visual, verbal, and behavioral cues), and (2) quality should be assessed relative to the intended learner's needs rather than as a universal, context-independent property.
AI.method: EduPanel employs a multi-agent LLM architecture grounded in evaluation rubrics. It decomposes the assessment task across specialized agents, each responsible for different aspects of teaching quality. The system conditions its judgments on learner personas, making evaluations learner-specific rather than universal.
AI.result: EduPanel achieves reliability comparable to a median human expert. When experts use its feedback, scoring accuracy improves (MAE from 0.87 to 0.73). Experts can reliably detect unreliable outputs (AUC = 0.77) rather than accepting them blindly, supporting its role as an assistant rather than a replacement.
AI.conclusion: EduPanel can serve as an effective assistive tool for educational evaluation, augmenting rather than replacing human experts. Its learner-conditioned, rubric-grounded design produces interpretable, multi-faceted assessments that improve human scoring accuracy while maintaining appropriate expert oversight.

title: AI Tool Discovery at Scale: All You Need is DNS
comment: keywords: AI tool discovery, ToolDNS, Agent, DNS
summary: The coming era of autonomous AI agents demands a discovery mechanism capable of navigating millions of tools, yet existing solutions buckle under O(N) complexity and centralized governance. Instead of building another fragile overlay, we propose ToolDNS, a radical framework that retrofits semantic tool discovery onto the Internet's most resilient substrate: the Domain Name System (DNS). By embedding functional intent and organizational trust into a hierarchical namespace, ToolDNS transforms an expensive semantic search into a series of lightweight, O(log N) name resolutions. We introduce three protocol-compliant enhancements to enable decentralized governance and semantic pruning: partially unfolded names, EDNS0 intent payloads, and logical subdomains. To rigorously evaluate this approach across the fragmented tooling landscape, we construct and release a large-scale heterogeneous benchmark comprising 33,688 real-world tools spanning MCP, A2A, RESTful, and Skill protocols. On this dataset, ToolDNS slashes the per-query search space by 95.26% while matching state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy. Furthermore, its UDP-native design reduces discovery latency by orders of magnitude compared to HTTP-based registries. Our work demonstrates that scalable AI interoperability requires not more middleware, but a smarter utilization of the infrastructure already beneath our feet.

AI.tldr: ToolDNS retrofits semantic tool discovery onto DNS, achieving O(log N) resolution, 95.26% search space reduction, and orders-of-magnitude lower latency than HTTP registries, while matching SOTA retrieval accuracy on a 33,688-tool benchmark.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents require discovery across millions of tools, but existing solutions suffer from O(N) complexity and centralized governance, making them unscalable and fragile for the coming era of massive tool ecosystems.
AI.method: ToolDNS embeds functional intent and organizational trust into a hierarchical DNS namespace, converting semantic search into O(log N) DNS resolutions. Three DNS-compliant enhancements are introduced: partially unfolded names, EDNS0 intent payloads, and logical subdomains, enabling decentralized governance and semantic pruning without breaking existing DNS infrastructure.
AI.result: Evaluated on a newly constructed benchmark of 33,688 real-world tools (MCP, A2A, RESTful, Skill protocols), ToolDNS reduces per-query search space by 95.26%, matches state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy, and achieves orders-of-magnitude lower discovery latency via its UDP-native design compared to HTTP-based registries.
AI.conclusion: Scalable AI tool interoperability is better achieved by leveraging existing infrastructure (DNS) rather than building additional middleware layers. ToolDNS demonstrates that a decentralized, hierarchical namespace atop DNS can efficiently solve large-scale tool discovery.

title: PLAID-PRF: Pseudo-Relevance Feedback with Centroid-like Tokens in PLAID
summary: Multi-vector dense retrieval models, such as ColBERT, achieve strong retrieval effectiveness by modelling fine-grained token-level interactions between queries and documents. Methods such as PLAID use centroid-based quantisation of each token's vector to reduce the index size and speed up retrieval while maintaining strong effectiveness. In this work, we introduce PLAID-PRF, a method that performs Pseudo-Relevance Feedback (PRF) over PLAID to reformulate ColBERT's query vectors based on the top-retrieved results. In contrast with prior methods that perform PRF on multi-vector retrieval models, PLAID-PRF keeps computational costs low by leveraging the internal PLAID centroid vectors, treating them similarly to tokens in traditional PRF methods. The method selects a small and diverse set of high-utility expansion vectors and appends them to the original query, rerunning PLAID to refine both candidate generation and final scoring. Extensive experiments on the standard in-domain MSMARCO and four out-of-domain BEIR benchmarks show that PLAID-PRF consistently improves retrieval effectiveness over various baselines. In particular, PLAID-PRF improves over PLAID by up to 4.3% nDCG@10 and 7.3% MRR@10, while introducing substantially less computation overhead than prior PRF methods. The results demonstrate that our proposed centroid-aware PRF method offers an effective and lightweight mechanism to improve the quality of top-ranked retrieved results. Overall, this work enables effective and efficient feedback-aware late-interaction retrieval without expensive query-time document-token clustering.

AI.tldr: PLAID-PRF introduces a lightweight pseudo-relevance feedback mechanism for ColBERT-style multi-vector retrieval by leveraging PLAID's internal centroid vectors as expansion tokens, improving nDCG@10 by up to 4.3% and MRR@10 by up to 7.3% with substantially lower computational overhead than prior PRF methods.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-vector dense retrieval models like ColBERT achieve strong effectiveness, but pseudo-relevance feedback (PRF) methods for these models are computationally expensive, often requiring costly query-time document-token clustering. The authors aim to develop a lightweight PRF mechanism that leverages PLAID's existing centroid-based infrastructure to perform efficient query reformulation without sacrificing retrieval quality.
AI.method: PLAID-PRF operates entirely within the PLAID centroid-based framework. It treats PLAID's centroid vectors analogously to tokens in traditional PRF. From the top-retrieved results of an initial PLAID run, it selects a small, diverse set of high-utility expansion centroid vectors and appends them to the original query representation. PLAID is then rerun with the augmented query to refine both candidate generation and final scoring — avoiding expensive document-token clustering at query time.
AI.result: On in-domain MSMARCO and four out-of-domain BEIR benchmarks, PLAID-PRF consistently improves over PLAID and other baselines, achieving gains of up to 4.3% nDCG@10 and 7.3% MRR@10, while introducing substantially less computation overhead than prior PRF methods for multi-vector retrieval.
AI.conclusion: PLAID-PRF demonstrates that centroid-aware pseudo-relevance feedback is an effective and efficient method for improving top-ranked retrieval quality in late-interaction models, enabling feedback-aware retrieval without the prohibitive cost of query-time token-level clustering.

title: Building a European Multilingual Evaluation Dataset: The MMLU Localisation Project within the EMT Network
summary: This paper reports on a collaboration between the Directorate-General for Translation (DGT) and the European Master's in Translation (EMT) to localise the MMLU dataset into 11 European languages. Beyond creating a more inclusive benchmark for LLM evaluation, the project offers master's students authentic, project-based professional training in translation, revision, project management, and multilingual coordination, while highlighting key methodological, administrative, and workflow challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a collaborative project between DGT and EMT to localize the MMLU benchmark into 11 European languages, serving dual purposes: creating a more inclusive multilingual LLM evaluation benchmark and providing authentic professional training for master's students in translation and project management.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of multilingual inclusivity in LLM evaluation benchmarks (specifically MMLU, which is English-centric) while simultaneously offering translation master's students hands-on, real-world professional experience in translation, revision, project management, and multilingual coordination.
AI.method: A collaborative institutional framework between DGT (a major EU translation body) and the EMT network, wherein master's students localize the MMLU dataset into 11 European languages through structured project-based workflows involving translation, revision, and coordination tasks.
AI.result: The project successfully produced a localized MMLU benchmark in 11 European languages and generated authentic training outcomes for students. It also revealed key methodological, administrative, and workflow challenges inherent in large-scale multilingual localization efforts.
AI.conclusion: Institutional collaboration between translation bodies and academic programs can effectively advance both LLM evaluation inclusivity and translator training, though careful attention must be paid to the methodological and administrative complexities involved.

title: Beyond Resolved Rate: A Non-Functional Quality Study
summary: Repository-level coding benchmarks typically measure progress in model capability by comparing the resolved rates of later and earlier models. However, this focus overlooks whether the non-functional quality of their generated patches has also changed across model generations. This study investigates whether later models produce functionally correct patches with better non-functional characteristics than earlier models on comparable repository-level repair tasks. We conducted two case studies involving four Claude and DeepSeek models on SWE-bench Lite. Using the same SWE-agent functional repair setting, we evaluated the generated patches with CodeQL, CodeScene, CPU time, and peak memory. Our primary analysis compared the models on commonly resolved instances. The static analysis results showed that most CodeQL paired differences were zero and that no CodeQL or CodeScene comparison remained significant after Holm correction. CPU time differences were small and inconsistent across model families, while peak memory usage was slightly higher for the later models under the benchmark test workload, with small absolute differences. Differences in individual CodeQL rules and CodeScene categories varied across model families and did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Overall, later models resolved more instances but showed no consistent improvement in the measured non-functional indicators on tasks solved by both models. Through this study, we hope to encourage a more comprehensive evaluation of models' practical software engineering capabilities.

AI.tldr: This study examines whether newer LLMs produce not only more functionally correct patches but also better non-functional quality (static analysis violations, code complexity, runtime performance) on SWE-bench Lite. Comparing Claude and DeepSeek model generations, the authors find no consistent improvement in non-functional indicators on commonly resolved instances, despite higher resolution rates in later models.
AI.motivation: Repository-level coding benchmarks like SWE-bench typically evaluate model progress solely by functional correctness (resolved rates), ignoring whether generated patches also improve in non-functional quality metrics such as static analysis compliance, code complexity, CPU time, and memory usage. This gap risks overestimating practical software engineering capability.
AI.method: Two case studies were conducted using four models from the Claude and DeepSeek families on SWE-bench Lite. All models used the same SWE-agent functional repair setting. Generated patches were evaluated with CodeQL (static analysis), CodeScene (code complexity/health), CPU time, and peak memory. The primary analysis compared model pairs on commonly resolved instances using paired difference tests with Holm correction for multiple comparisons.
AI.result: Most CodeQL paired differences were zero, and no CodeQL or CodeScene comparison remained statistically significant after Holm correction. CPU time differences were small and inconsistent across model families. Peak memory usage was slightly higher for later models under benchmark workloads, with small absolute differences. Individual rule/category differences did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Later models resolved more instances overall but showed no consistent non-functional improvement on commonly solved tasks.
AI.conclusion: Later-generation models improve functional resolution rates but do not consistently produce patches with better non-functional quality on tasks both models can solve. The authors advocate for incorporating non-functional metrics into model evaluation to better assess practical software engineering capabilities.

title: HALLMARK: Diagnosing Three Failure Modes in LLM Citation Verifiers
comment: 59 pages, 7 figures, 40 tables. Benchmark and code: https://github.com/rpatrik96/hallmark (v1.2.0); verification tool: https://github.com/rpatrik96/bibtexupdater (v1.5.0)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) now routinely draft literature reviews and assist with academic writing, which means a higher risk of fabricated references: GPTZero found 53 papers with hallucinated citations among NeurIPS 2025's accepted set. Rule- and LLM-based verifiers are emerging, but no shared benchmark compares them and gives detailed failure diagnostics. We close that gap with HALLMARK (Hallucination benchmark): 2,526 BibTeX entries spanning 14 hallucination types, three difficulty tiers, six diagnostic sub-tests per entry, and a contamination-resistant held-out split. On it we evaluate a DOI-lookup baseline, frontier LLMs zero-shot, tool-augmented agents, and our own rule-based, co-designed verifier bibtex-updater. Across the benchmark one result is consistent: the false-positive rate, not recall, decides whether a verifier is deployable. HALLMARK makes it concrete through three failure modes: agentic lookups buy recall but inflate false positives; at a venue-realistic base rate, the order-of-magnitude spread in false-positive rates (FPRs) -- not recall -- governs whether a verifier's flags are mostly true catches or mostly noise; and most LLMs over-flag papers published past their training cutoff, where only the two latest-cutoff models hold their false-positive rate near in-distribution levels (a signal we report as descriptive, since it is confounded with possible recall of those entries). Thus FPR is the deployment bottleneck, but an undetected fabrication remains the costlier error for the scientific record.

AI.tldr: HALLMARK is a benchmark of 2,526 BibTeX entries with 14 hallucination types and 6 diagnostic sub-tests, used to evaluate reference verifiers. The key finding: false-positive rate (FPR), not recall, determines deployability. Agentic lookups improve recall but inflate FPR; most LLMs over-flag papers past their training cutoff; while FPR is the deployment bottleneck, undetected fabrication remains the costlier error for science.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly draft academic literature reviews, leading to a rise in hallucinated citations (e.g., 53 found in NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers). While rule-based and LLM-based verifiers are being developed, no shared benchmark exists to compare them systematically or provide detailed failure diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors introduce HALLMARK, a benchmark comprising 2,526 BibTeX entries across 14 hallucination types, three difficulty tiers, six diagnostic sub-tests per entry, and a contamination-resistant held-out split. They evaluate a DOI-lookup baseline, frontier LLMs in zero-shot, tool-augmented agents, and their own rule-based verifier (bibtex-updater), measuring recall, FPR, and failure modes across configurations.
AI.result: Three consistent findings emerge: (1) agentic lookups boost recall but substantially inflate false positives; (2) at venue-realistic base rates, the order-of-magnitude spread in FPR — not recall — governs whether flagging is trustworthy; (3) most LLMs over-flag papers published after their training cutoff, while only the two most recent models maintain near in-distribution FPR on those entries.
AI.conclusion: FPR is the primary deployment bottleneck for citation verifiers, as high false-positive rates render flags unreliable. However, undetected fabrication (false negatives) remains the costlier error for the integrity of the scientific record, creating a tension between deployability and safety.

title: ChatMuse: Supporting In-Person Small-Group Conversation Experience with a Proactive Assistive AI Agent in Mixed Reality
summary: In-person small-group conversations occur across nearly every aspect of daily life and play a crucial role in social interaction. However, achieving effective in-person group conversations can be challenging and cognitively demanding. While recent Mixed Reality (MR) headsets show promise as a conversational support system by presenting relevant information through overlays, it remains unclear how such supporting information should be designed and generated for in-person group conversations. We propose ChatMuse, a novel MR-based proactive assistive system for in-person small-group conversation experience. ChatMuse analyzes verbal and non-verbal cues from all conversation participants and proactively provides real-time guidance on the user's verbal and non-verbal behaviors. The behavioral responses of the supported users are then used to improve ChatMuse's support capabilities in subsequent interactions. We conducted a within-subject study to evaluate and demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of ChatMuse in assisting users to engage in and contribute to in-person small-group conversations. Our research around ChatMuse represents a design exploration of a new interaction space that investigates the feasibility of supporting in-person small-group conversations through a proactive assistive AI agent in MR.

AI.tldr: ChatMuse is an MR-based proactive assistive system that analyzes verbal/non-verbal cues in real-time to provide behavioral guidance during in-person small-group conversations, demonstrating feasibility through a within-subject study.
AI.motivation: In-person small-group conversations are socially crucial yet cognitively demanding. While MR headsets can overlay supporting information, it is unclear how such information should be designed and generated specifically for group conversation contexts.
AI.method: The authors developed ChatMuse, an MR system that: (1) analyzes verbal and non-verbal cues from all participants, (2) proactively provides real-time behavioral guidance (both verbal and non-verbal) to the user via MR overlays, and (3) uses the user's behavioral responses as feedback to iteratively improve its support capabilities. A within-subject study was conducted to evaluate the system.
AI.result: The within-subject study demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of ChatMuse in assisting users to engage in and contribute to in-person small-group conversations.
AI.conclusion: ChatMuse represents a design exploration of a new interaction space investigating the feasibility of proactive assistive AI agents in MR for supporting in-person small-group conversations.

title: An Epistemic Position-Based Click Model: From Interactions to Epistemic Distributions of Relevance and Bias
summary: User interactions with rankings are affected by both items' relevances and display positions. Accordingly, click probabilities are often modeled as a product of relevance and position factors; and for improving recommendation and search, one needs to disentangle relevance from position bias. However, existing click models only provide frequentist point-estimates that do not capture any measure of epistemic uncertainty. Consequently, there is no indication of how much confidence one should have in their predictions. In this work, we introduce the first evidential deep-learning approach to form an epistemic alternative to the important position-based click model. Our learned model takes as input item and position features and outputs a beta-distribution for every relevance and position-bias variable of the position-based model. These distributions capture epistemic uncertainty about click probabilities and the underlying effects of attraction and position bias. The main challenge of our approach is its optimization for which we propose approximation and conditioning techniques to provide numerical stability and variance reduction. Our experiments indicate that our approach captures epistemic uncertainty in predictions on previously-unseen data, whereas standard policy gradients fail to learn meaningful distributions. We believe our contribution of the first contextual epistemic click model constitutes an important step in incorporating Bayesian uncertainty into click modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first evidential deep-learning approach for position-based click modeling that outputs beta distributions to capture epistemic uncertainty, overcoming the limitation of existing frequentist point-estimate models, with novel optimization techniques for numerical stability.
AI.motivation: Existing click models based on the position-based model (PBM) only provide frequentist point estimates of relevance and position bias, offering no measure of epistemic uncertainty. This leaves practitioners without any indication of confidence in predictions, which is critical for reliable recommendation and search systems.
AI.method: The authors propose an evidential deep-learning framework that takes item and position features as input and outputs beta distributions for every relevance and position-bias variable in the PBM. These distributions explicitly capture epistemic uncertainty. To address optimization challenges—numerical instability and high variance—they introduce approximation and conditioning techniques that stabilize training and reduce variance.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully captures epistemic uncertainty in predictions on held-out, previously unseen data. In contrast, standard policy gradient methods fail to learn meaningful distributions, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed optimization techniques.
AI.conclusion: This work constitutes the first contextual epistemic click model and represents an important step toward incorporating principled Bayesian uncertainty into click modeling, enabling more trustworthy and confidence-aware ranking systems.

title: Relay-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Multi-Domain Reasoning Chains
summary: Introducing Relay-Bench, an unsaturated, holistic, text-only benchmark that measures LLMs' ability to complete an assortment of tasks from distinct domains in a single prompt. The leading model, GPT-5.5 (xHigh), scores 43.3%. The test set entirely consists of composite problems: groups of single-domain subproblems that are strung together into challenges that require reasoning across multiple domains in combination. Many of these problems then have layers of complexity added through prompt encoding and deliberate context bloat. Domains tested include visual reasoning, coding, math, information extraction (with a focus on web search), problem-solving, general knowledge, and data analysis. No restrictions are imposed outside of the model harness, and models are explicitly encouraged to leverage code-execution, web searches, and all available tools. All problems are composed of two to thirteen subproblems and do not require multi-modal input or output.

AI.tldr: Relay-Bench is a new text-only benchmark featuring composite, multi-domain problems (2–13 subproblems) with added complexity via prompt encoding and context bloat. GPT-5.5 (xHigh) leads at 43.3%. Models are encouraged to use tools like code execution and web search.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks often saturate quickly and test isolated skills. Relay-Bench addresses this by creating unsaturated, holistic evaluations that require models to chain reasoning across multiple domains within a single prompt, better reflecting real-world, complex task requirements.
AI.method: The benchmark constructs composite problems by stringing together subproblems from distinct domains (visual reasoning, coding, math, information extraction, problem-solving, general knowledge, data analysis). Additional complexity is introduced through prompt encoding techniques and deliberate context bloat. Problems are text-only (no multi-modal I/O), contain 2–13 subproblems, and models are permitted unrestricted use of tools including code execution and web search.
AI.result: The best-performing model, GPT-5.5 (xHigh), achieves only 43.3% accuracy, indicating the benchmark remains highly unsaturated and challenging for current state-of-the-art LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Relay-Bench reveals significant headroom in LLMs' ability to handle composite, cross-domain reasoning tasks. The low top score (43.3%) demonstrates that even leading models struggle when multiple domains must be integrated within a single prompt, especially under conditions of encoding complexity and context bloat.

title: Semantic Drift in Bug Resolution: How Behavioral Signals Propagate from Reports to Tests and Patches
summary: Bug resolution is a cross-artifact process: natural-language reports must expose actionable behavioral cues that can be reproduced by tests and corrected by patches. Yet the extent to which these signals are preserved across artifacts remains largely unquantified. We introduce Desc2Fix, a framework for measuring semantic alignment between bug reports, triggering tests, and developer-written fixes. Alignment is operationalized through structured behavioral anchors (e.g., reproduction steps, API/exception cues, expected vs. actual behavior), deterministic similarity metrics (ROUGE, SBERT, CodeBERT, OpenAI embeddings), and LLM-based judgments grounded in coverage, correctness, and specificity. We analyze 2,857 report-test-patch triplets from Defects4J and SWT-Bench using GPT-4o and DeepSeek-Chat. LLMs reliably extract structured signals (up to 90% completeness) and exhibit strong cross-model consistency, yielding a stable semantic input contract for downstream reasoning. However, alignment is highly representation-sensitive: lexical similarity alone is insufficient; full diffs provide the most stable basis for judging report-patch correspondence; and structured summaries trade surface similarity for predicate-level salience. Across more than 182,000 LLM alignment ratings, both models show systematic optimism relative to humans (1-2 points on 5-point scales) and only modest rank agreement, motivating bias-aware evaluation. Our results demonstrate that behavioral alignment is measurable but not reducible to similarity, and that structured anchors combined with embedding-based proxies provide reproducible signals for ranking and filtering tests and candidate patches. By transforming alignment into a controllable engineering signal, Desc2Fix enables more reliable test generation, semantics-aware fault localization, principled patch ranking, and improved bug report authoring.

AI.tldr: Desc2Fix introduces a framework to quantify semantic alignment across bug reports, triggering tests, and patches, using structured behavioral anchors, similarity metrics, and LLM judgments. Analysis of 2,857 triples shows alignment is measurable, representation-sensitive, and not reducible to surface similarity, with LLMs exhibiting systematic optimism relative to human evaluators.
AI.motivation: Bug resolution spans multiple artifacts (reports, tests, patches), yet no quantitative framework exists to measure how well behavioral signals are preserved across these artifacts. This gap limits automated test generation, patch ranking, and fault localization.
AI.method: Desc2Fix operationalizes alignment via structured behavioral anchors (reproduction steps, API/exception cues, expected vs. actual behavior), deterministic similarity metrics (ROUGE, SBERT, CodeBERT, OpenAI embeddings), and LLM-based judgments (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-Chat) evaluated on coverage, correctness, and specificity. The framework is applied to 2,857 report-test-patch triplets from Defects4J and SWT-Bench, producing over 182,000 LLM alignment ratings.
AI.result: LLMs extract structured signals with up to 90% completeness and show strong cross-model consistency. However, alignment is representation-sensitive: lexical similarity alone is insufficient; full diffs provide the most stable basis for report-patch correspondence; structured summaries trade surface similarity for predicate-level salience. Both models exhibit systematic optimism (1–2 points above humans on 5-point scales) with only modest rank agreement, motivating bias-aware evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral alignment is measurable but not reducible to similarity. Structured anchors combined with embedding-based proxies yield reproducible signals for ranking and filtering tests/patches, enabling more reliable test generation, semantics-aware fault localization, principled patch ranking, and improved bug report authoring.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Phishing Email Detection: A Comparative Study of TF-IDF + Logistic Regression and Fine-Tuned DistilBERT
summary: Phishing emails remain one of the most persistent cybersecurity threats, and machine-learning classifiers are widely used to detect them. Most reported detection accuracies, however, are measured on clean, in-distribution test data rather than on emails deliberately altered to evade detection. This paper reports a controlled, pairwise comparison of two phishing-detection approaches a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression baseline and a fine-tuned DistilBERT transformer trained on a unified corpus of 82,255 emails drawn from six public datasets and evaluated under three conditions: normal in-distribution, synthetic phishing, and adversarial phishing. Both models exceeded 98% accuracy on clean data yet degraded sharply under adversarial testing: TF-IDF + LR fell to 64.00% (a 34.59-percentage-point drop) and DistilBERT fell to 63.64% (a 35.40-percentage-point drop) a gap of only 0.36 percentage points, equivalent to a single email in the 275-sample adversarial test set. LIME, SHAP, and attention-rollout analysis indicate the two models relied on different evidence yet showed similar vulnerability. Pairwise error analysis shows the models agreed on 54.9% of adversarial samples but each made a similar number of exclusive errors (24 and 25 respectively), indicating partly complementary rather than identical failure modes. The results show that clean-data accuracy does not predict adversarial robustness, and that adversarial testing should be a standard part of phishing-detection evaluation.

AI.tldr: Two phishing email classifiers — TF-IDF + Logistic Regression and fine-tuned DistilBERT — both achieve >98% clean-data accuracy but drop to ~64% under adversarial testing, a near-identical ~35-point degradation. LIME, SHAP, and attention analyses reveal different evidence reliance yet similar vulnerability, with only 54.9% overlap in adversarial errors, suggesting partly complementary failure modes.
AI.motivation: Most phishing detection studies report accuracy on clean, in-distribution test data, ignoring real-world scenarios where attackers deliberately craft emails to evade classifiers. The paper seeks to quantify how severely detection performance degrades under adversarial conditions and whether different model architectures exhibit distinct failure patterns.
AI.method: A controlled pairwise comparison using a unified corpus of 82,255 emails from six public datasets. Two models are evaluated: a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression baseline and a fine-tuned DistilBERT transformer. Testing occurs under three conditions: (1) normal in-distribution, (2) synthetic phishing, and (3) adversarial phishing (275-sample test set). Explainability tools — LIME, SHAP, and attention rollout — are used to analyze model decision rationales, and pairwise error analysis quantifies agreement and complementary errors.
AI.result: Both models exceed 98% accuracy on clean data. Under adversarial testing, TF-IDF + LR drops to 64.00% (−34.59 pp) and DistilBERT to 63.64% (−35.40 pp), a gap of only 0.36 pp. Explainability analyses show the models rely on different textual evidence. Pairwise error analysis reveals agreement on 54.9% of adversarial samples, with each model making a comparable number of exclusive errors (24 vs. 25), indicating partially complementary failure modes rather than identical ones.
AI.conclusion: Clean-data accuracy is not a reliable proxy for adversarial robustness in phishing detection. Adversarial testing should become a standard evaluation practice. The complementary error patterns between the two models suggest that ensemble or hybrid approaches may offer a path toward improved adversarial resilience.

title: From Agent Failure Paths to Quantified Residual Risk: A Compositional Framework for Resilient Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI is crossing trust boundaries faster than current risk models can represent. Existing approaches provide one of two partial views. They either describe failure mechanisms without producing a transferable residual-risk estimate, or they produce a risk estimate while treating the internal failure path as a black box. We couple those two views by proposing CPSAINT, a seven-layer integrity decomposition over Physical state, Sensors, Data, Compute, Actuators, Environment, and Time, paired with FRIESA-K, a residual-risk functional that maps each failure path to a quantified risk instance. FRIESA-K grounds the resistance term K in a controlled absorbing Markov model so that control effectiveness is derived from state dynamics rather than assigned as an informal score. The result is a concise mechanism-to magnitude pipeline for resilient agentic and embodied AI. We report governance observability through a separate additive penalty instead of inserting governance as a new variable in the resistance functional. We formalize structural composability linking valid failure paths to well-defined risk instances and show the framework on two contrasting scenarios a hard real-time warehouse robot and a governance-instrumented financial-services agent. Across both cases, the same layer grammar, variable semantics, and dynamic-resistance construction remain intact. Thus, we obtain a compact kernel that supports cross-domain reasoning, explicit assumptions, and quantitatively grounded formalism of composable trust.

AI.tldr: Proposes CPSAINT, a seven-layer integrity decomposition for agentic AI systems, paired with FRIESA-K, a residual-risk functional using a controlled absorbing Markov model to derive control effectiveness from state dynamics, enabling a mechanism-to-magnitude risk estimation pipeline demonstrated on warehouse robotics and financial-services agents.
AI.motivation: Current risk models for agentic AI are inadequate — they either describe failure mechanisms without producing transferable residual-risk estimates, or produce risk estimates while treating internal failure paths as black boxes. Agentic AI is crossing trust boundaries faster than these models can represent, creating a need for a unified approach that couples both views.
AI.method: Introduces CPSAINT: a seven-layer integrity decomposition (Physical state, Sensors, Data, Compute, Actuators, Environment, Time). Pairs it with FRIESA-K, a residual-risk functional that grounds the resistance term K in a controlled absorbing Markov model, deriving control effectiveness from state dynamics rather than informal scoring. Governance observability is handled via a separate additive penalty rather than inserting it into the resistance functional. Structural composability is formalized to link valid failure paths to well-defined risk instances.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on two contrasting scenarios: a hard real-time warehouse robot and a governance-instrumented financial-services agent. In both cases, the same layer grammar, variable semantics, and dynamic-resistance construction remain intact, yielding a compact kernel that supports cross-domain reasoning with explicit assumptions and quantitatively grounded formalism of composable trust.
AI.conclusion: CPSAINT + FRIESA-K provides a unified, cross-domain mechanism-to-magnitude pipeline for resilient agentic and embodied AI, enabling composable trust through a consistent layer grammar, rigorous semantics, and dynamic-resistance modeling grounded in state dynamics.

title: HALO: Interactive Co-abductive Reasoning in Scientific Hypothesis Generation
comment: To appear in the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST '26). 22 pages
summary: Scientific discovery is essential yet inefficient, primarily because generating hypotheses within a vast search space hinders breakthroughs. While current AI systems assist in generating new hypothesis candidates, they lack interactive support for the reasoning process by which users develop these outputs into promising hypotheses, resulting in surface-level hypotheses. To address this issue, we present co-abduction, a human-AI collaborative framework for abductive reasoning in scientific hypothesis generation. To operationalize co-abduction, we build HALO, a human-AI collaborative system for molecular hypothesis generation in drug discovery, enabling improved candidate clustering, strategy identification, and multi-strategy synthesis. In expert studies involving 10 medicinal chemists, HALO significantly facilitated abductive reasoning for hypothesis generation -- efficient candidate observation, systematic strategy identification, and coherent multi-strategy composition -- and enabled participants to produce higher-quality, more diverse candidate molecules.

AI.tldr: HALO introduces co-abduction, a human-AI collaborative framework for abductive reasoning in scientific hypothesis generation, applied to drug discovery. In a study with 10 medicinal chemists, HALO improved hypothesis quality, candidate diversity, and reasoning processes including candidate clustering, strategy identification, and multi-strategy synthesis.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is bottlenecked by inefficient hypothesis generation within vast search spaces. Current AI hypothesis generation systems lack interactive support for the reasoning process, leading to only surface-level hypotheses rather than deep, reasoned breakthroughs.
AI.method: The authors propose co-abduction, a human-AI collaborative framework grounded in abductive reasoning. They operationalize this through HALO, a system supporting molecular hypothesis generation with capabilities for candidate clustering, strategy identification, and multi-strategy synthesis. Expert evaluation involved 10 medicinal chemists.
AI.result: HALO significantly facilitated abductive reasoning: enabling efficient candidate observation, systematic strategy identification, and coherent multi-strategy composition. Participants produced higher-quality and more diverse candidate molecules compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Co-abduction via HALO effectively bridges the gap between AI-generated candidates and human reasoning, enabling deeper, more systematic hypothesis generation in scientific discovery, with demonstrated success in drug discovery contexts.

title: Engineering Trustworthy Agentic AI for Critical Systems
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems, capable of autonomous perception, planning, tool use, and multi-step action, are increasingly proposed for critical engineering domains where decisions carry physical, operational, or economic consequences. This survey addresses a gap in current literature by treating trustworthiness, whether agentic behavior can be verified, audited, and trusted under the constraints that engineering practice actually requires, as a first-class engineering property, rather than evaluating agentic AI by task capability alone. The study adopts a trustworthiness model organized around five cross-cutting dimensions: safety and constraint satisfaction; robustness and reliability; transparency and interpretability; accountability and auditability; and privacy and security. This is mapped onto an agentic assurance workflow spanning perception through audit. Building on this foundation, agentic systems architectures, threats, concrete trust mechanisms, and quantitative metrics are surveyed for direct application in agentic systems development and evaluation. These principles are then examined across four constraint-bound engineering domains: power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, high-performance computing, and communication networks, identifying recurring design patterns, shared failure modes, and domain-specific gaps. Synthesizing across those domains, agentic AI trustworthiness is shown to be a single problem, with a path outlined toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework analogous to the graded certification regimes used by mature safety-critical engineering fields.

AI.tldr: This survey frames trustworthiness as a first-class engineering property for agentic AI systems, organizing analysis around five dimensions (safety, robustness, transparency, accountability, privacy/security) mapped onto an assurance workflow. It surveys architectures, threats, mechanisms, and metrics, then examines four constraint-bound engineering domains to identify cross-domain patterns and advocate for a reusable, graded certification framework analogous to mature safety-critical fields.
AI.motivation: Existing literature evaluates agentic AI primarily by task capability, neglecting whether such systems can be verified, audited, and trusted under real-world engineering constraints. With agentic systems increasingly deployed in domains where failures carry physical, operational, or economic consequences, there is an urgent need to treat trustworthiness as a standalone, cross-cutting engineering property rather than an afterthought.
AI.method: The study constructs a trustworthiness model with five dimensions — safety/constraint satisfaction, robustness/reliability, transparency/interpretability, accountability/auditability, and privacy/security — and maps these onto an agentic assurance workflow from perception through audit. It then surveys agentic architectures, threat taxonomies, concrete trust mechanisms (e.g., shields, monitors, explainability methods), and quantitative metrics. These are applied across four domains (power systems, autonomous vehicles/robotics/UAVs, high-performance computing, communication networks) to extract recurring design patterns, shared failure modes, and domain-specific gaps.
AI.result: The cross-domain analysis reveals that agentic AI trustworthiness manifests as a single unified problem, not separate domain-specific challenges. Recurring design patterns and shared failure modes emerge across power systems, autonomous systems, HPC, and communication networks. Domain-specific gaps remain where current trust mechanisms lack maturity. The synthesis supports the feasibility of a generalized, reusable cross-domain assurance framework.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI trustworthiness should be treated as a unified engineering discipline. A path exists toward a reusable, cross-domain assurance framework modeled on graded certification regimes from mature safety-critical engineering fields (e.g., aerospace, nuclear), enabling systematic verification, auditing, and trust for agentic systems across diverse constraint-bound domains.

title: RAGAL: A Frugal, Fully Local Retrieval-Augmented Assistant for Technical Support at a Government Agency
summary: Public institutions hold large volumes of sensitive documents and support tickets that cannot leave the premises, ruling out cloud-hosted language models entirely. We report on RAGAL, a retrieval-augmented assistant for the technical-support team of AFIR, the Romanian Agency for Financing Rural Investments, built and operated under three hard constraints: zero data egress (no external API calls, even for synthetic data), a read-only mandate (the assistant drafts, humans execute), and a single 8 GB consumer laptop as the only development and training machine. Over a Romanian-language corpus of ~25,000 chunks -- 15,073 resolved support tickets and internal normative documents -- we show that the highest-leverage investments were retrieval engineering and retriever fine-tuning rather than a larger generator: hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with intent routing raised our internal evaluation from 62% to 81%, and fine-tuning the bge-m3 embedder on real ticket data improved recall@10 from 0.663 to 0.850 (MRR 0.489 to 0.684) after 72 minutes of training. We document a general pitfall: single-domain fine-tuning silently degraded retrieval on the untouched document domain below the stock baseline, detected only after building a per-domain evaluation set and repaired with locally generated queries (GenQ). We report two counter-intuitive findings -- PII masking improved generation quality, and a structural "anchor distillation" scheme made SQL hallucination impossible by construction -- along with a reproducible recipe for full embedder fine-tuning in 8 GB of VRAM. Finally, since zero egress also rules out a cloud judge, we describe a substitute: a 744B-parameter model run on CPU, too slow to serve interactively but affordable in overnight batch, used as a second opinion whose limits we quantify. We release the sanitized pipeline scripts for institutions facing similar data-locality constraints.

AI.tldr: RAGAL is a retrieval-augmented assistant built for a Romanian government agency under zero data egress, running entirely on an 8 GB laptop. Key gains came from retrieval engineering (hybrid dense-sparse + intent routing) and fine-tuning bge-m3 embeddings on real ticket data, boosting recall@10 from 0.663 to 0.850. The paper documents pitfalls like single-domain fine-tuning degrading cross-domain retrieval, and reports counter-intuitive findings including PII masking improving generation quality and a structural SQL anti-hallucination scheme.
AI.motivation: Public institutions hold sensitive documents that cannot leave premises, ruling out cloud-hosted LLMs. The authors needed a practical, deployable assistant for AFIR's technical-support team under three hard constraints: zero data egress (no external API calls), read-only mandate (human-in-the-loop for actions), and a single 8 GB consumer laptop as the sole compute resource.
AI.method: The system (RAGAL) combines hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with intent routing, fine-tuning of bge-m3 embeddings on real Romanian-language ticket data (~72 min on 8 GB VRAM), and a generator constrained to draft-only outputs. Key techniques include: (1) per-domain evaluation sets to detect cross-domain degradation from single-domain fine-tuning, (2) GenQ (locally generated queries) to repair degraded retrieval, (3) PII masking as a pre-processing step, (4) "anchor distillation" — a structural scheme that makes SQL hallucination impossible by construction, and (5) a 744B-parameter CPU-based model run in overnight batch as a substitute for a cloud judge.
AI.result: Hybrid dense-sparse retrieval with intent routing raised internal evaluation from 62% to 81%. Fine-tuning bge-m3 on ticket data improved recall@10 from 0.663 to 0.850 and MRR from 0.489 to 0.684 after 72 minutes of training. Single-domain fine-tuning silently degraded retrieval on the untouched document domain below the stock baseline, detected only via per-domain evaluation and repaired with GenQ. PII masking unexpectedly improved generation quality. Anchor distillation eliminated SQL hallucination structurally.
AI.conclusion: Under strict data-locality constraints, retrieval engineering and embedder fine-tuning yield higher returns than scaling the generator. Institutions facing similar constraints can replicate the approach using the released sanitized pipeline scripts. The paper also provides practical guidance on evaluating RAG systems without cloud access and mitigating domain-specific degradation from fine-tuning.

title: Computational models of pragmatic reasoning with flexible generation of meaning and expression alternatives
comment: 27 pages main text, 9 figures; 25 pages supplementary materials
summary: Pragmatic language use requires reasoning about alternatives: the alternative expressions a speaker might have chosen, or the alternative interpretations a listener might entertain. Formal and computational models of pragmatics must therefore specify the sets of alternatives that interlocutors reason over, which is often done through manual specification. Here we propose a framework, ScAffolded Generative models for Explanation (SAGE), that combines the explanatory transparency of cognitive models with the generative flexibility of language models (LMs). SAGE decomposes a pragmatic process into three kinds of modules: proposers, which use LMs to generate an open-ended space of candidate alternatives; evaluators, which assess those alternatives (e.g., their semantics, complexity, or typicality); and selectors, which implement the rule-based computational steps of a cognitively motivated task analysis. We assess SAGE in three case studies spanning pragmatic generation and interpretation-referential expression generation, manner (M-)implicatures, and Gricean conversational implicatures. SAGE models are evaluated critically using established methods from computational cognitive modeling, including ablations, baseline comparisons, and quantitative fit to human data. Across studies, SAGE models achieved high accuracy and often outperformed baselines, but component-level analyses reveal an asymmetry: LM proposers reliably generated alternatives well-suited to pragmatic modeling, whereas LM evaluators are better at providing intuitive judgements rather than judgements of theoretical or formal measures. We discuss the promise and the limitations of neuro-symbolic models as candidate explanatory accounts of human pragmatic language use.

AI.tldr: SAGE (ScAffolded Generative models for Explanation) is a neuro-symbolic framework that decomposes pragmatic reasoning into LM-based proposers (generating alternatives), evaluators (assessing those alternatives), and rule-based selectors (implementing cognitive task analyses). Tested on referential expression generation, M-implicatures, and Gricean implicatures, SAGE achieves high accuracy and often outperforms baselines, though LM evaluators excel at intuitive rather than formal/theoretical judgments.
AI.motivation: Pragmatic language use requires reasoning over sets of alternative expressions or interpretations, which in formal/computational models are typically specified manually. This manual specification is a bottleneck. The authors aim to automate alternative generation using LMs while retaining the explanatory transparency of cognitive models.
AI.method: SAGE decomposes pragmatic processing into three modules: (1) Proposers — LMs that generate open-ended candidate alternatives; (2) Evaluators — modules (including LMs) that assess alternatives on dimensions like semantics, complexity, or typicality; (3) Selectors — rule-based, cognitively-motivated computational steps that implement the final pragmatic choice. The framework is tested across three case studies (referential expression generation, M-implicatures, Gricean conversational implicatures) using ablations, baseline comparisons, and quantitative fit to human data.
AI.result: SAGE models achieved high accuracy and often outperformed baselines across all three case studies. However, component-level analysis revealed an asymmetry: LM proposers reliably generated alternatives well-suited for pragmatic modeling, while LM evaluators were better at providing intuitive judgments rather than theoretically or formally grounded measures.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic SAGE framework shows promise as an explanatory account of human pragmatic language use by combining LM flexibility with cognitive model transparency. However, the asymmetry between strong generation (proposers) and weaker formal evaluation (evaluators) highlights key limitations that must be addressed for such models to serve as full computational accounts of pragmatics.

title: LM2Alloy: Investigating LLM-Generated Formal Specifications for Automated Test Derivation in Production Software
summary:
We present an exploratory study on using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate Alloy formal specifications from both requirements documentation and production source code, and to derive executable test cases from those specifications. We evaluate on two real open-source Python libraries: Flipper, a feature flag management system, and Cerberus, a data validation library.
  In both cases, the LLM produced workable Alloy specifications and executable tests without any manual correction. For Flipper, our pipeline uncovered a genuine bug that the existing test suite had missed: the library silently accepts duplicate flag names, directly contradicting its documented uniqueness requirement. A direct LLM baseline--generating tests from the same README but skipping the Alloy step--achieved 68% branch coverage yet failed to catch this bug across all three independent runs. This suggests that introducing a formal intermediate representation can surface constraint-level defects that coverage-oriented generation may miss.
  For Cerberus, the code-derived specification captured an implicit abstraction over sized types that the documentation-derived spec omitted, producing two additional tests. Across both libraries, code-based specifications showed lower variance in test generation (mean SD = 2.15) than documentation-based ones (mean SD = 5.0), though whether this generalises remains an open question.
  Index Terms--formal specifications, Alloy, large language models, automated testing, specification drift, software validation.

AI.tldr: An exploratory study shows that LLMs can generate Alloy formal specifications from requirements docs and source code, then derive executable tests. Applied to two Python libraries, the pipeline uncovered a real bug missed by both existing tests and a direct LLM test-generation baseline, suggesting formal intermediate representations help surface constraint-level defects.
AI.motivation: Traditional LLM-based test generation focuses on code coverage but may miss constraint-level defects. The authors hypothesize that introducing a formal intermediate representation (Alloy specifications) between requirements/code and test generation can help surface deeper specification violations that coverage-oriented approaches overlook.
AI.method: A pipeline that uses LLMs to (1) generate Alloy formal specifications from either requirements documentation (README) or production source code, and (2) derive executable test cases from those Alloy specs. Evaluated on two open-source Python libraries (Flipper, Cerberus), with a baseline that generates tests directly from README without the Alloy intermediate step. Metrics include branch coverage, bug detection, and variance across runs.
AI.result: For Flipper, the Alloy pipeline caught a real bug (duplicate flag names silently accepted, violating documented uniqueness) that the existing test suite and the direct LLM baseline (68% branch coverage, 3 runs) both missed. For Cerberus, code-derived specs captured an implicit abstraction over sized types that doc-derived specs omitted, yielding two extra tests. Code-based specifications showed lower variance (mean SD=2.15) than documentation-based ones (mean SD=5.0) in test generation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can produce workable Alloy specifications and derived tests without manual correction. A formal intermediate representation can surface constraint-level bugs that coverage-driven generation misses. Code-derived specs may be more stable than documentation-derived ones, though generalizability remains an open question.

title: ChainMark: Model-Free LLM Watermarking with Closed-Form Calibration
summary: Regulatory regimes such as the EU AI Act mandate machine-readable marking of synthetic text, but existing watermark detectors rely on the generating LM and on heuristic thresholds with no closed-form calibration. We introduce ChainMark, an active watermark that partitions the vocabulary into S states via keyed SHA-256 and forces a hard Markov transition on a fraction rho of positions; the detector replays the partition from the same key in O(n) hash operations, with no LM access. We derive a closed-form S*(n, rho, alpha) mapping a target FPR, text length, and budget to the minimum state count (Theorem 1), prove a universal robustness threshold delta* = 1 - 1/sqrt(2) approximately 29.3% that is invariant in (S, rho, n) (Theorem 2), and generalise both to any k-regular transition topology (Theorem 3). Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and four domains, ChainMark strictly dominates KGW and SWEET under translation and random-substitution attacks at matched budget; a one-corpus empirical recalibration restores the 1% target FPR on natural-language text.

AI.tldr: ChainMark is an active watermarking scheme for synthetic text that uses keyed SHA-256 vocabulary partitioning with hard Markov transitions, providing closed-form calibration for false positive rates, a universal robustness threshold of ~29.3%, and strong empirical performance against translation and substitution attacks without requiring LM access for detection.
AI.motivation: Regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act require machine-readable marking of synthetic text, but existing watermark detectors depend on access to the generating language model and heuristic thresholds lacking closed-form calibration, limiting their practical deployability and statistical rigor.
AI.method: ChainMark partitions the vocabulary into S states via keyed SHA-256 hashing. During generation, it forces a hard Markov transition on a fraction ρ of token positions according to a deterministic state sequence. The detector replays the partition from the same secret key using O(n) hash operations, requiring no LM access. The authors derive closed-form expressions: S*(n, ρ, α) mapping target FPR α, text length n, and budget ρ to the minimum number of states (Theorem 1); a universal robustness threshold δ* = 1 − 1/√2 ≈ 29.3% invariant in (S, ρ, n) (Theorem 2); and generalizations to any k-regular transition topology (Theorem 3). Empirical recalibration on one corpus restores the 1% target FPR on natural-language text.
AI.result: ChainMark strictly dominates KGW and SWEET baselines under both translation and random-substitution attacks at matched watermarking budget across three instruction-tuned LLMs and four domains. A single-corpus empirical recalibration successfully restores the 1% target FPR when evaluated on natural-language text.
AI.conclusion: ChainMark provides the first watermarking method with fully closed-form calibration, no LM dependency for detection, and provable robustness guarantees, making it suitable for regulatory compliance in real-world deployment scenarios.

title: SAAG: Structured Agent Assessment and Grounding
comment: Accepted to KnowFM @ ACL 2026 workshop (Non-Archival). 16 pages in total
summary: Exact-match evaluation of agent-calling obscures qualitatively different failure modes: a model may select the right function yet hallucinate argument values, or satisfy a schema while choosing a agent for the wrong reason. Existing benchmarks collapse these distinctions into a single binary score, leaving practitioners unable to diagnose where agent calls fail. We propose SAAG a cascaded diagnostic framework that decomposes agent-calling evaluation into three sequential stages: registry conformance, structural completeness, and argument grounding, each producing interpretable stage-specific diagnostics. These diagnostics additionally enable iterative self-repair: on prediction failure, the stage-specific signal guides targeted correction without leaking ground-truth values. We evaluate this framework on a controlled benchmark derived from Glaive's function-calling dataset across registry sizes of 5, 10, and 15 agents using three local sub-4B-parameter models. Structured feedback consistently improves argument precision and reduces value hallucination relative to single-pass inference and uninformative binary feedback, while end-to-end F1 gains are modest and model-dependent. These results suggest that stage-decomposed diagnostic evaluation is a necessary lens for understanding and improving agent-calling reliability across model families and registry scales.

AI.tldr: SAAG introduces a three-stage cascaded diagnostic framework for evaluating agent/function calling that decomposes evaluation into registry conformance, structural completeness, and argument grounding, providing interpretable diagnostics that also enable targeted self-repair without leaking ground truth.
AI.motivation: Exact-match evaluation of agent-calling obscures qualitatively distinct failure modes (e.g., hallucinated argument values vs. wrong agent selection for incorrect reasons), and existing benchmarks collapse these into a single binary score, leaving practitioners unable to diagnose specific failure points.
AI.method: The paper proposes SAAG, a cascaded diagnostic framework with three sequential stages: (1) registry conformance — verifying the called function exists in the registry; (2) structural completeness — checking required arguments are present and schema-valid; (3) argument grounding — assessing whether argument values are factually grounded. Stage-specific diagnostic signals further enable iterative self-repair, where failures at each stage guide targeted correction without exposing ground-truth values. Evaluation uses a controlled benchmark derived from Glaive's function-calling dataset across registry sizes of 5, 10, and 15 agents with three sub-4B-parameter local models.
AI.result: Structured stage-specific feedback consistently improves argument precision and reduces value hallucination compared to single-pass inference and uninformative binary feedback. However, end-to-end F1 gains are modest and vary across models, indicating that while diagnostic decomposition aids understanding and targeted improvement, overall task performance gains are not uniformly large.
AI.conclusion: Stage-decomposed diagnostic evaluation is a necessary lens for understanding and improving agent-calling reliability across model families and registry scales. The framework surfaces failure modes that binary metrics mask and enables targeted self-repair, though end-to-end gains remain model-dependent.

title: Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision
summary: Bowed string instruments demand fine-grained bodily coordination that is typically taught through visual demonstration, creating persistent barriers for musicians with blindness and low-vision (BLV). To understand these challenges and explore new design opportunities, we conducted a design study with four advanced string musicians with BLV and three of their instructors. Our team, spanning violin performance and music education, disability studies in music, HCI design, and engineering employed a qualitative, multi-method approach including practice video analysis, lesson observation, expert interviews. Our analysis identifies recurring difficulties in right-hand bow control, left-hand coordination, score access, and memory-intensive practice. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory design ideation phase informed by empirical findings and feedback from one musician with BLV. We developed speculative design directions that could potentially address identified breakdowns, while acknowledging that these concepts require further evaluation with instructors and in deployed contexts.

AI.tldr: A design study with four BLV string musicians and three instructors identifies key challenges in bow control, coordination, score access, and memorization. The team proposes speculative design directions to address these barriers, pending further evaluation.
AI.motivation: Bowed string instruments require fine-grained bodily coordination traditionally taught through visual demonstration, creating persistent accessibility barriers for musicians with blindness and low-vision (BLV). The study aims to understand these specific challenges and explore design opportunities to address them.
AI.method: A qualitative, multi-method design study involving four advanced BLV string musicians and three instructors. The interdisciplinary team (violin performance, music education, disability studies, HCI, engineering) employed practice video analysis, lesson observation, and expert interviews. This was followed by an exploratory design ideation phase incorporating feedback from one BLV musician.
AI.result: The analysis identified recurring difficulties in four areas: right-hand bow control, left-hand coordination, score access, and memory-intensive practice demands. Based on these findings, speculative design directions were developed to address the identified breakdowns.
AI.conclusion: The study surfaces concrete, recurring breakdowns in BLV string pedagogy and offers preliminary speculative design directions. However, these concepts require further evaluation with instructors and in real-world deployed contexts before their efficacy can be established.

title: A Self-Evolving Default Action for Cooperative Tasks with Continuous Action Space
summary: Counterfactual credit assignment has proven effective in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for discrete action spaces, yet its extension to continuous-action cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing methods that approximate the counterfactual baseline via Monte Carlo sampling often introduce bias into policy gradients and fail to guarantee convergence to local optima, as the sampled actions may not have been sufficiently trained. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE, a novel MARL framework that employs a counterfactual baseline conditioned on a self-evolving default action sampled from each agent's experience buffer. This design naturally extends to continuous action spaces without relying on additional simulations, reward models, or environment-specific prior knowledge. The baseline accurately quantifies each agent's contribution, and introduces no bias into the deterministic policy gradient, ensuring convergence to local optima. Extensive experiments on cooperative vehicular tasks demonstrate that SAFE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: SAFE is a MARL framework that uses a self-evolving default action from experience buffers to construct an unbiased counterfactual baseline for continuous action spaces, ensuring convergence to local optima without extra simulations or prior knowledge.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual credit assignment in MARL has been successful for discrete actions but struggles in continuous-action cooperative tasks. Monte Carlo sampling-based approximations introduce policy gradient bias and fail to guarantee convergence since sampled actions may be insufficiently trained.
AI.method: SAFE conditions the counterfactual baseline on a self-evolving default action sampled from each agent's experience buffer, eliminating reliance on Monte Carlo sampling, additional simulations, reward models, or environment-specific priors. This baseline is unbiased for deterministic policy gradients.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on cooperative vehicular tasks show SAFE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models.
AI.conclusion: SAFE successfully extends counterfactual credit assignment to continuous-action MARL with unbiased gradient estimates and guaranteed local convergence, validated by superior empirical performance on vehicular cooperative tasks.

title: Beyond Noisy Signals: Dual-Level Denoising for Multi-modal Sequential Recommendation
summary: Multi-modal Sequential Recommendation (SR) incorporates rich side information (e.g., textual and visual features) to enhance dynamic user preference modeling. However, existing frameworks inevitably suffer from a \textbf{Dual-Noise Dilemma}: (1) \textit{Feature-level redundancy} stemming from the semantic gap between generic pre-trained representations and fine-grained recommendation intent; and (2) \textit{Sequence-level stochasticity} induced by spurious interactions such as accidental clicks. To break this bottleneck, we propose \textbf{DDMSR}, a novel \textbf{D}ual-level \textbf{D}enoising \textbf{M}ulti-modal \textbf{S}equential \textbf{R}ecommendation framework that systematically purifies signals from both feature-topological and sequence-frequency perspectives. Specifically, we first design a graph-based feature denoising module that leverages Laplacian smoothing on item semantic graphs as a structural low-pass filter, effectively suppressing high-frequency semantic noise while preserving salient features. For sequence purification, we introduce a frequency-domain sequence denoising module, utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform and a learnable frequency filter to adaptively modulate the interaction spectrum and attenuate anomalous signals. Furthermore, a multi-modal contrastive alignment objective is incorporated to bridge the heterogeneity gap and enforce cross-modal semantic consistency. Extensive experiments on four public benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDMSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, providing a highly robust and efficient solution for multi-modal sequential recommendation. The source code is available at: ~\href{https://github.com/jluo00/DDMSR}{\textcolor{blue}{https://github.com/jluo00/DDMSR}}.

AI.tldr: DDMSR is a dual-level denoising framework for multi-modal sequential recommendation that addresses both feature-level redundancy (via graph Laplacian smoothing as a low-pass filter) and sequence-level stochasticity (via FFT-based adaptive frequency filtering), enhanced by multi-modal contrastive alignment, achieving SOTA on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-modal sequential recommendation systems suffer from a Dual-Noise Dilemma: (1) feature-level redundancy caused by the semantic gap between generic pre-trained representations and fine-grained recommendation intent; (2) sequence-level stochasticity from spurious interactions like accidental clicks. Neither problem is adequately addressed by current frameworks.
AI.method: DDMSR employs two core denoising modules: (1) a graph-based feature denoising module that applies Laplacian smoothing on item semantic graphs as a structural low-pass filter to suppress high-frequency semantic noise while preserving salient features; (2) a frequency-domain sequence denoising module using Fast Fourier Transform with a learnable frequency filter to adaptively modulate the interaction spectrum and attenuate anomalous signals. A multi-modal contrastive alignment objective bridges cross-modal heterogeneity and enforces semantic consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four public benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDMSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, providing a highly robust and efficient solution for multi-modal sequential recommendation.
AI.conclusion: DDMSR effectively resolves the Dual-Noise Dilemma through dual-level (feature-topological and sequence-frequency) denoising, offering a robust and efficient framework that advances the state-of-the-art in multi-modal sequential recommendation.

title: Using Fine-Tuned LLMs to Identify Indicators of Vulnerability in UK Police Incident Logs
summary:
Purpose: Understanding how much of routine policing involves vulnerable people could inform resourcing, training, and multi-agency response, yet administrative data provide limited insight.
