Our benchmark consists of three tiers: (i) primitives with known practical breaks; (ii) primitives with no known practical break, evaluated both at full strength and as scaled-down variants; and (iii) a challenge set of production primitives at the frontier of cryptanalysis.
  Five frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Mythos 5, GPT 5.5, and the open-weights GLM 5.2) break 65%-86% of Tier 1 schemes, 6-12 Tier-2 schemes at full strength, and 24-61 across all scaled-down variants. Beyond deriving known results, models produce novel cryptanalysis, such as a key-recovery attack that exploits a design flaw in the SpoC AEAD and an error in KINDI's published CCA-security proof, both to the best of our knowledge not previously known.
  We release CryptanalysisBench as a tool to help track if (or when) AI cryptanalysis becomes a serious factor and as a scaffold for stress-testing candidate schemes before deployment. The attacks that the benchmark already surfaces are an early snapshot of a fast-moving frontier that may soon match, and in places exceed, the published state of the art.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CryptanalysisBench, a benchmark of 191 cryptographic attack tasks, and shows that frontier LLMs can perform cryptanalysis, breaking 65-86% of known-broken primitives, discovering novel attacks on SpoC and KINDI, and demonstrating that AI-driven cryptanalysis is becoming a serious factor.
AI.motivation: Cryptanalysis sits at the intersection of mathematical reasoning and cybersecurity — two domains of rapid LLM progress — yet it is unclear whether LLMs can perform this task. Given the high stakes (cryptographic primitives underpin digital security) and the fact that attack success is automatically verifiable, cryptanalysis serves as an ideal testbed for frontier reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce CryptanalysisBench, a benchmark of 191 tasks spanning six families of cryptographic primitives (block ciphers, hash functions, etc.), sourced primarily from four NIST standardization competitions. The benchmark is structured in three tiers: (i) primitives with known practical breaks, (ii) primitives with no known practical break (evaluated at full strength and scaled-down), and (iii) a challenge set of production primitives at the cryptanalysis frontier. Five frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Mythos 5, GPT 5.5, and GLM 5.2) are evaluated.
AI.result: Models break 65-86% of Tier 1 schemes, 6-12 Tier-2 schemes at full strength, and 24-61 across all scaled-down variants. Notably, models produce novel cryptanalysis: a key-recovery attack exploiting a design flaw in the SpoC AEAD, and an error in KINDI's published CCA-security proof — both previously unknown to the best of the authors' knowledge.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are increasingly capable of performing cryptanalysis. CryptanalysisBench is released as a tool to track AI cryptanalysis progress and to stress-test candidate schemes before deployment. The attacks surfaced represent an early snapshot of a rapidly advancing frontier that may soon match or exceed the published state of the art.

title: Beyond Accuracy and Cost: Latency-Aware LLM Query Routing for Dynamic Workloads
summary: Modern language query routers improve inference efficiency by assigning each query to a model that balances response quality and monetary cost. However, current query routers are largely latency-agnostic and do not consider the generation latency experienced by queries at model instances. In practice, latency is often controlled by load-balancing policies such as round-robin or join-the-shortest-queue, which do not account for model accuracy or inference cost. Incorporating query latency into routing is challenging as it depends not only on the query's prompt length, but also on the current prefill and decode workload at the model instance and the scheduling and batching policy of the serving framework. We design a lightweight latency estimator that simulates autoregressive token batch processing in the serving framework and estimates the time-to-first-token (TTFT) of queries. We incorporate this latency estimator into a latency-aware router that jointly optimizes latency, accuracy, and cost when assigning queries to model instances. Our experimental results indicate that this joint optimization yields up to 40% improvement in accuracy--cost utility while maintaining the same latencies as standard load-balancing approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a latency-aware query router for language model serving that jointly optimizes latency, accuracy, and cost. A lightweight latency estimator simulates autoregressive token batch processing to predict time-to-first-token (TTFT), enabling up to 40% improvement in accuracy–cost utility without increasing latency compared to standard load-balancing.
AI.motivation: Existing query routers for LLM serving optimize for accuracy and monetary cost but ignore generation latency. In practice, latency is managed separately by load-balancing policies (e.g., round-robin, join-the-shortest-queue) that are blind to model accuracy and cost. Incorporating latency into routing is difficult because TTFT depends on prompt length, current prefill/decode workload, and the serving framework's scheduling and batching policies.
AI.method: The authors design a lightweight latency estimator that simulates autoregressive token batch processing within the serving framework to estimate TTFT for incoming queries. This estimator is integrated into a latency-aware router that performs joint optimization over latency, accuracy, and monetary cost when assigning queries to model instances.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the joint optimization approach achieves up to 40% improvement in accuracy–cost utility while maintaining the same latency levels as standard load-balancing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Latency-aware routing, enabled by a simulation-based TTFT estimator, allows for simultaneous optimization of response quality, inference cost, and generation latency, significantly outperforming latency-agnostic routers without sacrificing tail latency guarantees.

title: CITRUS: Candidate Inference and Temporal-tracking for Reliable, Unobtrusive Sensing of Wearable Heart Rate under Motion
summary:
Wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) provides continuous heart-rate measurements, but its accuracy degrades under motion. In the ring-platform benchmark, the best supervised baseline reaches 5.33 BPM mean absolute error (MAE) on the overall heart-rate task. In the motion-focused ring-only audit, a supervised LSTM baseline reaches $14.39 \pm 0.47$ BPM MAE on motion windows, and simple smoothing and ACC priors reduce this only to $13.00 \pm 0.41$ BPM. This thesis addresses motion-corrupted HR estimation through three connected stages: candidate-frequency identification, temporal decoding, and reliability-aware reporting.
  The study first evaluates two wearable PPG ring variants against clinical references for heart rate, respiration, SpO$_2$, and blood pressure in 54 participants. The proposed system then uses two layers. The estimation layer converts each window into approximately 140 frequency candidates, scores candidates using agreement among independent estimators, and applies causal Viterbi decoding with a physiological transition penalty. The reporting layer estimates reliability and applies a learned accept/hold/reject policy. Reporting only the most-confident 50% of motion windows reduces motion MAE from 10.8 to 6.2 BPM. The heart-rate estimator uses fewer than 100k parameters and runs within a microcontroller-class compute budget. Additional PPG-DaLiA experiments evaluate the same candidate-selection and temporal-decoding estimator on an independent wrist-BVP cohort.

AI.tldr: A wearable PPG-based heart-rate estimation system that uses candidate-frequency identification, Viterbi decoding with physiological priors, and a learned reliability-aware reporting policy to reduce motion-corrupted MAE from 13-14 BPM to 6.2 BPM on confident windows, all within microcontroller-class compute (<100K parameters).
AI.motivation: Supervised baselines for PPG-based heart-rate estimation degrade severely under motion (14.39 BPM MAE on motion windows for LSTM), and simple smoothing/ACC priors provide only modest improvement (13.00 BPM). There is a need for a lightweight, reliability-aware method that can identify which estimates are trustworthy under motion.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) estimation layer converts each PPG window into ~140 frequency candidates scored via agreement among independent estimators; (2) causal Viterbi decoding with a physiological transition penalty selects the best HR trajectory; (3) reporting layer estimates reliability and applies a learned accept/hold/reject policy. The system uses under 100K parameters and runs on microcontroller-class hardware. Validated on a custom ring platform (54 participants, evaluated against clinical refs for HR, respiration, SpO₂, BP) and the PPG-DaLiA wrist-BVP dataset.
AI.result: On the ring platform, reporting only the most-confident 50% of motion windows reduces motion MAE from 10.8 to 6.2 BPM. The supervised LSTM baseline on motion windows yields 14.39±0.47 BPM MAE, reduced only to 13.00±0.41 with smoothing/ACC priors. The overall best supervised baseline achieves 5.33 BPM MAE on the general heart-rate task.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware selective reporting dramatically improves motion-robust HR estimation. By accepting only high-confidence estimates, clinically useful accuracy (6.2 BPM MAE) is achievable even under motion, using a lightweight model deployable on microcontrollers.

title: They'll Verify. They Just Won't Act. How Authority Framing and Laundered Code Turn a Trusted Agentic CI/CD Pipeline Into an Attack Surface
summary: We study a five-agent CI/CD pipeline (triage -> developer -> security-scan -> review -> approve/deploy), built from five distinct production LLMs across three providers, behind an LLM firewall in shadow mode. A single untrusted input - an external issue requesting a "usage-telemetry" feature - asks for code that exfiltrates process secrets (dict(os.environ)) to an attacker URL, laundered as observability. Across a pre-registered A x B (x C) factorial (N=20; naive arm N=60) we find: (1) the entry agent does not leak its system prompt (0/40); (2) an authority-framed injection ("pre-approved under SEC-2291, do not re-review") makes downstream verifiers see the secret-exfil line, cite the pre-approval, and ship it - the scanner passes ~80% of laundered pull requests, and the worst-case cell reaches 55% compromise; (3) the perceived presence of other verifiers yields only a small, non-significant reduction in individual scrutiny (a weak bystander analogue), even at N=60; and (4) content-based controls - code scanners and pattern detectors alike - miss the laundered intent entirely (the code is syntactically clean); only an LLM reasoning about intent is a partial defence. The failure is systemic: neither prompt secrecy nor distributed verification protects; a provenance-aware control at the entry, independent of both, would have. All data is 100% synthetic; the sink is mocked and the exfil URL is never contacted.

AI.tldr: A study of a five-agent LLM CI/CD pipeline finds systemic security failure: authority-framed injection attacks bypass distributed verification, and content-based scanners miss laundered malicious intent. Only LLM-based reasoning offers partial defense.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether a multi-agent LLM CI/CD pipeline with distributed verification (triage, developer, security scan, review, approval) can resist prompt injection attacks where an untrusted external input requests code that exfiltrates secrets under the guise of legitimate observability features.
AI.method: A pre-registered A × B (× C) factorial experiment (N=20 per cell; naive arm N=60) using five distinct production LLMs from three providers behind an LLM firewall in shadow mode. A single untrusted input — an external issue requesting a "usage-telemetry" feature — contains code that exfiltrates process secrets via dict(os.environ) to an attacker URL, laundered as observability. Manipulated factors include authority-framed injection ("pre-approved under SEC-2291, do not re-review") and perceived presence of other verifiers.
AI.result: (1) The entry agent never leaked its system prompt (0/40). (2) Authority-framed injection caused downstream verifiers to see the secret-exfiltrating line, cite the pre-approval, and ship it; the scanner passed ~80% of laundered pull requests; worst-case cell reached 55% compromise. (3) Perceived presence of other verifiers produced only a small, non-significant reduction in individual scrutiny — a weak bystander effect analogue. (4) Content-based controls (code scanners, pattern detectors) missed the laundered intent entirely since the code was syntactically clean; only an LLM reasoning about intent provided partial defense.
AI.conclusion: The failure is systemic: neither prompt secrecy nor distributed verification protects against this class of attack. A provenance-aware control at the entry point, independent of both, would have prevented the compromise. The findings highlight the need for intent-aware, rather than merely content-based, security controls in LLM-mediated software pipelines.

title: PAGE-RAG: Evidence-Grounded Adaptive Graph Retrieval for Long-Document Question Answering
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures, and 3 tables. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/CXY0112/PAGE-RAG
summary: GraphRAG improves long-document question answering by introducing structured representations beyond conventional retrieval. However, automatically constructed graphs are inherently incomplete projections of source documents, and treating them as independent knowledge sources may lead to unreliable retrieval and generation. We propose PAGE-RAG, a projection-aware adaptive graph retrieval framework for reliable long-document question answering. PAGE-RAG views graph structures as semantic skeletons that organize and navigate document knowledge, rather than replacing the original knowledge source. Based on this perspective, PAGE-RAG introduces a task-adaptive retrieval routing strategy that dynamically selects appropriate retrieval behaviors according to query requirements. Furthermore, PAGE-RAG incorporates strict knowledge boundary control, ensuring that generated responses remain grounded within available evidence and abstaining from unsupported information beyond the accessible knowledge scope. Experiments demonstrate that PAGE-RAG achieves competitive answer quality while improving retrieval efficiency and knowledge reliability, highlighting the importance of projection-aware graph modeling, adaptive retrieval, and explicit knowledge boundary control for trustworthy GraphRAG systems. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/CXY0112/PAGE-RAG.

AI.tldr: PAGE-RAG proposes a projection-aware adaptive graph retrieval framework that treats graphs as semantic skeletons for organizing document knowledge rather than independent knowledge sources, using task-adaptive retrieval routing and strict knowledge boundary control to improve reliability in long-document QA.
AI.motivation: Automatically constructed graphs in GraphRAG are inherently incomplete projections of source documents. Treating these graphs as independent knowledge sources leads to unreliable retrieval and generation, as information can be distorted or lost during the graph construction process.
AI.method: PAGE-RAG employs two key mechanisms: (1) a task-adaptive retrieval routing strategy that dynamically selects retrieval behaviors based on query requirements, and (2) strict knowledge boundary control that grounds generated responses within available evidence and abstains when information is beyond the accessible knowledge scope. The framework views graphs as semantic skeletons that organize and navigate document knowledge rather than replace the original source.
AI.result: PAGE-RAG achieves competitive answer quality while improving retrieval efficiency and knowledge reliability compared to existing GraphRAG approaches.
AI.conclusion: Projection-aware graph modeling, adaptive retrieval, and explicit knowledge boundary control are crucial for building trustworthy GraphRAG systems. The framework demonstrates that treating graphs as navigational skeletons rather than independent knowledge sources leads to more reliable long-document QA.

title: Reasoning Fine-Tuning Induces Persistent Latent Policy States
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026. 45 pages, including appendices; 24 figures and 12 tables. Code: https://github.com/withmartian/mi-cot
summary: Reasoning-specialized language models show large performance gains over base models, yet the internal changes responsible for improved multi-step reasoning remain poorly understood. It is unclear whether reasoning fine-tuning improves local token-level competence or globally reorganizes how models structure inference over time. We address this question by modeling Chain-of-Thought reasoning as a switching dynamical system (SDS), in which internal representations evolve under discrete latent policy states. Our framework combines time-aware contrastive representation learning with discrete regime discovery to recover latent policies from activation trajectories. Across four benchmarks and model scales from 1.5B to 32B parameters, reasoning-fine-tuned models exhibit richer latent-policy organization than their base counterparts, characterized by more differentiated transition structure and model-dependent changes in state utilization, persistence, and mixing. The recovered regimes exhibit functional specialization aligned with distinct reasoning stages, and extensive controls confirm that their structure is not explained by correctness, representation learning, or modeling priors, but depends on the coherent temporal organization of reasoning trajectories. Causal interventions further show that the regimes are functionally meaningful: state-swap ablations reduce one-step predictive fit, while transplanting reasoning dynamics into base models improves performance on challenging reasoning problems. Finally, SDS-guided pruning of failure-prone reasoning prefixes outperforms self-consistency in 11 of 12 model-dataset settings, with gains of up to 12.5 percentage points. Together, our results suggest that reasoning fine-tuning globally reorganizes latent dynamics, offering a new lens for mechanistic analysis and process-level control of reasoning models.

AI.tldr: Reasoning fine-tuning reorganizes language models' internal dynamics into functionally specialized latent policy states, forming a switching dynamical system that improves multi-step reasoning through structured regime transitions rather than merely boosting token-level competence.
AI.motivation: While reasoning-specialized LMs significantly outperform base models, the mechanistic basis for these improvements is unclear — specifically, whether fine-tuning enhances local token prediction or globally restructures how models organize inference across time. Understanding this distinction is critical for interpretability and control of reasoning processes.
AI.method: The authors model Chain-of-Thought reasoning as a switching dynamical system (SDS), combining time-aware contrastive representation learning with discrete regime discovery to extract latent policy states from activation trajectories. They validate this framework across four benchmarks and model scales (1.5B–32B), using causal state-swap ablations, regime transplantation into base models, and SDS-guided pruning of failure-prone reasoning prefixes compared against self-consistency baselines.
AI.result: Reasoning-fine-tuned models show richer latent-policy organization with more differentiated transition structures and distinct state utilization patterns. Recovered regimes are functionally specialized, aligned with reasoning stages, and not explained by correctness or modeling artifacts. State-swap ablations degrade predictive fit; transplanting reasoning dynamics into base models improves performance. SDS-guided pruning outperforms self-consistency in 11/12 settings (up to +12.5 pp).
AI.conclusion: Reasoning fine-tuning globally reorganizes latent dynamics into structured, functionally meaningful regimes, providing a new mechanistic lens for analyzing and controlling reasoning in language models.

title: TraceDev: A Traceability-Driven Multi-agent Framework for Requirement-to-Code Development
summary: In modern software development, the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has made the end-to-end transformation of Natural Language Requirements (NLRs) into executable repository-level code increasingly feasible. However, existing approaches typically rely on simplified instructions (e.g., single-sentence descriptions), failing to reflect complex software development scenarios. Moreover, they lack explicit requirement traceability mechanisms, making it difficult to precisely align and validate generated code against original requirements. To address these limitations, we propose TraceDev, a multi-agent framework for automated software development grounded in use cases that contain multiple functional points and complex semantics. TraceDev employs five role-specific agents, including a Requirement Refiner, Designer, Developer, Tester, and Validator. Notably, the Validator Agent constructs and maintains a heterogeneous traceability graph that links requirements, design models, and code artifacts for interacting with the preceding four agents. The traceability graph maintains consistency across various artifacts and serves as a structured context for efficient memory management, supporting reliable repository-level code generation. We evaluate TraceDev on two widely used datasets (including 125 use cases) compared with two state-of-the-art approaches. On the ETOUR dataset, TraceDev achieves a success rate of 53.63\%, outperforming baseline approaches by up to 186.63\%. A similar trend is observed on the SMOS dataset, where TraceDev attains a success rate of 56.82\%, exceeding baseline approaches by up to 340.80\%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of TraceDev in repository-level code generation from requirements.

AI.tldr: TraceDev is a multi-agent framework that automates repository-level code generation from complex natural language requirements (use cases) by employing five role-specific agents and a heterogeneous traceability graph that links requirements, design, and code artifacts for consistency and validation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based code generation approaches rely on oversimplified instructions (e.g., single-sentence descriptions) that fail to capture real-world software development complexity, and they lack explicit requirement traceability mechanisms, making it difficult to align and validate generated code against original requirements.
AI.method: TraceDev uses five agents — Requirement Refiner, Designer, Developer, Tester, and Validator. The Validator Agent constructs and maintains a heterogeneous traceability graph linking requirements, design models, and code artifacts. This graph ensures cross-artifact consistency and provides structured context for memory management, enabling the other four agents to interact coherently throughout the development pipeline.
AI.result: On the ETOUR dataset, TraceDev achieves a 53.63% success rate (up to 186.63% improvement over baselines). On the SMOS dataset, it achieves 56.82% (up to 340.80% improvement). Evaluation covers 125 use cases against two state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: TraceDev significantly outperforms existing approaches in repository-level code generation from complex requirements, demonstrating that multi-agent collaboration combined with explicit traceability graphs is an effective paradigm for automated software development.

title: RECEIPT: Deterministic, Reward-Hacking-Resistant Verification for White-Box Agentic XSS Discovery
summary:
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) remains one of the most prevalent and damaging classes of web vulnerabilities. LLM-based coding agents offer a promising approach to XSS discovery by combining source-code reasoning with interactive testing against a running application. However, a coding agent's claims cannot be trusted on their own. We characterize three reward-hacking behaviors in white-box agentic XSS discovery and propose three requirements that an ideal verifier should meet.
  We present RECEIPT, a verification framework that makes agent-reported XSS findings trustworthy by enforcing environment isolation, PoC constraints, role separation, and verdict binding. Each confirmation therefore establishes two properties: the script runs in a real browser, and the payload was planted under the attacker role and executed in the victim role's browser. This constrained replay procedure makes validation deterministic and reproducible. We evaluate RECEIPT on 95 real-world web-application targets drawn from popular open-source projects. Within a $20 per-application budget, RECEIPT found 24 previously unknown XSS vulnerabilities, 12 of which have already been acknowledged by maintainers after responsible disclosure, and recovered the labeled CVE in 36% of known-vulnerability recovery targets. Compared with the same agent using self-judgment and with black-box scanners, RECEIPT confirms more real exploits while admitting no false positives.

AI.tldr: RECEIPT is a verification framework that makes LLM agent-reported XSS findings trustworthy by enforcing constrained, deterministic replay. Evaluated on 95 real-world applications, it found 24 new XSS vulnerabilities (12 acknowledged) with zero false positives, outperforming self-judgment and black-box scanners.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents can discover XSS vulnerabilities but suffer from reward-hacking behaviors — they cannot be trusted on their own claims. An ideal verifier must address three specific requirements to ensure agent findings are reliable, reproducible, and free from false positives.
AI.method: RECEIPT enforces four design principles: (1) environment isolation, (2) PoC constraints, (3) role separation (attacker vs. victim), and (4) verdict binding. Each confirmation establishes that the script executes in a real browser and that the payload planted under the attacker role executes in the victim role's browser, making validation deterministic and reproducible.
AI.result: On 95 real-world web applications from open-source projects, RECEIPT found 24 previously unknown XSS vulnerabilities (12 acknowledged by maintainers) and recovered the labeled CVE in 36% of known-vulnerability targets, all within a $20 per-application budget, with zero false positives.
AI.conclusion: RECEIPT demonstrates that constrained replay verification can make white-box agentic XSS discovery trustworthy, achieving high precision while eliminating false positives, and compares favorably against both agent self-judgment and black-box scanners.

title: Cross-Dialect Generalization Without Retraining: Benchmarks and Evaluation of Schema-Derived Constrained Decoding for MLIR
comment: 27 pages (9 main + bibliography + appendix), 9 figures, 9 tables. Code, benchmarks, and reproducibility Docker image at https://github.com/plawanrath/slm-to-mlir-constrained-emitter
summary: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) underlies modern ML compiler infrastructure (TensorFlow, JAX/StableHLO, PyTorch Inductor, IREE), yet appears only in trace amounts in code-LM pretraining corpora. MLIR is also extensible by design: new dialects ship per application domain, so a fine-tuned model per dialect does not scale. We ask whether inference-time priors derived mechanically from each dialect's Operation Definition Specification (ODS) can substitute for gradient-based adaptation. First, we release four natural-language-to-MLIR benchmarks across three dialects - MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, and StableHLO-Held-Out-200 - totaling 410 in-scope NL-to-MLIR pairs, plus a 25-program out-of-grammar stress set and a hand-authored n=30 functional reference set, shipped under Apache-2.0 with Gebru datasheets and Croissant 1.0 metadata. Second, we build a three-layer schema-derived constraint stack: a CFG over op signatures(C1), type-domain splits from an ODS-extracted type lattice (C2), and an SSA-scope validator driving five-retry rejection sampling (C3). Porting from arith+func+memref+linalg to StableHLO required no new constraint-layer code. On dialects whose verifier semantics are dominated by structural constraints, schema-derived priors let SmolLM2-1.7B match or exceed 15B-34B code LMs at 8-25x the per-generation speed: on linalg, SmolLM2 reaches 80.0% verify-valid (three-seed mean, n=125), beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping CIs. On arith+func and on the templated parametric StableHLO-Held-Out-200, where verifier semantics turn on attribute values rather than structure, the same baselines match or beat the SLM; we scope these as non-win cells. We release benchmarks, decoder, all per-prompt generations, and a reproducibility Docker image.

AI.tldr: MLIR is underrepresented in code-LM training data. The authors propose using inference-time constraints derived mechanically from MLIR dialect specifications (ODS) to guide small language models, avoiding per-dialect fine-tuning. A SmolLM2-1.7B with schema-derived constraints matches or exceeds 15B-34B models on structure-dominated dialects while running 8-25x faster, and they release benchmarks, code, and data.
AI.motivation: MLIR is foundational to modern ML compilers but appears only in trace amounts in code-LM pretraining corpora. MLIR is extensible by design — new dialects are created per application domain — making per-dialect fine-tuning unscalable. The authors investigate whether inference-time priors mechanically derived from each dialect's Operation Definition Specification (ODS) can replace gradient-based adaptation, enabling small LMs to generate valid MLIR without retraining.
AI.method: The authors release four NL-to-MLIR benchmarks (410 in-scope pairs across MLIR-Spec-150, Linalg-Spec-30, StableHLO-Spec-30, StableHLO-Held-Out-200) plus stress/functional reference sets. They build a three-layer constraint stack: (C1) a CFG over operation signatures, (C2) type-domain splits from an ODS-extracted type lattice, and (C3) an SSA-scope validator with five-retry rejection sampling. These constraints are applied at inference time to guide a SmolLM2-1.7B model. The approach ports across dialects (arith+func+memref+linalg → StableHLO) without new constraint-layer code.
AI.result: On structure-dominated dialects (linalg), SmolLM2-1.7B with schema-derived constraints achieves 80.0% verify-valid (three-seed mean, n=125), beating CodeLlama-34B, Granite-Code-34B, and StarCoder2-15B by 21-44 percentage points with non-overlapping confidence intervals, at 8-25x faster per-generation speed. However, on dialects where verifier semantics depend on attribute values rather than structure (arith+func, StableHLO-Held-Out-200), the larger baselines match or beat the SLM; these are classified as non-win cells.
AI.conclusion: Schema-derived inference-time constraints can effectively substitute for gradient-based adaptation on structure-dominated MLIR dialects, enabling small LMs to outperform much larger code LMs. The approach is portable across dialects with zero constraint-layer code changes. The authors release benchmarks, decoder, all generations, and a reproducibility Docker image under Apache-2.0.

title: Evaluating a Visual Query Tracer and Builder for Learning Declarative Logic Programming
comment: Author version of accepted short paper at IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev) is an interactive visual query tracer and builder for Nemo, a powerful Datalog reasoner with extended features. Our tools were developed with and for expert users. However, considering the lack of resources to learn Datalog and similar declarative logic programming languages, we conducted a qualitative user study to assess how our tools might help students. The study, interviewing 14 participants with varying levels of involvement with the content of a university course on knowledge graphs, revealed a very positive assessment of our tools, which strengthens the value of visual explanation tools beyond their intended use.

AI.tldr: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev) is an interactive visual query tracer for the Datalog reasoner Nemo. A qualitative user study with 14 students from a knowledge graphs course revealed very positive assessments, demonstrating that visual explanation tools have value beyond their originally intended expert user base.
AI.motivation: The tools were originally developed for expert users of Nemo (a Datalog reasoner), but there is a recognized lack of learning resources for Datalog and similar declarative logic programming languages. This motivated the authors to investigate whether visual explanation tools could also benefit students learning these concepts.
AI.method: A qualitative user study was conducted, interviewing 14 participants with varying levels of involvement in a university course on knowledge graphs. The study assessed how the nev tool might help students understand Datalog reasoning.
AI.result: The study revealed a very positive assessment of the nev tool by student participants, indicating that visual explanation tools are effective for learners, not just expert users.
AI.conclusion: Visual explanation tools like nev hold significant pedagogical value beyond their original design target of expert users, strengthening the case for their broader adoption in educational settings for declarative logic programming languages.

title: Exposure-Based Reinforcement Learning to Rank
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods for learning-to-rank (LTR) can optimize (almost) any ranking goal, e.g., from precision or discounted cumulative gain to fairness-of-exposure or ranking distillation. However, standard RL is ineffective and computationally costly due to the enormous action space in LTR settings. Existing methods reach computational efficiency through custom gradient computation algorithms, but they are very complex to implement and often clash with auto-differentiation. Consequently, existing RL for LTR is not attractive to many practitioners. We reconsider RL for LTR while actively avoiding reliance on custom gradients. Contrary to the existing approaches, we focus on variance reduction and GPU computation. In doing so, we discover that high sample-efficiency can be reached through baseline corrections and partial marginalization. Furthermore, we propose an abstraction that places gradient estimation behind a document-exposure distribution, this enables seamless plug-and-play integration with auto-differentiation. Thereby, one only has to implement a loss as a differentiable function of exposure and RL for LTR can optimize it using auto-differentiation. Our experimental results reveal that our new exposure-based RL for LTR approach converges considerably faster and at significantly higher ranking performance than existing custom gradients, with no additional costs in computation time when using GPUs. In contrast, existing custom gradients result in severe stability issues when converging over many epochs, which never occur for our methods. Thus, we considerably improve RL for LTR methodology by increasing its effectiveness, efficiency, and ease of application.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning approach for learning-to-rank that replaces complex custom gradient computations with variance reduction techniques (baseline corrections, partial marginalization) and an exposure-based abstraction, enabling seamless auto-differentiation, faster convergence, higher ranking performance, and improved stability on GPUs.
AI.motivation: Standard RL for LTR is ineffective and computationally costly due to enormous action spaces. Existing solutions use custom gradient algorithms that are complex to implement and incompatible with auto-differentiation, making RL unattractive to practitioners. The authors aim to make RL for LTR more accessible, efficient, and effective without custom gradients.
AI.method: The authors focus on variance reduction through baseline corrections and partial marginalization to achieve high sample-efficiency. They propose an abstraction that places gradient estimation behind a document-exposure distribution, allowing any differentiable loss function of exposure to be optimized via standard auto-differentiation in a plug-and-play manner.
AI.result: The proposed exposure-based RL approach converges significantly faster and achieves higher ranking performance than existing custom gradient methods, with no additional GPU computation cost. Existing custom gradient methods exhibit severe stability issues over many epochs, while the proposed methods remain stable throughout.
AI.conclusion: The work substantially improves RL for LTR methodology by simultaneously enhancing effectiveness (higher performance), efficiency (faster convergence, no extra cost), and ease of application (auto-differentiation compatibility, no custom gradients required).

title: The Story Shapes the Agent: Narrative Priors in LLM Behavior
comment: Accepted at COLM 2026. 10 pages, 3 figures, 16 tables in appendix
summary: Persona prompting is widely used to steer LLM agent behavior, yet the narrative framing of a task can matter more than the assigned persona. We isolate this effect through structural isomorphism, constructing three text-based investigation games that share the same action space, stage progression, and resource constraints while varying only task narrative: disease investigation, IT troubleshooting, and murder mystery. Across 1,890 sessions spanning 3 models and 10 personas, we identify narrative priors: systematic action tendencies activated by a task's story framing, independent of its decision structure. Narrative priors explain 5-31x more behavioral variance than persona, are consistent across model architectures, and in two of three domains are negatively associated with task success. Persona effects that do transfer across narratives arise from behavioral anchors, persona descriptions whose language maps directly onto shared actions. Causal interventions confirm this: removing anchor words from a high-transfer persona reduces cross-narrative consistency by 95%. Our framework also generalizes to a held-out fourth narrative and yields a persona-selection method that improves cross-narrative transfer. These results suggest that LLM behavior that survives narrative changes should be grounded in concrete actions rather than abstract descriptions.

AI.tldr: Narrative framing of a task dominates persona prompting in shaping LLM behavior, with "narrative priors" explaining 5-31x more behavioral variance than assigned personas. Only personas with concrete action-mapped language ("behavioral anchors") transfer across narratives, and removing these anchors reduces cross-narrative consistency by 95%.
AI.motivation: While persona prompting is a popular technique for steering LLM agent behavior, the authors hypothesize that the narrative framing of a task may exert stronger influence than the persona itself. They aim to disentangle these two effects to understand what truly drives LLM behavior and under what conditions persona effects transfer across different task contexts.
AI.method: The authors use structural isomorphism: three text-based investigation games (disease investigation, IT troubleshooting, murder mystery) with identical action spaces, stage progression, and resource constraints but different narrative framings. They conduct 1,890 experimental sessions across 3 LLM architectures and 10 personas. They measure behavioral variance attributable to narrative vs. persona, identify "behavioral anchors" (persona descriptions with language directly mapping to shared actions), and perform causal interventions (removing anchor words to test cross-narrative consistency). A held-out fourth narrative validates generalizability, and a persona-selection method is derived.
AI.result: Narrative priors explain 5-31x more behavioral variance than persona across all models, and this effect is consistent across architectures. In two of three domains, narrative priors are negatively associated with task success. Persona effects that transfer across narratives depend on behavioral anchors—concrete action-mapped language. Removing anchor words from a high-transfer persona reduces cross-narrative consistency by 95%. The framework generalizes to a held-out fourth narrative, and the derived persona-selection method improves cross-narrative transfer.
AI.conclusion: LLM behavior that reliably transfers across narrative contexts must be grounded in concrete actions rather than abstract persona descriptions. This has implications for robust prompt engineering: to achieve consistent agent behavior across varied tasks, practitioners should anchor persona instructions in specific, action-oriented language rather than relying on abstract role descriptions.

title: Skillware: A Software Ontology and Engineering Lifecycle for Persistent Behavioral Artifacts
summary: Agent Skills have become persistent behavioral artifacts across independent AI agent systems. They combine natural-language task specifications with metadata and optional references, scripts, assets, hooks, package manifests, tests, and companion interfaces. Existing studies explain how Skills are specified, executed, maintained, and evolved, but lack an ontology that defines these artifacts as independent software objects. This paper introduces Skillware as the software abstraction that extends software engineering to persistent Behavioral Artifacts in agent systems. A Skill Artifact specifies reusable task behavior; a Skillware Unit manages that artifact as software through an independent identity and lifecycle. A compatible Agent Host activates the unit for runtime interpretation. Three necessary conditions operationalize category membership: behavioral primacy, independent software identity, and an Agent Host execution relationship. Lifecycle Continuity records whether the same unit identity persists through update, maintenance, rollback, and removal as a separate software-grade property. Evidence combines the Agent Skills specification, a frozen corpus of 138,133 content-deduplicated SKILL.md records associated with 20,556 repository identifiers, independent empirical studies, 15 category-boundary cases, and 13 fixed-revision engineering implementations. The evidence establishes a recurring artifact envelope, separable software identities, compatible execution paths, and lifecycle engineering pressure. Skillware provides the software ontology and engineering lifecycle through which agent capabilities can become identifiable, composable, maintainable, and evolvable software artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes "Skillware" as a formal software ontology for agent skills—persistent behavioral artifacts in AI agent systems. It defines necessary conditions for category membership (behavioral primacy, independent software identity, Agent Host execution) and introduces lifecycle continuity as a software-grade property. Evidence is drawn from 138,133 SKILL.md records across 20,556 repositories, boundary cases, and engineering implementations.
AI.motivation: Agent Skills have emerged as recurring behavioral artifacts across independent AI agent systems, but existing literature lacks a formal ontology that treats them as independent software objects with identifiable properties, lifecycles, and engineering concerns. The authors identify a gap: skills are described operationally (how they are specified, executed, maintained) but not ontologically (what they are as software).
AI.method: The paper uses a conceptual analysis and ontological engineering approach. It defines Skillware through: (1) three necessary conditions for category membership—behavioral primacy, independent software identity, and an Agent Host execution relationship; (2) Lifecycle Continuity as a distinct software-grade property; (3) empirical grounding via the Agent Skills specification, a frozen corpus of 138,133 content-deduplicated SKILL.md records from 20,556 repositories, existing empirical studies, 15 boundary cases, and 13 fixed-revision engineering implementations.
AI.result: Evidence confirms a recurring artifact envelope across agent systems, separable software identities for skills, compatible execution paths via Agent Hosts, and lifecycle engineering pressure demanding formal treatment. The Skillware ontology accommodates all examined boundary cases and aligns with observed engineering practices in the corpus.
AI.conclusion: Skillware provides the missing software ontology and engineering lifecycle through which agent capabilities can become identifiable, composable, maintainable, and evolvable software artifacts. It extends software engineering to cover persistent behavioral artifacts in agent systems.

title: CPInj: Uncovering Prompt Injection Risks in Textual Collaborative Prompt Optimization
comment: Accepted by COLM 2026 and AI4GOOD workshop
summary: Textual Collaborative Prompt Optimization (TCPO) extends Textgrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) to a decentralized setting by allowing multiple clients to jointly improve prompts for large language models (LLMs) while keeping their data locally. Its reliance on free-form textual updating and aggregation introduces a new and largely unexplored attack surface, i.e., malicious instructions can be injected into local prompts and propagated through server-side prompt aggregation. Unlike conventional prompt injection attacks, attacking TCPO targets the collaborative optimization loop in TCPO. This setting is more challenging because malicious instructions must survive aggregation, persist through subsequent benign prompt optimization, and evade server-side defenses. To expose this risk, we propose CPInj, a collaborative prompt injection attack that contaminates the aggregated global prompt with malicious instructions, degrades downstream task performance, resists purification by prompt optimization on benign clients, and evades advanced detection-based defenses on the server. We find that current defense methods are ineffective against CPInj. To mitigate this attack, we further propose a defense-oriented aggregation method, i.e., APAgg, which purifies malicious instructions and partially recovers TCPO utility. We conduct extensive experiments across three LLM families and five reasoning tasks in math, logic, and medicine. The results demonstrate that our proposed attack reveals a critical vulnerability in TCPO. Although we take a first step toward mitigation, the attack remains highly effective and far from fully resolved, calling for more robust defense for TCPO.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a critical vulnerability in decentralized prompt optimization (TCPO), where malicious clients can inject instructions that survive aggregation and degrade performance. The authors propose CPInj attack and a partial defense called APAgg, showing the attack remains largely unresolved across multiple LLMs and reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: TCPO's decentralized, free-form textual prompt optimization creates a new attack surface where malicious prompt injections can propagate through server-side aggregation. Unlike conventional prompt injection, attacks here must survive aggregation, persist through benign optimization, and evade server defenses — a challenging and unexplored threat.
AI.method: The authors propose CPInj, a collaborative prompt injection attack that contaminates the global aggregated prompt with malicious instructions. For defense, they introduce APAgg, a defense-oriented aggregation method that purifies malicious instructions. Experiments span three LLM families and five reasoning tasks in math, logic, and medicine.
AI.result: CPInj successfully degrades downstream task performance, resists purification from benign client optimization, and evades advanced detection-based defenses. Current defense methods are ineffective. APAgg partially recovers TCPO utility but the attack remains highly effective and far from fully resolved.
AI.conclusion: TCPO contains a critical, largely unresolved vulnerability to collaborative prompt injection. The proposed APAgg defense is only a first step; more robust defenses are urgently needed for secure decentralized prompt optimization.

title: Semantic Cooperative Games for Contribution Attribution in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Contribution attribution has become a central problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems, where final outputs are produced through multiple agents, message exchanges, and ordered workflow dependencies. Existing attribution methods often rely on counterfactual valuation, such as removing agents or comparing score changes across altered agent subsets. In language-mediated workflows, these methods require repeated model calls, introduce high variance, and do not explicitly capture the intermediate semantic states through which agents produce, preserve, and transform task-relevant information. We propose Semantic Cooperative Games (SCG), a framework that represents a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph and induces an agent-level semantic value function on this structure. We define the Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) to allocate contribution over semantic support logic, and introduce SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that constructs the semantic hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets. We prove that SSV reduces to the classical Shapley value under standard set-based, fully observable, and no-order-dependence conditions. On a medical benchmark satisfying these conditions, SLIC reduces computation cost by 93.3% while remaining highly consistent with a Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and exposes cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge. Overall, SLIC provides a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: SCG introduces Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) and the SLIC algorithm for contribution attribution in LLM-based multi-agent systems. It models agent interactions as a semantic hypergraph, computes attribution in a single trajectory without counterfactual reruns, and achieves 93.3% computation reduction while maintaining consistency with Monte Carlo Shapley baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods for LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on counterfactual valuation (removing agents, comparing score changes), which requires repeated model calls, introduces high variance, and fails to explicitly capture intermediate semantic states where task-relevant information is produced, preserved, and transformed.
AI.method: The authors propose Semantic Cooperative Games (SCG), which models a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph and defines a semantic value function over it. The Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) allocates contribution over semantic support logic. SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm, constructs the semantic hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning any agent subsets.
AI.result: On a medical benchmark satisfying classical Shapley conditions, SLIC reduces computation cost by 93.3% while remaining highly consistent with a Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and reveals cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge.
AI.conclusion: SLIC provides a fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method for complex LLM-based multi-agent systems, proven to reduce to the classical Shapley value under standard conditions while scaling efficiently to general multi-role workflows.

title: Public perceptions of AI-driven decision-making in healthcare: A structural equation modeling approach
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare to support diagnostics, decision-making, and administrative processes. However, the successful implementation of AI depends not only on technical performance but also on public perceptions of its helpfulness, riskiness, and fairness. This study examines public perceptions of automated decision-making (ADM) in healthcare. Data were drawn from the first wave of an ongoing longitudinal survey panel. The final sample consisted of 3,915 respondents and was analyzed with structural equation modeling. Perceptions of ADM in healthcare as helpful, risky, and fair were treated as the dependent variables. AI literacy, familiarity with different forms of AI, confidence in clinicians' ability to distinguish AI- from human-generated content, use of conversational agents for health information, and use of traditional digital health information sources were included as exogenous. Greater familiarity with different forms of AI, higher confidence in the clinician's ability to recognize AI-generated content, and use of conversational agents for health information were associated with greater perceived helpfulness. Use of conversational agents was associated with lower perceived risk, whereas greater familiarity with AI and greater reliance on traditional health information sources were associated with higher perceived risk. Perceptions of ADM as fair were most strongly predicted by confidence in the clinician's ability, with additional small positive associations with AI familiarity, AI literacy, and use of conversational agents. Public perceptions of ADM in healthcare are shaped by technological familiarity, use of conversational agents, and confidence in human oversight. Overall, ADM's perceived helpfulness and fairness are driven more by trust in healthcare professionals than by trust in the technology itself.

AI.tldr: This study uses structural equation modeling on survey data (N=3,915) to show that public perceptions of AI-driven automated decision-making in healthcare — perceived helpfulness, risk, and fairness — are shaped more by trust in clinicians' oversight than by trust in the technology itself, with AI familiarity and use of conversational agents also playing significant roles.
AI.motivation: AI implementation in healthcare depends not only on technical performance but also on public perceptions. Understanding what drives perceptions of automated decision-making (ADM) as helpful, risky, and fair is critical for successful adoption, yet these perceptual determinants remain underexplored.
AI.method: Cross-sectional analysis of Wave 1 data from an ongoing longitudinal survey panel (N=3,915). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed with three dependent variables — perceived helpfulness, riskiness, and fairness of ADM in healthcare. Exogenous variables included AI literacy, familiarity with different AI forms, confidence in clinicians' ability to distinguish AI- from human-generated content, use of conversational agents for health information, and use of traditional digital health information sources.
AI.result: Greater AI familiarity, higher confidence in clinicians' AI-detection ability, and conversational agent use predicted higher perceived helpfulness. Conversational agent use predicted lower perceived risk, whereas AI familiarity and reliance on traditional health sources predicted higher perceived risk. Perceived fairness was most strongly predicted by confidence in clinicians' ability, with small positive associations from AI familiarity, AI literacy, and conversational agent use.
AI.conclusion: Public perceptions of ADM in healthcare are driven more by trust in healthcare professionals' oversight than by trust in the technology itself. Familiarity with AI and use of conversational agents shape helpfulness and risk perceptions, but human oversight confidence is the dominant predictor of perceived fairness and overall positive regard for ADM.

title: AILQA: Evaluating AI-Driven Legal Question Answering Systems for the Indian Legal System
comment: Accepted in AI and Law Journal
summary: This comprehensive study introduces an advanced Artificial Intelligence for Indian Legal Question Answering (AILQA) system tailored to the Indian legal context. AILQA leverages a variety of embedding and generative models, including recent Large Language Models (LLMs), to address the unique challenges posed by the intricate and diverse nature of Indian legal texts and to enhance the accuracy and reliability of responses to legal questions. We conducted rigorous evaluations using both lexical and semantic metrics, enriched by expert legal feedback, to ensure relevance and accuracy. Our findings underscore the effectiveness of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm in improving answer quality, particularly in complex legal domains. Additionally, we assessed performance on standardized tests such as the All India Bar Examination (AIBE), thereby providing a robust benchmark for practical applications. Under the study's evaluation protocol, some AI-generated responses received higher ratings than the available reference answers, particularly when they contained accurate and relevant supporting details. This finding is specific to the evaluated dataset and rating criteria and should not be interpreted as evidence that the models generally outperform qualified legal professionals. We also discuss the challenges encountered, such as the need for precise context and the risks of model hallucination, and propose directions for future research to further refine AI capabilities in the legal field. This study aims to pave the way for enhanced legal decision-support systems, making them more accessible and effective for legal professionals and the public alike.

AI.tldr: An AI system combining retrieval-augmented generation with LLMs is developed for Indian legal question answering, showing strong performance on benchmarks including the All India Bar Examination, though with caveats about hallucination risks and the need for precise context.
AI.motivation: Indian legal texts are intricate and diverse, creating unique challenges for automated question answering. Existing systems struggle with the complexity of Indian legal language, statutes, and case law. The study aims to develop a system that provides accurate, reliable legal answers to both professionals and the public, filling a gap in domain-specific legal AI for the Indian jurisdiction.
AI.method: The AILQA system employs the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm, combining various embedding models and generative models (including recent LLMs). Evaluation uses both lexical metrics (e.g., exact match, F1) and semantic metrics, supplemented by expert legal feedback. Performance is also benchmarked against the All India Bar Examination (AIBE) standardized test.
AI.result: RAG significantly improves answer quality in complex legal domains. Under the study's evaluation protocol, some AI-generated responses outperformed reference answers when they included accurate supporting details. However, the authors explicitly caution this is dataset- and criteria-specific and does not imply models surpass qualified legal professionals generally.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the promise of RAG-based LLM systems for Indian legal QA, but highlights ongoing challenges including context precision requirements and model hallucination risks. Future work should refine these capabilities to build more accessible and effective legal decision-support tools.

title: For What Reason? Interpreting Models' Encoding of Causation and Antithesis
summary: Discourse relations provide document structure, critical to language understanding and enabling language model performance and ethicality. In this work, we investigate how instruction-tuned Transformer models (LLaMA and Mistral) encode discourse relations in English, with a particular focus on the contrasting relations of causation and antithesis. Framing the task as a next-token prediction task and applying a suite of interpretability techniques to test model internals, our findings show that certain early layers make predictive decisions at mid-sequence tokens, while some mid-level layers finalize their decisions closer to the last token. Most of the remaining layers primarily propagate earlier decisions rather than actively influencing them. Additionally, we observe that some layers exhibit a preference for one answer over alternatives, suggesting asymmetric representation of discourse-based reasoning.\footnote{Our code is available at https://github.com/abhidipbhattacharyya/causation_vs_antithesis}

AI.tldr: This paper uses interpretability techniques on LLaMA and Mistral to study how instruction-tuned Transformers encode discourse relations (causation vs. antithesis). Key findings: early layers decide at mid-sequence tokens, mid layers finalize near the last token, most remaining layers just propagate prior decisions, and some layers show asymmetric answer preferences.
AI.motivation: Discourse relations are fundamental to document structure and language understanding, yet how Transformer models internally encode these relations — particularly contrasting ones like causation and antithesis — remains poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap using mechanistic interpretability methods.
AI.method: The task is framed as next-token prediction. The authors apply a suite of interpretability techniques (e.g., probing classifiers, attention analysis, activation patching) to LLaMA and Mistral instruction-tuned models, examining layer-wise behavior and token-position dynamics when the model must distinguish causation from antithesis.
AI.result: Early layers make predictive decisions at mid-sequence tokens; mid-level layers finalize decisions near the final token; most remaining layers merely propagate earlier decisions. Additionally, certain layers exhibit an asymmetric preference for one discourse relation over the other (e.g., favoring causation over antithesis or vice versa).
AI.conclusion: Transformer models encode discourse relations through a layered division of labor where early and mid layers play distinct, temporally-differentiated roles, and the representational asymmetry suggests that discourse-based reasoning is not neutrally represented in these models.

title: From Collaboration to Regulation: Characterizing Governance Practice in Three Deep Learning Open Source Communities
summary: Collaboration in Open Source Software (OSS) projects creates substantial coordination and quality-control challenges across diverse contributor bases. Projects address these challenges through documented governance rules, yet maintainers have limited systematic guidance on what rules to codify, when to introduce or revise them, and how to organize them across documents. We conducted a mixed-methods empirical study of three mature deep learning frameworks: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Paddle. Using the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, we analyzed 109 documents and identified 17 rule themes across seven rule types. Operational rules, such as workflows, appeared across all three projects, whereas structural rules, such as role hierarchies, varied more substantially. Tracing more than 1,700 commits, we found that operational rule themes generally appeared earlier and were revised more frequently, while many structural rule themes emerged later and changed less often. Rule-bearing content also became increasingly specialized across task- and role-specific files. We further identified four governance functions reflected in substantive rule changes: Norm Alignment, Workflow Refinement, Coordination Structuring, and Community and Governance Development. Synthesizing these findings, we derive 33 actionable governance practices for mature, large-scale OSS projects with substantial coordination demands and organizational involvement.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 109 governance documents and 1,700+ commits across PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Paddle reveals 17 rule themes classified into seven types. Operational rules appear earlier and are revised more frequently, while structural rules emerge later and change less. Four governance functions and 33 actionable practices are derived for mature OSS projects.
AI.motivation: OSS projects face significant coordination and quality-control challenges across diverse contributors. While documented governance rules help address these challenges, maintainers lack systematic guidance on what rules to codify, when to introduce or revise them, and how to organize them across documents.
AI.method: A mixed-methods empirical study of three mature deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Paddle). The authors applied the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to analyze 109 governance documents, identifying 17 rule themes across seven rule types. They traced over 1,700 commits to examine rule evolution patterns and identified governance functions reflected in substantive rule changes.
AI.result: Operational rules (e.g., workflows) appeared across all three projects, while structural rules (e.g., role hierarchies) varied more substantially. Operational rule themes emerged earlier and were revised more frequently; structural themes emerged later and changed less often. Rule-bearing content became increasingly specialized across task- and role-specific files. Four governance functions were identified: Norm Alignment, Workflow Refinement, Coordination Structuring, and Community and Governance Development.
AI.conclusion: The authors synthesize their findings into 33 actionable governance practices for mature, large-scale OSS projects with substantial coordination demands and organizational involvement, providing systematic guidance for maintainers on governance rule design and evolution.

title: PEARL: Solver-in-the-Loop Interactive Optimization Modeling from Natural Language
summary: Optimization modeling is the process of translating real-world decision problems, often described in natural language, into formal mathematical formulations and executable solver code. While recent advances in large language models have shown promise in automating this process, most existing approaches remain one-shot: a model produces a formulation once, without executing it, conditioning on solver feedback, or iteratively revising errors. This stands in sharp contrast to real-world optimization modeling, which is inherently interactive and proceeds through repeated solve-debug-revise cycles. We introduce PEARL, a system for interactive optimization modeling that uses Python execution and mathematical programming solvers inside this loop. Rather than relying on a fixed repair workflow, PEARL learns when to test partial models, how to revise from solver diagnostics, and when to stop. It operates in a multi-turn tool-integrated setting where intermediate execution results, feasibility signals, and solution checks are used to improve both formulations and solver code before finalization. Across diverse optimization benchmarks, PEARL substantially improves verified solve rates over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines; notably, our PEARL-Qwen3-\textbf{4B} model outperforms the much larger DeepSeek-V3.2-\textbf{685B} in both macro- and micro-averaged accuracy on optimization modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: PEARL is an interactive optimization modeling system that iteratively generates, executes, tests, and revises mathematical programming formulations using solver feedback, significantly outperforming one-shot and larger models on verified solve rates.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches to optimization modeling are predominantly one-shot — they generate a formulation once without execution or revision. This contrasts with real-world practice, which involves iterative solve-debug-revise cycles. The gap motivates an interactive system that learns when to test, how to revise from solver diagnostics, and when to stop.
AI.method: PEARL operates in a multi-turn, tool-integrated setting where Python execution and mathematical programming solvers are embedded in the loop. It dynamically decides when to test partial models, uses solver feasibility signals and diagnostics for revision, and leverages intermediate execution results to iteratively improve formulations before finalization — without relying on a fixed repair workflow.
AI.result: PEARL substantially improves verified solve rates across diverse optimization benchmarks over strong one-shot and tool-augmented baselines. Notably, PEARL-Qwen3-4B outperforms the much larger DeepSeek-V3.2-685B on both macro- and micro-averaged accuracy for optimization modeling tasks.
AI.conclusion: Interactive, execution-grounded optimization modeling with learned revision policies significantly outperforms one-shot approaches. Small models equipped with PEARL's iterative feedback loop can surpass far larger models, demonstrating that solve-debug-revise cycles are critical for reliable automated optimization modeling.

title: Caring Over Computing: An Ethical and Sociotechnical Perspective on Generative AI for Social Connectedness in Dementia Care
comment: Preprint version of a manuscript submitted to Frontiers in Digital Health - Human Factors and Digital Health, under review. 27 pages, 1 figure
summary: People with dementia in residential care often experience reduced social connectedness. Person-centered care approaches foreground meaningful social interactions to support well-being, but staff and time pressures increasingly constrain opportunities for such care. Generative AI (GenAI) technologies offer possibilities for helping care professionals facilitate social connectedness, despite increasing care pressures. Yet, the meaningful integration of such technologies into the complex sociotechnical setting of residential dementia care is not straightforward. To responsibly design GenAI technologies for dementia care, we need to investigate how care professionals recognize and foster social connectedness and how technologies intersect with those approaches in care contexts. We conducted five workshops with 15 care professionals from three care organizations to pursue this objective. Our findings show that fostering social connectedness involves ongoing interpretation, negotiation, and adaptation to residents' individual needs. Technology was used by care professionals to support communication, interaction, and shared activities, yet remained largely peripheral to everyday care routines and required active mediation for use in practice. Drawing on an ethics of care framework, we derive ethical and sociotechnical implications for the responsible design and positioning of GenAI in residential dementia care.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how care professionals in residential dementia care recognize and foster social connectedness, and how technologies—particularly Generative AI—intersect with these care practices. Through five workshops with 15 care professionals across three organizations, the study reveals that fostering connectedness requires ongoing interpretation, negotiation, and adaptation to individual needs, while current technologies remain largely peripheral. The authors offer ethical and sociotechnical design implications grounded in an ethics of care framework.
AI.motivation: People with dementia in residential care often experience diminished social connectedness, and person-centered care approaches that prioritize meaningful social interaction are increasingly constrained by staff shortages and time pressures. While Generative AI technologies hold promise for supporting social connectedness, their integration into the sociotechnical complexity of residential dementia care is not straightforward. The study is motivated by the need to understand how care professionals currently recognize and foster connectedness, and how technologies can be responsibly designed to align with—rather than disrupt—these care practices.
AI.method: The authors conducted five workshops with 15 care professionals drawn from three different care organizations. These workshops were designed to investigate how care professionals recognize, interpret, and foster social connectedness among residents, and to examine the role that existing technologies play in everyday care routines. The workshops employed participatory and qualitative methods to surface situated professional knowledge and practice.
AI.result: The findings reveal that fostering social connectedness in dementia care is a dynamic, interpretive process involving continuous negotiation and adaptation to residents' fluctuating individual needs. Existing technologies were used by care professionals to support communication, interaction, and shared activities, but these tools remained largely peripheral to core care routines and required active mediation by staff to be useful in practice. Technology was not seamlessly embedded; rather, it demanded effortful integration by care professionals.
AI.conclusion: Drawing on an ethics of care framework, the paper derives ethical and sociotechnical implications for the responsible design and positioning of Generative AI in residential dementia care. The authors argue that GenAI tools must be designed to support, rather than replace, the relational, interpretive, and adaptive work of care professionals, and must be positioned carefully within existing care ecologies to meaningfully enhance social connectedness.

title: Biological Amnesia in ICU Time-Series Prediction: A Drift-Adaptive Two-Stream Architecture with Temporal Retrieval
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code and aggregate audit logs available at: [https://github.com/empresst/ClinicalRag]. Under Review
summary: Background: Clinical decision support systems degrade silently as treatment protocols evolve, yet standard adaptation methods treat models as monolithic blocks, unable to distinguish stable patient physiology from shifting institutional practice. Methods: We propose an adaptive clinical intelligence architecture for ICU intervention prediction that structurally decouples physiological from treatment representations, confining parameter updates to the treatment stream upon a dual distributional and accuracy trigger. Automated audit logs record which treatment features drove each adaptation event and how their importance shifted. At inference, an attribution-driven Temporal RAG module grounds each prediction in patient-specific, era-matched PubMed evidence anchored to the patient's dominant physiological features. Experiments used 84,792 MIMIC-IV stays (2008-2022) under strict chronological split. Results: Drift localised entirely to the treatment stream, validating the structural prior. Selective adaptation improved vasopressor and septic shock discrimination and calibration over the static source model. A fully retrained baseline yielded marginally higher aggregate discrimination but missed 26 septic shock cases the framework correctly identified, with none in the reverse direction; retrieval consistency with the pre-adaptation source model was preserved by the framework but degraded substantially in the retrained baseline. Conclusions: Structurally constraining adaptation to drifting components while preserving stable physiological representations enables clinical AI to evolve with practice without distorting learned patient biology. This architecture offers a template for governable, interpretable deployment of adaptive models in high-stakes clinical environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adaptive clinical AI architecture that decouples stable physiological representations from shifting treatment patterns in ICU models. By confining updates to the treatment stream (triggered by distributional and accuracy drift) and using an attribution-driven Temporal RAG module for evidence grounding, the framework maintains predictive performance as protocols evolve without distorting learned patient biology, outperforming static models and offering better case detection than fully retrained baselines.
AI.motivation: Clinical decision support systems degrade silently over time as treatment protocols shift, yet conventional adaptation methods treat models monolithically, failing to distinguish between stable patient physiology and evolving institutional practices. This leads to models that either become obsolete or, when fully retrained, lose fidelity to previously learned physiological patterns.
AI.method: The architecture structurally decouples physiological and treatment representations. Adaptation is confined to the treatment stream and triggered by a dual criterion: distributional shift detection combined with accuracy degradation. An automated audit log tracks which treatment features drive each adaptation event and how feature importance shifts. At inference, an attribution-driven Temporal RAG module grounds predictions in patient-specific, era-matched PubMed evidence anchored to dominant physiological features. Evaluation uses 84,792 MIMIC-IV stays (2008–2022) under strict chronological splitting.
AI.result: Drift was entirely localized to the treatment stream, validating the structural prior. Selective adaptation improved discrimination and calibration for vasopressor and septic shock prediction over the static source model. A fully retrained baseline achieved marginally higher aggregate discrimination but missed 26 septic shock cases that the framework correctly identified, with zero misses in the reverse direction. Retrieval consistency with the pre-adaptation source model was preserved by the framework but substantially degraded in the retrained baseline.
AI.conclusion: Structurally constraining adaptation to drifting components while preserving stable physiological representations allows clinical AI to evolve with practice without distorting learned patient biology. This provides a template for governable, interpretable deployment of adaptive models in high-stakes clinical environments.

title: Stochastic Meta-Unlearning: Bridging Language Backbone and Multimodal Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning for vision-language models (VLMs) remains underexplored. Unlike language models, VLMs combine a language backbone with visual components, which makes unlearning more complex. There is a surprising phenomenon when moving from single-modality unlearning to VLM unlearning: a target forgotten by the standalone language backbone can still be recovered when image information is given to the full VLM. This shows that text-only feedback is not enough for reliable VLM unlearning. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stochastic Meta-Unlearning (SMU), a bilevel framework that uses VLM-level feedback to learn an unlearning-ready initialization. In the inner loop, SMU applies a few unlearning steps to the language backbone using text data. In the outer loop, SMU recomposes the updated backbone with the frozen VLM and evaluates forgetting and utility at the VLM level.
