This design makes the unlearning update aware of the final multimodal behavior, while still keeping the update local to the language backbone. Experiments on two VLMs, two multimodal meme datasets, and three baselines show that SMU achieves the best overall forget-retain trade-off. Compared with the strongest baseline for each metric, SMU reduces average Forget accuracy by 10.52 points and improves average Retain and Test accuracy by 20.10 and 17.01 points, respectively. More importantly, SMU also transfers to new forgetting targets and to different meta-test unlearning methods. These results suggest that VLM-level feedback can make language-backbone unlearning more reliable and more transferable for VLMs.

AI.tldr: SMU is a bilevel meta-unlearning framework for VLMs that uses VLM-level feedback to learn an unlearning-ready initialization of the language backbone, preventing visual recovery of forgotten targets and achieving superior forget-retain trade-offs with strong transferability.
AI.motivation: Text-only unlearning in VLMs is unreliable: a target forgotten by the standalone language backbone can be recovered when visual input is provided to the full VLM. This reveals that single-modality feedback is insufficient, motivating the need for VLM-level supervision during unlearning.
AI.method: Stochastic Meta-Unlearning (SMU) is a bilevel optimization framework. The inner loop performs a few unlearning steps on the language backbone using text-only data. The outer loop recomposes the updated backbone with the frozen VLM's visual components and evaluates forgetting and utility at the full VLM level, providing multimodal feedback to learn a robust initialization.
AI.result: On two VLMs, two multimodal meme datasets, and three baselines, SMU achieves the best forget-retain trade-off: it reduces average Forget accuracy by 10.52 points and improves average Retain and Test accuracy by 20.10 and 17.01 points, respectively, over the strongest baselines. SMU also transfers to new forgetting targets and different meta-test unlearning methods.
AI.conclusion: VLM-level feedback during unlearning makes language-backbone updates more reliable and transferable. SMU's bilevel design ensures the unlearning update remains local to the language backbone while being aware of downstream multimodal behavior, establishing a new state-of-the-art for VLM unlearning.

title: SciCodePile: A 128GB Corpus and Executable Benchmark for Challenging Scientific Code Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at general-purpose code generation, yet how well they handle scientific code remains an open question. Existing datasets and benchmarks are limited in scale, domain coverage, or executable verification, leaving the true gap between current LLMs and reliable scientific code generators inadequately assessed. To address these limitations, we present SciCodePile, the largest scientific code corpus to date, constructed from 37,737 public repositories and collectively comprising 128GB of code that spans multiple computational science disciplines. From this corpus, we further curate an executable benchmark of 200 tasks, each equipped with a sandboxed execution environment and an automated test harness for functional verification. We evaluate 15 LLMs from both open-source and closed-source families on three tasks: prefix-to-suffix completion, fill-in-the-middle infilling, and executable code generation. Results show that scientific code generation remains highly challenging: The best CodeBLEU reaches only 38.13 and 38.37 on the two completion tasks, while the strongest model achieves just 12.30\% Pass@1 on the executable benchmark, underscoring how far current models remain from reliable scientific code generation. To demonstrate the training utility of SciCodePile, we further show that continued pretraining on our corpus improves CodeBLEU by $\times$2.84 on scientific code completion, and instruction tuning on our data improves Pass@1 by $\times$4.79 on the executable benchmark. All code and data are available at https://huggingface.co/SciCodePile.

AI.tldr: SciCodePile introduces a 128GB scientific code corpus from 37K+ repos and a 200-task executable benchmark. Evaluating 15 LLMs reveals poor scientific code generation (best Pass@1: 12.30%). Continued pretraining and instruction tuning on this data yield substantial gains (×2.84 CodeBLEU and ×4.79 Pass@1 improvements).
AI.motivation: Existing code benchmarks lack scale, domain coverage, and executable verification for scientific code. The true capability gap between LLMs and reliable scientific code generation remains poorly quantified.
AI.method: Construct SciCodePile (37,737 repos, 128GB) spanning multiple computational science disciplines. Curate a 200-task executable benchmark with sandboxed environments and automated test harnesses. Evaluate 15 open/closed-source LLMs on prefix-to-suffix completion, fill-in-the-middle infilling, and executable code generation. Perform continued pretraining and instruction tuning to demonstrate corpus utility.
AI.result: Scientific code generation is highly challenging: best CodeBLEU reaches 38.13/38.37 on completion tasks; best Pass@1 is only 12.30% on the executable benchmark. Continued pretraining on SciCodePile improves CodeBLEU by ×2.84; instruction tuning improves Pass@1 by ×4.79.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs remain far from reliable scientific code generation. SciCodePile serves as both a valuable training resource and a rigorous benchmark, with demonstrated gains from domain-specific continued pretraining and instruction tuning.

title: When to Trust the Map: Confidence-Aware LLM Routing for Automotive CVE-to-ATM Mapping
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables; Accepted at ESCAR EUROPE 2026
summary: Public CVE descriptions report the technical conditions and impact of vulnerabilities, whereas the Auto-ISAC Automotive Threat Matrix (ATM) expresses an adversary's tactics and techniques. Because the two representations are not directly aligned, incorrect automated mappings in safety-critical environments may distort threat interpretation and mitigation prioritization, motivating a confidence-aware approach that distinguishes auto-confirmable mappings from uncertain cases. This paper reformulates automotive CVE-to-ATM mapping as a selective automation problem. The proposed framework generates candidate mappings via hierarchical in-context learning, then fuses self-consistency and LLM-based evidence verification signals into a calibrated meta-model. The resulting calibrated confidence score routes each candidate into AUTO, REVIEW, or HOLD. On the evaluation set, the proposed system substantially improved candidate-set precision at matched recall over a Flat zero-shot GPT-5.2 baseline. In the High-Confidence operating mode, the AUTO tier achieved a precision of 0.878, more than double the candidate-set base rate, and the calibrated confidence score achieved an AUROC of 0.868 in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidates. These results show that the framework can support selective automation by isolating auto-confirmable mappings from those requiring analyst review.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates automotive CVE-to-ATM mapping as a selective automation problem, using hierarchical in-context learning to generate candidate mappings and a calibrated meta-model fusing self-consistency with LLM-based evidence verification to route candidates into AUTO, REVIEW, or HOLD tiers, achieving 0.878 precision in AUTO mode and 0.868 AUROC for confidence calibration.
AI.motivation: CVE descriptions and the Auto-ISAC Automotive Threat Matrix (ATM) represent vulnerabilities in fundamentally different ways — technical conditions/impact vs. adversary tactics/techniques. Since these representations are not directly aligned, automated mappings in safety-critical automotive environments risk distorting threat interpretation and mitigation prioritization. A confidence-aware approach is needed to separate auto-confirmable mappings from uncertain ones requiring human review.
AI.method: The framework operates in two stages: (1) Candidate generation via hierarchical in-context learning (LLM-based prompting) that produces CVE-to-ATM mappings. (2) A calibrated meta-model that fuses two signals — self-consistency (agreement across multiple LLM samples) and LLM-based evidence verification — into a confidence score. This score is then used to route each candidate mapping into one of three tiers: AUTO (high confidence, auto-confirmable), REVIEW (uncertain, needs analyst), or HOLD (low confidence, suppressed).
AI.result: Against a Flat zero-shot GPT-5.2 baseline, the system substantially improved candidate-set precision at matched recall. In High-Confidence operating mode, the AUTO tier achieved 0.878 precision (more than double the candidate-set base rate). The calibrated confidence score achieved an AUROC of 0.868 for distinguishing correct from incorrect mappings.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively supports selective automation by reliably isolating auto-confirmable CVE-to-ATM mappings from those requiring human analyst review, demonstrating that confidence-calibrated LLM pipelines with tiered routing are viable for safety-critical vulnerability management workflows.

title: S2T-RLHF: Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Stable Preference-Based RLHF
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with preference-based reward models often exhibits unstable training dynamics. A key contributing factor is that standard RLHF relies on a single sequence-level scalar reward, which is propagated to token-level policy updates and leaves credit assignment within a response inherently ambiguous. Recent work has attempted to address this issue by refining rewards into denser token-level supervision, often relying on the implicit assumption that finer-grained credit assignment improves optimization. We argue that this assumption is incomplete: when preference signals are noisy and only defined at the response level, overly fine-grained reward refinement can amplify reward uncertainty and destabilize learning. To address this problem, we propose a granularity-aware principle for hierarchical credit assignment, emphasizing stability-oriented reward design rather than maximal allocation precision. Under this principle, sentences serve as a natural intermediate granularity, balancing semantic coherence with robustness to token-level noise. Guided by this view, we introduce S2T-RLHF. This sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework first allocates sequence-level preference rewards across sentences and then applies bounded token-level refinement within each sentence, without reward-model retraining or token-level supervision. Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings show that S2T-RLHF improves training stability and robustness while maintaining competitive preference alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes S2T-RLHF, a hierarchical credit assignment framework that decomposes sequence-level preference rewards first across sentences then to tokens, improving RLHF training stability by avoiding the noise amplification of overly fine-grained reward refinement.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF uses a single sequence-level scalar reward, creating ambiguous token-level credit assignment. While recent methods densify rewards to token-level supervision, the authors argue this can backfire: when preference signals are noisy and sequence-level, overly fine-grained refinement amplifies reward uncertainty and destabilizes learning. A granularity-aware approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose a granularity-aware principle favoring stability over maximal precision. They introduce S2T-RLHF, a sentence-to-token reward decomposition framework that (1) first allocates sequence-level preference rewards across sentences as an intermediate granularity, (2) then applies bounded token-level refinement within each sentence. This requires no reward-model retraining or token-level supervision.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and optimization settings demonstrate that S2T-RLHF improves training stability and robustness while maintaining competitive preference alignment compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Sentence-level intermediate granularity strikes an effective balance between semantic coherence and robustness to token-level noise. Stability-oriented reward design, rather than maximal allocation precision, is key to improving RLHF training dynamics.

title: Sequential Learner Modeling Using Multi-Relational Graph Convolutional Networks
summary: User modeling is a critical task in a variety of personalized systems. Recognizing their effectiveness in learning from graph-structured data, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), are increasingly employed for user modeling. However, existing approaches typically treat different relation types in a graph as homogeneous, limiting their ability to capture richer semantics and construct more informative user models. While multi-relational GNNs (MR-GNNs) have been adopted for representation learning and recommendation, their application for user modeling remains unexplored. Moreover, existing GNN-based user modeling approaches ignore the user interaction sequence. To address these research gaps, in this work we propose MR-ConceptGCN, a novel fully unsupervised approach focused on concept-based sequential learner modeling using multi-relational GCNs (MR-GCNs). MR-ConceptGCN effecively combines Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs), MR-GCNs, and the pre-trained language model SBERT to obtain enhanced relation- and semantic-aware representations of the PKG items. The enriched embeddings of the knowledge concepts that a learner did not understand when interacting with learning materials in CourseMapper are then used to construct a sequential learner model that combines long-term and short-term learner interactions. We report the results of an online user study (n = 31), demonstrating the benefits of MR-ConceptGCN in terms of several important user-centric aspects including accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and satisfaction with an educational recommender system.

AI.tldr: MR-ConceptGCN proposes an unsupervised, multi-relational GCN approach for concept-based sequential learner modeling that combines Personal Knowledge Graphs, MR-GCNs, and SBERT to capture richer relational semantics and interaction sequences, demonstrating improved user-centric metrics in an educational recommender system study.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based user modeling approaches suffer from two key limitations: (1) they treat different relation types in graphs as homogeneous, losing rich semantic information, and (2) they ignore user interaction sequences. While MR-GNNs exist for recommendation, their application to user modeling remains unexplored.
AI.method: MR-ConceptGCN integrates Personal Knowledge Graphs (PKGs) with multi-relational GCNs and the pre-trained language model SBERT to produce relation- and semantic-aware embeddings of PKG items. Enriched embeddings of uncomprehended knowledge concepts from learner interactions in CourseMapper are used to construct a sequential learner model combining both long-term and short-term interaction patterns.
AI.result: An online user study (n=31) demonstrated that MR-ConceptGCN outperforms baselines on user-centric metrics including accuracy, usefulness, diversity, and user satisfaction within an educational recommender system.
AI.conclusion: MR-ConceptGCN effectively addresses the gaps of homogeneous relation treatment and sequence ignorance in GNN-based user modeling, with the fully unsupervised approach showing practical benefits for personalized educational recommendation.

title: LatentMT: Machine Translation with Latent Reasoning
summary: Latent-reasoning looped language models (LoopLMs) offer a different scaling path for machine translation (MT): instead of increasing parameter count or emitting explicit chain-of-thought tokens, they spend additional recurrent computation inside hidden states. We introduce LatentMT, the first systematic study of latent-reasoning LoopLMs for machine translation. LatentMT adapts a small 2.6B-parameter backbone model with lightweight training. Across 32 translation directions spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, LatentMT achieves performance comparable to models three to five times larger. It is competitive in a high-resource language and achieves state-of-the-art performance on both mid-resource and low-resource languages. Studying the behavior of scaling the number of recurrent reasoning steps, we find that recurrent computation consistently improves translation quality in early steps, then saturates quickly afterwards. Our mechanistic analysis shows that hidden-representation differences shrink along the recurrent reasoning-step axis, supporting the observed saturation in performance. Finally, our efficiency analysis shows that LatentMT requires lower training and inference compute than much larger non-latent-reasoning models with similar performance, making latent recurrent computation a promising path toward compact, efficient, and strong machine translation.

AI.tldr: LatentMT adapts a small 2.6B-parameter language model with recurrent latent reasoning for machine translation, achieving performance comparable to models 3-5× larger across 32 translation directions, with state-of-the-art results on mid- and low-resource languages while requiring less compute.
AI.motivation: Scaling MT models traditionally requires more parameters or explicit chain-of-thought tokens, both of which are computationally expensive. The authors explore latent-reasoning looped language models (LoopLMs) as an alternative scaling path that spends additional recurrent computation in hidden states rather than growing model size.
AI.method: LatentMT adapts a small 2.6B-parameter backbone model with lightweight training to enable latent recurrent reasoning. The approach is systematically evaluated across 32 translation directions covering high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. The study also includes mechanistic analysis of hidden-representation dynamics across reasoning steps and efficiency analysis comparing compute requirements.
AI.result: LatentMT matches or exceeds models 3-5× larger: it is competitive on high-resource languages and achieves state-of-the-art on mid- and low-resource languages. Recurrent reasoning steps improve translation quality initially but saturate quickly. Hidden-representation differences shrink along the recurrent-step axis, explaining the saturation. LatentMT requires lower training and inference compute than much larger non-latent-reasoning models with similar performance.
AI.conclusion: Latent recurrent computation is a promising path toward compact, efficient, and strong machine translation, offering a compute-efficient alternative to parameter scaling for improving MT quality, particularly in mid- and low-resource settings.

title: EmbeddedKittens: An Evaluation of Code Embeddings for Scratch
comment: Submitted to ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary: The trend of embedding source code for machine learning applications also enables new opportunities in learning analytics in programming education, but which code embedding approach is most suitable for learning analytics remains an open question. A common approach to embedding source code lies in treating the code as a token sequence similar to natural language when training large language models~(LLMs). However, in case of visual block-based programming languages like Scratch, this approach cannot be applied directly. While text-based representations of block-based code can be created to apply LLMs to this problem, other dedicated embedding models could potentially exhibit improved performance by capturing additional structural information. In this paper, we therefore instantiate four LLMs and five different popular embedding approaches for Scratch programs, create a token-prediction and two different classification tasks with corresponding datasets, and empirically evaluate the models on them. Our experiments demonstrate that a transfer of code embeddings to the educational environment of Scratch is feasible. The embedding models trained on large open Scratch datasets capture relevant structural and semantic information about the code to enable learning analytics like predicting functional correctness of student programs, in the typically small classroom setting without requiring further task-specific model fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four LLMs and five embedding approaches for Scratch block-based programs, finding that code embeddings transfer effectively to educational settings, enabling tasks like predicting functional correctness in small classrooms without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: While embedding source code is common for ML applications, it's unclear which approach works best for learning analytics in programming education. The challenge is compounded for visual block-based languages like Scratch, where standard token-sequence approaches used for text-based code cannot be directly applied.
AI.method: The authors instantiate four LLMs and five embedding approaches for Scratch programs, create a token-prediction task and two classification tasks with corresponding datasets, and conduct an empirical evaluation comparing all models across these tasks.
AI.result: Code embeddings successfully transfer to the Scratch educational environment. Models trained on large open Scratch datasets capture relevant structural and semantic code information, enabling learning analytics (e.g., predicting functional correctness of student programs) in small classroom settings without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Transfer of code embeddings to block-based educational environments like Scratch is feasible and effective, with pretrained embeddings on large-scale Scratch data providing sufficient signal for downstream learning analytics tasks in resource-constrained classroom contexts.

title: GLID: Gated Local Intrinsic Dimension Repairs the Blind Spots of Face-Forgery Detectors
summary: Fine-tuned foundation-model detectors dominate face-forgery benchmarks, yet they stay blind to generator families absent from training. We present GLID, a detector that repairs this blind spot with geometry instead of data. GLID treats the patch tokens of a single image as a sample from a manifold and estimates their local intrinsic dimension (LID) at several depths of a frozen vision transformer. This 12-dimensional, training-free signal enters a fine-tuned detector through a confidence gate whose strength is calibrated purely in-distribution. On a 16-axis cross-generator benchmark, GLID reaches 0.805 mean AUC, first among retrained state-of-the-art baselines and never significantly behind the strongest of them on any axis. It lifts the generation axes by +0.084 AUC while moving reenactment by only -0.005. Two empirical laws explain the design. First, forged faces bend the token manifold at family-specific depths: GAN artifacts peak at the last layer, diffusion artifacts peak mid-network, and the pattern survives four backbones, three dimension estimators, and non-face imagery. Second, fine-tuning absorbs auxiliary gains exactly where training data covers: injecting 1% target-family images erases a +0.100 gain, so geometric signals matter precisely where data is unavailable. The deterministic signal also cuts the cross-seed spread of accuracy 5.5x. Code, preregistered analysis gates, and per-image scores accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: GLID is a training-free geometric detector that estimates local intrinsic dimension (LID) of ViT patch token manifolds to detect forged faces, excelling on generator families unseen during training — achieving 0.805 mean AUC across 16 cross-generator axes and outperforming fine-tuned baselines where training data is absent.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned foundation-model detectors for face forgery perform poorly on generator families not represented in their training data ("blind spots"). The authors aim to close this generalization gap without relying on additional training data, instead exploiting geometric properties of the internal representations of frozen vision transformers.
AI.method: GLID extracts LID estimates from patch tokens at multiple depths of a frozen ViT, producing a 12-dimensional, training-free signal. This signal is combined with a fine-tuned detector via a confidence gate calibrated solely on in-distribution data. Two empirical findings underpin the approach: (1) forged faces distort the token manifold at generator-family-specific depths (GAN artifacts peak at last layer, diffusion at mid-network), and (2) fine-tuning absorbs auxiliary gains only where training data exists — injecting merely 1% target-family images eliminates geometric gains.
AI.result: GLID achieves 0.805 mean AUC on a 16-axis cross-generator benchmark, ranking first among retrained SOTA baselines and never significantly behind the strongest baseline on any axis. It improves generation axes by +0.084 AUC while losing only -0.005 on reenactment. The LID signal is robust across four ViT backbones, three dimension estimators, and non-face imagery. The deterministic geometric signal also reduces cross-seed accuracy variance by 5.5×.
AI.conclusion: Geometric signals from frozen foundation models provide a principled, data-free route to generalization across unseen forgery generators. The two empirical laws — family-specific manifold distortion depths and the erasure of geometric gains by even minimal target-family exposure — establish that geometry matters precisely where data is unavailable, offering a complementary paradigm to data-hungry fine-tuning.

title: Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering for Trustworthy LLM Inference
summary: Steering vectors (SVs), an inference-time intervention technique for large language models (LLMs), guide the generation process by adding a concept-specific direction vector to intermediate activations during inference. However, existing SV methods frequently yield representation-incoherent behaviors that undermine interpretability and fine-grained control, largely because prior work has focused on binary positive-negative steering evaluation while employing discrete clustering metrics that fail to capture the continuous spectrum of semantic alignment. In this work, we present the Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS) framework for LLM inference. PCS preserves original task competence while providing controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias through concept-driven steering-vector retrieval and probabilistic strength calibration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS), a framework that improves steering vectors for LLMs by using probabilistic strength calibration and concept-driven retrieval to address representation incoherence, enabling finer-grained, interpretable, and safety-oriented semantic control.
AI.motivation: Existing steering vector (SV) methods suffer from representation-incoherent behaviors that reduce interpretability and fine-grained control. Prior work relies on binary positive-negative evaluation and discrete clustering metrics, which fail to capture the continuous spectrum of semantic alignment.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Probabilistic Concept-Aware Steering (PCS) framework, which combines concept-driven steering-vector retrieval with probabilistic strength calibration to inject controllable, safety-oriented semantic bias during LLM inference while preserving original task competence.
AI.result: Not explicitly detailed in the provided abstract excerpt.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract excerpt; the abstract focuses on introducing the PCS framework and its intended benefits.

title: Fusion Embedding: A Unified Embedding Space for Text, Image, Video, and Audio
summary: A single embedding space that covers text, images, video, and audio lets one index serve every query a user can pose. Embedding models built on vision-language backbones now lead text/image/video retrieval benchmarks but lack audio entirely, while audio-text retrieval is led by specialist systems that serve no other modality. We present the Fusion Embedding family, which adds audio to a frozen vision-language embedding base whose parameters are never updated: generation 1 (fusion-embedding-1) trains only a 16.4M-parameter connector between a frozen audio tower and the frozen base, and generation 2 (fusion-embedding-2) adds modality-gated deep adapters (44.2M parameters) whose branch never executes on text, image, or video inputs: their outputs are bit-for-bit those of the released base, verified after every training run. Because the base already binds text, images, and video, aligning audio to text alone makes audio-image retrieval emerge, with zero paired audio-visual training data. Alongside the recipe we map its design space with controlled negative results (rewriting training captions with an LLM, substituting a leaderboard-stronger audio tower, and widening the connector each reduce retrieval) and with training-protocol findings that we expect to transfer to any frozen decoder-LM embedding backbone. Both generations train in hours on a single GPU. Weights, code, and the evaluation harness are openly released.

AI.tldr: Fusion Embedding introduces a family of multimodal embedding models that add audio capabilities to a frozen vision-language backbone via lightweight connectors/adapters, enabling a single index to serve text, image, video, and audio queries without degrading existing modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language embedding models excel at text/image/video retrieval but lack audio; audio-text retrieval relies on specialist models that don't serve other modalities. The goal is a unified embedding space covering all four modalities without retraining or degrading the base model.
AI.method: Two generations: (1) fusion-embedding-1 trains a 16.4M-parameter connector between a frozen audio tower and a frozen vision-language embedding base; (2) fusion-embedding-2 adds modality-gated deep adapters (44.2M params) whose branches never execute on text/image/video, preserving bit-for-bit identical outputs to the base. Audio is aligned to text only, enabling emergent zero-shot audio-image retrieval without paired audio-visual data. Controlled negative results map the design space.
AI.result: Both generations train in hours on a single GPU. Aligning audio to text alone causes audio-image retrieval to emerge with zero paired audio-visual training data. Negative results show that rewriting captions with LLMs, substituting a stronger audio tower, and widening the connector all reduce retrieval performance.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, modular extension of frozen vision-language backbones with audio is effective and efficient. The gated adapter approach guarantees zero regression on existing modalities. Findings on training protocols are expected to generalize to any frozen decoder-LM embedding backbone. Weights, code, and evaluation harness are open-sourced.

title: Cross-Agent Campaign Attribution: Linking Asynchronous Attacks Across LLM Agents
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
summary: LLM-agent defenses are typically evaluated one session at a time. In deployment, however, attacks can be distributed across independent agents, teams, and runtimes, leaving each local guardrail with only a sparse fragment. We formalize cross-agent asynchronous campaign attribution: linking sessions from the same latent adversarial campaign without shared runtime state, test-time campaign labels, or attacker identity oracles. We introduce Asynchronous Attribution Fingerprint Vectors ($A^2FV$), a lightweight proxy-side reference protocol for scoring pairwise campaign similarity from proxy-observable tool-use, timing, and prompt residue. We also construct SCD-v1, a controlled persona-matched benchmark with benign traffic, isolated attacks, multi-session campaigns, matched non-oracle evasion, and leakage audits. On SCD-v1, $A^2FV$ achieves 0.82 pairwise AUC for campaign linking, while score-only adaptations of per-session detectors and chunked LLM judges remain near chance under the same task. The strongest fixed signal is carried by structural and stylometric residue, while timing is retained as a diagnostic channel for richer proxy traces. Crossed-style controls show that the signal is partly style-sensitive but not reducible to style alone. Static and dimension-aware non-oracle stress tests further show that pairwise separability persists under controlled evasion. These results establish cross-agent campaign attribution as a distinct evaluation layer for securing LLM agents in the wild.

AI.tldr: Proposes A²FV, a lightweight proxy-side protocol that links sessions from the same adversarial campaign across independent LLM agents without shared state, achieving 0.82 pairwise AUC for campaign attribution where existing per-session detectors fail.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-agent defenses are evaluated per-session, but real-world attacks span multiple independent agents, teams, and runtimes, fragmenting evidence across local guardrails. No existing method addresses cross-agent campaign attribution without shared runtime state or attacker identity labels.
AI.method: Introduces Asynchronous Attribution Fingerprint Vectors (A²FV), a proxy-side protocol that scores pairwise campaign similarity using proxy-observable signals: tool-use patterns, timing, and prompt residue (structural and stylometric). Constructs SCD-v1, a controlled benchmark with benign traffic, isolated attacks, multi-session campaigns, non-oracle evasion, and leakage audits. Compares against score-only adaptations of per-session detectors and chunked LLM judges.
AI.result: A²FV achieves 0.82 pairwise AUC on SCD-v1; per-session detectors and chunked LLM judges remain near chance. Structural and stylometric residue carry the strongest signal; timing serves as a diagnostic channel. Crossed-style controls show signal is partly style-sensitive but not reducible to style alone. Static and dimension-aware stress tests confirm pairwise separability persists under controlled evasion.
AI.conclusion: Cross-agent campaign attribution constitutes a distinct and necessary evaluation layer for securing deployed LLM agents, complementary to per-session defenses, and A²FV provides a viable first protocol for this task.

title: FindStatBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Combinatorial Code Synthesis
summary: We introduce FindStatBench, an execution benchmark for evaluating large language models on combinatorial code synthesis. Built from FindStat, it contains 2,329 tasks across 24 collections and 5.52M hidden instances, covering statistic synthesis, which maps objects to integers, and map synthesis, which maps objects to objects. Each task gives a mathematical description and at most five public input-output examples; a model must emit one Python solve function with no retrieval, tool use, execution feedback, voting, or reranking. Submissions are scored by exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects. We evaluate eleven systems: four closed-source production models and seven open-weight models served through one inference provider. FindStatBench reveals three main patterns. First, the strongest open- and closed-source systems converge within 1 pp instance accuracy, and both an oracle over all systems and five-way sampling from one mid-tier model yield only limited task-accuracy gains. Second, examples can hurt: several classical bijections are solved perfectly with zero examples but fail under five-example prompts. Third, some failures reflect output-budget mechanics, as reasoning can exhaust the visible response before code is emitted. Overall, statistic synthesis is much easier than map synthesis, some collections remain near-zero, long prompts cause a sharp accuracy cliff, and exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.

AI.tldr: FindStatBench is an execution benchmark of 2,329 combinatorial code synthesis tasks (statistic and map synthesis) with 5.52M hidden instances. Evaluating eleven LLMs reveals: open/closed-source systems converge within 1pp accuracy; examples can hurt performance on classical bijections; reasoning exhausts output budgets; statistic synthesis proves far easier than map synthesis; and exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle.
AI.motivation: Existing code synthesis benchmarks lack rigorous evaluation of LLMs on combinatorial algorithm generation requiring exact symbolic reasoning. The authors aim to systematically measure whether LLMs can translate mathematical descriptions of combinatorial statistics and maps into correct Python functions, isolating pure synthesis ability without retrieval, tool use, or execution feedback.
AI.method: FindStatBench is constructed from the FindStat database, comprising 2,329 tasks across 24 collections. Each task provides a mathematical description and up to five public input-output examples; models must emit a single Python `solve` function. Evaluation uses exact sandboxed execution on held-out combinatorial objects, with no retrieval, tool use, execution feedback, voting, or reranking permitted. Eleven systems are evaluated: four closed-source production models and seven open-weight models served through one inference provider.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The strongest open- and closed-source systems converge within 1 percentage point instance accuracy; oracle aggregation and five-way sampling yield only limited task-accuracy gains. (2) Examples can be detrimental — several classical bijections are solved perfectly with zero examples but fail under five-example prompts. (3) Some failures stem from output-budget mechanics, where reasoning consumes the visible response window before code emission. (4) Statistic synthesis is significantly easier than map synthesis; some collections remain near-zero accuracy. (5) Long prompts cause a sharp accuracy cliff, and exact symbolic rule induction remains brittle overall.
AI.conclusion: FindStatBench demonstrates that current LLMs struggle with exact combinatorial code synthesis, particularly map synthesis and tasks requiring precise symbolic rule induction. The convergence of open and closed-source systems, the counterproductive effect of examples in certain cases, and the output-budget bottleneck highlight fundamental limitations of current models on this class of problems, offering a challenging benchmark for future work.

title: AutoJourn: Multi-Perspective Summarisation, Bias Detection and Bias Neutralisation for LLM-Generated News in Automated Journalism
summary: We present AutoJourn, a demonstration system for multi-perspective news generation and bias-aware evaluation using large language models (LLMs). The system tackles three core challenges in responsible automated journalism: extracting diverse perspectives from unstructured social media discussions, generating summaries that preserve viewpoint diversity, and detecting or mitigating bias in AI-generated news. The pipeline integrates advanced prompt engineering with optional retrieval augmentation to produce semantically diverse perspective sets, a multi-perspective summarisation module that merges conflicting viewpoints into balanced summaries, and a bias analysis suite supporting sentence-level bias detection and type classification in the generated news article, and automatic neutralisation. Users can inspect perspective clusters, compare stance-specific summaries, generate news articles, and apply bias-aware rewrites directly in the interface. We evaluate each component with intrinsic metrics -- semantic diversity, summary quality, and bias reduction and show improvements over strong baselines while maintaining content fidelity. A live, publicly accessible demo accompanies the paper to facilitate reproducibility and further research on socially responsible automated journalism.

AI.tldr: AutoJourn is a demonstration system that uses LLMs for multi-perspective news generation with built-in bias detection, classification, and neutralization, extracting diverse viewpoints from social media and producing balanced summaries with measurable improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Automated journalism faces three core challenges: (1) extracting diverse perspectives from unstructured social media, (2) generating summaries that preserve viewpoint diversity rather than collapsing into a single narrative, and (3) detecting and mitigating bias in AI-generated news. Existing systems lack integrated solutions addressing all three simultaneously in a socially responsible manner.
AI.method: AutoJourn employs a multi-stage pipeline: (a) advanced prompt engineering with optional retrieval augmentation to extract semantically diverse perspective sets from social media discussions; (b) a multi-perspective summarisation module that merges conflicting viewpoints into balanced summaries; (c) a bias analysis suite providing sentence-level bias detection, bias type classification, and automatic neutralisation. All components are exposed through an interactive interface where users can inspect clusters, compare stance-specific summaries, and apply bias-aware rewrites. Evaluation uses intrinsic metrics: semantic diversity, summary quality, and bias reduction.
AI.result: AutoJourn demonstrates improvements over strong baselines across all three evaluation dimensions — semantic diversity of extracted perspectives, summary quality, and bias reduction — while maintaining content fidelity. The system preserves viewpoint diversity in generated summaries and effectively detects and neutralises bias at the sentence level.
AI.conclusion: AutoJourn provides an integrated, publicly accessible demonstration of responsible automated journalism, showing that LLMs can be effectively harnessed for multi-perspective news generation with robust bias mitigation, thereby facilitating further research and reproducibility in socially responsible AI-driven news production.

title: Rationale-Guided Knowledge Distillation for Cross-Lingual Stance Detection
summary: Stance detection aims to identify whether a text expresses a favorable or opposing attitude toward a given target, and serves as an important task for various downstream applications. Although existing studies have achieved strong performance in monolingual settings, especially in English, many low-resource languages such as Catalan still lack sufficient annotated data for training effective models. Cross-lingual stance detection alleviates this problem by transferring stance knowledge from resource-rich languages to low-resource languages. However, most existing methods mainly rely on semantic alignment between texts and targets, while ignoring the reasoning process required for reliable stance inference. Although Large Language Models provide strong reasoning ability, their high computational cost and inference latency limit practical deployment. To address these limitations, we propose a rationale-guided knowledge distillation framework for cross-lingual stance detection. Specifically, we use Chain-of-Thought prompting to guide Large Language Models in generating informative rationales, and distill the resulting reasoning knowledge into a compact student model. We further design a dual-path distillation mechanism to align rationale-enhanced and rationale-free representations, together with their prediction distributions. In addition, two contrastive learning strategies are introduced to improve stance discrimination. Experiments on multilingual benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes a rationale-guided knowledge distillation framework that transfers reasoning knowledge from LLMs to a compact student model for cross-lingual stance detection, using Chain-of-Thought prompting, dual-path distillation, and contrastive learning.
AI.motivation: Cross-lingual stance detection suffers from scarce annotated data in low-resource languages; existing methods focus on semantic alignment but neglect the reasoning process needed for reliable stance inference. LLMs offer reasoning but are computationally prohibitive for deployment.
AI.method: A rationale-guided knowledge distillation framework: (1) Chain-of-Thought prompting elicits informative rationales from LLMs; (2) a dual-path distillation mechanism aligns rationale-enhanced and rationale-free representations along with their prediction distributions; (3) two contrastive learning strategies enhance stance discrimination; all distilled into a compact student model.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms competitive baselines on multilingual benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Distilling LLM-generated reasoning rationales via the proposed dual-path framework effectively transfers cross-lingual stance detection capability into efficient, deployable models.

title: Spaghetti Architect: A Contamination-Resistant, By-Construction-Labelled, Multi-Language Code Dataset Generator
comment: 32 pages. Under review at the Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR). Code: https://github.com/KurathSec/Spaghetti-Architect (artifact archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21033174)
summary: Mined code corpora are abundant but uncontrolled: a snippet's semantics, surface "messiness," and difficulty are whatever the wild contained; there is no known-optimal reference to grade against; and any public sample may already sit in a model's training set. We present Spaghetti Architect, a tool that mints code datasets with the control such corpora lack. An anti-optimization transpiler maps a clean, language-agnostic JSON intermediate representation to deliberately redundant, fully-flattened programs in five languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C++); every program is compiled, run, and checked against a reference oracle, so each instance is correct by construction. The clean IR is a known-optimal reference, messiness is dialed by strictly-nested anti-pattern profiles, each instance is labelled along two orthogonal difficulty axes, intrinsic (problem size) and incidental (presentation at fixed semantics), and contamination is resisted by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed. We give construct-validity evidence that the quality order moves established complexity and readability metrics, and report baselines on a four-model open ladder: exact match rises with scale, and the intrinsic knob collapses arithmetic-aggregation accuracy of even the strongest model to zero. Further, development-set scores equal freshly re-minted held-out counterparts within $|Δ|\le 0.012$ (comprehension) and $\le 0.011$ (refactoring); on identical programs, refactoring equivalence ($0.73 \rightarrow 0.99$) is scale-invariant while output prediction collapses; and ablating the generator's self-annotations shows they inflate the weakest model an order of magnitude more than the strongest ($-0.173$ vs $-0.017$): the annotated ladder resolves one of three adjacent pairs where the unannotated resolves all three. Open source (MIT), dependency-free, archived under a persistent DOI.

AI.tldr: Spaghetti Architect is a code dataset minting tool that transforms clean JSON intermediate representations into deliberately obfuscated, multi-language programs with controlled messiness, orthogonal difficulty axes, and built-in correctness guarantees, enabling contamination-resistant evaluation of code LLMs.
AI.motivation: Mined code corpora lack control: semantics, messiness, and difficulty are uncontrolled; there is no optimal reference for grading; and public samples risk training-set contamination. Researchers need controllable, correct-by-construction code benchmarks for rigorous model evaluation.
AI.method: An anti-optimization transpiler converts a clean, language-agnostic JSON IR into deliberately redundant, fully-flattened programs across five languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C++). Each program is compiled, executed, and validated against a reference oracle. Messiness is controlled via nested anti-pattern profiles, and difficulty is labeled along two orthogonal axes: intrinsic (problem size) and incidental (presentation at fixed semantics). Contamination is resisted by minting fresh variants from a private held-out seed.
AI.result: Construct validity is demonstrated via established complexity/readability metrics. Exact match scores rise with model scale. The intrinsic difficulty knob collapses arithmetic-aggregation accuracy of the strongest model to zero. Dev-set scores match freshly re-minted held-out sets within |Δ| ≤ 0.012 (comprehension) and ≤ 0.011 (refactoring). Refactoring equivalence on identical programs improves from 0.73 to 0.99 and is scale-invariant, while output prediction collapses. Ablating self-annotations hurts the weakest model an order of magnitude more than the strongest (−0.173 vs −0.017).
AI.conclusion: Spaghetti Architect provides a principled, contamination-resistant, controllable framework for evaluating code LLMs. It reveals that scaling helps exact match but not intrinsic difficulty, and that model-generated annotations disproportionately benefit weaker models. The tool is open-source (MIT), dependency-free, and archived under a persistent DOI.

title: Data Leakage Prevention in Agentic Applications via Preemptive Hardening
summary: Agentic systems integrate LLM driven planning with interfaces to external tools, making data leakage and tool misuse feasible via instruction/data boundary failures and prompt injection attacks. Enforcing required controls consistently is particularly challenging in workflows spanning many codebases and heterogeneous agents. To address this challenge in multi agentic systems, we present a pre-deployment pipeline for scanning, hardening, and validation of agentic applications. The pipeline analyzes prompt templates, tool interfaces, and tool-invocation code to identify leakage-enabling patterns and generate actionable patches. The hardened application is then validated through adversarial prompt injection attacks and benign input variations ensuring that mitigations do not disrupt intended behavior. In the hardening stage, high-risk tools are prioritized, and minimally invasive mitigations are applied, including schema tightening, boundary sanitization, allowlist-based tool gating, and least-privilege checks. In the validation stage, the pipeline automatically generates attack inputs that mimic jailbreaks, instruction overrides, and tool-targeted manipulation, along with benign task variants, to confirm that the functionality of the hardened application is preserved after remediation. We evaluated the pipeline on five real-world agentic applications, as well as on the AgentDojo benchmark. Across all applications, the proposed pipeline identified recurring leakage-enabling patterns and generated patches that can be integrated without disrupting the intended application behavior. The resulting modifications of application code were shown to eliminate leaks when targeted by basic jailbreak and instruction-override attacks, achieving a 100% reduction in leakage, and reduce leaks by 91% under conditions of stress-induced manipulation, without the need of continuous runtime policy enforcement.

AI.tldr: A pre-deployment pipeline for multi-agentic systems that scans, hardens, and validates agentic applications against data leakage and prompt injection attacks. The pipeline identifies leakage patterns, applies minimally invasive patches (schema tightening, sanitization, allowlists, least-privilege), and validates via adversarial attacks and benign inputs. Evaluated on five real-world applications and AgentDojo, achieving 100% leakage reduction against basic attacks and 91% reduction under stress manipulation.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems combining LLM-driven planning with external tools are vulnerable to data leakage and tool misuse through instruction/data boundary failures and prompt injection. Consistently enforcing controls across heterogeneous agents and codebases is challenging, motivating a systematic pre-deployment approach rather than relying solely on runtime enforcement.
AI.method: A three-stage pre-deployment pipeline: (1) Scanning — analyzes prompt templates, tool interfaces, and tool-invocation code to detect leakage-enabling patterns; (2) Hardening — applies prioritized, minimally invasive mitigations including schema tightening, boundary sanitization, allowlist-based tool gating, and least-privilege checks; (3) Validation — automatically generates adversarial inputs (jailbreaks, instruction overrides, tool-targeted manipulation) and benign task variants to verify mitigations don't break intended functionality.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-world agentic applications and the AgentDojo benchmark. The pipeline identified recurring leakage-enabling patterns and produced integrable patches without disrupting application behavior. Achieved 100% reduction in leakage against basic jailbreak and instruction-override attacks, and 91% reduction under stress-induced manipulation — all without requiring continuous runtime policy enforcement.
AI.conclusion: A systematic pre-deployment hardening and validation pipeline can effectively eliminate data leakage vulnerabilities in multi-agentic systems, achieving strong security guarantees against prompt injection without runtime overhead, while preserving intended application functionality.

title: When JSON Is Not Enough: Semantic Reliability of Schema-Constrained LLM Ordering Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used as transaction compilers: a user states an intent in natural language, and the model emits a structured object that an API can execute. JSON Schema and provider-level structured-output modes are useful because they remove a large class of parse failures, but they do not by themselves decide whether the object is a safe, faithful transaction. We introduce OrderBench, a deterministic benchmark for restaurant ordering agents that separates syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, exact item semantics, constraint preservation, and unsafe acceptances. Across 2,400 Nebius Token Factory calls to four open models in prompt-only and JSON-schema modes, we find that schema-valid output can still have large semantic error rates. In the strongest model, both modes achieve 100% schema validity, yet semantic success remains near 80%; in weaker models, schema-valid unsafe acceptances occur in double digits. The result is a concrete engineering warning: structured output is a necessary interface layer, not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution.

AI.tldr: OrderBench is a restaurant-ordering benchmark revealing that JSON Schema validation ensures syntactic correctness but does not prevent serious semantic errors (e.g., wrong items, unsafe acceptances), with even the best models achieving only ~80% semantic success despite 100% schema validity.
AI.motivation: LLM-based transaction compilers (natural language intent → structured API calls) rely on JSON Schema to eliminate parse failures, but schema validity alone cannot guarantee semantic correctness, constraint preservation, or safety. There is a need to systematically quantify the gap between syntactic and semantic reliability in agentic transactions.
AI.method: The authors introduce OrderBench, a deterministic benchmark for restaurant ordering agents that evaluates six dimensions: syntactic validity, schema validity, status decisions, exact item semantics, constraint preservation, and unsafe acceptances. They test 2,400 calls via Nebius Token Factory across four open models in prompt-only and JSON-Schema modes.
AI.result: Schema-valid outputs can carry large semantic error rates. The strongest model achieves 100% schema validity in both modes but only ~80% semantic success. Weaker models exhibit double-digit rates of schema-valid unsafe acceptances.
AI.conclusion: Structured output (e.g., JSON Schema) is a necessary interface layer for LLM agents but is not a substitute for domain verification and fail-closed execution. Semantic validation must remain a separate, mandatory engineering concern.

title: Find Before You Fine-Tune: A Diagnostic Study of Small LLMs for Cybersecurity QA
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly fine-tuned for critical-domain Question-Answering (QA), yet choosing which small model to adapt, before paying the cost of adaptation, remains difficult. Fine-tuning can improve domain alignment, but it may also erode prior knowledge, weaken instruction-following, or increase hallucination, especially when labeled data are scarce or rapidly evolving as in cybersecurity. We present FiT (Find before Fine-Tune), a task-oriented diagnostic framework that characterizes small LLMs along three capabilities required for cybersecurity QA: vocabulary recognition, parametric knowledge, and contextualization of retrieved information. Using FiT, we conduct an empirical study of five open-weight 7-billion-parameter models under two fine-tuning regimes. We find that fine-tuning does not uniformly help: it consistently degrades vocabulary and parametric knowledge in small models, and the two regimes trade off differently. Knowledge-focused tuning causes moderate, rank-preserving degradation, whereas instruction-focused tuning collapses measured knowledge through induced abstention, inverting the knowledge ranking while leaving retrieval-grounded contextualization essentially intact. We quantify these regime-specific patterns with rank-correlation analysis and show that pre-fine-tuning FiT scores anticipate the direction of post-tuning change. Our results suggest that task-oriented diagnosis can screen out unsuitable models, avoid unnecessary fine-tuning, and support safer deployment of small LLMs in cybersecurity QA pipelines.

AI.tldr: FiT is a pre-fine-tuning diagnostic framework that characterizes small LLMs on vocabulary, parametric knowledge, and contextualization. Applied to five 7B models in cybersecurity QA, it reveals that fine-tuning degrades vocabulary/knowledge, with knowledge-focused and instruction-focused tuning producing distinct trade-offs. Pre-tuning FiT scores predict post-tuning outcomes, enabling model screening and safer deployment.
AI.motivation: Choosing which small LLM to fine-tune for critical-domain QA (e.g., cybersecurity) is difficult and costly. Fine-tuning can improve domain alignment but risks eroding prior knowledge, weakening instruction-following, or increasing hallucination—especially with scarce or rapidly evolving labeled data. A pre-tuning diagnostic is needed to screen models before incurring adaptation costs.
AI.method: FiT (Find before Fine-Tune) is a task-oriented diagnostic framework that evaluates small LLMs on three axes: (1) vocabulary recognition, (2) parametric knowledge, and (3) contextualization of retrieved information. An empirical study applies FiT to five open-weight 7B-parameter models under two fine-tuning regimes—knowledge-focused tuning and instruction-focused tuning—with analysis via rank-correlation to quantify regime-specific degradation patterns.
AI.result: Fine-tuning does not uniformly help: it consistently degrades vocabulary and parametric knowledge in small models. Knowledge-focused tuning causes moderate, rank-preserving degradation; instruction-focused tuning collapses measured knowledge through induced abstention, inverting the knowledge ranking while leaving retrieval-grounded contextualization largely intact. Pre-fine-tuning FiT scores predict the direction of post-tuning change.
AI.conclusion: Task-oriented diagnosis via FiT can screen out unsuitable models before fine-tuning, avoid unnecessary adaptation costs, and support safer deployment of small LLMs in cybersecurity QA pipelines. The distinct degradation patterns between tuning regimes highlight the need for regime-aware model selection.

title: Graph-Based Agentic AI with LangGraph: Workflow Pathways for Long-Running Stateful Business Processes
summary: This paper is a practitioner guide to graph-based workflow pathways for long-running, stateful, multi-step generative AI systems in business processes. Rather than treating LangGraph, a low-level orchestration framework for stateful agents, as a model-quality benchmark target, we present three executable recipes -- SQL analytics with repair loops, agentic retrieval-augmented generation with evidence gating, and human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupt and checkpoint recovery -- to show how typed state, conditional routing, deterministic tools, retries, interrupts, checkpoints, and traces fit together. LangGraph is positioned by workflow-complexity fit, not as a universal default: simpler ReAct-style or plain SDK loops may be better for basic tool use, schema-first tools for structured extraction and validation, and DSPy when prompt or program optimization is the main goal. Each recipe explains when LangGraph is worth the extra structure and which implementation patterns make routes, pauses, and audit trails explicit product behavior rather than hidden prompt logic.

AI.tldr: A practitioner guide presenting three executable LangGraph recipes for stateful, multi-step generative AI workflows in business contexts, with guidance on when LangGraph's structural overhead is justified versus simpler alternatives like ReAct loops, schema-first tools, or DSPy.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between LangGraph's technical capabilities and practical business deployment by providing concrete, reproducible workflow patterns rather than treating it as a model benchmark target. The authors aim to help practitioners decide when LangGraph's typed state, conditional routing, interrupts, and checkpointing justify the added complexity over simpler orchestration approaches.
AI.method: The paper presents three executable recipes: (1) SQL analytics with repair loops — demonstrating deterministic tools and retry patterns; (2) agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with evidence gating — showing conditional routing and typed state management; and (3) human-in-the-loop policy review with interrupt and checkpoint recovery — illustrating pauses, audit trails, and state persistence. Each recipe is analyzed for implementation patterns that make routes, pauses, and audit trails explicit product behavior rather than hidden prompt logic.
AI.result: The work establishes a workflow-complexity fit framework positioning LangGraph as appropriate for long-running, stateful, multi-step processes requiring explicit routing and recovery, while recommending simpler ReAct-style or plain SDK loops for basic tool use, schema-first tools for structured extraction/validation, and DSPy for prompt or program optimization as the primary goal.
AI.conclusion: LangGraph is best deployed when workflow complexity — specifically the need for typed state, conditional routing, interrupts, checkpoints, and audit trails — outweighs the overhead of its structural requirements. Practitioners should select orchestration patterns based on workflow-complexity fit rather than defaulting to LangGraph universally.

title: Tracing the Shadows: Automatic Tracking and Analysis of Crypto Money Laundering via Transaction Semantic Analysis
summary:
With the rapid advancement of decentralized finance (DeFi), security incidents related to cryptocurrency have become increasingly prevalent. After such incidents, attackers typically attempt to rapidly move stolen assets, concealing the origin of illicit funds and ultimately converting them into fiat currency. However, existing anti-money laundering (AML) methods struggle to cope with the semantic complexity of DeFi transactions. They either rely heavily on low-level token transfers, or perform protocol-agnostic money flow analysis, failing to capture the high-level intent of transactions.
  In this paper, we propose AMLGuard, a semantic-aware AML framework for account-based blockchains. AMLGuard tracks illicit fund flows from known malicious addresses by performing semantic analysis on complex DeFi transactions, enabling accurate and continuous laundering tracking. Given a complex transaction, AMLGuard combines static rule-based analysis with retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) reasoning to infer implicit DeFi semantics, transforming raw transaction data into high-level semantic representations. Furthermore, for cross-chain transactions where laundering intent is not explicitly exposed, AMLGuard parses transaction parameters and performs argument parsing to recover cross-chain semantics, enabling seamless tracking across ledgers. Based on the inferred semantics, AMLGuard abstracts each transaction into a DeFi Semantic Unit (DSU). We evaluate the effectiveness of AMLGuard on 82 real-world laundering cases, involving illicit assets worth over $1 billion. Specifically, AMLGuard reconstructs compact illicit fund-flow topologies with destination precision of 94.4% and 87.6%, while achieving the highest address recall of 98.4% and 95.8% and destination recall of 94.1% and 93.8% on single-chain and cross-chain datasets.

AI.tldr: AMLGuard is a semantic-aware anti-money laundering framework for account-based blockchains that uses static rule-based analysis combined with retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning to infer DeFi transaction semantics, abstracting transactions into DeFi Semantic Units (DSUs) for accurate tracking of illicit fund flows across both single-chain and cross-chain scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing AML methods for DeFi either rely on low-level token transfers or perform protocol-agnostic money flow analysis, failing to capture the high-level semantic intent of complex DeFi transactions. This makes them ineffective at tracking illicit funds through sophisticated laundering schemes, especially cross-chain ones.
AI.method: AMLGuard combines (1) static rule-based analysis with retrieval-augmented LLM reasoning to infer DeFi transaction semantics, converting raw transaction data into high-level semantic representations; (2) cross-chain argument parsing to recover bridging semantics from transaction parameters; and (3) abstraction of each transaction into a DeFi Semantic Unit (DSU) to construct compact, semantically meaningful fund-flow topologies.
AI.result: Evaluated on 82 real-world laundering cases involving over $1 billion in illicit assets. On single-chain datasets: 94.4% destination precision, 98.4% address recall, and 94.1% destination recall. On cross-chain datasets: 87.6% destination precision, 95.8% address recall, and 93.8% destination recall.
AI.conclusion: AMLGuard demonstrates that semantic-aware analysis significantly improves illicit fund tracking in DeFi by capturing high-level transaction intent. The framework achieves high precision and recall in both single-chain and cross-chain laundering scenarios, enabling more effective AML enforcement in the decentralized finance ecosystem.

title: ProbSPARQL: Querying Knowledge Graphs with Multi-dimensional, Uncertain Numeric Data
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Preprint. Supplementary material and reproducibility artifacts are available online
summary: The SFB 1574 Circular Factory is building a shared knowledge graph infrastructure for integrating data about returned products. A central challenge is that circular-factory data include numeric measurements that (i) originate from sensors or are derived from sensor-based measurements, (ii) are frequently multi-dimensional, and (iii) are inherently uncertain, while downstream triage, validation, reliability-modeling, and reassembly-planning modules require queryable uncertainty representations. Current RDF and SPARQL technologies lack native support for harmonized querying and analysis of such uncertain numeric measurement data. To address this gap, we present ProbSPARQL, an upward-compatible SPARQL extension developed as an early-stage query-layer pilot for this infrastructure. ProbSPARQL models uncertain numeric values as random variables whose distributions are encoded by probabilistic RDF literal datatypes, and supports distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins. We implement ProbSPARQL on Apache Jena ARQ and expose it through a Fuseki-compatible execution layer. We assess real-data applicability using project-derived measurement fragments covering GMM-encoded uncertainty and histogram-based empirical roughness distributions, and evaluate scalability separately on controlled ontology-conformant benchmarks with up to 5,000 angle-grinder instances and 1.5M triples. The results show feasible in-engine execution, filter-pushdown speedups over application-layer post-processing, and latency-accuracy trade-offs among divergence-join decision strategies.

AI.tldr: ProbSPARQL extends SPARQL with native support for uncertain numeric data through probabilistic RDF datatypes, distribution-aware expressions, and divergence-based joins, enabling queryable uncertainty representations for circular-factory data within a Fuseki-compatible execution layer.
AI.motivation: Circular-factory data from returned products contain multi-dimensional, sensor-derived numeric measurements that are inherently uncertain. Existing RDF/SPARQL technologies lack native querying and analysis capabilities for such uncertain numeric data, hindering downstream tasks like triage, validation, reliability modeling, and reassembly planning that require queryable uncertainty representations.
AI.method: ProbSPARQL models uncertain numeric values as random variables with distributions encoded via probabilistic RDF literal datatypes (GMM and histogram-based). It introduces distribution-aware expressions, probabilistic filters, and divergence-based joins as upward-compatible SPARQL extensions, implemented on Apache Jena ARQ with a Fuseki-compatible execution layer. Evaluation uses project-derived measurement fragments and controlled benchmarks scaling to 5,000 instances and 1.5M triples.
AI.result: ProbSPARQL achieves feasible in-engine execution, demonstrates filter-pushdown speedups over application-layer post-processing, and reveals latency-accuracy trade-offs among divergence-join decision strategies on benchmarks up to 1.5M triples.
AI.conclusion: ProbSPARQL successfully fills the gap in native SPARQL support for uncertain numeric data, providing a practical query-layer infrastructure for the SFB 1574 Circular Factory knowledge graph, with demonstrated scalability and performance benefits.

title: Dual Attention Residuals
summary: Recent work extends Transformer residual pathways along two complementary axes: historical retrieval selects information from earlier depths, whereas multi-stream methods maintain multiple residual trajectories. These capabilities have largely been studied in isolation, and assigning an independent retriever to each stream still prevents one trajectory from influencing depth selection in another. We propose Dual Attention Residuals (DAR), which brings multi-stream interaction into historical retrieval through reciprocal cross-stream addressing. For each target stream, DAR computes depth weights from normalized states in the opposite stream and applies them to values from the target stream's own history. The retrieved states are combined for an unchanged Transformer branch and updated through constrained gated writes; a block-form variant operates on block-level histories to control overhead. Across dense models from 0.1B to 1B parameters and a 7B sparse-MoE model, DAR consistently improves validation loss over standard residual Transformers and Attention Residuals. Routing ablations show that the gain cannot be explained by an additional stream or value projection alone. Representation and intervention analyses further show that reciprocal cross-stream selection preserves depth-wise diversity and avoids the redundancy or functional imbalance observed in alternative two-stream designs.

AI.tldr: Dual Attention Residuals (DAR) enables cross-stream interaction in historical retrieval by letting each stream compute depth weights from the opposite stream's states, improving Transformer performance without the redundancy seen in isolated multi-stream designs.
AI.motivation: Existing work extends Transformer residuals along two axes — historical retrieval (selecting information from earlier depths) and multi-stream methods (maintaining multiple residual trajectories) — but these have been studied in isolation. Assigning independent retrievers to each stream prevents cross-stream influence on depth selection, limiting interaction between trajectories.
AI.method: DAR introduces reciprocal cross-stream addressing: for each target stream, depth weights are computed from normalized states in the opposite stream and applied to values from the target stream's own history. Retrieved states are combined for an unchanged Transformer branch and updated via constrained gated writes. A block-form variant operates on block-level histories to manage computational overhead.
AI.result: DAR consistently improves validation loss over standard residual Transformers and Attention Residuals across dense models (0.1B–1B parameters) and a 7B sparse-MoE model. Routing ablations demonstrate the gain cannot be attributed solely to an additional stream or value projection. Representation and intervention analyses show DAR preserves depth-wise diversity and avoids the redundancy or functional imbalance observed in alternative two-stream designs.
AI.conclusion: Reciprocal cross-stream depth selection is an effective mechanism for integrating multi-stream interaction into historical retrieval, yielding consistent gains across model scales and architectures while maintaining representational diversity across depths.

title: Chi-MERA: Defending Orbit-Based Authentication of LEO Satellites with the Space Oddity of MLAT (Long Version)
summary:
An active research area, physical layer security can be a last resort in insecure legacy systems, a resource-efficient alternative, or a complementary backup for cryptographic techniques. In this paper, we demonstrate that previously established authentication schemes for LEO satellites are vulnerable to attackers that control multiple devices. In extensive experiments, such attackers produce false positive rates (FPR) of up to 40%.
  Based on a root cause analysis, we develop a novel scheme, called Chi-MERA, that improves authentication performance and is robust against multi-device attackers. Our scheme uses two enhancements: (1) multilateration (MLAT) to clearly distinguish between attackers and legitimate satellites, and (2), a new resilient signature scheme without dependency on a single dedicated reference receiver. Our evaluation shows that exploiting MLAT characteristics such as residual analysis to classify vastly different signal source categories (orbit vs. non-orbit) is highly effective. In extensive simulations, we show that the new authentication achieves low FPR of $<$2% and false negative rates of $<$3% for accidentally rejecting valid signals. Furthermore, our scheme's defense scales linearly: $n$ receivers reliably withstand spoofing (FPR $< 1%$) from attackers with $\frac{n}{2}$ devices.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies vulnerabilities in existing LEO satellite physical layer authentication schemes against multi-device attackers (up to 40% FPR) and proposes Chi-MERA, a novel scheme combining multilateration (MLAT) with a resilient signature mechanism to achieve robust authentication (<2% FPR, <3% FNR) that scales linearly with the number of receivers.
AI.motivation: Existing physical layer authentication schemes for LEO satellites are vulnerable to attackers controlling multiple devices, producing false positive rates as high as 40%. There is a need for a robust authentication mechanism that can withstand such multi-device spoofing attacks while maintaining low error rates.
AI.method: Chi-MERA employs two key enhancements: (1) multilateration (MLAT) to spatially distinguish between legitimate satellites (orbit-based signals) and attackers (non-orbit signals) through residual analysis, and (2) a new resilient signature scheme that eliminates dependency on a single dedicated reference receiver, making it robust against coordinated multi-device attackers.
AI.result: The scheme achieves a false positive rate below 2% and a false negative rate below 3%. MLAT-based residual analysis effectively classifies signal sources into orbit vs. non-orbit categories. The defense scales linearly: n receivers can withstand spoofing from attackers with n/2 devices while maintaining FPR under 1%.
AI.conclusion: Chi-MERA significantly improves LEO satellite physical layer authentication by leveraging spatial signal characteristics via MLAT and a resilient signature design, providing scalable, robust defense against multi-device attackers where prior schemes fail.

title: Position: AI/ML Deepfake Research is Misaligned with AI-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AIG-NCII)
comment: Position paper accepted to ICML 2026, Spotlight
summary: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) is not adequately addressed in AI/ML literature regarding AI-generated media, commonly referred to as "deepfakes". While research on deepfakes currently focuses on its epistemic harms -- or harms relating to truth and authenticity -- this is misaligned with the dominant reality of generative AI abuse involving sexualized imagery. We conduct a landscape analysis of highly-cited works to demonstrate that technical interventions addressing deepfakes almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII, limiting the research ecosystem to authenticity detection tools. In this position paper, we argue that existing interventions address viewer-centric epistemic harms, such as fraud or scams, but ignore subject-centric dignity harms, such as AIG-NCII. We illustrate that knowing an image is synthetic does not mitigate harms to subjects and may, in some cases, even exacerbate them. We conclude by offering recommendations to realign the field, including updating threat models to consider subject-centric harms and addressing AIG-NCII in AI safety research. Finally, we caution that researchers should only engage in this high-risk domain if they implement safety guardrails for both subjects and researchers and establish partnerships with domain experts in sexual violence prevention.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI/ML deepfake research overwhelmingly focuses on epistemic harms (truth/authenticity) while ignoring the dominant real-world abuse: AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII). Current technical interventions centered on authenticity detection fail to address subject-centric dignity harms and may even worsen them. The authors call for realigning threat models, incorporating AIG-NCII into AI safety research, and adopting ethical guardrails.
AI.motivation: The deepfake research community is misaligned with reality: most generative AI abuse involves sexualized, non-consensual intimate imagery, yet the technical literature predominantly addresses epistemic harms like fraud and disinformation. This gap means the dominant intervention paradigm — authenticity detection — is irrelevant or harmful to victims of AIG-NCII.
