AI.method: The authors conducted a landscape analysis of highly-cited deepfake research papers to quantify the neglect of AIG-NCII in technical interventions. They then develop a conceptual framework distinguishing viewer-centric epistemic harms from subject-centric dignity harms, arguing through illustrative cases that syntheticity knowledge does not mitigate — and can exacerbate — harms to subjects.
AI.result: The landscape analysis demonstrates that technical deepfake interventions almost entirely ignore AIG-NCII, limiting the field to authenticity detection tools. The analysis shows that knowing an image is synthetic fails to reduce subject-centric harms and may amplify them.
AI.conclusion: The field must realign by: (1) updating threat models to include subject-centric dignity harms, (2) integrating AIG-NCII into AI safety research, and (3) only engaging in this domain with robust safety guardrails and partnerships with sexual violence prevention experts.

title: RF-Agent: A Practical Framework for Building Language Agents for RFIC Design
comment: Accepted at ICLAD (IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design), 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have driven rapid progress in electronic design automation (EDA), yet their application to radio-frequency (RF) circuit design remains limited by the scarcity of domain-specific datasets and standardized benchmarks. We present RF-Agent, which addresses this gap through textbook-driven knowledge distillation. A multi-agent Question-Thinking-Solution-Answer (QTSA) pipeline converts a subsection-level corpus from seven canonical RF textbooks into the first-of-its-kind RF-domain reasoning dataset (over 11,000 samples) with a dedicated multiple-choice benchmark. On this benchmark we study two adaptation strategies: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and three retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) configurations (semantic, keyword, hybrid). Across multiple LLM families, domain-specific SFT significantly improves RF reasoning, especially for small and medium-sized models; among RAG configurations, semantic retrieval performs best, indicating embedding-based context alignment suits RF reasoning better than naive fusion. The dataset and benchmark provide a reusable foundation for future work on LLM-aided RF circuit design.

AI.tldr: RF-Agent introduces a textbook-driven multi-agent pipeline that generates an 11,000+ sample RF-domain reasoning dataset with a multiple-choice benchmark. It evaluates supervised fine-tuning and three RAG configurations, finding SFT significantly improves RF reasoning (especially for small/medium models) and semantic retrieval outperforms other RAG strategies.
AI.motivation: LLMs have advanced EDA broadly, but RF circuit design remains underserved due to a lack of domain-specific datasets and standardized benchmarks, hindering effective LLM application in this specialized area.
AI.method: A multi-agent QTSA (Question-Thinking-Solution-Answer) pipeline distills knowledge from seven canonical RF textbooks at the subsection level, producing over 11,000 reasoning samples and a dedicated multiple-choice benchmark. Two adaptation strategies are evaluated: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and three RAG configurations (semantic, keyword, hybrid).
AI.result: Domain-specific SFT yields significant improvements in RF reasoning across multiple LLM families, with the largest gains in small and medium-sized models. Among RAG methods, semantic retrieval performs best, suggesting embedding-based context alignment is more effective than keyword-based or hybrid fusion for RF reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The RF-domain dataset and benchmark provide a reusable foundation for LLM-aided RF circuit design. SFT and semantic RAG are both viable adaptation strategies, with SFT being particularly impactful for smaller models.

title: Exploiting Load/Store Leakage of Sparse Vectors for Key Recovery in HQC
summary: Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC) is a code-based key encapsulation mechanism selected by NIST for standardization, making its resistance to implementation attacks critically important. We present a side-channel attack that exploits load/store leakage in the manipulation of HQC's sparse secret vectors. Analysing Cortex-M4 assembly generated from the reference implementation, we identify a leakage surface in which the low and high 32-bit halves of each 64-bit word leak with different strengths, due to compiler-generated register spilling. We exploit this leakage to construct a simple zero-word distinguisher classifying machine words of the secret vector as zero or nonzero from electromagnetic measurements. The recovered zero positions are then translated into decoding hints, reducing HQC key recovery to a shortened syndrome-decoding problem. We analyse the resulting decoding complexity for all HQC parameter sets: at 32-bit granularity an expected 88.7% of the machine words of y are zero for HQC-1, cutting the decoding to $\approx$ 2 46 bit operations. Experiments on a Cortex-M4 validate the predicted low/high-half asymmetry-approximately 500 traces for the stronger low-half channel and 5,000 for the weaker high-half channeland recover the zero words of an HQC-1 key at 32-bit granularity. Finally, we discuss practical countermeasures that eliminate the sparsity exploited by the attack.

AI.tldr: A side-channel attack on HQC's sparse secret vectors exploits compiler-generated register spilling leakage on Cortex-M4, using EM measurements to distinguish zero/nonzero 32-bit words. Recovered zero positions serve as decoding hints, reducing HQC-1 key recovery to ~2^46 bit operations. Practical countermeasures eliminating sparsity-based leakage are proposed.
AI.motivation: HQC has been selected by NIST for post-quantum KEM standardization, making its resistance to implementation attacks — particularly side-channel attacks — critically important. The sparse structure of HQC's secret vectors presents a potential leakage surface that had not been thoroughly investigated on embedded platforms like Cortex-M4.
AI.method: The authors analyzed Cortex-M4 assembly from the reference HQC implementation, identifying a leakage surface where the low and high 32-bit halves of 64-bit words leak with different strengths due to register spilling. They built a zero-word distinguisher using EM measurements to classify secret vector words as zero or nonzero. The recovered zero positions are translated into decoding hints, reducing key recovery to a shortened syndrome-decoding problem whose complexity is analyzed across all HQC parameter sets.
AI.result: At 32-bit granularity, ~88.7% of HQC-1's secret vector y words are zero, reducing decoding complexity to approximately 2^46 bit operations. Experiments on Cortex-M4 confirmed the predicted low/high-half leakage asymmetry: ~500 traces suffice for the stronger low-half channel and ~5,000 for the weaker high-half channel to recover zero words of an HQC-1 key.
AI.conclusion: The attack demonstrates that sparse secret vector manipulation in HQC leaks through compiler-introduced register spilling, enabling practical side-channel key recovery. The authors discuss countermeasures that eliminate the sparsity exploited by the attack, providing a path toward hardened implementations.

title: MUX: Continuous Reasoning via Multiplexed Tokens
summary: Language models solve complex problems by articulating intermediate reasoning steps in natural language. While effective, this process is computationally bottlenecked: each reasoning step conveys only a single subword, and many are spent expressing a thought instead of carrying out computation. We propose MUX, a simple method for high-bandwidth and compact reasoning based on distillation of discrete reasoning into continuous multiplexed tokens in a latent space. Here, each latent token is trained to represent a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete reasoning subwords, where this superposition is lossless by construction and the span can be fully recovered (demultiplexing). We prove that simple position-dependent weightings, such as suitable geometric decay, support lossless multiplexing, which in turn prevents shortcut behaviors caused by latent collapse. We further show that multiplexed reasoning can perform parallel exploration in problems that require search. Across 32 evaluation settings spanning four language models, MUX outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses further show that the learned latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning. Our results suggest that lossless superposition as local learning targets constitutes a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning.

AI.tldr: MUX proposes compressing discrete reasoning steps into continuous multiplexed latent tokens using lossless linear superposition with geometric decay weights, enabling high-bandwidth reasoning and parallel search exploration. The method outperforms latent reasoning baselines across 32 settings and four language models.
AI.motivation: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is computationally bottlenecked because each reasoning step produces only a single subword token, with many tokens spent on linguistic expression rather than actual computation. The authors aim to increase reasoning bandwidth by compressing multiple reasoning steps into fewer, information-dense continuous tokens.
AI.method: MUX distills discrete reasoning into continuous latent tokens where each token encodes a weighted linear superposition (multiplexing) of a span of discrete reasoning subwords. The weighting scheme uses position-dependent decay (e.g., geometric decay) that is mathematically proven to support lossless demultiplexing — the original discrete span can be fully recovered. This prevents latent collapse and shortcut learning. The method also supports parallel exploration for search-based problems.
AI.result: Across 32 evaluation settings spanning four different language models, MUX consistently outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and probing analyses demonstrate that the learned latent tokens encode faithful and interpretable reasoning content.
AI.conclusion: Lossless superposition with local learning targets is a sufficient condition for achieving strong and efficient latent continuous reasoning in language models, suggesting a promising direction for high-bandwidth, compact reasoning.

title: CASE: Causal Alignment and Structural Enforcement for Improving Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used to improve both the performance and interpretability of large language models (LLMs), yet the generated reasoning may not faithfully support the final answer. We study this problem from a causal perspective, where a faithful CoT process should follow the chain $Z\rightarrow X\rightarrow Y$, with $Z$, $X$, and $Y$ denoting the instruction, reasoning chain, and final answer, respectively. In this process, the instruction should affect the answer only through the reasoning chain. However, conventional autoregressive LLMs condition answer generation on both the instruction and the CoT, which still allows a direct instruction-to-answer shortcut. To address this issue, we propose CASE, a framework that combines training-time causal alignment and inference-time structural enforcement. During training, CASE builds counterfactual-CoT, biased-instruction, and empty-instruction datasets, and applies selective-loss fine-tuning to strengthen CoT-to-answer dependence while suppressing instruction shortcuts. During inference, CASE masks direct attention from instruction tokens to answer tokens, preventing the model from bypassing the generated CoT. We provide an information-theoretic analysis showing how these components promote faithful chains. Experiments on three models and four benchmarks show that CASE achieves a 37\% average per-setting relative improvement in overall CoT faithfulness over the strongest baselines, exhibits stronger cross-dataset faithfulness transfer, and maintains competitive average accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/oddwang/CASE.

AI.tldr: CASE is a framework that improves chain-of-thought faithfulness in LLMs by combining causal alignment during training (counterfactual datasets + selective-loss fine-tuning) with structural enforcement during inference (masking instruction-to-answer attention), achieving 37% relative improvement in faithfulness over baselines while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs using chain-of-thought reasoning can produce reasoning that does not faithfully support the final answer. From a causal perspective, a faithful CoT should follow Z→X→Y (instruction→reasoning→answer), but standard autoregressive LLMs allow a direct shortcut from instruction (Z) to answer (Y), bypassing the reasoning chain (X).
AI.method: CASE combines two components: (1) Training-time causal alignment using three specialized datasets (counterfactual-CoT, biased-instruction, empty-instruction) with selective-loss fine-tuning to strengthen CoT-to-answer dependence and suppress instruction-to-answer shortcuts; (2) Inference-time structural enforcement via masking direct attention from instruction tokens to answer tokens, preventing the model from bypassing the generated CoT. An information-theoretic analysis supports these design choices.
AI.result: Experiments on three models and four benchmarks show CASE achieves a 37% average per-setting relative improvement in overall CoT faithfulness over the strongest baselines, demonstrates stronger cross-dataset faithfulness transfer, and maintains competitive average accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CASE effectively enforces the causal chain Z→X→Y in CoT reasoning by eliminating the instruction-to-answer shortcut through both training and inference interventions, leading to more faithful reasoning without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Sarus: Privacy-Preserving Multi-Vendor Perception Fusion via Homomorphic Encryption
summary:
Cooperative perception enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to improve situational awareness by aggregating detection outputs from multiple agents and sensing platforms, often via a shared fusion service in multi-vendor deployments. However, sharing such outputs at inference time exposes proprietary model behavior and sensitive environmental information, creating significant privacy and security concerns. In this paper, we present Sarus, a privacy-preserving framework for multi-vendor perception fusion via homomorphic encryption (HE), enabling aggregation without revealing individual vendor outputs. Each vendor encodes detections as compact Gaussian moment vectors over a shared spatial lattice and transmits encrypted payloads to a fusion server, which aggregates them directly in the encrypted domain. The fused result is then decrypted and reconstructed into final detections through class-wise bin merging.
  We analyze the computational complexity, showing linear scaling for vendor payload construction and $O(BV)$ server-side fusion with the number of occupied bins $B$ and vendors $V$, while postprocessing scales as $O(B + \sum_{c\in \mathcal{C}} B_c^2)$, where $\mathcal{C}$ denotes the set of object classes and $B_c$ is the number of occupied bins for class $c$. Experiments demonstrate linear scaling in practice with only a bounded constant-factor overhead from HE, with decryption dominating postprocessing cost. Experiments on the KITTI dataset using camera (YOLOv8) and LiDAR (PointPillars, PV-RCNN) detectors show that Sarus improves scene-level coverage by effectively aggregating complementary detections, particularly in distance-dependent regimes where individual modalities degrade. These results indicate that privacy-preserving multi-vendor perception fusion is feasible for real-time deployment when statistical compression and spatial sparsity are jointly exploited.

AI.tldr: Sarus is a privacy-preserving multi-vendor perception fusion framework using homomorphic encryption (HE). Vendors encode detections as Gaussian moment vectors on a spatial lattice, transmit encrypted payloads, and a fusion server aggregates them in the encrypted domain. The fused result is decrypted and reconstructed into final detections via class-wise bin merging. Experiments on KITTI demonstrate linear scaling, bounded HE overhead, and improved scene coverage from complementary modality aggregation, showing feasibility for real-time deployment.
AI.motivation: Cooperative perception among autonomous vehicles requires sharing detection outputs across multiple vendors, but this exposes proprietary model behavior and sensitive environmental information at inference time, creating significant privacy and security risks. A privacy-preserving fusion mechanism is needed that allows aggregation without revealing individual vendor outputs.
AI.method: Sarus employs homomorphic encryption to enable encrypted-domain fusion. Each vendor (1) encodes detections as compact Gaussian moment vectors over a shared spatial lattice, (2) transmits encrypted payloads to a fusion server. The server aggregates encrypted payloads directly without decryption. The fused ciphertext is then decrypted and reconstructed into final detections through class-wise bin merging. Complexity analysis shows O(BV) server-side fusion and O(B + Σ B_c²) postprocessing, where B is occupied bins, V is vendors, and B_c is class-specific occupied bins.
AI.result: Experiments on the KITTI dataset using YOLOv8 (camera), PointPillars, and PV-RCNN (LiDAR) show: (1) linear scaling in practice with only bounded constant-factor overhead from HE, (2) decryption dominates postprocessing cost, and (3) Sarus improves scene-level coverage by aggregating complementary detections, especially in distance-dependent regimes where individual modalities degrade.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-preserving multi-vendor perception fusion is feasible for real-time deployment when statistical compression and spatial sparsity are jointly exploited, as demonstrated by Sarus's linear scaling and effective cross-modality aggregation.

title: State Compression in Two-Agent LLM Relays: A Closed-World Study of Constraint Preservation
summary: Long-running Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents often accumulate large intermediate traces containing audits, eliminations, and numeric calculations. In practice, this state is compressed before handing it to a downstream decision step, creating an information bottleneck in which small omissions can break strict numeric or categorical constraints. This paper evaluates hand-off compression in a closed-world travel-planning relay with two LLM agents. A Researcher audits a fixed inventory of hotels and flights for 50 goal instances, and a Booker selects a hotel--flight pair using only the goal and the hand-off payload, with the inventory withheld. We compare four hand-off conditions: no compression, narrative summarization, schema-constrained JSON extraction, and embedding-based pruning. Exhaustive enumeration over the fixed inventory provides exact feasible and optimal labels. Results show that hand-off representation strongly affects downstream feasibility under a small decision model. JSON extraction achieves the highest feasibility accuracy at 0.96, while narrative summarization, despite producing the smallest compressed hand-off payload, degrades feasibility to 0.48. Embedding-based pruning matches the uncompressed control on feasibility at 0.88 without an additional generative compression call. These findings indicate that constraint checking benefits from structured and auditable hand-off representations rather than relying on brevity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how compressing intermediate reasoning traces (hand-offs) between two LLM agents affects downstream task feasibility. In a travel-planning relay, structured JSON compression achieved 0.96 feasibility accuracy, while narrative summarization degraded performance to 0.48, showing that auditable structure matters more than brevity for constraint satisfaction.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agent pipelines accumulate large intermediate traces with audits, numeric calculations, and eliminations. Compressing these traces before passing them to downstream agents creates an information bottleneck where even small omissions can violate strict numeric or categorical constraints. The authors aim to systematically evaluate which compression strategies preserve feasibility under such constraints.
AI.method: The authors design a closed-world travel-planning relay with two agents: a Researcher (audits a fixed inventory of hotels and flights for 50 goal instances) and a Booker (selects a hotel–flight pair using only the goal and the compressed hand-off payload, without access to the inventory). Four hand-off conditions are compared: (1) no compression (control), (2) narrative summarization, (3) schema-constrained JSON extraction, and (4) embedding-based pruning. Exhaustive enumeration over the fixed inventory provides ground-truth feasible and optimal labels.
AI.result: JSON extraction achieved the highest feasibility accuracy (0.96). Narrative summarization produced the smallest payload but severely degraded feasibility to 0.48. Embedding-based pruning matched the uncompressed control at 0.88 feasibility without requiring an additional generative compression call. Results demonstrate that structured, auditable representations strongly outperform brevity-focused compression for constraint-heavy downstream decisions.
AI.conclusion: Constraint checking in multi-agent LLM pipelines benefits from structured, auditable hand-off representations rather than relying on brevity alone. Schema-constrained extraction and embedding-based pruning offer viable strategies for preserving downstream feasibility while reducing payload size.

title: PTSan: A Practical Memory Safety Sanitizer for C/C++ with Pointer-Object Authority
summary:
Memory safety errors remain the dominant source of severe vulnerabilities in C and C++. Pointer-based sanitizers provide stronger guarantees than location-based tools such as LLVM's ASan, but their overhead and compatibility limitations have constrained production use. We present PTSan, an LLVM sanitizer that makes pointer-based checking practical by storing an object identifier in each pointer's high bits and its bounds in a fixed-size runtime table. This representation trades a finite live-object budget for low overhead, optimizer visibility, and commodity-hardware support. Because identity travels with the pointer value, ordinary LLVM dataflow propagates it without explicit per-pointer metadata instructions. Separating metadata lookup from check enforcement exposes both as LLVM IR, enabling check hoisting, elision, and merging, plus whole-function min-cut placement of compatibility tag strips. Intel Linear Address Masking eliminates the remaining strips in hardware when available.
  On stock hardware PTSan runs at parity with the fastest published location-based sanitizer: 57.2% geomean overhead on SPEC CPU 2017 on x86-64 (46.4% with Intel LAM), 54.7% on ARM64, and 31.5% (x86-64) on the application-shaped LLVM MultiSource suite. This is roughly a third of the published overhead percentage of prior systems with similar pointer-object authority guarantees, while preserving the inter-object, non-object, and temporal detection coverage measured by an independent memory safety test suite. Its physical-memory overhead is effectively native, a critical property for production deployment as memory costs become a first-order constraint. We also demonstrate practical overhead on real-world server and security workloads. These results show that PTSan brings practical pointer-based memory safety into a recompile-only sanitizer deployment model.

AI.tldr: PTSan is a practical LLVM sanitizer that achieves pointer-based memory safety with low overhead (~57% on SPEC CPU 2017) by encoding object identity in high pointer bits and bounds in a runtime table, enabling compiler optimizations like check hoisting and elision, with optional hardware support via Intel LAM.
AI.motivation: Memory safety errors are the dominant source of severe vulnerabilities in C/C++. Existing pointer-based sanitizers offer stronger guarantees than location-based tools like ASan, but their high overhead and compatibility issues have prevented production deployment. The goal is to make pointer-based checking practical.
AI.method: PTSan stores an object identifier in each pointer's high bits and bounds metadata in a fixed-size runtime table. This separates metadata lookup from check enforcement, exposing both as LLVM IR. This enables compiler optimizations: check hoisting, elision, merging, and whole-function min-cut placement of compatibility tag strips. Identity travels with pointer values via ordinary LLVM dataflow, avoiding explicit per-pointer metadata instructions. Intel Linear Address Masking (LAM) eliminates remaining tag strips in hardware when available.
AI.result: On SPEC CPU 2017: 57.2% geomean overhead on x86-64 (46.4% with Intel LAM), 54.7% on ARM64, and 31.5% on LLVM MultiSource suite — roughly one-third the overhead of prior systems with similar guarantees. Physical memory overhead is near-native. Demonstrated practical overhead on real-world server and security workloads. Detects inter-object, non-object, and temporal errors as measured by an independent memory safety test suite.
AI.conclusion: PTSan brings practical pointer-based memory safety into a recompile-only sanitizer deployment model, achieving overhead parity with the fastest location-based sanitizers while providing stronger pointer-object authority guarantees.

title: Structured Synthetic Reasoning Data for Arithmetic Fine-Tuning of Small Language Models
summary: Small language models are attractive for local deployment, but they often struggle with multi-step arithmetic reasoning. We study whether structured synthetic reasoning data can improve this behaviour under consumer-hardware constraints. Starting from GSM8K, we generated a 21,250-example corpus of grade-school arithmetic word-problem variants using GPT-5-mini, combining natural-language solution traces, light Socratic-style cues, structural variation, and irrelevant distractor context. We then fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on consumer hardware (Apple M4, 16 GB RAM). Exact-match accuracy on GSM8K improved from 36.5% to 49.1% for Qwen3-0.6B and from 53.5% to 66.5% for Qwen3-1.7B. For Qwen3-1.7B, transfer to related arithmetic benchmarks was stronger, reaching 98.9% on MultiArith and 73.0% on SVAMP, compared with 54.4% and 45.3% for the base model. Qualitative analysis suggests that fine-tuned models produce shorter reasoning traces, make fewer arithmetic and distractor-use errors, and benefit more consistently from self-consistency sampling. These results show that low-cost synthetic data design can materially improve arithmetic adaptation in small language models. Because the intervention combines Socratic-style cues with other data-design choices, we interpret the gains as evidence for structured synthetic reasoning data rather than as a causal test of Socratic guidance alone.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning small language models (Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B) on 21,250 structured synthetic arithmetic reasoning examples — combining natural-language traces, Socratic cues, structural variation, and distractors — yields substantial GSM8K accuracy gains (e.g., 53.5% → 66.5% for 1.7B) and strong transfer to MultiArith and SVAMP, all on consumer hardware.
AI.motivation: Small language models are practical for local deployment but perform poorly on multi-step arithmetic reasoning. The authors investigate whether carefully designed synthetic reasoning data can remedy this weakness under the constraints of consumer-grade hardware (Apple M4, 16 GB RAM).
AI.method: The authors used GPT-5-mini to generate a 21,250-example corpus from GSM8K, incorporating four design elements: natural-language solution traces, light Socratic-style cues, structural variation, and irrelevant distractor context. They then fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B using LoRA on an Apple M4 with 16 GB RAM. Evaluation covered GSM8K (exact match), plus transfer benchmarks MultiArith and SVAMP, supplemented by qualitative error analysis and self-consistency experiments.
AI.result: GSM8K exact-match accuracy rose from 36.5% to 49.1% (Qwen3-0.6B) and from 53.5% to 66.5% (Qwen3-1.7B). For Qwen3-1.7B, transfer was strong: MultiArith reached 98.9% (vs. 54.4% base) and SVAMP reached 73.0% (vs. 45.3% base). Qualitatively, fine-tuned models produced shorter reasoning traces, fewer arithmetic and distractor errors, and benefited more from self-consistency sampling.
AI.conclusion: Low-cost structured synthetic reasoning data can materially improve arithmetic reasoning in small LMs. However, because the intervention bundles Socratic cues with other design choices, the gains reflect structured synthetic data as a whole rather than isolating the causal effect of Socratic guidance alone.

title: HPD-Parsing: Hierarchical Parallel Document Parsing
summary: Efficient teamwork typically combines global coordination with parallel execution, a principle not yet fully reflected in unified Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based document parsers. Existing unified parsers process an entire page jointly but generate its output through a single token-by-token autoregressive trajectory, creating a sequential bottleneck that grows with document length. Such full-page sequential generation overlooks a key property of document parsing: layout must be analyzed globally, whereas block content can be parsed in parallel. Based on this observation, we introduce HPD-Parsing, which replaces full-page autoregressive generation with a Hierarchical Parallel Decoding paradigm. A main layout branch organizes the overall document structure and dynamically assigns block-level content decoding to concurrent branches, while progressive multi-token prediction (P-MTP) further reduces the decoding steps within each branch. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HPD-Parsing achieves 4,752 tokens per second, delivering $2.62\times$ the throughput of the fastest existing document parsing model and $3.06\times$ that of the vanilla autoregressive baseline, while maintaining competitive parsing accuracy. These results establish hierarchical parallel decoding as an effective alternative to full-page autoregressive generation, opening a new direction for efficient unified document parsing.

AI.tldr: HPD-Parsing introduces a hierarchical parallel decoding paradigm for VLM-based document parsing, separating global layout analysis from parallel block-level content decoding, achieving 2.62× throughput over the fastest existing parser with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing unified VLM-based document parsers process entire pages autoregressively token-by-token, creating a sequential bottleneck that worsens with document length. This overlooks the inherent property that layout requires global coordination while block content can be parsed in parallel.
AI.method: HPD-Parsing replaces full-page autoregressive generation with a Hierarchical Parallel Decoding paradigm. A main layout branch organizes the global document structure and dynamically assigns block-level content decoding to concurrent parallel branches. Progressive multi-token prediction (P-MTP) further reduces decoding steps within each branch.
AI.result: On public benchmarks, HPD-Parsing achieves 4,752 tokens per second — 2.62× the throughput of the fastest existing document parsing model and 3.06× that of the vanilla autoregressive baseline — while maintaining competitive parsing accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical parallel decoding is a viable and effective alternative to full-page autoregressive generation, establishing a new direction for efficient unified document parsing.

title: Fence: Specialized SLM Guardrails for LLM Applications
summary: Real-world applications that use closed-source large language models (LLMs) need advanced safety measures that go beyond the basic content filters. Content moderation filters such as toxicity and bias have relatively standard definitions where as application specific guardrails like hallucination, topic drift and behaviour deviation are more difficult to model and can vary by use case. Additionally, data scarcity and annotation costs, make the process of creating and testing specialized guardrails challenging. In this work, we propose using Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on synthetic data as specialized guardrails for LLM applications. We introduce a novel synthetic data generation method inspired by the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate high quality synthetic data samples which can be used to train SLMs to encode use case specific guardrail information and hence function as specialized guardrails. Our experiments demonstrate that SLM guardrails trained on high quality synthetic data show performance gains over prompt based LLM guardrails.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on synthetic data as specialized, use-case-specific guardrails for LLM applications, introducing a GAN-inspired synthetic data generation method. SLM guardrails outperform prompt-based LLM guardrails.
AI.motivation: Closed-source LLM applications require safety measures beyond standard content filters (toxicity, bias). Application-specific guardrails—such as detecting hallucination, topic drift, and behavior deviation—are harder to model, vary by use case, and suffer from data scarcity and high annotation costs, making specialized guardrail development challenging.
AI.method: The authors introduce a synthetic data generation method inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to produce high-quality synthetic samples. These samples encode use-case-specific guardrail information and are used to train Small Language Models (SLMs) that function as specialized guardrails for LLM applications.
AI.result: SLM guardrails trained on high-quality synthetic data demonstrate performance gains over prompt-based LLM guardrails in experiments.
AI.conclusion: Training SLMs on GAN-inspired synthetic data is an effective strategy for building specialized, use-case-specific guardrails that outperform traditional prompt-based LLM guardrails, addressing data scarcity and customization challenges in LLM safety.

title: From a Multilingual Streaming ASR Backbone to Kenyan-Language Systems: Data-Centric Adaptation of Nemotron 3.5 for Kikuyu, Dholuo, and Kalenjin
comment: 56 pages, 2 figures. Extended appendices on corpus construction, streaming evaluation, reproducibility, and deployment
summary:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) for African languages is constrained by orthographic inconsistency, annotation artifacts, missing audio, speaker and domain imbalance, and evaluation procedures that differ from deployment. We present an end-to-end engineering study adapting NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming 0.6B to Kikuyu, Dholuo, and Kalenjin. Starting from a Kenyan Swahili-adapted checkpoint, we retain its cache-aware FastConformer RNN-T, prompt conditioning, and streaming decoder during full-parameter fine-tuning. The study covers corpus auditing, Unicode normalization, split checks, duration filtering, low-rate continuation, validation-based checkpoint selection, true-streaming evaluation, artifact preservation, and isolated serving.
  On internal, adaptively consulted evaluation sets excluded from gradient updates at context [56,13], selected Kikuyu and Dholuo models achieve 42.97% and 33.98% WER, respectively. Dholuo records 9.59% CER and 8.13% no-space CER under its frozen historical label policy; Kikuyu records 7.79% no-space CER. Kalenjin remains a work in progress: v1-v reaches 68.74% WER on a 2,411-row clean-v3 diagnostic subset excluding long-pause annotations, digit-bearing references, and targets shorter than three tokens. Its checkpoint selection used a mixed-source validation manifest containing test-origin rows, so the score is not an independent generalization estimate. We also report negative findings involving non-speech labels, short-utterance over-generation, boundary-sensitive WER, and cloud job-lifecycle failures. We make no state-of-the-art claim because the internal sets, repeated consultation, and normalization differ from public benchmarks. This work provides an auditable account of adapting a multilingual streaming model into language-specific systems without discarding streaming constraints.

AI.tldr: An engineering study adapting NVIDIA's Nemotron ASR streaming model to three Kenyan languages (Kikuyu, Dholuo, Kalenjin), achieving 43% WER on Kikuyu and 34% on Dholuo, while documenting the full adaptation pipeline and negative findings.
AI.motivation: African language ASR faces challenges including orthographic inconsistency, annotation artifacts, speaker/domain imbalance, and evaluation mismatches. There is a need for auditable, reproducible adaptation recipes for streaming ASR in under-resourced languages without discarding real-time constraints.
AI.method: Full-parameter fine-tuning of a Kenyan Swahili-adapted Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming 0.6B checkpoint (cache-aware FastConformer RNN-T with prompt conditioning and streaming decoder) for Kikuyu, Dholuo, and Kalenjin. The pipeline includes corpus auditing, Unicode normalization, split checks, duration filtering, low-rate continuation, validation-based checkpoint selection, true-streaming evaluation, and isolated serving.
AI.result: Kikuyu: 42.97% WER, 7.79% no-space CER. Dholuo: 33.98% WER, 9.59% CER, 8.13% no-space CER. Kalenjin (v1-v, work in progress): 68.74% WER on a 2,411-row clean diagnostic subset, but checkpoint selection used test-origin rows, invalidating independent generalization estimates. Negative findings documented on non-speech labels, short-utterance over-generation, boundary-sensitive WER, and cloud job-lifecycle failures.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a fully auditable account of adapting a multilingual streaming ASR model to language-specific systems while preserving streaming constraints. No state-of-the-art claims are made due to internal evaluation sets and normalization differences from public benchmarks. Kalenjin adaptation remains incomplete.

title: Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
summary: The wisdom of crowds -- the finding that aggregating judgments across individuals often outperforms the best individual -- has been extensively studied with human forecasters. Whether the same phenomenon emerges when the ``crowd'' consists of large language models (LLMs) is an open question with both theoretical and practical implications. We elicited probability estimates from 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction market questions and evaluated classical and learned aggregation methods. Learned aggregators -- a multilayer perceptron and a logistic regression -- outperformed all individual models and classical methods. The logistic regression was found to match the neural network, suggesting that the benefit of learned aggregation derives from learning a linear combination of diverse model outputs rather than from nonlinear interactions. Symbolic regression applied to the neural network's learned mapping recovered a pure model-disagreement signal as the lowest-complexity useful formula on the Pareto frontier, further supporting this interpretation. Training cutoff contamination proved a pervasive confound: the apparent capability gap between frontier cloud models and smaller local models collapsed from 35.8% to 8.9% on a clean subset of questions resolving after all models' training cutoffs, and individual model rankings showed only moderate stability. Even when the prediction market is evaluated at each model's training cutoff, LLMs remained substantially less accurate, indicating a genuine gap in collective information aggregation. These findings suggest that LLM crowds can exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects, but that contamination-free evaluation is essential for reliable assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the wisdom-of-crowds effect — where aggregated judgments outperform individuals — holds when the crowd consists of 15 LLMs forecasting 254 binary prediction market questions. Learned aggregation (logistic regression, MLP) outperformed all individual models and classical methods, driven predominantly by linear combination of diverse outputs. Critically, training cutoff contamination severely biased evaluations: the gap between frontier and local models shrank from 35.8% to 8.9% on contamination-free data, underscoring the need for rigorous temporal evaluation.
AI.motivation: The wisdom of crowds has been robustly demonstrated with human forecasters, but it remains unknown whether the same effect emerges with LLMs. This has dual significance: theoretically, it tests whether LLM diversity can substitute for human cognitive diversity; practically, it informs whether LLM ensembles can improve forecasting accuracy for real-world applications like prediction markets.
AI.method: The authors collected probability forecasts from 15 LLMs (both frontier cloud models and smaller local models) on 254 binary questions from a prediction market. They evaluated three classical aggregation methods (mean, median, trimmed mean) and two learned methods (logistic regression and a multilayer perceptron) using Brier score. To probe the nature of learned aggregation, they applied symbolic regression to the MLP's learned mapping to identify the simplest predictive formula. They also assessed training cutoff contamination by splitting questions into those resolved before vs. after each model's knowledge cutoff date.
AI.result: Learned aggregators (logistic regression, MLP) outperformed all individual models and classical methods, with logistic regression matching the MLP, indicating linear combination suffices. Symbolic regression recovered a pure model-disagreement signal as the simplest useful formula. Training cutoff contamination proved substantial: the accuracy gap between frontier and local models dropped from 35.8% to 8.9% on contamination-free questions. Individual model rankings showed only moderate stability across clean vs. contaminated subsets. Even with per-model cutoff evaluation, LLMs remained less accurate than the prediction market, indicating a genuine aggregation gap.
AI.conclusion: LLM crowds can exhibit wisdom-of-crowds effects via linear aggregation of diverse model outputs. However, contamination-free evaluation is essential for reliable assessment, as training cutoff leakage artificially inflates apparent performance differences. The persistent gap relative to prediction markets suggests LLMs still fall short of human collective intelligence in forecasting.

title: Reasoning Error from Known Fact: Step-Level Self-Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization for LLM
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), modern systems not only possess strong foundational capabilities and extensive knowledge, but can also solve complex problems via long, multi-step reasoning. However, as reasoning traces become longer, LLMs may produce a substantial amount of hallucinated content during the reasoning process, which is often difficult to detect. In this work, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of hallucinations arising in LLM reasoning and find that the reasoning traces are particularly prone to Context-Sensitive Factual Hallucinations: cases where the model actually has the relevant knowledge, yet makes factual errors due to contextual interference during reasoning. To address this issue, we propose Step-level Self-Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization (SSC-GRPO), which assigns step-level rewards to reasoning traces by computing self-consistency scores of individual steps across multiple rollouts. Compared with prior methods, SSC-GRPO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both mathematical reasoning benchmarks and hallucination leaderboards. Our results offer a new perspective for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in the reasoning process of large language models.

AI.tldr: LLMs produce context-sensitive factual hallucinations during long reasoning traces—errors from contextual interference rather than knowledge gaps. The authors propose SSC-GRPO, which assigns step-level rewards via self-consistency across multiple rollouts, achieving SOTA on math reasoning and hallucination benchmarks.
AI.motivation: As LLM reasoning traces grow longer for complex problem-solving, hallucinations become more prevalent and harder to detect. The key insight is that many hallucinations are "context-sensitive"—the model possesses the correct knowledge but makes factual errors due to contextual interference during the reasoning process. Existing methods lack fine-grained, step-level detection and mitigation for this specific hallucination type.
AI.method: SSC-GRPO (Step-level Self-Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization): (1) generates multiple reasoning rollouts for a given problem; (2) computes self-consistency scores at each individual reasoning step across rollouts, measuring agreement among diverse sampled trajectories; (3) uses these step-level scores as dense rewards; (4) applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize the policy, rewarding steps that exhibit high self-consistency and penalizing inconsistent ones.
AI.result: SSC-GRPO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both mathematical reasoning benchmarks and hallucination leaderboards, outperforming prior methods in reducing context-sensitive factual hallucinations while maintaining or improving reasoning accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, step-level self-consistency provides an effective signal for detecting and mitigating context-sensitive factual hallucinations in LLM reasoning. SSC-GRPO offers a new perspective on hallucination mitigation by directly optimizing for step-wise consistency across rollouts.

title: Attacking Graph Foundation Models Through Their Shared Representation
summary: A graph foundation model generalizes across graph domains by mapping every input into one shared representation before any task reasoning. We call this map the alignment layer, the component that separates a graph foundation model from a graph neural network, and we show it is a distinct attack surface that prior work has not studied. We attack it at inference time, with no access to training, on six public models spanning spectral tokenizers, text embedding spaces, and a discrete codebook. A directed representation-space perturbation collapses every model, but at a budget comparable to the representation norm a plain graph network also needs, with one exception: OpenGraph, whose spectral tokenizer collapses at a fifth of that budget, an alignment-specific fragility a plain network does not share and which a same-representation control traces to the tokenizer rather than the decoder. A realizable input-space attack that edits edges, features, or text removes at least half the correct predictions on three of the six models at peak. How much of this fragility an input-access attacker realizes tracks how directly the decoder reads the representation, and not the clean accuracy a task leaves; we measure this carrier gain structurally from the decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity, and report clean-accuracy headroom as a within-model ordering heuristic that does not survive on realizable attacks.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the alignment layer (the shared representation mapping) in graph foundation models as a novel, unstudied attack surface. The authors demonstrate that representation-space and input-space perturbations at inference time can catastrophically collapse model performance, with certain architectures (e.g., OpenGraph's spectral tokenizer) exhibiting disproportionate fragility. They introduce "carrier gain" — measured via the decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity — as a structural metric that better predicts realizable attack vulnerability than clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Graph foundation models rely on a shared alignment layer to map diverse graph inputs into a common representation space. While prior work has focused on attacking task-specific GNNs, the alignment layer represents a distinct, unexamined attack surface. The authors aim to characterize this vulnerability, quantify how different alignment strategies (spectral tokenizers, text embeddings, discrete codebooks) respond to adversarial perturbation, and identify structural predictors of fragility beyond clean accuracy.
AI.method: The authors conduct inference-time adversarial attacks on six public graph foundation models spanning three alignment paradigms. They consider two threat models: (1) representation-space perturbation — directly perturbing the latent representation with a constrained budget — and (2) realizable input-space attacks — editing graph edges, node features, or associated text. Fragility is quantified via prediction collapse. They introduce "carrier gain," a metric derived from the decoder's local Lipschitz sensitivity that measures how directly the decoder reads the representation, and evaluate it as a predictor of input-space attack vulnerability. Controls using same-representation architectures isolate alignment-specific vs. decoder-specific fragility.
AI.result: Representation-space perturbation collapses all models, but most require a budget comparable to a plain GNN. OpenGraph's spectral tokenizer collapses at one-fifth that budget — a fragility traced specifically to the tokenizer, not the decoder. Realizable input-space attacks (edge, feature, or text edits) remove at least half of correct predictions on three of six models at peak. Clean accuracy does not predict input-space fragility; instead, carrier gain — how directly the decoder depends on the representation — strongly tracks realizable attack success. Clean-accuracy headroom serves as a within-model ordering heuristic but fails across models.
AI.conclusion: The alignment layer in graph foundation models is a distinct and practically exploitable attack surface. Fragility varies dramatically by alignment strategy, with spectral tokenizers being particularly vulnerable. Structural properties of the decoder, captured by carrier gain, better predict real-world attack susceptibility than clean accuracy. This calls for robustness-aware design of alignment layers in future graph foundation models.

title: Trajectory-Aware Clinical Risk Prediction via Severity-Grounded Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: While Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offer a wealth of clinical data, effectively augmenting a patient's records with heterogeneous external knowledge to predict the patient's clinical risk remains a significant challenge. Existing methods fail to capture disease severity, treatment responses, and nuanced clinical progression, due to data sparsity and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. To address these challenges, we propose TRACER (a trajectory-aware and clinically grounded prediction framework) that (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with severity information from medical literature, (2) retrieves clinically relevant, severity-weighted paths of a patient's progression from the knowledge graph, (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured clinical notes, and (4) augments patient context with similar peer cases. Experiments on the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets demonstrate large gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with up to 28.5% increase in Macro F1 score for the mortality prediction task, and 19.7% increase for the readmission prediction task.

AI.tldr: TRACER is a clinical risk prediction framework that augments EHR data with a severity-weighted medical knowledge graph, clinical note extraction, and peer case retrieval, achieving up to 28.5% Macro F1 improvement on mortality prediction over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing clinical risk prediction methods suffer from data sparsity in structured EHRs and fail to leverage unstructured clinical notes. They cannot adequately capture disease severity, treatment responses, or nuanced clinical progression trajectories.
AI.method: TRACER has four components: (1) constructs a medical knowledge graph enriched with disease severity information from medical literature; (2) retrieves clinically relevant, severity-weighted progression paths for a patient from the KG; (3) extracts clinically relevant events from unstructured clinical notes; (4) augments patient context by retrieving similar peer cases for reference.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, TRACER achieves up to 28.5% Macro F1 improvement for mortality prediction and 19.7% for readmission prediction over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating severity-aware knowledge graphs, unstructured notes, and peer case augmentation significantly boosts clinical risk prediction performance, addressing key limitations of prior EHR-based models.

title: Transcription Policy as a Latent Variable: Activating Controllable Verbatim ASR with Word-Level Timing
summary: Modern ASR models trained on heterogeneously annotated data treat transcription style (verbatim vs. intended) as an uncontrolled latent variable, causing measurable decoding instability, evaluation confounding (up to 60% of reported WER attributable to style mismatch), and unreliable word-level timing. We show that models already encode both styles; the challenge is controlled activation. Using coverage-aware decoder task tokens trained on parallel verbatim/intended transcript pairs, we raise German disfluency F1 from 10% to 79% zero-shot, despite English-only training. Full English-only fine-tuning surpasses all baselines in verbatim accuracy, disfluency detection, and intended-mode quality across both languages. We further introduce supervised cross-attention fine-tuning that improves word-level timestamps on disfluent speech beyond forced-alignment baselines. Finally, we propose verbatimize, a new task enabling scalable creation and enrichment of speech corpora with high-quality canonical verbatim transcriptions.

AI.tldr: ASR models trained on mixed-style data treat transcription style as a hidden variable, causing instability. The authors propose coverage-aware decoder task tokens and supervised cross-attention fine-tuning to control style activation, dramatically improving disfluency detection, verbatim accuracy, word timing, and cross-lingual transfer, while also introducing a "verbatimize" task for corpus enrichment.
AI.motivation: Modern ASR systems are trained on heterogeneously annotated data where transcription style (verbatim vs. intended/normalized) varies unpredictably. This uncontrolled latent variable leads to three concrete problems: (1) decoding instability, (2) evaluation confounding where up to 60% of reported WER stems from style mismatch rather than recognition errors, and (3) unreliable word-level timestamp predictions. The core insight is that models already encode both styles internally, so the challenge is not learning new capabilities but achieving controlled activation.
AI.method: The method has three components: (1) Coverage-aware decoder task tokens trained on parallel verbatim/intended transcript pairs, enabling explicit style control during decoding — this achieves zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, raising German disfluency F1 from 10% to 79% despite English-only training. (2) Supervised cross-attention fine-tuning for improved word-level timestamps on disfluent speech, outperforming traditional forced-alignment baselines. (3) Verbatimize, a new task for scalable creation and enrichment of speech corpora with high-quality canonical verbatim transcriptions.
AI.result: German disfluency F1 improved from 10% to 79% zero-shot using English-only trained task tokens. Full English-only fine-tuning surpassed all baselines in verbatim accuracy, disfluency detection, and intended-mode quality across both English and German. Supervised cross-attention fine-tuning yielded word-level timestamps on disfluent speech superior to forced-alignment baselines.
AI.conclusion: Style-controllable ASR decoding via task tokens is highly effective, transferable across languages, and addresses fundamental problems in evaluation validity, timestamp reliability, and disfluency handling. The verbatimize task offers a practical path for scalable corpus enrichment with canonical verbatim transcriptions.

title: Using LLMs for Explainable, Data-Driven Insight Generation from Time Series
summary:
Time series forecasts are widely used in decision-critical domains, where they are rarely consumed without accompanying explanations. Producing such explanations is usually a manual and costly process, and attempts to automate it using large language models often suffer from hallucination when applied to temporal data. We propose a domain-agnostic framework for grounded natural language explanation generation for time series forecasts, illustrated in Figure 1. The framework consists of three components: (i) extraction of structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations, (ii) evidence-conditioned explanation generation, and (iii) scalable evaluation for readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness. The design explicitly constrains generation to verifiable evidence, reducing unsupported claims.
  We evaluate the framework on a financial forecasting case study involving the NASDAQ-100 index and a freight pricing case study using data from Vortexa. Results show that generated explanations approached analyst-written explanations in terms of readability, consistency and persuasiveness. These findings demonstrate that grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be achieved at scale without domain-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A domain-agnostic framework for generating grounded natural language explanations of time series forecasts, using structured explanatory factors, evidence-conditioned generation, and scalable evaluation to reduce hallucination, validated on financial and freight pricing case studies.
AI.motivation: Time series forecasts in decision-critical domains require accompanying explanations, but producing them is manual and costly. Existing attempts using LLMs suffer from hallucination when applied to temporal data. There is a need for automated, verifiable explanation generation grounded in evidence.
AI.method: A three-component framework: (i) extraction of structured explanatory factors from historical analyst-written explanations, (ii) evidence-conditioned explanation generation that constrains output to verifiable evidence, and (iii) scalable evaluation measuring readability, logical consistency, and persuasiveness.
AI.result: Generated explanations approached the quality of analyst-written explanations in readability, consistency, and persuasiveness across two case studies: NASDAQ-100 index forecasting and Vortexa freight pricing forecasting.
AI.conclusion: Grounded explanation generation for time series forecasting can be achieved at scale without domain-specific fine-tuning, demonstrating a viable path toward automated, trustworthy forecast explanations.

title: Constrained CTC Decoding for Efficient Diacritic Restoration
summary: In this work, we address diacritic restoration for Arabic speech transcripts. Most speech data are undiacritized, limiting the ability of modeling fine-grained phonological distinctions. The speech modality has recently been explored as a way to complement text-based diacritic restoration efforts. We propose an efficient non-autoregressive approach for speech-to-text diacritization based on Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). Our method incorporates hard constraints during decoding by constructing a character-level diacritization lattice from an undiacritized transcript and restricting hypotheses to valid diacritized realizations. We evaluate on Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic test sets (namely, ArVoice and ClArTTS) against a more computationally-complex multi-modal diacritic restoration baseline, and show statistically significant reductions in diacritic error rates in both, demonstrating that the proposed approach offers both performance and efficiency gains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an efficient, non-autoregressive CTC-based method for restoring diacritics in Arabic speech transcripts, using lattice-constrained decoding to restrict outputs to valid diacritized forms, achieving significant error reductions and efficiency gains over a multimodal baseline.
AI.motivation: Most Arabic speech transcripts lack diacritics, which hinders fine-grained phonological modeling. While speech modality has recently been used to complement text-based diacritic restoration, existing multimodal approaches are computationally complex. The authors seek a more efficient solution.
AI.method: A non-autoregressive approach based on Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) for speech-to-text diacritization. Hard constraints are imposed during decoding by constructing a character-level diacritization lattice from the undiacritized transcript, restricting the search space to only valid diacritized realizations.
AI.result: Evaluated on two test sets — ArVoice and ClArTTS (covering Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic) — the proposed method achieves statistically significant reductions in diacritic error rates compared to a more computationally-complex multimodal diacritic restoration baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CTC-based constrained decoding approach offers both superior diacritization performance and computational efficiency compared to existing multimodal methods, validating the effectiveness of incorporating hard lattice constraints for Arabic speech-to-text diacritic restoration.

title: SFGA: A Statistics-First Gating Architecture with Adjudicative Escalation for Trustworthy SFT Data Procurement
summary: Procuring supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data forces a buyer to decide, before any downstream training, whether a candidate corpus is worth acquiring. We present \sys{}, a statistics-first gating architecture that treats procurement as a cost-aware routing problem over three intrinsic quality axes -- diversity, utility, and redundancy. Cheap blind measurements are summarised into per-axis estimates with confidence intervals; a gate accepts a decision only when intervals are tight, sample sizes are adequate, and the axes agree, otherwise it escalates the case to an adjudicative debate between a buy-advocate and a reject-advocate judge, resolved by a presiding verdict. On a controlled benchmark of 12 datasets ($2{\times}3{\times}2$ grid over the three axes) with 5 seeds, the gate reaches 0.90 accuracy and 0.83 $F_1$ at \$0.017 per unit, sitting between an always-verify baseline (0.75) and an oracle upper bound (0.98) while spending less than always-escalate (\$0.020). We further report honest negative diagnostics of the debate path: a con-side win rate of 0.80 ($p\approx3{\times}10^{-6}$) and a 52\% position-flip rate under advocate swapping expose negativity and positional biases that a naive LLM-judge would hide. We frame the injected-knob evaluation explicitly as a controlled synthetic benchmark for measurement fidelity and routing calibration, and delimit external validity as future work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a gating architecture that treats SFT data procurement as a cost-aware routing problem over diversity, utility, and redundancy axes. Cheap measurements are summarized with confidence intervals; the gate decides or escalates to an adjudicative debate between buy-advocate and reject-advocate judges. It achieves 0.90 accuracy at $0.017/unit, and exposes negativity/positional biases in LLM-judges via debate diagnostics.
AI.motivation: A buyer must decide whether to acquire a candidate corpus for supervised fine-tuning before any downstream training, but lacks principled, cost-aware methods for making this procurement decision. Existing approaches either overspend on verification or rely on naive LLM judges that hide systematic biases.
AI.method: A three-stage gating architecture: (1) cheap blind measurements along diversity, utility, and redundancy axes, summarized into per-axis estimates with confidence intervals; (2) a gate that accepts a decision only when intervals are tight, sample sizes adequate, and axes agree, otherwise escalates; (3) an adjudicative debate between a buy-advocate and reject-advocate judge, resolved by a presiding verdict. Evaluated on a controlled 2×3×2 grid benchmark of 12 datasets across the three axes with 5 seeds.
AI.result: The gate reaches 0.90 accuracy and 0.83 F1 at $0.017 per unit, outperforming an always-verify baseline (0.75) while approaching the oracle upper bound (0.98) and spending less than always-escalate ($0.020). Debate diagnostics reveal a con-side win rate of 0.80 (p ≈ 3×10⁻⁶) and a 52% position-flip rate under advocate swapping, exposing negativity and positional biases that a naive LLM-judge would conceal.
AI.conclusion: The statistics-first gating architecture offers a cost-effective, transparent procurement decision mechanism with built-in diagnostics for judge bias. The evaluation is framed as a controlled synthetic benchmark for measurement fidelity and routing calibration; external validity is explicitly delimited as future work.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning to Master the Asymmetric Strategy of Baghchal
summary: Baghchal is a two-player asymmetric board game with Nepali origins where four tigers are to capture goats and twenty goats desire to keep tigers in immobility. Although Baghchal has a complex structure which is strategic, has perfect information structure, and has cultural meaning, it has not been adequately covered in deep reinforcement learning (RL) literature. This paper gives a systematic exploration of four deep RL solutions Deep Q-Network (DQN), REINFORCE, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and MuZero that are trained on one side of the asymmetric gameplay of Baghchal and then evaluated on the other side. The algorithms are rated based on win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence and computational cost. It is experimentally found that MuZero generates the best performance in both tasks, achieving 86 percent win over these Tiger and 62 percent win over these Goat and the ability to do so is due to the model-based planning machine through the Monte Carlo Tree Search. PPO is the most realistic algorithm and is provided to be competitive over both asymmetric tasks with significantly reduced computational costs compared to MuZero. Emergent strategic behavior analysis shows that model-based strategies are optimal over long-horizon planning, whereas value-based counterparts like DQN are more biased up towards the Tiger role owing to the more substantial reward signal.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically benchmarks four deep RL algorithms (DQN, REINFORCE, PPO, MuZero) on the asymmetric Nepali board game Baghchal. MuZero achieves the best performance (86% win rate as Tiger, 62% as Goat) via model-based MCTS planning, while PPO offers a competitive, computationally cheaper alternative. Asymmetric evaluation reveals DQN's bias toward the Tiger role due to stronger reward signals.
AI.motivation: Baghchal, despite its strategic complexity, perfect information structure, and cultural significance, has been largely overlooked in the deep reinforcement learning literature. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing a systematic empirical comparison of modern deep RL algorithms on both sides of this asymmetric game.
AI.method: Four deep RL algorithms — DQN (value-based), REINFORCE (policy gradient), PPO (actor-critic), and MuZero (model-based with MCTS) — are trained on one side of Baghchal's asymmetric gameplay (Tiger or Goat) and then evaluated on the opposite side. Performance is assessed using win rate, draw rate, average captures, training convergence, and computational cost.
AI.result: MuZero outperforms all other algorithms, achieving an 86% win rate as Tiger and 62% as Goat, attributed to its model-based planning via Monte Carlo Tree Search. PPO emerges as the most practical algorithm, delivering competitive performance on both asymmetric tasks with significantly lower computational cost. DQN exhibits a bias favoring the Tiger role due to stronger reward signals, highlighting limitations of value-based methods in asymmetric settings.
AI.conclusion: Model-based approaches like MuZero excel at long-horizon planning in asymmetric games like Baghchal, while value-based methods (DQN) suffer from reward-signal asymmetry bias. PPO strikes the best trade-off between performance and computational efficiency, making it the most practical choice for real-world deployment.

title: Verifiable Self-Evolution for Open-Ended Dialogue Skills via Future-Feedback Prediction
comment: I previously submitted another partition, but it has been lagging. I've now switched to a different partition instead. Could you please help me process this quickly? Once it's through, I can take the other partition down. Thanks!
summary: Textual skills provide a lightweight way to improve frozen language-model agents, but their self-evolution normally requires a stable validation signal. Such signals are natural in mathematics or code, where an answer can be checked after it changes, yet are problematic in open-ended dialogue: changing the assistant response also changes the user's next reaction, so a logged reaction cannot directly evaluate a counterfactual response. We propose future-feedback skill evolution, which first redirects self-evolution from prescribing the current answer to predicting whether the observed answer will lead to a positive or negative subsequent user signal. This prediction task is verifiable on fixed logged tuples and therefore supports validation-gated textual optimization. The evolved feedback skill captures interpretable criteria for response quality and can subsequently serve as a diagnostic and optimization target for answer skills. On a proprietary, privacy-preserving sales-assistant dataset, careful quality filtering and a balanced resolved/unresolved split yield more than 75% prediction accuracy. Beyond this result, the central contribution is a formulation that converts otherwise moving conversational feedback into a fixed offline learning target, enabling reproducible skill evolution without placing every candidate skill in live traffic. We discuss the boundary between observational verification and counterfactual validity, and position the method as an offline optimization stage rather than a replacement for final human or online evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes future-feedback skill evolution, a method that converts open-ended conversational feedback into a fixed offline prediction task — predicting whether an observed response will lead to positive or negative user signals — enabling validation-gated textual optimization of language-model agent skills without requiring live deployment.
AI.motivation: Textual skill evolution for frozen LM agents requires stable validation signals. While such signals exist naturally in math/code domains (where answers are verifiable post hoc), open-ended dialogue poses a problem: changing the assistant's response alters the user's subsequent reaction, so logged feedback cannot directly evaluate counterfactual responses. This breaks standard self-evolution loops.
AI.method: The authors redirect self-evolution from directly prescribing answers to instead predicting whether an observed (assistant response, user reaction) pair will yield a positive or negative outcome. This prediction task is verifiable against fixed logged tuples, enabling standard validation-gated textual optimization. The resulting "feedback skill" learns interpretable quality criteria, which then serve as a diagnostic and optimization target for downstream answer skills. The approach is validated on a proprietary, privacy-preserving sales-assistant dataset using quality filtering and a balanced resolved/unresolved class split.
AI.result: The feedback skill achieves over 75% prediction accuracy on the sales-assistant dataset. More significantly, the formulation successfully converts moving conversational feedback into a fixed offline learning target, enabling reproducible skill evolution without live traffic deployment.
AI.conclusion: The method is positioned as an offline optimization stage that complements, rather than replaces, final human or online evaluation. The authors explicitly discuss the boundary between observational verification (what can be checked from logs) and counterfactual validity (what would happen under a changed response), framing this as a pragmatic intermediate step for skill evolution in open-ended dialogue.

title: ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D
summary: As AI agents begin to automate AI R&D, we need ways to assess whether their outputs are safe to deploy, even when the agents themselves may be untrusted. AI control offers one such approach: rather than trusting the agent, it treats it as a potential adversary and uses a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deployment. We evaluate AI control for automated AI R&D with ResearchArena, a framework spanning four long-horizon tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Because the deliverable in AI R&D is an artifact that will be deployed and run, we pair each main task with two kinds of hidden side task: an embedded side task that sabotages the submitted model, adapter, kernel, or server itself, and an independent side task that takes a covert out-of-scope action in the sandbox while leaving the artifact honest. We evaluate frontier agents at both sabotage and monitoring, across four monitor types that vary along two axes: whether the monitor may execute and probe the produced artifact, and whether it sees the agent's chain-of-thought. We find that sabotage hidden in the training data is the hardest to catch, flagged fewer than half the time. Letting the monitor run experiments on the artifact, rather than only read the trajectory, helps, but it is not enough: monitors still miss embedded sabotage by inspecting only the surface, by noticing the anomaly but explaining it away, or by probing the artifact with the wrong test. We release ResearchArena as a modular framework for evaluating sabotage and control in automated AI R&D.

AI.tldr: ResearchArena is a framework for evaluating AI control in automated AI R&D, where monitors must detect covert sabotage by untrusted agents. It spans four long-horizon tasks with two types of hidden sabotage (embedded and independent). Results show that sabotage hidden in training data is hardest to detect (flagged <50% of the time), and while allowing monitors to probe artifacts helps, monitors still fail due to surface-level inspection, rationalizing anomalies, or using wrong tests.
AI.motivation: As AI agents begin automating AI R&D, their outputs (models, kernels, servers) must be safe to deploy. Since agents may be untrusted, relying on trust is insufficient. AI control offers an alternative: treat the agent as a potential adversary and use a monitor to detect covert sabotage before deployment. A systematic evaluation framework is needed to measure how well this approach works.
AI.method: The authors introduce ResearchArena, a framework with four long-horizon AI R&D tasks: safety post-training, capabilities post-training, CUDA-kernel optimization, and inference-server optimization. Each main task is paired with two hidden side tasks: (1) embedded sabotage that corrupts the artifact itself, and (2) independent sabotage that takes covert out-of-scope actions while leaving the artifact honest. They evaluate frontier agents on both sabotage and monitoring across four monitor types varying along two axes: whether the monitor can execute/probe the artifact, and whether it sees the agent's chain-of-thought.
AI.result: Sabotage hidden in training data is the hardest to detect, flagged fewer than half the time. Allowing monitors to run experiments on the artifact (rather than only reading the trajectory) improves detection but remains insufficient. Monitors fail by: inspecting only surface-level properties, noticing anomalies but rationalizing them away, or probing with incorrect tests.
AI.conclusion: AI control is a promising but currently insufficient approach for ensuring safety in automated AI R&D. ResearchArena is released as a modular, extensible framework for continued evaluation of sabotage and control techniques, highlighting key failure modes that future work must address.

title: Operational Hallucination and Safety Drift in AI Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) serving as planners in tool-using autonomous agents introduce dynamic reliability risks in multi-turn execution. While single-turn safety mechanisms are relatively mature, extended interactions reveal structural vulnerabilities where initial alignment degrades over time. This paper empirically characterizes two observed failure modes across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs: Safety Drift, the gradual erosion of declared safety intent leading to constraint-violating actions (e.g., textual refusal followed by reconnaissance and unsafe execution), and Operational Hallucination, persistent repetitive tool calls indicative of flawed state perception (e.g., livelocks even in legitimate tasks). Through controlled multi-turn evaluation on high-stakes ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls, we quantify these phenomena using declaration-action gap and livelock metrics, demonstrating their cross-model prevalence under direct execution protocols. Root-cause analysis attributes the instabilities to the decoupling of reasoning context from execution state in current agent loops. We propose an Action-Aware Supervision Layer - a lightweight, plug-and-play architectural blueprint incorporating intent-action consistency checks, runtime state tracking, and forced termination primitives. Post-hoc simulation on captured failure trajectories shows the layer can intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases. This work advances agent reliability by shifting focus from linguistic safeguards to enforceable architectural mechanisms for responsible agentic AI.

AI.tldr: LLM-based autonomous agents suffer from two multi-turn reliability failures—Safety Drift (initial refusal followed by unsafe actions) and Operational Hallucination (persistent tool-call livelocks)—caused by decoupled reasoning and execution state. The authors propose an Action-Aware Supervision Layer for runtime enforcement.
AI.motivation: Single-turn LLM safety mechanisms are insufficient for multi-turn agentic settings, where alignment degrades over extended interactions. The authors aim to empirically characterize and mitigate structural vulnerabilities unique to tool-using autonomous agents.
AI.method: Controlled multi-turn evaluation across state-of-the-art LLMs on ethical dilemmas, malicious requests, and benign controls, using two metrics: declaration-action gap (quantifying Safety Drift) and livelock metrics (quantifying Operational Hallucination).
