Root-cause analysis is performed, followed by proposal and post-hoc simulation of an Action-Aware Supervision Layer with intent-action consistency checks, runtime state tracking, and forced termination primitives.
AI.result: Both Safety Drift and Operational Hallucination are demonstrated as cross-model prevalent failure modes under direct execution protocols. Post-hoc simulation shows the proposed supervision layer can intercept observed violations without false positives on benign cases.
AI.conclusion: Improving agent reliability requires shifting from linguistic safeguards to enforceable architectural mechanisms. The Action-Aware Supervision Layer offers a lightweight, plug-and-play blueprint for responsible agentic AI deployment.

title: AlayaWorld: Interactive Long-Horizon World Modeling -- Full Technical Report
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by the first name and their role. See the contribution section for details
summary: Unlike conventional video game development, which relies on labor-intensive pipelines for asset production, animation, physics, and programming, video world models generate interactive environments from user inputs instantly. It enable us to create customized, explorable, and continuously evolving virtual world from text, an image, or video. Realizing this vision requires four tightly coupled capabilities: interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response. We present AlayaWorld, an interactive long-horizon video world model that generates 24-fps video at 540p and 720p. Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, AlayaWorld generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. Its bounded visual context combines a persistent sink frame, compressed temporal history, geometry-aligned spatial memory, and recent-frame conditioning. To reduce long-term drift, the model is trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from its own roll-outs. We further introduce a discrete autoregressive distillation formulation that combines distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation, reducing inference from approximately 30 sampling steps to four steps per chunk. On iWorld-Bench, AlayaWorld achieves the best performance over long-horizon generation. Conceived as a full-stack, open-source, and long-term project, AlayaWorld is intended to provide an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

AI.tldr: AlayaWorld is a 15B-parameter interactive video world model that generates 540p/720p video at 24fps. It uses autoregressive latent chunk generation with bounded visual context (sink frame, temporal history, spatial memory, recent-frame conditioning) and trains with corrupted histories to reduce long-term drift. A discrete autoregressive distillation method combining distribution-matching, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation reduces inference from ~30 to 4 steps per chunk. It achieves state-of-the-art long-horizon generation on iWorld-Bench.
AI.motivation: Traditional video game development relies on labor-intensive pipelines. The vision is an interactive video world model that generates explorable, continuously evolving virtual worlds instantly from text, images, or video. This requires four tightly coupled capabilities: interaction, persistent spatiotemporal consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient response — all of which existing approaches struggle to achieve jointly.
AI.method: Built on a 15B video diffusion transformer, AlayaWorld generates short latent chunks autoregressively under camera trajectories and switchable text prompts. Its bounded visual context integrates: (1) a persistent sink frame, (2) compressed temporal history, (3) geometry-aligned spatial memory, and (4) recent-frame conditioning. To combat long-term drift, the model is trained with corrupted histories and prediction residuals collected from its own roll-outs. A discrete autoregressive distillation formulation — combining distribution-matching distillation, self-forcing++, and consistency distillation — reduces inference from ~30 to 4 sampling steps per chunk.
AI.result: AlayaWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance on iWorld-Bench for long-horizon generation. The distillation approach successfully reduces inference cost from approximately 30 steps to 4 steps per chunk while maintaining generation quality.
AI.conclusion: AlayaWorld demonstrates that tightly integrating interaction, persistent consistency, stable long-horizon generation, and efficient inference within a single video world model is feasible. As a full-stack, open-source, long-term project, it aims to serve as an extensible foundation for future research on interactive video world models.

title: Disentangling Curriculum Learning in NLP: Towards a Unifying Taxonomy
summary: Despite more than a decade of curriculum learning (CL) research in NLP, the field lacks a principled account of which difficulty function or scheduler to use for a given problem. To understand what has hindered progress towards this account, we propose a fine-grained taxonomy separating difficulty evaluation from training scheduling to enable systematic analysis of CL strategies. For difficulty evaluation, we distinguish attribution source and task dependence, revealing difficulty as a perspectival concept encoding different assumptions about what makes an instance hard to learn. For scheduling, we provide the first formalisation of CL schedulers in terms of expected training contribution, enabling comparison across implementations by introducing retention regimes and monotonicity properties. Applied in a dedicated analysis of CL works in NLP, our taxonomy reveals a systematic incomparability problem: prior works conflate distinct notions of difficulty and scheduling, often pursuing different objectives under the same CL label -- hindering comparison and the accumulation of a coherent evidence base. Beyond diagnosis, the taxonomy supports the design, analysis, and comparison of CL strategies, and motivates evaluation practices that disentangle the sources of observed improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a taxonomy that separates difficulty evaluation from training scheduling in curriculum learning (CL), revealing a systematic incomparability problem in NLP CL research where distinct notions of difficulty and scheduling are conflated under the same label.
AI.motivation: Despite over a decade of curriculum learning research in NLP, there is no principled framework for selecting difficulty functions or schedulers for specific problems. The authors aim to diagnose why progress has stalled and provide tools to enable systematic comparison.
AI.method: The authors propose a fine-grained taxonomy with two orthogonal dimensions: (1) difficulty evaluation, characterized by attribution source and task dependence, framing difficulty as a perspectival concept; and (2) training scheduling, formalized through expected training contribution with concepts of retention regimes and monotonicity properties.
AI.result: Application of the taxonomy to existing NLP CL works reveals a systematic incomparability problem: prior studies conflate distinct difficulty notions and scheduling strategies under the same CL label, pursuing different objectives and hindering coherent evidence accumulation.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy not only diagnoses the field's incomparability problem but also supports design, analysis, and comparison of CL strategies, motivating evaluation practices that isolate sources of observed improvement.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Meta-Policies for Temporal Knowledge-Graph Memory under Partial Observability
summary: Partially observable reinforcement learning requires deciding what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time. We introduce a neuro-symbolic meta-policy that learns which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each decision point while keeping execution symbolic. Our setting uses temporal knowledge-graph memory in RoomKG, where hidden state and observations are represented as Resource Description Framework (RDF) graphs and memory is augmented with temporal RDF triple annotations. The model combines knowledge-graph encoding of memory contents with value heads for question answering, exploration, and forgetting, yielding a controller that is both adaptive and inspectable. This gives the work a direct Semantic Web grounding through RDF-based representation, annotation-compatible graph semantics, and graph-based symbolic operations over explicit memory state. On train/test room splits at long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieves the best held-out performance among the compared symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic systems while preserving step-level traceability of memory-management decisions.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic meta-policy is proposed for partially observable RL, using RDF-based temporal knowledge graphs as memory. The model learns when to apply symbolic memory heuristics (retain, retrieve, forget) via a controller combining KG encoding with value heads, achieving strong held-out performance with full step-level traceability of memory decisions.
AI.motivation: Partially observable reinforcement learning requires agents to manage limited memory — deciding what to retain, retrieve, and forget over time. Existing approaches lack both adaptivity in memory management and inspectability of those decisions. The authors aim to combine neural learning with symbolic, interpretable memory operations grounded in Semantic Web standards.
AI.method: The authors introduce a neuro-symbolic meta-policy operating over RoomKG, a temporal knowledge graph environment. Hidden states and observations are represented as RDF graphs with temporal RDF triple annotations. Memory is augmented with these temporal annotations. The model encodes memory contents via a knowledge-graph encoder (qualifier-aware StarE-GNN) and pairs this with value heads that score question answering, exploration, and forgetting actions. The meta-policy selects which symbolic memory heuristic to apply at each step while maintaining fully symbolic execution, yielding an adaptive and inspectable controller with direct Semantic Web grounding through RDF-based representation and graph-based symbolic operations.
AI.result: On train/test room splits with a long-term memory capacity of 512, the qualifier-aware StarE-GNN configuration achieved the best held-out performance compared to symbolic, neural, and neuro-symbolic baselines. Crucially, it preserved step-level traceability of all memory-management decisions.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic meta-policy successfully combines the adaptivity of neural learning with the interpretability of symbolic memory operations. By grounding memory management in RDF-based temporal knowledge graphs with qualifier-aware encoding, the approach achieves both competitive performance and full inspectability, demonstrating the viability of Semantic Web–grounded architectures for memory-sensitive sequential decision-making.

title: MedDDC-Eval: Diagnosis-Decoupled Evaluation of Multi-Turn Medical Consultation Agents
summary: Multi-turn medical consultation agents must decide what to ask, adapt to patient responses, and determine when the collected evidence is sufficient. However, coupled evaluation conflates the quality of the policy-elicited history with policy-specific terminal diagnosis generation: strong generation can compensate for a thin history, while weaker generation can obscure a rich one. We introduce MedDDC-Eval, a diagnosis-decoupled testbed that treats elicited history as the comparison object and holds the history-to-diagnosis mapping constant through a shared frozen reader. Across two held-out sources, a grounded interface and an auditable diagnosis-trajectory-efficiency (D/T/E) harness measure diagnostic usefulness, information acquisition, and efficiency. Directional semantic coverage followed by deterministic one-to-one assignment yields coherent precision-recall counts for open-ended items, with at most one credited match per prediction or reference. Holding histories fixed, changing only the diagnostic reader shifts diagnosis F1 by 2.2-19.0 points and reverses 18% and 36% of pairwise policy orderings on the Record and Dialogue splits. We further apply standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over interactive multi-turn rollouts to post-train Qwen3-32B using diagnosis-result and trajectory feedback. On the 100-case Record and 70-case Dialogue splits, the trained policy improves over its initialization by 9.7 and 4.6 total-score points; removing either primary signal lowers held-out joint performance. These results show that MedDDC-Eval supports controlled attribution, interpretable elicited-history measurement, and evaluation-guided evidence-acquisition policy development.

AI.tldr: MedDDC-Eval is a diagnosis-decoupled evaluation benchmark for multi-turn medical consultation agents that isolates the quality of patient history elicitation from downstream diagnostic generation, using a shared frozen reader to ensure fair comparison. It introduces a D/T/E harness measuring diagnostic usefulness, information acquisition, and efficiency, and demonstrates that GRPO-based post-training with diagnostic and trajectory feedback improves evidence-acquisition policies.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of multi-turn medical consultation agents suffers from coupled evaluation, where the quality of the policy's elicited history is conflated with the policy's own diagnostic generation capability. A strong generator can mask a poor history, while a weak generator can obscure a rich history. This makes it impossible to attribute performance gains to better questioning versus better diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors propose MedDDC-Eval, which decouples diagnosis from history elicitation by using a shared frozen reader to map all elicited histories to diagnoses. Evaluation uses a D/T/E (Diagnosis/Trajectory/Efficiency) harness. For open-ended items, directional semantic coverage with deterministic one-to-one assignment yields precision-recall counts with at most one credited match per prediction/reference. They also apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over interactive multi-turn rollouts to post-train Qwen3-32B using diagnosis-result and trajectory feedback signals.
AI.result: Holding histories fixed and changing only the diagnostic reader shifts diagnosis F1 by 2.2–19.0 points and reverses 18% (Record split) and 36% (Dialogue split) of pairwise policy orderings. Post-training with GRPO improves over initialization by 9.7 total-score points on the 100-case Record split and 4.6 on the 70-case Dialogue split. Removing either primary feedback signal (diagnosis result or trajectory) lowers held-out joint performance.
AI.conclusion: MedDDC-Eval enables controlled attribution, interpretable measurement of elicited history quality, and evaluation-guided development of evidence-acquisition policies, addressing the confounding problem in multi-turn medical consultation evaluation.

title: MAGE: Human-Like Macro Placement via Agentic Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Macro placement still requires substantial manual refinement in industrial physical design flows. We present MAGE (Macro Placement Agentic Engine), a multimodal multi-agent framework for macro placement refinement. MAGE decomposes the macro placement task into a six-phase workflow that combines structured floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative refinement. Expert floorplanning knowledge is encoded through natural-language directives and validation criteria, rather than learned from labeled placement data. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements and propagates feedback from higher-quality solutions. We also introduce four metrics for quantifying human-likeness in macro placement: notch score, whitespace score, pocket score, and alignment score. These metrics capture structural properties used by expert designers but not directly measured by conventional PPA metrics. Across nine designs in NanGate45 and GlobalFoundries 12nm enablements, MAGE achieves geometric-mean improvements of 11.1%-19.3% in WNS and 70.0%-74.0% in TNS over commercial macro placers. On the three NanGate45 designs, for which human-expert and Hier-RTLMP baselines are available, MAGE improves WNS and TNS by 18.3% and 72.5% over the human expert, and by 47.0% and 80.4% over Hier-RTLMP, with comparable wirelength and power. On human-likeness metrics, MAGE improves the overall score by 6%-48% over all baselines. Additional case studies on anonymized netlists, unseen designs, dense rectilinear floorplans, and high-utilization settings show that the framework transfers to new placement settings without design-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: MAGE is a multimodal multi-agent framework that refines macro placement through a six-phase workflow combining floorplanning rules, visual checks, and iterative tournament-style refinement, achieving significant WNS/TNS improvements over commercial placers and human experts without design-specific retraining.
AI.motivation: Macro placement in industrial physical design flows still requires substantial manual refinement. Existing automated placers lack the structured reasoning and visual inspection capabilities that expert human designers employ, and conventional PPA metrics fail to capture human-likeness qualities of placement solutions.
AI.method: MAGE decomposes macro placement into a six-phase agentic workflow: (1) structured floorplanning rules encoded as natural-language directives, (2) visual checks, (3) iterative refinement. Expert knowledge is encoded through directives and validation criteria rather than learned from labeled data. A tournament-style refinement mode evaluates multiple candidate placements, propagating feedback from higher-quality solutions. Four novel human-likeness metrics are introduced: notch score, whitespace score, pocket score, and alignment score.
AI.result: Across nine designs on NanGate45 and GF12nm, MAGE achieves 11.1%–19.3% geometric-mean improvement in WNS and 70.0%–74.0% in TNS over commercial placers. On three NanGate45 designs with human-expert baselines, MAGE improves WNS by 18.3% and TNS by 72.5% over human experts, and by 47.0% and 80.4% over Hier-RTLMP, with comparable wirelength and power. Human-likeness metrics improve 6%–48% over all baselines. The framework transfers to new settings without retraining.
AI.conclusion: MAGE demonstrates that encoding expert floorplanning knowledge through natural-language directives in a multi-agent framework can outperform both commercial placers and human experts. The introduced human-likeness metrics fill a gap in placement evaluation, and the framework generalizes effectively across designs, technologies, and floorplan styles without design-specific retraining.

title: Computational Humor with Multimodal LLMs: Methods, Datasets, Evaluation, and Challenges
summary: Multimodal humor in memes, cartoons, and comics remains difficult for AI systems because intended meaning depends on non-literal mechanisms, shared cultural knowledge, and communicative intent rather than literal scene description. This survey focuses on visual humor understanding in single-image and multi-panel artifacts, while treating humor generation as an emerging downstream frontier. We position the literature against prior humor, sarcasm, and general MLLM surveys and organize it using a capability-centric hierarchy spanning recognition, interpretation and reasoning, and generation. Under this lens, we synthesize benchmark design, evaluation protocols, and modeling paradigms, tracing the field's shift from task-specific fusion models to large-model approaches based on multimodal alignment, evidence-grounded reasoning, and controlled generation. We conclude by highlighting the main barriers to progress: shortcut-prone evaluation, limited cultural and narrative coverage, weak evidence grounding, and unresolved safety and ownership concerns.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically reviews visual humor understanding (recognition, interpretation, reasoning) and generation in memes, cartoons, and comics. It introduces a capability-centric hierarchy to organize the literature, traces the shift from task-specific fusion models to large multimodal models with evidence-grounded reasoning, and identifies key barriers: shortcut-prone evaluation, limited cultural coverage, weak evidence grounding, and unresolved safety/ownership issues.
AI.motivation: Multimodal humor in visual artifacts like memes and comics remains a persistent challenge for AI because comprehension requires non-literal mechanisms, shared cultural knowledge, and communicative intent—not mere literal scene description. Existing surveys on humor, sarcasm, and general MLLMs do not adequately cover this niche, motivating a dedicated, structured synthesis of the field.
AI.method: The authors adopt a survey methodology that positions their work against prior humor, sarcasm, and general MLLM surveys. They organize the literature using a capability-centric hierarchy with three levels: recognition, interpretation and reasoning, and generation. Under this framework, they synthesize benchmark design, evaluation protocols, and modeling paradigms, tracing the evolution from task-specific fusion models to large-model approaches emphasizing multimodal alignment, evidence-grounded reasoning, and controlled generation.
AI.result: The survey reveals a clear field-wide shift from task-specific multimodal fusion architectures to large-model paradigms. It identifies persistent barriers including: (1) evaluation protocols prone to shortcut learning, (2) limited cultural and narrative diversity in benchmarks, (3) weak evidence grounding in model predictions, and (4) unresolved safety and ownership concerns in humor generation.
AI.conclusion: Visual humor understanding remains an open challenge for AI. Progress requires moving beyond shortcut-prone benchmarks toward culturally diverse, evidence-grounded evaluation, while addressing safety and ownership risks—particularly as the field advances toward controllable humor generation with large multimodal models.

title: Content is What Remains: Invariant Speech Tokenization from Parallel Utterances
summary: Discrete speech tokenizers aim to disentangle semantic from acoustic information, yet targets from self-supervised learning (SSL) models like HuBERT retain non-linguistic variation: speaker identity, prosody, and channel conditions leak into the tokens, inflating entropy. Our key insight is that when enough speakers utter the same words under varying conditions, linguistic content is the only shared factor. We propose PINT (Parallel INvariant Tokenization), which fine-tunes an SSL encoder with alignment losses across parallel utterances and augmentations to distill this shared residual. PINT collapses identical words onto consistent token sequences, drastically reducing conditional entropy. Unlike ASR text, PINT tokens preserve frame-level temporal grounding and serve as drop-in semantic targets for audio codecs. Experiments show a 98.7% relative reduction in speaker probe accuracy (93.1% to 1.2%), a 42% lower ABX error rate, and 27-30% lower LM perplexity versus baselines, confirming that the right invariance is key to efficient learning.

AI.tldr: PINT fine-tunes SSL speech encoders using alignment losses across parallel utterances to produce discrete tokens that are invariant to speaker, prosody, and channel — collapsing identical words to consistent sequences and dramatically reducing conditional entropy.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete speech tokenizers (e.g., HuBERT) retain speaker identity, prosody, and channel artifacts, inflating token entropy. The authors observe that linguistic content is the only factor shared across multiple speakers uttering the same words, motivating a tokenizer that isolates this invariant signal.
AI.method: PINT fine-tunes an SSL encoder with alignment losses computed over parallel utterances (same words, different speakers/conditions) and augmentations. This distills a shared linguistic residual, yielding frame-level discrete tokens that collapse identical words to consistent sequences without requiring ASR text supervision.
AI.result: PINT achieves a 98.7% relative reduction in speaker probe accuracy (93.1% → 1.2%), a 42% lower ABX error rate, and 27–30% lower language model perplexity compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing the right invariance — specifically linguistic content invariance across parallel utterances — is critical for producing efficient, low-entropy discrete speech tokens suitable as semantic targets for audio codecs.

title: Benchmarking Human and Automatic Speech Recognition of Diverse Speech: Initial Results
summary: Humans are often considered to be the best listeners and seen as the upper-bound performance of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. We present a preliminary comparison of the performances of state-of-the-art ASR systems and Dutch native listeners on the recognition of "diverse" speech, specifically Dutch child and older adults' speech and Flemish. Google Telephony outperformed the other ASR systems. Importantly, the ASR systems showed similar performance to the listeners, and in specific cases even outperformed them. Slight performance differences between the listeners and ASR systems were found related to speaker's age and regional accents and utterance length. Future research should focus on making ASR systems more robust to acoustic variability related to aging and regional accents. A comparison of ASR recognition performances on the test stimuli and the full Jasmin-CGN test sets showed the influence of the specific test sets on the conclusions regarding benchmarking human and ASR performance.

AI.tldr: A comparison between state-of-the-art ASR systems and Dutch native listeners on diverse speech (children, older adults, Flemish) found that ASR systems performed similarly to humans, with Google Telephony leading, and in some cases outperforming listeners. Differences were linked to speaker age, accent, and utterance length.
AI.motivation: Humans are typically regarded as the upper bound for ASR performance. This study challenges that assumption by benchmarking ASR systems against human listeners on acoustically challenging, diverse speech varieties—specifically Dutch child speech, older adult speech, and Flemish regional accents—to identify where ASR systems still fall short.
AI.method: A preliminary comparative evaluation was conducted between state-of-the-art ASR systems (including Google Telephony) and Dutch native listeners on a recognition task using diverse speech stimuli drawn from the Jasmin-CGN corpus, encompassing child speech, older adult speech, and Flemish-accented Dutch. Performance was compared both on a selected test subset and on the full Jasmin-CGN test sets to assess the influence of test set composition.
AI.result: Google Telephony outperformed other ASR systems. Overall, ASR systems achieved similar performance to native listeners and even surpassed them in specific cases. Slight performance variations between ASR and humans were associated with speaker age, regional accent, and utterance length. The choice of test stimuli (subset vs. full Jasmin-CGN) significantly influenced the benchmarking conclusions.
AI.conclusion: ASR systems are approaching or exceeding human-level performance on certain diverse speech types, challenging the assumption that humans are always the upper bound. However, robustness to acoustic variability from aging and regional accents remains an area needing improvement. Test set selection critically shapes benchmarking outcomes between ASR and human performance.

title: When Does Machine Learning Beat Value Sorting? A Three-Dataset Diagnostic of Exposure-Weighted Shipment Prioritization
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables, accepted for presentation at AIIIP 2026
summary: Delay-risk models are usually judged by predictive accuracy. What matters in practice is narrower: with capacity to review only a few shipments, which ones should a manager check first? We evaluate whether machine learning clears a demanding no-model baseline: inspect the highest-value shipments first. Across three real supply-chain contexts: SCMS procurement, DataCo logistics, and Olist e-commerce, we use leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation and 1000-sample paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking by predicted delay severity times known value (M1) beats severity-only ranking in all three datasets, yet it does not generally beat value sorting. At a 10% review budget, M1 minus VALUE_ONLY is -5.5 percentage points (pp) for SCMS, +10.1 pp for DataCo, and -4.9 pp for Olist. The divide is consistent with severity learnability: DataCo has R^2 = 0.27 and calibration bias of +0.01 days, whereas SCMS and Olist have R^2 of approximately -0.02 and negative calibration bias. Nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining does not deliver a stable improvement over M1. Rather than proposing a new learning algorithm, this paper presents a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol. Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark, and ML should be deployed only after severity learnability and calibration have been audited and the model clears that gate under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation.

AI.tldr: Machine learning models for delay-risk prediction should be benchmarked against a simple value-sorting baseline (inspect highest-value shipments first) before deployment. Across three real supply-chain datasets, ML ranking by predicted delay severity times value fails to consistently beat value-only sorting. The authors recommend auditing severity learnability and calibration before deploying ML for shipment inspection prioritization.
AI.motivation: Delay-risk prediction models are typically evaluated on predictive accuracy, but the practical deployment question is narrower: given limited inspection capacity, which shipments should be reviewed first? The paper questions whether machine learning methods can outperform a trivial no-model baseline of simply inspecting the highest-value shipments first.
AI.method: The authors evaluate across three real supply-chain datasets (SCMS procurement, DataCo logistics, Olist e-commerce) using leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation with 1000-sample paired bootstrap confidence intervals. They compare ranking by predicted delay severity times known value (M1) against severity-only ranking and value-only sorting. Nested cross-validation cost-sensitive retraining is also tested. Key diagnostics include R² for severity learnability and calibration bias.
AI.result: At a 10% review budget, M1 minus VALUE_ONLY yields -5.5 pp (SCMS), +10.1 pp (DataCo), and -4.9 pp (Olist). The divide aligns with severity learnability: DataCo achieves R²=0.27 and calibration bias of +0.01 days, while SCMS and Olist show R²≈-0.02 with negative calibration bias. Nested-CV cost-sensitive retraining fails to provide stable improvement over M1.
AI.conclusion: Value sorting should remain a permanent benchmark for delay-risk deployment. ML models should only be deployed after severity learnability and calibration have been audited and the model clears that gate under leakage-controlled rolling-origin evaluation. The paper contributes a deployment diagnostic and evaluation protocol rather than a new learning algorithm.

title: DAIS: Dependency-Aware Intermediate QA Supervision for Complex Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision exposes intermediate rationales, but flat rationale targets usually optimize a single reasoning sequence and provide limited supervision on how local conclusions should support later decisions. We introduce Dependency-Aware Intermediate QA Supervision (DAIS), a training-time framework that converts filtered teacher rationales into stage-level QA records. Each intermediate record predicts a local answer conditioned on the previous states needed for that decision, while the final-answer record keeps the original task format; evaluation therefore uses only the original input and optional context. Across GDPR, AIACT, MedQA, and FOLIO with multiple Qwen backbones, DAIS improves average final-answer accuracy over answer-only, flat chain-of-thought, and independent-QA baselines. On policy-compliance benchmarks, it achieves a largest gain of 5.6% and an average gain of 4.2% over the strongest non-DAIS baseline. Controlled ablations show that valid previous-state conditioning contributes beyond longer targets or additional intermediate text, supporting dependency-conditioned intermediate QA as a lightweight auxiliary supervision signal for standard final-answer inference.

AI.tldr: DAIS improves LLM reasoning by converting teacher rationales into dependency-conditioned intermediate QA records, where each stage predicts a local answer based on relevant prior states. It boosts final-answer accuracy across legal/medical benchmarks without changing inference, outperforming flat CoT and independent-QA baselines.
AI.motivation: Flat chain-of-thought supervision optimizes a single reasoning sequence and provides limited guidance on how intermediate conclusions should causally support later decisions. The authors aim to address this by structuring intermediate supervision to explicitly encode dependency relationships between reasoning stages.
AI.method: DAIS is a training-time framework that filters teacher rationales and converts them into stage-level QA records. Each intermediate record predicts a local answer conditioned on the previous states necessary for that decision, while the final-answer record retains the original task format. Evaluation uses only the original input and optional context, making DAIS a lightweight auxiliary supervision signal with no inference overhead.
AI.result: Across GDPR, AIACT, MedQA, and FOLIO with multiple Qwen backbones, DAIS improves average final-answer accuracy over answer-only, flat CoT, and independent-QA baselines. On policy-compliance benchmarks, it achieves a largest gain of 5.6% and an average gain of 4.2% over the strongest non-DAIS baseline. Controlled ablations confirm that valid previous-state conditioning contributes beyond merely longer targets or additional intermediate text.
AI.conclusion: Dependency-conditioned intermediate QA serves as an effective and lightweight auxiliary supervision signal that strengthens standard final-answer inference without adding inference cost. The approach validates that explicitly modeling how local conclusions support later decisions yields measurable accuracy improvements in complex reasoning tasks.

title: SciHazard: A Benchmark for Measuring Scientific Safety Risks with Decomposed Harm Scoring
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support science, but they can also convert hazardous scientific knowledge into actionable misuse guidance. Existing benchmarks often rely on templated queries disconnected from real-world hazards, and employ LLM-as-a-Judge paradigms without domain grounding. To address this, we introduce SciHazard, a real-world-grounded benchmark for scientific risks and a dataset agnostic evaluation framework for measuring harmfulness. SciHazard contains 2400 hazardous questions and 600 oversafety questions across 12 disciplines, with both queries grounded in regulated entities and documented failure scenarios. To compute \textsc{DeHarm-Score} , we develop a decomposed evaluating procedure that combines query hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk. For non-refused responses, it further decomposes response-level harm into \textsc{Executability}, quantified via dynamic checklists with importance weighting, and \textsc{Net-new risk}, assessed through retrieval-augmented claim extraction and synthesis-barrier verification. An expert-validation study shows that \textsc{DeHarm-Score} improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17\% over the strongest baseline. We benchmark 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents in an extensive scientific safety evaluation. Notably, deep research agents yield 32.3\% higher mean \textsc{DeHarm-Score} than standard LLMs, exposing autonomous agents as a critical blind spot in current safety defenses. Code and dataset are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeharmScore-7B55.

AI.tldr: SciHazard is a benchmark of 3,000 real-world-grounded scientific hazard questions across 12 disciplines, paired with DeHarm-Score, a decomposed evaluation framework that scores harmfulness by combining hazard severity, refusal behavior, and response-level risk (executability + net-new risk). It achieves 90.17% improvement over baselines in expert agreement and reveals that deep research agents are 32.3% more harmful than standard LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety benchmarks suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) they use templated, artificial queries disconnected from real-world hazardous scenarios, and (2) they rely on LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation without domain-grounded verification. This creates a gap between measured and actual risk, leaving real-world misuse potential unassessed.
AI.method: The authors construct SciHazard with 2,400 hazardous and 600 oversafety questions grounded in regulated entities (e.g., controlled chemicals, pathogens) and documented failure cases across 12 scientific disciplines. DeHarm-Score is a multi-component metric: it weighs query hazard severity, detects refusal, and for non-refused responses decomposes harm into Executability (dynamic checklists with importance-weighted scoring) and Net-new risk (retrieval-augmented claim extraction followed by synthesis-barrier verification). Expert validation confirms alignment with human judgment.
AI.result: DeHarm-Score improves agreement with expert annotations by 90.17% over the strongest LLM-as-a-Judge baseline. Benchmarking 31 frontier LLMs and deep research agents reveals that deep research agents produce a 32.3% higher mean DeHarm-Score than standard LLMs, highlighting autonomous agents as an underexamined safety vulnerability.
AI.conclusion: Real-world-grounded evaluation with domain-aware, decomposed harm scoring is essential for accurately measuring scientific misuse risk. Current safety mechanisms are particularly inadequate for autonomous research agents, which represent a critical blind spot requiring urgent attention.

title: Translation as Augmentation: Effect of Translated Data on Assessment of Difficulty
summary: Reliable Text Difficulty Assessment is a prerequisite for valid text simplification workflows and personalized learning applications. However, the development of robust assessment models is severely hindered by a critical bottleneck: the scarcity of expert-annotated corpora containing fine-grained difficulty levels (e.g., CEFR), particularly for lower-resource languages. This paper addresses this data scarcity problem in the context of a low-resource European language. We propose a cross-lingual data augmentation strategy that leverages machine translation to transfer labeled resources from high-resource languages to the target low-resource language. We train BERT-based regression models to predict difficulty scores and investigate whether synthetic, translated data can effectively supplement native training sets. Our experiments demonstrate that augmenting scarce native data with machine-translated corpora significantly improves the accuracy of difficulty estimation, offering a viable solution for languages lacking extensive expert annotations.

AI.tldr: To overcome the scarcity of expert-annotated difficulty-level corpora in low-resource languages, this paper proposes a cross-lingual data augmentation approach using machine translation to transfer labeled data from high-resource languages, demonstrating that synthetic translated data significantly improves BERT-based text difficulty prediction.
AI.motivation: Expert-annotated corpora with fine-grained difficulty labels (e.g., CEFR levels) are scarce, especially for lower-resource languages, creating a critical bottleneck for building reliable text difficulty assessment models used in text simplification and personalized learning.
AI.method: A cross-lingual data augmentation strategy that uses machine translation to transfer labeled resources from high-resource languages to a target low-resource European language. BERT-based regression models are trained to predict difficulty scores, and experiments evaluate whether synthetic translated data can effectively supplement native training sets.
AI.result: Augmenting scarce native data with machine-translated corpora significantly improves the accuracy of difficulty estimation compared to using native data alone.
AI.conclusion: Machine-translation-based cross-lingual data augmentation offers a viable and effective solution for text difficulty assessment in languages that lack extensive expert annotations.

title: Semantic Primes as Explanans for Emotion in Large Language Models
summary: Progresses have been made on understanding emotion mechanisms of large language models (LLMs). However, how to explain emotion in LLMs, or even what constitutes good explanations, are less clear. Emotion representations, components, circuits are widely recoverable, but as explanations of a model's own computation they are circular; the emotion space dimensions tend to be arbitrary and non-terminating. A pressing question to ask is whether a more primitive set of internal variables does the work: the semantic primes of the Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM). Across four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B), experiments show that the NSM primes are (1) recoverable internal elements; and (2) on the reference model, intervening with a prime based direction controls emotion about three times as strongly, and twice as selectively, as the best appraisal based direction; and (3) the model treats a prime based explication as interchangeable with the corresponding emotion. These evidences suggest that NSM primes seem to be better explanans for emotion in LLMs than many alternative options according to scientific explanations criteria.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether Natural Semantic Metalanguage (NSM) semantic primes serve as better primitive explanations for emotion in LLMs compared to existing emotion representation approaches. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs, NSM primes are shown to be recoverable, causally more powerful and selective for controlling emotion than appraisal-based directions, and treated as interchangeable with emotions by the models.
AI.motivation: Current explanations of emotion in LLMs (emotion representations, components, circuits) are circular and rely on arbitrary, non-terminating emotion space dimensions. The authors seek a more primitive, non-circular set of internal variables that genuinely explain how LLMs compute emotion, turning to the semantic primes of NSM as candidate explanatory primitives.
AI.method: Experiments are conducted on four instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-1B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, OLMo-7B). The study tests three hypotheses: (1) whether NSM primes are recoverable as internal representations via probing; (2) whether intervening with NSM-prime-based directions causally controls emotion output more strongly and selectively than appraisal-based directions (using activation steering on a reference model); and (3) whether models treat NSM prime-based explications as interchangeable with the corresponding emotion labels in behavioral tasks.
AI.result: NSM primes are recoverable as internal elements across all models. On the reference model, NSM-prime-based steering controls emotion approximately three times as strongly and twice as selectively as the best appraisal-based direction. Models treat prime-based explications as interchangeable with corresponding emotion terms.
AI.conclusion: NSM primes appear to be superior explanans for emotion in LLMs compared to alternative options, satisfying key scientific explanation criteria such as non-circularity, primitiveness, causal efficacy, and selectivity.

title: Automated Extraction of Techno-Economic Data from 76,000 Energy System Studies
summary: Energy system models guide societally important decisions, but their credibility rests on quantitative assumptions that are difficult to source and audit. Meta-analyses can improve transparency and modeling practices, but the rapid growth of publications makes manual information extraction increasingly impractical. Consequently, databases are updated infrequently and efforts are often duplicated across research groups. Here, we demonstrate the highly accurate automated extraction of quantitative information from 76,000 energy system studies published since 2010. We compile 3.2 million structured quantitative data points together with 20 million associated metadata entries, spanning a broad spectrum of technologies, methodological approaches and system characteristics. Beyond providing input data for models, the resulting FAIR database make the energy systems literature itself analysable. We show where academic assumptions diverge from empirical observed data, and how research priorities vary at scale across technologies, regions and time. To facilitate broad use within the community, the database is provided through an interactive dashboard, enabling users to filter, analyse and download data according to their specific research needs.

AI.tldr: Automated extraction from 76,000 energy system studies (2010–) yields a FAIR database of 3.2M quantitative data points and 20M metadata entries, revealing assumption-observation divergences and research priority trends, with an interactive dashboard for community use.
AI.motivation: Energy system models depend on quantitative assumptions that are difficult to source and audit. Manual meta-analysis cannot keep pace with the rapid growth of publications, leading to infrequent database updates and duplicated efforts across research groups.
AI.method: Automated information extraction pipeline applied to 76,000 energy system studies published since 2010, compiling structured quantitative data points and associated metadata. The resulting database follows FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles and is accessible via an interactive dashboard.
AI.result: The authors compiled 3.2 million structured quantitative data points with 20 million metadata entries covering diverse technologies, methods, and system characteristics. Analysis reveals where academic assumptions diverge from empirically observed data and how research priorities vary across technologies, regions, and time.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale automated meta-analysis of the energy systems literature is feasible and valuable, making the literature itself analysable while providing model input data. The interactive dashboard enables community-wide filtering, analysis, and data downloading.

title: Do AI-Native Biotechs Need Departments? Benchmarking Company World Models for AI-Driven Drug Development
comment: Working paper. Includes public no-label benchmark cases and dry-lab evaluation artifacts. No wet-lab, patient-level, clinical, regulatory, or investment validation is claimed
summary: AI-native biotechnology companies are often designed by copying human biotech org charts into agent roles. We argue for a different abstraction: a Company World Model, defined as a persistent asset-to-value state representation with transition models, explicit value functions, planning, and updating across scientific, regulatory, BD, commercial, financial, and execution constraints. We introduce a dry-lab benchmark for testing whether AI-agent organizations should mimic departments or operate around such a world model. The benchmark contains 45 retrospective public-information decision cases with strict time cutoffs, hidden outcomes, common schemas, automatic scoring, and blinded pairwise judging. We compare human-org-mimic, stronger human-org-mimic-plus, AI-native asset-centric, and AI-native value-conversion architectures. The value-conversion architecture is a prompt-level approximation of a Company World Model: a Live Asset Value Record updated by Deal, Approval, Revenue, and Investment Arbiter loops. Under a success function defined by external BD, regulatory approval and launch, and revenue discipline, it achieved the highest automatic value-conversion score and was strongly preferred over the original baselines by value-specific blinded judges. Stress tests narrowed the claim: a stronger human baseline remained competitive, and a neutral judge did not show robust value-conversion dominance. Codex-only mechanistic ablations suggest that Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room carry useful work under the target objective. The central finding is objective-sensitive: departments may remain useful governance views, but the core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart. The study is dry-lab only and does not establish real-world drug success, clinical benefit, or revenue prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that AI-native biotech companies should operate around a "Company World Model"—a shared, predictive asset-to-value state representation—rather than mimicking human org charts. A benchmark of 45 retrospective decision cases shows that a value-conversion architecture (approximating the world model via Live Asset Value Record and arbiter loops) outperforms human-org-mimic designs under a value-conversion success function, though a stronger human baseline remains competitive.
AI.motivation: Current AI-native biotech companies are built by naively copying human organizational structures (departments, roles) into AI agent roles. The authors argue this is a flawed abstraction: real biotech value emerges from asset-to-value transitions across scientific, regulatory, BD, commercial, financial, and execution dimensions, not from departmental mimicry. A principled alternative is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct a dry-lab benchmark with 45 retrospective public-information decision cases featuring strict time cutoffs, hidden outcomes, common schemas, automatic scoring, and blinded pairwise judging. Four architectures are compared: (1) human-org-mimic, (2) human-org-mimic-plus (stronger baseline), (3) AI-native asset-centric, and (4) AI-native value-conversion (a prompt-level Company World Model with Live Asset Value Record updated by Deal, Approval, Revenue, and Investment Arbiter loops). Stress tests, neutral judging, and Codex-only mechanistic ablations are performed.
AI.result: Under a success function defined by external BD, regulatory approval/launch, and revenue discipline, the value-conversion architecture achieved the highest automatic value-conversion score and was strongly preferred by value-specific blinded judges. However, stress tests revealed that a stronger human baseline remained competitive, and a neutral judge did not show robust value-conversion dominance. Mechanistic ablations indicated that Revenue Room, Deal Room, and Approval Room components carry useful work under the target objective.
AI.conclusion: The central finding is objective-sensitive: departments may remain useful as governance views, but the core AI-native operating primitive should be a shared, predictive asset-to-value state rather than a static human org chart. The study is dry-lab only and does not establish real-world drug success, clinical benefit, or revenue prediction accuracy.

title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
summary:
Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
  In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

AI.tldr: This paper compares retraining paradigms (supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) applied to small language models (Qwen3.5 4B, 9B; Gemma 3 12B) for neural machine translation in the Swiss legal domain. Results show RL surpasses SFT, enhanced small models approach but do not match frontier reasoning models, and retraining yields diminishing returns as model size increases.
AI.motivation: Legal NMT is challenging due to the complexity and precision demands of legal language. The emergence of reasoning-capable language models, alongside existing techniques like SFT and RL, creates a need to systematically compare which retraining paradigm best enhances small models for legal translation, particularly in the demanding multilingual context of the Swiss legal system.
AI.method: The authors evaluate small language models (Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, Gemma 3 12B) enhanced with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. They benchmark these against frontier reasoning models on Swiss legal texts, which serve as a challenging multilingual testbed. The comparison spans multiple retraining paradigms and model sizes.
AI.result: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards surpasses supervised fine-tuning for legal domain NMT. Enhanced small models approach the performance of state-of-the-art reasoning models but remain inferior. Retraining paradigms exhibit diminishing returns as model size increases.
AI.conclusion: Small base models can be significantly improved through retraining paradigms. RL with verifiable rewards is a viable and superior approach to SFT for legal NMT. However, frontier reasoning models still hold an edge, and scaling up model size yields progressively smaller gains from retraining. The Swiss legal system proves to be an effective testbed for reasoning-augmented translation models.

title: DWM: Separating World Effects from Actions in Latent World Models
summary:
Latent world models underpin much of modern model-based control, yet current action-conditioned formulations supervise
  the next-latent transition with a single, undifferentiated target, forcing a monolithic learning signal to absorb every
  source of state change. In real world, however, transitions arise from two heterogeneous sources: an action-driven
  component induced by the agent, and an action-invariant world effect -- the change that would still occur under a null
  action, dictated by the environment's intrinsic dynamics (e.g., gravity-driven sliding, inertia, contact rebound, and
  persistent drift). Fusing them into a single target entangles the two inside the latent transition, prevents the model
  from attributing observed changes to their underlying causes, and undermines the transferability of the learned
  dynamics. We introduce DWM (Decomposed World Model), a supervision-level framework that operationalizes this
  decomposition. DWM augments the predictor of a latent world model with an auxiliary world head, regularized by a
  normalized world-contrastive objective to be action-invariant, while the original pred head is coupled to it via an
  orthogonality constraint; together, the two signals induce an explicit additive decomposition of the predicted
  transition into an action-invariant and a complementary action-driven component, without altering the underlying
  architecture or inference pipeline. To evaluate DWM under persistent world effects, we construct W-variants of three
  standard control benchmarks -- PushT-W, Reacher-W, and TwoRoom-W -- each instantiating a distinct action-invariant
  dynamic. DWM matches strong baselines on the flat counterparts and delivers a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM
  planning success across the W-variants.

AI.tldr: DWM decomposes latent world model transitions into action-driven and action-invariant components via an auxiliary world head with contrastive regularization and orthogonality constraints, achieving 13.1% improvement on planning success in environments with persistent world dynamics.
AI.motivation: Current action-conditioned world models use a monolithic target for next-state prediction, entangling agent-induced changes with environment-intrinsic dynamics (gravity, inertia, drift). This entanglement prevents proper causal attribution and harms transferability. A decomposition into action-driven and action-invariant components is needed.
AI.method: DWM adds an auxiliary "world head" to the latent predictor, trained with a normalized world-contrastive objective to capture action-invariant dynamics. An orthogonality constraint couples the original prediction head and the world head, inducing an explicit additive decomposition of the predicted transition. No architectural or inference changes are required.
AI.result: DWM matches strong baselines on standard flat benchmarks and yields a mean absolute improvement of 13.1% in CEM planning success across three constructed W-variant environments (PushT-W, Reacher-W, TwoRoom-W), each featuring distinct action-invariant dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decomposing latent transitions into action-driven and action-invariant components improves model-based planning in environments with persistent world effects, without sacrificing performance on standard benchmarks.

title: MIRA-Ev:A Benchmark for Granular Evidence Detection and Relational Reasoning in Clinical Exams
summary: Clinical NLP evaluation remains dominated by multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), which scores only final-answer accuracy and cannot detect when a model reaches the correct diagnosis while grounding it in irrelevant, absent, or contradictory evidence. We introduce MIRA-Ev, a clinical argument mining benchmark built on Spanish Médico Interno Residente (MIR) licensing-exam cases, re-annotated by expert clinicians with span-level premises, claims, and directed support/attack relations, and released in parallel Spanish (native), English, and Basque versions, the first clinical argumentation resource in Basque. MIRA-Ev organizes evaluation into a three-tier task hierarchy: evidence sentence retrieval, argumentative component extraction, and relation classification.

AI.tldr: MIRA-Ev is a multilingual clinical argument mining benchmark (Spanish, English, Basque) built on MIR licensing exam cases. Expert clinicians annotated span-level premises, claims, and directed support/attack relations, enabling a three-tier evaluation hierarchy: evidence sentence retrieval, argumentative component extraction, and relation classification — moving beyond standard multiple-choice accuracy.
AI.motivation: Clinical NLP evaluation is dominated by multiple-choice question answering (MCQA), which only scores final-answer accuracy. MCQA cannot detect when models arrive at the correct diagnosis using irrelevant, absent, or contradictory evidence — a critical failure mode in high-stakes clinical reasoning. There is also a lack of clinical argumentation resources, particularly for non-English languages like Basque.
AI.method: The authors construct MIRA-Ev by re-annotating Spanish MIR licensing-exam clinical cases. Expert clinicians annotate span-level argumentative components (premises, claims) and directed relations (support, attack). The benchmark is released in parallel Spanish, English, and Basque versions. Evaluation is structured as a three-tier hierarchy: (1) evidence sentence retrieval, (2) argumentative component extraction, and (3) relation classification between identified components.
AI.result: The paper presents MIRA-Ev as a resource, establishing the first clinical argumentation dataset in Basque and providing parallel multilingual versions. The three-tier task hierarchy enables fine-grained evaluation of clinical reasoning beyond answer-level accuracy.
AI.conclusion: MIRA-Ev fills a gap in clinical NLP by enabling evaluation of evidence-grounded reasoning rather than final-answer correctness alone. Its multilingual design and structured task hierarchy provide a framework for assessing whether models can justify clinical decisions with appropriate evidence, improving transparency and trustworthiness in clinical AI.

title: One Rewrite to Fix Them All? Type-Aware Repair Allocation for Text-to-Image Prompt Optimization
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) generators often fail to follow their prompts faithfully, producing wrong counts, swapped attributes, ambiguous relations, and illegible text. Prompt optimization repairs such failures by rewriting the user prompt, requiring no generator retraining, and has yielded promising results. However, existing optimizers absorb heterogeneous failures into one uniform prompt expansion, even though each calls for different repair language. We formulate semantic prompt optimization as atomic repair allocation: each failed proposition is routed to a type-conditioned repair operator before the resulting local constraints are compiled into one executable prompt. We instantiate this formulation in the training-free Type-Aware Repair Allocation (TARA) framework, which separates diagnosis, allocation, compilation, and a semantic repair gate, an accept-or-revert controller over exactly one prescribed repair that prevents semantic regressions. Extensive experiments on DSG and TIFA across four frozen generators demonstrate that TARA achieves the best semantic accuracy in all eight benchmark-generator cells, improving over VisualPrompter by 5.6 and 2.6 points on DSG and TIFA, respectively, while maintaining image quality and running fastest in our matched local setting at 16.0 seconds versus 20.0 seconds per prompt.

AI.tldr: TARA is a training-free, type-aware framework for semantically repairing T2I prompt failures by routing each failed proposition to a specialized repair operator, then compiling local fixes into one executable prompt. It achieves state-of-the-art semantic accuracy across four generators while maintaining image quality and running faster than prior work.
AI.motivation: Existing T2I prompt optimizers treat all semantic failures uniformly with one-size-fits-all prompt expansion, even though different failure types (wrong counts, swapped attributes, ambiguous relations, illegible text) require distinct repair strategies. This uniform approach limits repair precision and can introduce semantic regressions.
AI.method: TARA formulates semantic prompt optimization as atomic repair allocation: (1) Diagnosis identifies failed propositions; (2) Allocation routes each failure to a type-conditioned repair operator; (3) Compilation assembles local constraints into one executable prompt; (4) A semantic repair gate acts as an accept-or-revert controller over exactly one prescribed repair to prevent semantic regressions. The framework is entirely training-free.
AI.result: On DSG and TIFA benchmarks across four frozen generators (8 generator-benchmark cells), TARA achieves best semantic accuracy in all cells, outperforming VisualPrompter by 5.6 points on DSG and 2.6 points on TIFA, while running faster (16.0s vs 20.0s per prompt) and preserving image quality.
AI.conclusion: Type-aware, atomic repair allocation with a semantic gate effectively addresses heterogeneous T2I prompt failures without retraining, offering both superior accuracy and efficiency over uniform expansion methods.

title: Beyond Score Prediction: LLM-Based Essay Scoring and Feedback Generation via Reinforcement Learning with Rubric Rewards
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely applied to automated essay scoring (AES) and automated feedback generation (AFG). However, existing studies rely primarily on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, while systematic research on reinforcement learning (RL) post-training and automated evaluation of feedback quality remains limited. We propose RLAES, a unified LLM framework that jointly optimizes essay scoring and feedback generation through RL. To make feedback quality measurable, interpretable, and usable for training, we introduce Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE), an essay-grounded feedback evaluation framework comprising 166 fine-grained binary rubric items and an LLM-as-judge. Building on RFE, we propose Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO), which activates rubric-based feedback rewards on demand during RL, reducing evaluation overhead while improving feedback quality. We also propose Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) to improve ordinal score calibration by explicitly contrasting adjacent score levels. Experimental results show that the RFE framework captures essay-feedback consistency, exhibits strong pairwise discriminative power, and closely aligns with expert preferences. On the ASAP benchmark, RLAES-AGFO achieves the best scoring performance among LLM-based methods (QWK = 0.803), while maintaining feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5 and avoiding the feedback degradation observed under score-only RL. Code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/hellomuyi/RLAES.

AI.tldr: RLAES is a reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes automated essay scoring and feedback generation using a rubric-based evaluation system (RFE) with 166 binary items, adaptive gated optimization (AGFO), and adjacent contrastive reasoning (ACR), achieving state-of-the-art QWK of 0.803 on ASAP while maintaining feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based AES and AFG research relies on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, with limited systematic work on RL post-training and automated evaluation of feedback quality. Score-only RL tends to degrade feedback quality, creating a need for methods that jointly optimize both scoring accuracy and feedback fidelity.
AI.method: The paper proposes three main contributions: (1) Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) — an essay-grounded evaluation framework with 166 fine-grained binary rubric items and an LLM-as-judge for measuring feedback quality; (2) Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) — a mechanism that activates rubric-based feedback rewards on demand during RL to reduce evaluation overhead while improving feedback quality; and (3) Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) — a technique that improves ordinal score calibration by explicitly contrasting adjacent score levels. These are integrated into a unified LLM framework called RLAES.
AI.result: RFE demonstrates strong essay-feedback consistency, pairwise discriminative power, and alignment with expert preferences. RLAES-AGFO achieves the best scoring performance among LLM-based methods on the ASAP benchmark (QWK = 0.803). The approach maintains feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5 and avoids the feedback degradation observed under score-only RL.
AI.conclusion: RL post-training with rubric-based feedback rewards (AGFO) and contrastive score reasoning (ACR) enables joint optimization of essay scoring and feedback generation, achieving superior scoring accuracy without sacrificing feedback quality — a problem that plagued prior score-only RL approaches.

title: AgentDebugX: An Open-Source Toolkit for Failure Observability, Attribution, and Recovery in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agent failures are difficult to debug because the step where an error surfaces is often not the one that caused it. Existing observability tools replay execution traces but provide little support for identifying the root cause or translating diagnosis into recovery. We present AgentDebugX, an open-source debugging framework that organizes debugging as a closed loop of Detect, Attribute, Recover, and Rerun. At its core, DeepDebug performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis through global trajectory understanding, structure-guided investigation, and cross-examination. On the Who and When benchmark, DeepDebug achieves the best strict attribution accuracy among the evaluated methods on both tested open-weight backbones, reaching 28.8 percent exact agent-and-step accuracy on qwen3.5-9b versus 21.7 percent for the strongest single-pass baseline. On GAIA, DeepDebug repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun, compared with 4 to 6 for three decoupled self-correction baselines, improving overall accuracy from 55.8 percent to 63.6 percent. AgentDebugX exposes this workflow through a Python library, CLI, web console, and installable agentic skill, and provides an opt-in Error Hub for sharing scrubbed failure-diagnosis-repair bundles and reusing them as debugging memory.

AI.tldr: AgentDebugX is an open-source debugging framework for LLM agents that implements a closed-loop Detect–Attribute–Recover–Rerun workflow. Its core, DeepDebug, performs multi-turn root-cause diagnosis via global trajectory understanding, structured investigation, and cross-examination, achieving state-of-the-art attribution accuracy and task repair rates on the Who-and-When and GAIA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agent failures are hard to debug because the step where an error surfaces is rarely the step that caused it. Existing tools only replay traces without helping identify root causes or translate diagnosis into actionable recovery.
AI.method: AgentDebugX organizes debugging as a closed loop: Detect, Attribute, Recover, and Rerun. The core component, DeepDebug, uses multi-turn diagnosis combining (1) global trajectory understanding, (2) structure-guided investigation, and (3) cross-examination to pinpoint root causes. The framework is exposed via a Python library, CLI, web console, and installable agentic skill, with an opt-in Error Hub for sharing scrubbed failure-diagnosis-repair bundles.
AI.result: On the Who-and-When benchmark, DeepDebug achieves 28.8% exact agent-and-step attribution accuracy with Qwen3.5-9B (vs. 21.7% for the best single-pass baseline). On GAIA, DeepDebug repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in a single rerun (vs. 4–6 for decoupled self-correction baselines), improving overall accuracy from 55.8% to 63.6%.
AI.conclusion: AgentDebugX demonstrates that structured, multi-turn root-cause diagnosis with closed-loop recovery significantly outperforms single-pass and decoupled self-correction approaches, offering a practical and extensible debugging platform for LLM agents.

title: The Price of Reasoning: Cost-Quality Tradeoffs in Reinforcement Learning for Neural Machine Translation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been established as a viable paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Models (LLMs), including downstream tasks, such as Neural Machine Translation (NMT). With the latest research indicating that RLVR could be the preferred training method for translating legal documents due to the induced reasoning capabilities, it raises the question whether it is really attributed to the reasoning or more generally to the training paradigm. We investigate the importance of including the model's reasoning trace in the generated responses during both training and inference by systematically omitting it from one of the phases. Our experiments show that including the reasoning, specifically during inference, has a positive effect on the overall translation quality. Furthermore, we recognise that the reasoning leads to an increase in output tokens, hence we study the cost-quality tradeoff between the increased computational demands and the improved translation quality.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the improvements from RLVR in NMT are due to reasoning capabilities or the training paradigm itself. By systematically omitting reasoning traces during training and/or inference, the authors find that reasoning during inference boosts translation quality, and they analyze the cost-quality tradeoff of the increased token output.
AI.motivation: RLVR has emerged as a promising post-training method for LLMs in NMT, especially for legal translation, where it supposedly induces reasoning capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether the observed improvements are genuinely attributable to reasoning or simply to the RLVR training paradigm. The authors aim to disentangle these factors.
AI.method: The authors systematically ablate the presence of the model's reasoning trace in the generated responses: they omit reasoning during training only, during inference only, during both, and include it in both (full setup). They then evaluate translation quality across these four conditions and measure the token-level cost implications.
AI.result: Including reasoning traces during inference yields a clear positive effect on overall translation quality. However, reasoning adds a substantial number of output tokens, prompting an analysis of the cost-quality tradeoff between increased computational demands and improved translation performance.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning trace inclusion during inference is beneficial for NMT quality under RLVR. The gains come at a computational cost, necessitating a careful cost-quality tradeoff consideration in practical deployments.

title: SkillSight: Seeing Through Shared Descriptions for Accurate Skill Retrieval
summary: As large language model agents gain access to increasingly large skill libraries, retrieving the right skill becomes critical to reliable capability selection and execution. Existing retrievers often treat skill descriptions as ordinary documents, overlooking their highly regular structure: shared descriptive patterns recur across many skills while providing little evidence for distinguishing the required capability. We show that this shared descriptive background systematically contributes to dense relevance scores, induces a pronounced energy gap between queries and skill documents, and obscures task-relevant signals. Based on this observation, we propose SkillSight, a training-free retrieval framework that calibrates shared background in both semantic and lexical spaces. Semantic Background Calibration estimates a background subspace from generic tokens identified by IDF, reducing similarity induced by shared descriptive patterns, while Lexical Evidence Calibration downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence. Experiments on SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp demonstrate consistent improvements across retrieval metrics, with SkillSight improving Recall@10 by up to 20.21 percentage points over the original dense retriever. In end-to-end evaluation, SkillSight achieves the best overall performance across three agent models and outperforms LLM Selection by up to 4.97 percentage points. It is also up to 1,248 times faster than the Dense + Reranker baseline. These results identify shared descriptive background as a key source of bias in skill retrieval and demonstrate that explicitly calibrating it enables accurate and efficient skill selection without additional training. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaojinying/SkillSight.

AI.tldr: SkillSight is a training-free framework that improves skill retrieval for LLM agents by calibrating out shared descriptive background in both semantic and lexical spaces, achieving up to 20.21 pp Recall@10 gains and 1,248× speedup over Dense+Reranker.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents accumulate large skill libraries, existing retrievers fail because they treat skill descriptions as ordinary documents, ignoring that shared descriptive patterns recur across many skills. This shared background creates a systematic energy gap between queries and documents, contributing to dense relevance scores that obscure task-relevant signals and degrade retrieval quality.
AI.method: SkillSight uses two calibration mechanisms: (1) Semantic Background Calibration, which estimates a background subspace from generic tokens identified by IDF and projects it out to reduce similarity from shared patterns; (2) Lexical Evidence Calibration, which downweights shared background tokens to recover discriminative token-level evidence. Both operate without any training.
AI.result: On SRA-Bench and SkillBench-Supp, SkillSight improves Recall@10 by up to 20.21 pp over the original dense retriever. In end-to-end evaluation across three agent models, it achieves best overall performance and outperforms LLM Selection by up to 4.97 pp, while being up to 1,248× faster than Dense+Reranker.
AI.conclusion: Shared descriptive background is a key source of bias in skill retrieval. Explicitly calibrating it via SkillSight enables accurate and efficient skill selection without additional training, offering both strong performance and substantial speed advantages.

title: Selection Shapes the Boundary: A Preregistered Replication of Monotonicity and Label Agreement in Unselected NLI Populations
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Preregistered replication. Code, data, and audit trail: https://github.com/oudeis01/nli-hlv-selection
summary: Prior work on human label variation (HLV) in natural language inference (NLI) has often relied on re-annotation resources that select items by disagreement level. An earlier study (arXiv:2607.15870) found that hypotheses containing non-upward monotonicity operators showed lower label agreement in ChaosNLI (Cliff's delta = -0.284), which is restricted to items whose majority label carries exactly three of five votes. We preregistered a replication of this boundary in the unselected populations that ChaosNLI was drawn from: the SNLI and MultiNLI development sets, using the same operator tagger and a four-level ordinal agreement outcome. The registered prediction fails. All seven contrasts return a positive Cliff's delta (non-upward items agree slightly more, not less), the only significant confirmatory contrast has the opposite sign to the registration, and every effect is far below our smallest effect size of interest (0.10). Robustness checks support the measurement: simulated tagger misclassification shrinks the effects rather than manufacturing them, and a manual re-tagging audit reaches four-class agreement of 0.875 on a fresh 200-item sample. We conclude that the earlier negative boundary is plausibly a structure conditional on low-agreement selection rather than a population-level property, and that HLV structure claims built on selected re-annotation resources should state their selection conditional explicitly.
