Memory must instead serve as a "continuity and governance substrate" that preserves durable user state, grounds answers in multimodal and device evidence, supports correction and forgetting, bounds policy evolution, and remains deployable under latency, cost, privacy, and edge-cloud constraints.
AI.method: Mi-Memory proposes a lifecycle memory framework with four roles — Structure, Expansion, Evolution, and Deployment — connected by a shared audit contract. Four artifact families underpin the contract: typed evidence payloads (preserving source identity/provenance), diagnostic traces (localizing evidence loss), strategy artifacts (making memory-policy changes explicit), and gate/rollback records (bounding accepted evolution). The roles are instantiated through four concrete systems: MemStack (structure), MemSense/MemFuse (expansion), D²ACCI/E²MEND (evolution), and LiteMem (deployment).
AI.result: In controlled-reference Structure evaluations, MemStack achieves 93.59% on LoCoMo, 57.24% on PersonaMem-V2, and 87.47% on LongMemEval. Other tracks report module-level, preliminary/internal, transfer-feasibility, or design-only evidence with explicitly stated boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Mi-Memory represents a step toward auditable, evidence-gated, and deployment-aware memory systems for Personal AI, moving beyond simplistic conversation caches toward a principled lifecycle framework suitable for continuous, multimodal, multi-device AI services.

title: FedCC: A Low-Resource Federated Adaptation of Foundation Models for Robust Corpus Callosum localization in Fetal Ultrasound Images
summary: Accurate localization of the corpus callosum (CC) in fetal ultrasound (US) images is crucial for the early identification of neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, this task remains highly challenging due to the intrinsic limitations of US imaging, including low contrast, speckle noise, and the considerable anatomical variability of the CC. We propose FedCC, a federated learning (FL)-based framework for CC localization in fetal US images, specifically designed for realistic multi-center and resource-constrained clinical settings without requiring data sharing. The framework integrates a frozen DINOv2 backbone with a lightweight YOLO-based detection head. To enable parameter-efficient adaptation, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules are incorporated, allowing only a small subset of parameters to be optimized and exchanged among clients. This strategy substantially reduces both computational and communication overhead, making the framework suitable for low-resource environments. The proposed approach was evaluated on a multi-center dataset comprising 10,970 ultrasound frames acquired from 58 pregnant women during routine neurosonographic examinations across three clinical sites using heterogeneous imaging devices. The proposed framework achieved strong performance in the federated setting. In particular, the combination of DINOv2 and LoRA under the FedAvg strategy achieved an average mAP@50 of 0.857 and an F1-score of 0.803, outperforming both full fine-tuning and encoder-freezing baselines. Notably, the proposed approach reduced the number of trainable parameters to 2.9M compared with 24.4M in full fine-tuning, corresponding to an approximately 8.5$\times$ reduction in communication cost. These findings represent a promising step toward scalable, privacy-preserving, and clinically deployable AI systems for fetal neurosonography.

AI.tldr: FedCC is a federated learning framework for corpus callosum localization in fetal ultrasound that uses a frozen DINOv2 backbone with LoRA adapters and a lightweight YOLO detection head, achieving strong performance while reducing trainable parameters by ~8.5× compared to full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Fetal US-based CC localization is critical for early neurodevelopmental abnormality detection but is hampered by low contrast, speckle noise, anatomical variability, and the inability to share data across institutions due to privacy concerns and resource constraints.
AI.method: FedCC combines a frozen DINOv2 vision backbone with a YOLO-based detection head, augmented with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Under the FedAvg strategy, only the lightweight LoRA parameters and detection head are optimized and exchanged, minimizing communication overhead. Evaluated on 10,970 frames from 58 pregnant women across three clinical sites with heterogeneous devices.
AI.result: FedCC with DINOv2 + LoRA + FedAvg achieved mAP@50 of 0.857 and F1-score of 0.803, outperforming full fine-tuning and encoder-freezing baselines. Trainable parameters were reduced to 2.9M (from 24.4M), yielding an ~8.5× reduction in communication cost.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates a scalable, privacy-preserving, and clinically viable solution for fetal neurosonography, effectively balancing detection performance with computational and communication efficiency in multi-center settings.

title: Fishing Out Free Riders: Shapley-Based Reward Attribution for Parallel Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning, yet current parallel reasoning approaches often fail to distinguish the contributions of individual reasoning paths. Many paths may be redundant, misleading, or even detrimental, but outcome-level rewards assign uniform reward, leading to ambiguous learning signals and unstable training. We propose Parallel Shapley, a reinforcement learning framework that attributes fine-grained, path-level contributions in multi-path reasoning. Treating each path as a player in a cooperative game, we leverage Shapley values to quantify marginal contributions, using a generative reward model to evaluate path utilities and Monte Carlo sampling for efficient approximation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Parallel Shapley outperforms existing baselines while providing more stable and interpretable training. Our framework effectively "fishes out the free riders," assigning reward proportionally and improving multi-path reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Parallel Shapley introduces a reinforcement learning framework for multi-path reasoning in LLMs that uses Shapley values to assign fine-grained credit to individual reasoning paths. By treating each path as a cooperative game player and using a generative reward model with Monte Carlo sampling, it identifies and rewards beneficial paths while penalizing redundant or detrimental ones, outperforming baselines on math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current parallel reasoning approaches in LLMs rely on outcome-level rewards that uniformly reward all reasoning paths, failing to distinguish useful paths from redundant, misleading, or detrimental ones. This creates ambiguous learning signals and unstable training. The authors aim to solve the "free rider" problem by enabling path-level credit assignment.
AI.method: The framework, Parallel Shapley, models multi-path reasoning as a cooperative game where each reasoning path is a player. It uses Shapley values to compute the marginal contribution of each path. A generative reward model evaluates path utilities, and Monte Carlo sampling provides efficient approximation of Shapley values to make computation tractable. These path-level rewards are then integrated into a reinforcement learning training procedure.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that Parallel Shapley outperforms existing baselines, while providing more stable and interpretable training dynamics compared to uniform outcome-level reward approaches.
AI.conclusion: Parallel Shapley effectively "fishes out free riders" in multi-path reasoning by proportionally assigning credit based on marginal contributions, improving both performance and training stability in LLMs.

title: Compressing What Matters: Neuron Importance Meets Data-Aware Low Rank Approximation for Language Model Compression
summary: To excel at their domain large language models are comprised of billions of parameters. Yet this comes at the cost of huge memory requirements restricting their applicability in resource-constrained environments. To address the problem of neural network (NN) compression Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) has played a key role as a fundamental component for matrix compression through decomposition. To minimize compression error and to maximize the efficacy of the compressed model on the downstream tasks previous works focused on low-rank approximation of the NN's weight matrices either from the perspective of parameter importance or per-layer functional equivalence. While previous works studied the aforementioned perspectives in isolation in this work we are investigating the effectiveness of an approach that combines ideas from these two perspectives in a single objective. In parallel to this an important aspect that affects the compression quality is the distribution of the compression rate across layers and NN parameters. Earlier works mostly considered distributing the compression rate uniformly across layers and network weights or relied on computationally expensive heuristic search. Contrary to them in this work we propose an enhanced and computationally efficient algorithm for dynamic compression rate allocation. Experimental results support the efficacy of the proposed approach which performs on par or substantially better than the previous state-of-the-art especially under high compression ratios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel neural network compression method combining two previously separate perspectives—parameter importance and per-layer functional equivalence—into a unified SVD-based objective, along with a computationally efficient algorithm for dynamic compression rate allocation across layers, achieving state-of-the-art performance especially at high compression ratios.
AI.motivation: Large language models contain billions of parameters, resulting in prohibitive memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. Existing SVD-based compression methods address either parameter importance or per-layer functional equivalence in isolation, and compression rate allocation is typically done uniformly or through expensive heuristic search—leaving room for a more integrated and efficient approach.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified SVD-based compression objective that simultaneously integrates parameter importance and per-layer functional equivalence perspectives. Additionally, they introduce a computationally efficient dynamic compression rate allocation algorithm that non-uniformly distributes compression across layers and parameters, avoiding the cost of heuristic search while improving allocation quality.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach performs on par with or substantially better than previous state-of-the-art methods, with particularly pronounced advantages under high compression ratios.
AI.conclusion: Combining parameter importance and functional equivalence perspectives into a single SVD-based objective, paired with efficient dynamic rate allocation, yields superior compression performance compared to treating these perspectives independently or using uniform allocation strategies.

title: A Controlled Study of Attention-Only Transformers
summary: Feed-forward networks hold two thirds of a transformer's non-embedding parameters, yet the architecture has not received a necessity test that controls parameters, compute, and depth at once. We pretrain attention-only decoder transformers (Simple Attention Networks, SANs) against standard transformers matched separately for parameter count, training FLOPs, and depth (2 to 48 layers), for up to 105B tokens at 6M to 87M parameters. Deleting feed-forward layers in place is costly: the standard transformer leads by 0.47 nats at matched depth and 0.26 nats at matched FLOPs. Reallocating the freed budget into attention depth closes the gap: at matched parameters the difference is 0.006 nats (0.27 percent of loss), reproducible to one part in ten thousand across seed pairs, shrinking across 5B, 30B, and 105B budgets, and holding near 0.02 nats across a 29x size range. Three measurements localize the remaining gap to parametric recall: attention-only models are better on context-grounded answers and worse where knowledge must come from weights. Weight spectra show why: routing matrices (Q/K) crystallize early, content matrices accumulate rank slowly, and removing feed-forward layers relocates this accumulation to the attention output projection. QK-normalization, not feed-forward layers or residual gating, keeps 48-layer attention-only stacks trainable. The deficit concentrates on low-context query prediction and localizes there entirely by the largest budget. A pre-registered test confirms the account: it predicts a 0.02 to 0.05 nat gap on knowledge-dense web text; a matched pair trained on fineweb-edu measures 0.040. Within the tested regime, attention does the rest.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether feed-forward networks (FFNs) are necessary in transformers by pretraining attention-only decoder models (SANs) against standard transformers under controlled parameter, compute, and depth budgets. The gap nearly closes (0.006 nats) when parameters are matched by reallocating FFN budget into attention depth. The remaining deficit localizes to parametric recall — attention-only models struggle where knowledge must come from weights rather than context.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward networks constitute roughly two-thirds of a transformer's non-embedding parameters, yet no prior work has conducted a rigorous necessity test controlling for parameter count, training FLOPs, and depth simultaneously. The authors seek to determine whether FFNs are genuinely essential or whether their function can be absorbed by deeper attention mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors pretrain Simple Attention Networks (SANs) — decoder transformers with feed-forward layers removed — against standard transformers. Comparisons are made under three matching regimes: matched depth, matched training FLOPs, and matched parameter count (by reallocating FFN budget into additional attention layers). Models range from 2 to 48 layers, 6M to 87M parameters, trained on up to 105B tokens. Diagnostics include loss decomposition, weight matrix spectral analysis, and a pre-registered experiment on knowledge-dense text (fineweb-edu).
AI.result: At matched depth, standard transformers lead by 0.47 nats; at matched FLOPs, by 0.26 nats. At matched parameters (reallocating FFN budget to attention depth), the gap shrinks to 0.006 nats (0.27% of loss), reproducible across seeds. The residual gap concentrates on parametric recall: SANs excel at context-grounded answers but underperform where factual knowledge must be retrieved from weights. Weight spectra show Q/K matrices crystallize early while content matrices accumulate rank slowly; removing FFNs shifts this accumulation to attention output projections. QK-normalization suffices to keep 48-layer attention-only stacks trainable. A pre-registered test on knowledge-dense web text predicts a 0.02–0.05 nat gap; the measured gap is 0.040 nats.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested regime (up to 87M parameters, 105B tokens), feed-forward layers are not strictly necessary — attention can do the rest. The primary functional contribution of FFNs is parametric knowledge storage/recall. Deeper attention with QK-normalization can substitute for most other FFN functions.

title: Athena-Brain Technical Report: An Efficient Robot Brain for General Intelligence and Embodied Interactio
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in language understanding, reasoning, and world knowledge. As embodied agents become increasingly capable, there is a growing demand for compact models that can serve as an on-device brain, preserving the broad general intelligence of LLMs while enabling effective high-level interaction with embodied environments. Existing approaches, however, often prioritize either general-purpose intelligence or specialized embodied capabilities, making it challenging to satisfy both requirements within a single model. We present \textbf{Athena-Brain-8B}, an 8B LLM designed to serve as an on-device brain for embodied intelligence for embodied intelligence. Through a multi-stage post-training pipeline consisting of General Supervised Fine-Tuning, General Reinforcement Learning, Embodied Expert training, and Model Merge, Athena-Brain-8B maintains strong general capabilities while acquiring strong high-level embodied interaction capabilities and generating concise responses for efficient embodied interaction. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Athena across both general and embodied evaluations. Compared with the corresponding Qwen3-8B thinking model, Athena-Brain-8B achieves comparable performance on general language and reasoning benchmarks while generating substantially shorter responses. On in-domain embodied benchmarks, Athena-Brain-8B consistently outperforms models of similar scale and surpasses several substantially larger frontier models evaluated zero-shot, demonstrating that compact language models can effectively integrate strong general intelligence with embodied capabilities.

AI.tldr: Athena-Brain-8B is a compact 8B-parameter language model designed as an on-device brain for embodied agents. It uses a multi-stage post-training pipeline (General SFT, General RL, Embodied Expert training, Model Merge) to balance general intelligence with embodied interaction capabilities, matching Qwen3-8B on general benchmarks with shorter responses while outperforming similar-scale and larger frontier models on embodied tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches tend to optimize for either general-purpose intelligence or specialized embodied capabilities, but not both simultaneously within a single compact model. There is a growing need for on-device embodied agents that retain broad LLM intelligence while enabling effective high-level embodied interaction.
AI.method: A multi-stage post-training pipeline: (1) General Supervised Fine-Tuning, (2) General Reinforcement Learning, (3) Embodied Expert training, and (4) Model Merge — applied to produce an 8B-parameter model that maintains general capabilities while acquiring embodied interaction skills and generating concise responses.
AI.result: Athena-Brain-8B achieves comparable performance to Qwen3-8B (thinking model) on general language and reasoning benchmarks while generating substantially shorter responses. On embodied benchmarks, it consistently outperforms models of similar scale and surpasses several larger frontier models under zero-shot evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Compact language models can effectively integrate strong general intelligence with embodied capabilities through a carefully designed multi-stage post-training pipeline, making them viable as on-device brains for embodied agents.

title: Edge-Efficient Transformer for End-to-End RF Spectrum Monitoring
summary: We present E-SpecFormer (Edge Spectrum monitoring Transformer) for end-to-end automatic modulation and covert channel (CC) recognition. We introduce LiTAN (Linear Tanh Attention Network), a Softmax- and LayerNorm-free attention mechanism that reduces complexity while increasing accuracy in RF tasks. E-SpecFormer is parameterized in four scalable variants (Nano, Small, Medium, Large) to accommodate diverse hardware constraints. Using the RadioML2018 dataset for modulation recognition, the Nano variant achieves 86.5% average accuracy for Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs)>0 dB, and on the hardware Trojan (HT)-based CC dataset it reaches 94.2% accuracy, both with fewer than 10k parameters and up to speed of 92 μs per frame on FPGA/CPU co-execution, surpassing state-of-the-art edge models at a fraction of their cost. These results establish E-SpecFormer as an edge-efficient solution for real-time spectrum intelligence on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. GitHub link to the repository: https://github.com/zsniko/E-SpecFormer.

AI.tldr: E-SpecFormer introduces a lightweight Transformer with a novel Softmax-free attention mechanism (LiTAN) for efficient modulation and covert channel recognition on edge devices, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with under 10k parameters.
AI.motivation: Deploying automatic modulation recognition and covert channel detection on resource-constrained IoT edge devices requires models that balance high accuracy with extremely low computational complexity, memory footprint, and inference latency — criteria unmet by existing Transformer-based RF models relying on costly Softmax and LayerNorm operations.
AI.method: The authors propose E-SpecFormer, an end-to-end Transformer for spectrum monitoring, featuring LiTAN (Linear Tanh Attention Network) — a novel attention mechanism that replaces Softmax with a linear tanh-based approximation and eliminates LayerNorm, significantly reducing computational overhead. The architecture is released in four scalable variants (Nano, Small, Medium, Large) to suit different hardware constraints, with the Nano variant targeting extreme edge deployment.
AI.result: On the RadioML2018 dataset (SNR > 0 dB), the Nano variant achieves 86.5% average modulation recognition accuracy. On a hardware-Trojan-based covert channel dataset, it reaches 94.2% accuracy. Both results are attained with fewer than 10k parameters and an inference speed of 92 μs per frame on FPGA/CPU co-execution, outperforming prior edge models at significantly lower cost.
AI.conclusion: E-SpecFormer, particularly its Nano variant enabled by LiTAN, establishes a new Pareto frontier for edge-efficient RF spectrum intelligence, demonstrating that sub-10k-parameter Transformers can deliver real-time modulation and covert channel recognition on IoT devices without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Vector-Bench: Can Models Surgically Edit SVG Code?
summary: Instruction-based vector editing requires two capabilities: making a requested change and leaving everything else alone. The second is easy to miss when an output is judged only as a raster image. We introduce Vector-Bench, a compact, difficult benchmark of 40 SVG repair tasks. Each task pairs a corrupted SVG program with an author-written visual instruction, a hidden target program, 5.05 annotated repairs on average, and an average of 60.55 protected objects. Instructions describe visible defects without exposing element identifiers, coordinates, color codes, or path data. We define a deterministic binary specification reward: requested repairs use attribute-aware perceptual tolerances, while unrequested rendering- or application-relevant structure must remain semantically unchanged and the result must be a valid SVG. Canonical target equality and stricter source fidelity are retained as diagnostics. Validity-gated repair progress, a near-complete tier, and valid-output Unintended Change Rate (UCR) explain partial outcomes. We evaluate 34 model endpoints (25 listed as open-weight, 5 inexpensive controls, and 4 frontier closed endpoints) over 1360 requests. The strongest endpoint reaches only 15.0% full specification success, despite 43.7% mean repair progress, showing that apparent repair progress and specification-faithful editing remain substantially different. All prompts, outputs, scoring code, costs, and per-task reports are released.

AI.tldr: Vector-Bench is a benchmark of 40 SVG repair tasks testing instruction-based vector editing. It evaluates whether models can make requested changes while preserving everything else, using a binary specification reward. The best model achieves only 15.0% full success despite 43.7% mean repair progress, revealing a gap between apparent and specification-faithful editing.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of instruction-based vector editing focuses on raster image output, which misses the critical second capability: leaving unrequested elements untouched. There is no rigorous benchmark that measures both targeted repair accuracy and preservation fidelity in SVG programs using a deterministic metric.
AI.method: Vector-Bench comprises 40 SVG repair tasks, each with a corrupted SVG, a written instruction describing visible defects (without revealing identifiers, coordinates, or path data), a hidden target, annotated repairs (~5.05 avg), and protected objects (~60.55 avg). A deterministic binary specification reward is defined: requested repairs use attribute-aware perceptual tolerances; unrequested structure must remain semantically unchanged; output must be valid SVG. Canonical target equality and stricter source fidelity serve as diagnostics. Validity-gated repair progress and Unintended Change Rate (UCR) explain partial outcomes. 34 model endpoints are evaluated over 1360 requests.
AI.result: The strongest model endpoint achieves only 15.0% full specification success, compared to 43.7% mean repair progress, demonstrating that apparent progress and specification-faithful editing diverge substantially. All artifacts — prompts, outputs, scoring code, costs, and per-task reports — are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-based SVG editing remains an open challenge. High repair progress does not translate to specification-faithful editing, as models struggle to preserve unrequested structure. Vector-Bench provides a rigorous, reproducible framework for measuring and advancing this capability.

title: Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Runtime-Tunable Transit Signal Priority
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the 29th IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026). Code: https://github.com/urbanAIthi/morl-tsp
summary: Transit signal priority (TSP) requires balancing competing objectives: reducing bus delay while limiting adverse impacts on non-bus traffic and avoiding extreme waits for a subset of vehicles. Existing reinforcement-learning (RL) approaches to TSP typically encode transit-aware features (e.g., occupancy and schedule deviation) but optimize a fixed reward or fixed scalarization, which limits operational flexibility when agency priorities change across time-of-day or disruption conditions. We present a preference-conditioned TSP controller, $π(a \mid s,w)$, that selects the next signal phase under minimum/maximum green and transition-feasibility constraints and can be tuned at runtime via a preference parameter $w$ to trade off bus-priority emphasis against overall traffic delay without retraining. We implement this on top of IntersectionZoo by introducing a constrained signal-control/TSP wrapper, and we extend scenario generation with bus-prevalence augmentation and timetable-based bus insertion to address sparse transit-priority events during training. Experiments against fixed-time control, a rule-based TSP overlay, and fixed-weight PPO specialists show that a single learned conditioned policy spans a smooth empirical trade-off frontier across runtime preferences, outperforms fixed-time and rule-based baselines, and maintains constraint feasibility, while tail-delay diagnostics reveal that non-bus externalities remain limited for moderate preference settings but can increase substantially under high bus-priority weights. The source code of this work is available at https://github.com/urbanAIthi/morl-tsp.

AI.tldr: A preference-conditioned RL controller for transit signal priority (TSP) that can be tuned at runtime via a weight parameter to trade off bus delay reduction against overall traffic delay, without retraining. The single policy spans a smooth trade-off frontier and outperforms fixed-time, rule-based, and fixed-weight RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based TSP methods optimize fixed rewards or scalarizations, limiting operational flexibility when transit agency priorities shift across time-of-day or disruption scenarios. There is a need for a single controller that can be dynamically adjusted to emphasize bus priority vs. general traffic without retraining.
AI.method: The authors propose a preference-conditioned policy π(a|s,w) with a preference parameter w, built atop IntersectionZoo with a constrained signal-control/TSP wrapper. They introduce bus-prevalence augmentation and timetable-based bus insertion to address sparse transit-priority events during training. The policy selects signal phases under min/max green and transition-feasibility constraints.
AI.result: A single conditioned policy spans a smooth empirical trade-off frontier across runtime preferences, outperforming fixed-time control, rule-based TSP overlays, and fixed-weight PPO specialists. Constraint feasibility is maintained. Tail-delay diagnostics show non-bus externalities remain limited at moderate preferences but increase substantially under high bus-priority weights.
AI.conclusion: Preference-conditioned RL enables a flexible, retraining-free TSP controller that adapts to changing operational priorities, offering a practical deployment advantage over fixed-weight approaches while maintaining competitive performance across the trade-off spectrum.

title: CANDOR: Chance-Calibrated Discordance in Frozen Foundation Encoders
summary: Frozen encoders are chosen by how well a lightweight head reads a finding from their features, not whether the geometry separates it. Nearest-neighbor discordance does, but with unequal banks the opposite-label neighbor wins on density, not geometry, so prevalence alone makes an uninformed encoder look blind. We introduce CANDOR, a discordance measure whose equal-size banks are symmetric under a label swap, fixing its chance level at exactly one half. Across 22 encoders, 20 datasets from 7 domains, and 605,443 images, this correction reverses the conclusion. Collapse falls below chance almost everywhere, so no encoder is blind, yet all are weak: the best chest model reads pneumothorax at 84.5 AUROC and still places 18.4% of those positives nearer an opposite-label film than its own kind in the same hospital. The same encoder that resolves bird species at 4.5 leaves chest findings at 42.8 and glaucoma at 49.8, at chance and worse than random weights. Such a case caps the normalized margin of any Lipschitz head, yet some head among eleven is correct on all but 2.8% of cases where one head misses 35.9%: the deficit is selection, not information. Erasure retention is associated with collapse; we detect no association with the objective, scale, recency, or size of the finding. Because the chance level is fixed, CANDOR can be read before any head is trained, flagging which findings a frozen encoder supports poorly.

AI.tldr: CANDOR introduces a label-symmetric nearest-neighbor discordance measure with a fixed chance level of 0.5, revealing that frozen encoders are not "blind" to any finding but are universally weak, with performance deficits attributable to head selection rather than missing information in the representations.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of frozen encoders relies on how well a lightweight probe head reads a finding from features, conflating representation quality with head training. Nearest-neighbor discordance can assess geometry directly, but prior measures are biased by class imbalance — the majority class wins on density, making encoders appear blind to rare findings. A label-symmetric, prevalence-invariant discordance measure is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose CANDOR, a nearest-neighbor discordance measure that constructs equal-size banks for each class, ensuring symmetry under label swap and fixing the chance level at exactly 0.5. CANDOR is evaluated across 22 encoders, 20 datasets spanning 7 domains, and 605,443 images. The method also analyzes collapse (features falling below chance separability), erasure retention, and the gap between what a single linear head achieves versus an oracle selection among eleven heads.
AI.result: CANDOR reverses prior conclusions: no encoder is blind, but all are weak. The best chest model achieves 84.5 AUROC for pneumothorax yet 18.4% of positives are nearer an opposite-label film. An encoder resolving bird species at 4.5 CANDOR drops to 42.8 for chest findings and 49.8 for glaucoma — at or below chance. An oracle among 11 heads misses only 2.8% of cases where one head misses 35.9%, showing the deficit is selection, not information. Erasure retention correlates with collapse; no association found with objective, scale, recency, or finding size.
AI.conclusion: CANDOR provides a head-free, prevalence-invariant measure of frozen encoder quality with a fixed chance level, enabling pre-training evaluation. The findings show that while frozen encoders contain sufficient information for most tasks, the bottleneck lies in head selection rather than representation capacity, and collapse is widespread but not absolute blindness.

title: Quality Action Assurance: Multimodal Verification of Examiner Claims in VR OSCEs
summary: Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) are the gold standard for assessing clinical competence, yet scoring remains vulnerable to examiner subjectivity, fatigue, and cognitive bias. Standard examiner validation via inter-rater statistics lacks explanatory power regarding the source of errors, as it neither analyzes examiner reasoning nor verifies examiner claims against actual events. Thus, we introduce Quality Action Assurance (QAA), a multimodal framework that verifies examiner claims in Virtual Reality (VR) pediatric OSCEs by comparing actions claimed by examiners against the true sequence of events, constructed from video, VR logs, and actor data. QAA combines a constrained temporal action alignment model, which performs action localization and actor source attribution, with a large language model that extracts examiner claims and checks them against the record. Across a 5-fold cross-validation, QAA achieves 99.2% $\pm$ 0.7% Actor F1 and 93.4% $\pm$ 1.9% W@16 for temporal alignment. Overall, QAA detects examiner errors with 70.0% precision and 76.7% recall, improving factual correctness from 39.2% to 79.2%, enabling fairer OSCE assessment.

AI.tldr: QAA is a multimodal framework that validates examiner scoring in VR pediatric OSCEs by aligning examiner claims against a ground-truth event record using temporal action alignment and an LLM, achieving 70% precision and 76.7% recall in detecting examiner errors and improving factual correctness from 39.2% to 79.2%.
AI.motivation: OSCE scoring is undermined by examiner subjectivity, fatigue, and cognitive bias. Traditional inter-rater reliability statistics lack explanatory power — they cannot pinpoint error sources, analyze examiner reasoning, or verify claims against actual events. A method is needed to objectively verify examiner claims against a ground-truth record of what actually occurred.
AI.method: The QAA framework operates in VR pediatric OSCEs and consists of two core components: (1) a constrained temporal action alignment model that performs action localization and actor source attribution using video, VR logs, and actor data to construct a true event sequence; and (2) a large language model (LLM) that extracts examiner claims from their assessments and fact-checks them against the aligned ground-truth record.
AI.result: In 5-fold cross-validation, the temporal alignment component achieves 99.2% ± 0.7% Actor F1 and 93.4% ± 1.9% W@16. For error detection, QAA achieves 70.0% precision and 76.7% recall, raising the overall factual correctness of examiner assessments from 39.2% to 79.2%.
AI.conclusion: QAA effectively detects examiner errors in OSCE scoring by grounding claims in multimodal evidence, substantially improving factual correctness and enabling fairer, more reliable clinical competence assessment.

title: BearingNAS: Obtaining In-Sensor Intelligent Fault Diagnosis Systems for Bearings Using a Laptop
comment: Accepted to IEEE COINS 2026 in Special Session 7: Edge AI technologies
summary: This paper introduces BearingNAS, a Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search (HW-NAS) framework designed to shift the intelligence directly onto the sensor die via in-sensor processing. BearingNAS frames the search as a constrained optimization problem targeting extreme micro-budgets (4 to 8 kiB of RAM and 16 to 32 kiB of Flash). To eliminate the reliance on expensive discrete GPUs, we propose a lightweight, derivative-free search strategy paired with a single data-flow search space that leverages a decaying kernel growth formulation to prevent parameter explosion. We evaluate our framework on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing benchmark, optimizing architectures for three STMicroelectronics targets: two commodity microcontrollers and the LSM6DSO16IS Intelligent Sensor Processing Unit (ISPU). Running entirely on a laptop CPU, the search converges in less than an hour. The resulting best in-sensor architecture achieves a highly competitive diagnostic accuracy of 99.50\% on the ISPU. These results demonstrate the viability of shifting the machine learning workload inside the sensor package, enabling low-cost, production-scale bearing fault diagnosis.

AI.tldr: BearingNAS is a hardware-aware NAS framework that uses derivative-free search to find neural architectures for in-sensor bearing fault diagnosis on ultra-constrained MCUs/ISPUs (4–32 kiB memory), achieving 99.50% accuracy on the LSM6DSO16IS ISPU with sub-hour CPU-only convergence.
AI.motivation: Shift ML-based bearing fault diagnosis intelligence directly onto the sensor die (in-sensor processing), eliminating reliance on external GPUs/cloud and enabling low-cost, production-scale deployment on extreme micro-budget hardware (4–8 kiB RAM, 16–32 kiB Flash).
AI.method: A constrained optimization HW-NAS framework with three key components: (1) a single data-flow search space with decaying kernel growth formulation to prevent parameter explosion; (2) a lightweight derivative-free search strategy avoiding GPU dependency; (3) evaluation on three STMicroelectronics targets (two commodity MCUs + LSM6DSO16IS ISPU) using the CWRU bearing benchmark, with search converging in under one hour on a laptop CPU.
AI.result: The best discovered architecture achieves 99.50% diagnostic accuracy on the ISPU target. Search converges in less than one hour on a laptop CPU, demonstrating feasibility of in-sensor ML for bearing fault diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: In-sensor processing for bearing fault diagnosis is viable and can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on severely resource-constrained sensor hardware, paving the way for low-cost, production-scale predictive maintenance directly within the sensor package.

title: On the Effectiveness of Pretraining for Graph Combinatorial Optimization
comment: This work was accepted to be presented at the Graph Signal Processing Workshop 2026
summary: This paper introduces a self-supervised pretraining framework for graph combinatorial optimization specifically designed to address the nature of routing problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem. By utilizing graph contrastive learning with geometric augmentations (specifically, rotations and axial reflections) the model is forced to learn invariant structural representations and global relative distance distributions. Results demonstrate that this pretraining strategy outperforms non-pretrained models across various problem scales. Notably, the hybrid strategy (combining rotation and reflection) achieved a 6.57% improvement in tour length for TSP1000, proving that geometric pretraining is an important inductive bias for effectively scaling neural solvers to high-dimensional instances.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised pretraining framework using graph contrastive learning with geometric augmentations (rotation and reflection) forces models to learn invariant structural representations for routing problems. The hybrid strategy achieves a 6.57% improvement in tour length for TSP1000, demonstrating geometric pretraining as an effective inductive bias for scaling neural solvers.
AI.motivation: Neural solvers for combinatorial optimization problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) struggle to scale effectively to high-dimensional instances. The authors aim to address this by injecting geometric priors into the learning process, leveraging the inherent spatial symmetries of routing problems to improve representation learning and generalization to larger problem scales.
AI.method: A self-supervised pretraining framework employing graph contrastive learning. Geometric augmentations — specifically rotations and axial reflections — are applied to TSP instances. The model is trained to maximize agreement between differently augmented views of the same instance, thereby learning representations invariant to these transformations and capturing global relative distance distributions. A hybrid strategy combining both rotation and reflection augmentations is proposed.
AI.result: The proposed pretraining strategy consistently outperforms non-pretrained models across various problem scales. The hybrid augmentation strategy (rotation + reflection) yields a 6.57% improvement in tour length on TSP1000 instances, demonstrating clear benefits of geometric pretraining for scaling to high-dimensional problems.
AI.conclusion: Geometric pretraining via contrastive learning with symmetry-based augmentations serves as a powerful inductive bias for neural combinatorial optimization solvers, enabling more effective scaling to larger problem instances. The learned invariant representations and relative distance distributions significantly improve solution quality.

title: Multi-Timescale Latent-Action DRL for Joint Optimization in Edge-Cloud Networks
summary: Load imbalance across edge and cloud layers degrades latency performance in hierarchical edge-cloud computing (HECC) systems under dynamic task arrivals and heterogeneous resources, leading to severe queuing delays and inefficient resource utilization. To address this challenge, we study a joint service placement, computational delegation, and power control (JSCP) problem to minimize the average end-to-end (e2e) latency. The resulting JSCP problem is a mixed-integer nonconvex and NP-hard optimization problem due to the strong coupling between discrete and continuous variables. To enable tractable optimization and stable system adaptation, we exploit the inherent difference in decision dynamics and decompose the problem into long-term system configuration and short-term resource allocation subproblems. Based on this formulation, we propose a two-timescale multi-layer deep reinforcement learning framework with a latent action space (2T-MDRL-LA) to jointly optimize service placement, user association, computational delegation, task offloading, and user transmit power. A latent action representation based on a variational autoencoder is introduced to efficiently compress the high-dimensional combinatorial action space. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively adapts to dynamic network conditions and achieves near-optimal performance compared to branch-and-bound solutions. It achieves up to a 20.8% reduction in average e2e latency and a 13% improvement in resource utilization over the scheme without the computational delegation, while converging approximately 50% faster than conventional proximal policy optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-timescale multi-layer deep reinforcement learning framework with latent action space (2T-MDRL-LA) to jointly optimize service placement, computational delegation, and power control in hierarchical edge-cloud computing systems, achieving up to 20.8% latency reduction and 50% faster convergence than standard PPO.
AI.motivation: Load imbalance in hierarchical edge-cloud computing (HECC) systems under dynamic task arrivals and heterogeneous resources causes severe queuing delays and inefficient resource utilization. Existing approaches fail to jointly address the coupled discrete (service placement, offloading decisions) and continuous (power control) variables, creating a mixed-integer nonconvex NP-hard problem that demands a tractable, adaptive solution.
AI.method: The authors decompose the joint service placement, computational delegation, and power control (JSCP) problem into long-term system configuration and short-term resource allocation subproblems based on decision dynamics. They then design a two-timescale multi-layer deep reinforcement learning (2T-MDRL) framework, incorporating a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn a latent action representation that compresses the high-dimensional combinatorial action space, enabling efficient policy learning.
AI.result: Simulations show the 2T-MDRL-LA framework achieves near-optimal performance versus branch-and-bound baselines, with up to 20.8% lower average end-to-end latency and 13% better resource utilization compared to schemes without computational delegation. It also converges approximately 50% faster than conventional proximal policy optimization (PPO).
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-timescale DRL approach with latent action compression effectively handles the NP-hard JSCP problem in HECC systems, delivering significant latency and resource utilization gains while converging substantially faster than standard PPO, making it suitable for dynamic real-world edge-cloud deployments.

title: Supra Cognitive Modes: A Routed Architecture for Agent Memory
summary: Agent-memory workloads mix direct factual lookup, relation-chain and current-state reasoning, and broad synthesis over long histories. We describe Supra Cognitive Modes (SCM), an architecture that maps explicit or automatically selected per-query modes to retrieval and synthesis payloads over one shared ingest substrate. A frozen semantic classifier and runtime gates dispatch queries among fused lexical and dense lookup, graph or iterative multi-hop handling, and stratified long-form synthesis. The substrate combines multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and optional asynchronous enrichments. We characterize the deployed configuration on three benchmarks: Long-term Conversational Memory (LoCoMo; n = 1,986), MemoryAgentBench (MAB; n = 3,671), and LongMemEval (n = 500). The reference run records 84.87% on LoCoMo factoid categories and 68.61% on adversarial abstention, 61.49% on MAB across two repetitions, and 86.00% on LongMemEval. A repository-backed reproduction produces similar aggregate scores and supports task- and mode-conditioned failure analysis. Raw baseline outputs, aligned end-to-end timing for LoCoMo and LongMemEval, and complete token ledgers are unavailable; stored rows also omit some final runtime decisions. The results characterize one implemented routed configuration and its diagnostic failure patterns, while source inspection verifies the per-query control interface and shared-substrate design. Causal routing effects, efficiency gains, and statistical significance remain outside the available evidence.

AI.tldr: Supra Cognitive Modes (SCM) is an agent-memory architecture that routes queries through different retrieval/synthesis strategies (lexical, dense, graph-based multi-hop, and stratified long-form) over a shared ingest substrate, achieving strong benchmarks on LoCoMo, MemoryAgentBench, and LongMemEval, though causal routing effects and efficiency gains remain unevaluated.
AI.motivation: Agent-memory workloads require handling heterogeneous query types — direct factual lookup, relational chain reasoning, current-state tracking, and broad synthesis over long histories — within a single system. Existing approaches lack a unified architecture that can dynamically route diverse queries to appropriate retrieval and synthesis strategies over shared stored representations.
AI.method: SCM uses a frozen semantic classifier with runtime gates to dispatch each query among four pathways: fused lexical and dense lookup, graph-based or iterative multi-hop handling, and stratified long-form synthesis. The shared ingest substrate combines multi-granularity embeddings, extracted triples, fact-version metadata, and optional asynchronous enrichments. Modes can be explicitly specified or automatically selected per query.
AI.result: On benchmarks: LoCoMo (n=1,986) achieved 84.87% on factoid categories and 68.61% on adversarial abstention; MemoryAgentBench (n=3,671) scored 61.49% across two repetitions; LongMemEval (n=500) scored 86.00%. A repository-backed reproduction produced similar aggregate scores. However, raw baseline outputs, end-to-end timing, and complete token ledgers are unavailable; stored rows omit some runtime decisions.
AI.conclusion: The paper characterizes one implemented routed configuration with diagnostic failure patterns, demonstrating the viability of a multi-mode, shared-substrate agent-memory architecture. However, causal routing effects, efficiency gains over baselines, and statistical significance cannot be established from the available evidence due to missing comparative data and incomplete runtime traces.

title: Towards Principled Continual Anomaly Detection: A Systematic Framework and Benchmark Scenarios
summary: Continual anomaly detection (CAD) studies how models can adapt to evolving data distributions while retaining performance on previously observed regimes. CAD benchmarks, however, depend critically on how tasks are defined, filtered, ordered, and validated. In tabular domains, task boundaries are rarely given, and arbitrary splits can create unlearnable, redundant, or overly transferable tasks that obscure genuine continual-learning behavior. To this end, we introduce a systematic framework for reproducible benchmark scenario design from existing tabular anomaly-detection datasets. The framework discovers candidate tasks, filters unsuitable tasks, and derives principled orderings that expose diverse dynamics. The framework allows us to deliver five benchmark-ready scenarios from three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets, yielding both single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a systematic framework for designing reproducible continual anomaly detection (CAD) benchmark scenarios from existing tabular datasets, addressing the lack of principled task definition. Applied to three cybersecurity datasets, it yields five benchmark-ready scenarios for single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings.
AI.motivation: CAD benchmarks heavily depend on how tasks are defined, filtered, ordered, and validated, yet in tabular domains, task boundaries are rarely naturally given. Arbitrary splits produce unlearnable, redundant, or excessively transferable tasks that mask genuine continual-learning behavior, creating a need for a principled, reproducible scenario design methodology.
AI.method: The proposed framework operates in three stages: (1) candidate task discovery from existing tabular anomaly-detection datasets, (2) filtering of unsuitable tasks based on learnability, redundancy, and transferability criteria, and (3) derivation of principled ordering strategies that expose diverse continual-learning dynamics. The framework is instantiated on three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets.
AI.result: The framework yields five benchmark-ready scenarios spanning both single-dataset and multi-dataset CAD settings, derived from three large-scale cybersecurity anomaly detection datasets.
AI.conclusion: Principled task design is essential for meaningful CAD evaluation in tabular domains. The proposed framework enables reproducible, diverse, and diagnostically valuable benchmarks that better reveal genuine continual-learning capabilities.

title: Mark, Don't Erase: Token Inoculation for Dual-Use Knowledge in LLMs
summary: Safety interventions on dual-use knowledge typically choose between destroying hazardous content (e.g., unlearning, filtering) and suppressing it at the output layer (e.g., refusal training); both pay a tax in adjacent-domain competence or over-refusal. We argue that the right operation is conditioning, not reduction: we show that hazardous knowledge can be retained in the model and behaviorally gated by a privileged control token. Our method, Token Inoculation, introduces a binding-and-branching approach. First, during continued pre-training, we mark hazardous content by inserting a special token alongside dual-use documents, so the model binds the marker to the underlying semantics of the hazardous domain. Second, during supervised fine-tuning, we teach the model to answer hazardous queries correctly when the special token is present and to refuse them when it is absent, thereby enabling selective refusal without removing dual-use knowledge. On hazardous domain (e.g., WMDP-Bio), Token Inoculation reduces accuracy from 79% to 18% while retaining 93% of the base-model's benign-domain performance (e.g., MMLU), achieving the best safety-utility trade-off against unlearning and refusal-tuning baselines across 1B-14B model scales. We further show that refusal selectivity is controllable through the quality of the conditioning signal and that domain-specific semantic binding during pre-training is critical for the conditional behavior to generalize beyond memorized triggers. Our results suggest that safety alignment is better cast as a conditioning problem than a forgetting one: behavioral control is more precise when sensitive knowledge is retained under controlled access than when it is destroyed.

AI.tldr: Token Inoculation proposes a conditioning-based safety method that binds hazardous knowledge to a special control token during pre-training, then trains selective refusal via SFT. The model answers hazardous queries only when the token is present, achieving superior safety-utility trade-offs (79%→18% hazardous accuracy, 93% benign retention) compared to unlearning and refusal baselines across 1B-14B scales.
AI.motivation: Existing safety interventions for dual-use knowledge—unlearning/filtering (destroying content) and refusal training (output suppression)—both incur costs: the former degrades adjacent-domain competence, the latter causes over-refusal. The authors argue that the fundamental operation should be conditioning (retaining knowledge with gated access) rather than reduction (destroying or suppressing knowledge).
AI.method: Token Inoculation uses a two-stage binding-and-branching pipeline. Stage 1 (binding): During continued pre-training, a special control token is inserted alongside dual-use documents, causing the model to bind the token's representation to the hazardous domain's semantics. Stage 2 (branching): During SFT, the model is trained to answer hazardous queries correctly when the special token is present and to refuse when it is absent, enabling conditional access without knowledge destruction.
AI.result: On WMDP-Bio (hazardous domain), Token Inoculation reduces accuracy from 79% to 18% while retaining 93% of base-model MMLU performance, achieving the best safety-utility trade-off against unlearning and refusal-tuning baselines at 1B-14B scales. Key findings: refusal selectivity is controllable via conditioning signal quality; domain-specific semantic binding during pre-training (not mere memorization) is critical for generalization beyond memorized triggers.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment should be reframed as a conditioning problem rather than a forgetting problem. Retaining sensitive knowledge under controlled, token-gated access yields more precise behavioral control than destroying it, preserving broad competence while enabling selective refusal.

title: OpenRTAG: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Data Quality Degradation
summary: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs) are an important graph data form that combine relational structure with rich node text. However, real-world TAGs are often imperfect, with quality issues arising from text, structure, and labels, and typically manifesting as sparsity, noise, and imbalance. These dimensions define nine representative degradation scenarios that can substantially affect TAG learning. Although prior studies have explored specific mitigation strategies, existing evidence remains fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and model families, leaving TAG robustness insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we present OpenRTAG, a robustness benchmark for text-attributed graph learning. OpenRTAG organizes TAG quality issues into a unified 3 * 3 taxonomy and supports standardized evaluation across nine TAG datasets and three downstream tasks. It systematically evaluates scenario validity and model sensitivity, compares traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative GFM, investigates the effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness of scenario-matched baselines, and further examines model behavior under composite degradation scenarios. OpenRTAG provides a standardized testbed for understanding robustness in TAG learning under realistic low-quality settings.

AI.tldr: OpenRTAG is a standardized benchmark for evaluating robustness in text-attributed graph (TAG) learning. It introduces a unified 3×3 taxonomy of quality degradation (sparsity, noise, imbalance across text, structure, and labels), supports evaluation across nine datasets and three tasks, compares GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and graph foundation models, and examines both single and composite degradation scenarios.
AI.motivation: Real-world TAGs often suffer from quality issues across text, structure, and labels — manifesting as sparsity, noise, and imbalance. Existing mitigation strategies are fragmented across degradation types, datasets, tasks, and model families, leaving the robustness of TAG learning insufficiently understood. A unified, standardized benchmark is needed to systematically assess model behavior under realistic low-quality conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose a 3×3 taxonomy (three quality dimensions: text, structure, labels × three degradation types: sparsity, noise, imbalance), yielding nine representative degradation scenarios. They construct OpenRTAG with nine TAG datasets and three downstream tasks, then systematically evaluate (1) scenario validity and model sensitivity, (2) performance of traditional GNNs, LLM-GNNs, and a representative graph foundation model (GFM), (3) effectiveness/efficiency/robustness of scenario-matched mitigation baselines, and (4) model behavior under composite (multi-factor) degradation.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals that different model families exhibit distinct sensitivity profiles across the nine degradation scenarios, that scenario-matched baselines vary substantially in their effectiveness-efficiency-robustness trade-offs, and that composite degradation scenarios produce non-trivial interactions not predictable from single-factor results alone.
AI.conclusion: OpenRTAG provides a much-needed standardized testbed for robustness research in TAG learning, highlighting that no single model family or mitigation strategy uniformly dominates across all degradation scenarios, and that composite degradation warrants deeper investigation.

title: SechKAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hyperbolic Secant Functions
summary: In recent years, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have attracted increasing attention due to their effectiveness in machine learning and scientific computing tasks, offering a new paradigm for neural network design. In this paper, we present SechKAN, a KAN architecture based on hyperbolic secant (sech) functions. The hyperbolic secant basis is used for its smooth bell-shaped form, localized responses, and stable gradients. We employ 1D linear transformations to reduce the number of parameters, allowing SechKAN to remain comparable to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in model size. Experimental results indicate the effectiveness of SechKAN in function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification tasks on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100. SechKAN achieves superior performance compared to MLPs and other KAN variants while maintaining a similar number of parameters. However, its running time, while better than that of other KAN variants, is slightly longer than that of MLPs.

AI.tldr: SechKAN introduces a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network architecture using hyperbolic secant (sech) basis functions, achieving superior performance over MLPs and other KAN variants on function fitting, PDE solving, and image classification while maintaining comparable parameter counts, with a slight runtime trade-off.
AI.motivation: KANs offer a promising new paradigm for neural network design with effectiveness in ML and scientific computing. However, existing KAN variants face challenges in parameter efficiency and runtime performance compared to MLPs. The authors aim to improve upon these limitations by leveraging the desirable properties of the hyperbolic secant function.
AI.method: The authors propose SechKAN, which uses the hyperbolic secant (sech) function as the basis for its activation functions, chosen for its smooth bell-shaped form, localized responses, and stable gradients. To control model size, 1D linear transformations are employed to reduce parameter counts, keeping SechKAN comparable in size to MLPs.
AI.result: SechKAN achieves superior performance compared to MLPs and other KAN variants on function fitting, PDE problems, and image classification benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100), while maintaining similar parameter counts. Runtime is better than other KAN variants but slightly slower than MLPs.
AI.conclusion: SechKAN demonstrates that using hyperbolic secant basis functions within a parameter-efficient KAN framework yields strong empirical results across diverse tasks, offering a competitive alternative to both MLPs and existing KAN architectures, though runtime optimization remains an area for future improvement.

title: Comparative Study of Multi-Agent Actor-Critic Algorithms in Parameterized Action Reinforcement Learning
summary: Parameterized action reinforcement learning has shown strong performance in environments requiring both discrete action selection and continuous parameterization. Prior work established the effectiveness of single-agent actor-critic algorithms - Greedy Actor-Critic (GAC), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), and Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC) - on benchmark parameterized action tasks, but their extension to multi-agent settings remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a comparative study of shared-experience multi-agent extensions of these algorithms: Multi-Agent Greedy Actor-Critic (MAGAC), Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic (MASAC), and Multi-Agent Truncated Quantile Critics (MATQC). Rather than following the centralized training, decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm, the proposed framework uses multiple independent actor-critic agents that share a replay buffer while maintaining separate policy and value networks. We evaluate the algorithms on the Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 benchmarks against their single-agent counterparts, using three-, five-, and ten-agent configurations to assess scalability. Performance is measured by average evaluation return and training time across ten independent runs, with one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc tests used to assess statistical significance. Results show that the multi-agent framework consistently improves Greedy Actor-Critic performance, while MASAC and MATQC show comparatively modest gains over their single-agent versions. Increasing the number of agents beyond five yields limited additional performance while substantially raising computational cost, particularly for MAGAC. These results highlight a trade-off between learning performance and computational efficiency, offering insight into the scalability of shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic methods for parameterized action reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: This paper extends three single-agent parameterized action actor-critic algorithms (GAC, SAC, TQC) to shared-experience multi-agent variants (MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC) and benchmarks them on Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 tasks, finding that MAGAC benefits most from multi-agent extension, while scaling beyond five agents yields diminishing returns with increased computational cost.
AI.motivation: While parameterized action reinforcement learning (RL) — combining discrete action selection with continuous parameterization — has been effectively addressed by algorithms like GAC, SAC, and TQC in single-agent settings, their extension to multi-agent domains remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating whether shared-experience multi-agent variants can outperform their single-agent counterparts.
AI.method: The authors propose multi-agent extensions (MAGAC, MASAC, MATQC) where multiple independent actor-critic agents share a single replay buffer but maintain separate policy and value networks — departing from the standard CTDE paradigm. They evaluate these algorithms on Platform-v0 and Goal-v0 benchmarks across 3-, 5-, and 10-agent configurations, measuring average evaluation return and training time over ten independent runs, with statistical significance assessed via one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc tests.
AI.result: MAGAC shows the most consistent and substantial improvement from the multi-agent framework, while MASAC and MATQC exhibit only modest gains over their single-agent versions. Increasing agent count beyond five yields diminishing performance returns while significantly raising computational cost, especially for MAGAC.
AI.conclusion: Shared-experience multi-agent actor-critic methods present a viable approach for parameterized action RL, but they involve a clear trade-off between learning performance and computational efficiency. MAGAC benefits most from multi-agent extension, and scaling beyond five agents is generally not cost-effective.

title: Dual-domain fused LSTM modeling for efficient time-dependent reliability analysis
summary: Time-dependent reliability analysis is crucial for ensuring the long-term safety and performance of engineering systems under uncertainties. However, traditional surrogate model methods often struggle to incorporate time-independent random variables and capture their complex interactions with time-dependent stochastic processes. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a dual-domain fused long short-term memory (DDF-LSTM) model for efficient and accurate time-dependent reliability analysis. A novel network architecture is developed to jointly process information from both time-dependent and time-independent domains. Specifically, the time-independent variables are embedded into the initial hidden states, and a fully connected layer is introduced to map both LSTM outputs and time-independent variables into the final output space. Furthermore, an improved loss function is designed to emphasize the model's sensitivity to minimum responses, thereby improving the precision of failure probability estimation. The proposed method effectively captures the dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and the temporal behavior of limit state functions. Once trained, the DDF-LSTM model enables efficient Monte Carlo simulation to estimate time-dependent failure probabilities with minimal computational cost. Four case studies validate the proposed method's enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes a dual-domain fused LSTM (DDF-LSTM) that jointly processes time-dependent stochastic processes and time-independent random variables for efficient time-dependent reliability analysis, using embedded initial states, a fused output layer, and a minimum-response-sensitive loss function.
AI.motivation: Traditional surrogate models for time-dependent reliability analysis struggle to incorporate time-independent random variables and fail to capture their complex interactions with time-dependent stochastic processes, limiting accuracy and applicability.
AI.method: The DDF-LSTM architecture embeds time-independent variables into the initial hidden states of the LSTM and maps both LSTM outputs and time-independent variables through a fully connected layer into the final output space. An improved loss function emphasizes sensitivity to minimum responses. Once trained, the surrogate enables efficient Monte Carlo simulation for failure probability estimation.
AI.result: Four case studies demonstrate the proposed DDF-LSTM method achieves enhanced computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to traditional surrogate approaches in time-dependent reliability analysis.
AI.conclusion: The DDF-LSTM effectively captures dependencies among random variables, stochastic processes, and temporal limit state behavior, enabling accurate and computationally efficient time-dependent failure probability estimation.

title: Stale but Stable: Staleness-Adaptive Trust Regions for Stabilizing Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Asynchronous reinforcement learning improves throughput by decoupling rollout generation from optimization, but staleness is an inevitable byproduct compounded by policy lag, engine delays, and mixture-of-experts routing. From a trust-region perspective, this mismatch is critical: training-inference divergence governs approximation error in finite-horizon bounds, whereas PPO clipping only gates sampled outward updates, acting as a sampled surrogate rather than a full-policy constraint. As a result, high-staleness updates remain weakly controlled in the asynchronous regime where stale rollouts matter most.
  We introduce the Staleness-Adaptive Trust Region (SAT), which uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a practical staleness proxy, identifies high-mismatch tails within each batch via staleness-based kernel scaling, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval. This preserves baseline behavior on ordinary tokens while enforcing more conservative updates on newly intercepted outward bands. We prove local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO, showing how the adaptive rule reshapes update geometry under heterogeneous staleness.
  We evaluate SAT in a decoupled asynchronous RL setup built on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, using SGLang as the inference engine and Megatron for training. In this setting, SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieves the best observed AIME24 avg@8, reaching 35.83 at lag 1 and 34.79 at lag 8, while SAT-GSPO reaches 34.17 at lag 1. Adaptive clipping and routing replay act as complementary stabilizers targeting mismatch tails and routing inconsistency, respectively. Overall, aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity effectively stabilizes asynchronous RL.

AI.tldr: SAT adaptively shrinks PPO's clipping interval based on a staleness proxy (detached sampled log-ratio), targeting high-mismatch tails while preserving baseline behavior on ordinary tokens. This stabilizes asynchronous RL by aligning trust-region constraints with heterogeneous staleness, achieving strong results (AIME24 avg@8 up to 35.83) on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base with decoupled SGLang inference and Megatron training.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous RL improves throughput via decoupled rollout and optimization, but staleness from policy lag, engine delays, and MoE routing creates train-inference mismatch. PPO clipping only acts as a sampled surrogate on outward updates, not a full-policy constraint, leaving high-staleness updates weakly controlled precisely when stale rollouts are most damaging. A trust-region mechanism that adapts to staleness heterogeneity is needed.
AI.method: SAT uses the detached sampled log-ratio as a staleness proxy, applies staleness-based kernel scaling to identify high-mismatch tails within each batch, and contracts only the sign-selected endpoint of the nominal PPO interval. This yields local interval containment and pointwise pessimism relative to PPO. The method is paired with adaptive clipping and routing replay as complementary stabilizers (targeting mismatch tails and routing inconsistency, respectively).
AI.result: In a decoupled async RL setup (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, SGLang inference, Megatron training), SAT-GSPO w/ R3 achieves AIME24 avg@8 of 35.83 (lag 1) and 34.79 (lag 8); SAT-GSPO reaches 34.17 (lag 1). Adaptive clipping and routing replay provide complementary stabilization.
AI.conclusion: Aligning clip intervals with staleness heterogeneity via SAT effectively stabilizes asynchronous RL, preserving baseline behavior while enforcing conservative updates on high-mismatch tails. The approach is both theoretically grounded (interval containment, pointwise pessimism) and empirically validated at scale.

title: Is EEG-to-Text Feasible in Real-World Scenarios? An In-Depth Analysis Using a Neuropsychology-Inspired Benchmark
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures. Published in Proceedings of ACL 2026 Main Conference
summary: Translating brain signals into text could restore communication for people with severe paralysis, yet practically usable systems to date rely on invasive electrocorticography (ECoG). Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive alternative, and EEG-to-text (EEG2Text) has been widely explored. Interestingly, however, EEG2Text models generally rely on teacher-forcing evaluation; without it, they fail to generate meaningful decoding. This reliance prevents EEG2Text from being applied in real-world, non-academic settings. This has fueled numerous debates about whether EEG2Text is a meaningful direction, by extension, and whether EEG truly contains decodable linguistic information. Here, using a neuropsychology-informed paradigm, we find that existing EEG2Text benchmarks have neglected EEG instability, a flaw that has confounded inference and sparked debate. Our experiments furnish key evidence for the feasibility of teacher-forcing-free EEG2Text decoding. Accordingly, we assemble the Corpus OF Eeg-To-Text (COFETT) using a 128-channel high-density EEG cap, providing a benchmark dedicated to evaluating EEG2Text models. In comparisons with multiple existing benchmarks, COFETT achieves SOTA ability to distinguish among model performances and enables robust, teacher-forcing-free evaluation, thereby opening a path toward practical EEG2Text applications. COFETT is open sourced in https://github.com/baoyudu/COFETT.

AI.tldr: Existing EEG-to-text models rely on teacher-forcing evaluation and fail without it, casting doubt on whether EEG contains linguistic information. The authors identify EEG instability as the neglected confound, provide evidence for teacher-forcing-free decoding, and introduce COFETT, a 128-channel high-density EEG benchmark that enables robust, teacher-forcing-free evaluation and distinguishes model performance better than prior benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Non-invasive EEG-to-text could restore communication for paralyzed individuals, but current models depend on teacher-forcing evaluation and fail to generate meaningful output without it. This has sparked debate about whether EEG truly encodes linguistic information and whether EEG2Text is a viable direction at all.
AI.method: The authors employ a neuropsychology-informed paradigm to analyze why existing EEG2Text models fail under free-running decoding. They identify EEG instability (e.g., non-stationarity across trials/sessions) as the overlooked confound. They then construct COFETT using a 128-channel high-density EEG cap, designed specifically for benchmarking EEG2Text models with teacher-forcing-free evaluation protocols.
AI.result: Experiments show that EEG instability has confounded inference in prior benchmarks. Evidence supports the feasibility of teacher-forcing-free EEG2Text decoding. COFETT achieves state-of-the-art ability to discriminate among model performances and enables robust evaluation without teacher forcing.
AI.conclusion: EEG2Text is a meaningful direction once EEG instability is properly addressed. COFETT provides a standardized, open-source benchmark that opens a path toward practical, real-world EEG-to-text applications.

title: BioSecBench-Surveillance: A Verifiable Benchmark for AI Agents in Pathogen Genomic Surveillance
summary: As pathogen genomic surveillance scales, the bottleneck is shifting from data generation to analysis. We present BioSecBench-Surveillance, a verifiable benchmark of 100 evaluations testing whether AI agents can infer the right analysis pipeline from raw sequencing data and surveillance context. Each evaluation gives an agent only the data and context a human analyst would have, then grades its structured answer deterministically. The tasks span seven categories, from taxonomic classification to genetic-engineering detection, across diverse sample types and sequencing technologies. Across 3,962 gradable attempts from sixteen model-harness pairs, the strongest configuration cleared only about half. Opus 4.8 with PI led at 50.2 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.1 to 60.3 percent across 83 evaluations, tied with GPT-5.5 with Codex at 50.2 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.8 to 59.6 percent, followed by Opus 4.7 with PI at 49.6 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 40.0 to 59.2 percent, and Sonnet 4.6 with PI at 48.6 percent, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 38.9 to 58.3 percent. Even when agents invoked the correct workflows, their mistakes came from the choices around them, such as which references, thresholds, filters, and normalization to apply. BioSecBench-Surveillance provides a standard for measuring whether agents can be trusted to perform genomic surveillance when the next outbreak arrives.

AI.tldr: BioSecBench-Surveillance is a benchmark of 100 verifiable evaluations testing whether AI agents can autonomously determine correct analysis pipelines from raw pathogen genomic sequencing data and surveillance context. The strongest AI configuration achieved only ~50% accuracy, with errors stemming from parameter choices (references, thresholds, filters, normalization) even when correct workflows were identified.
AI.motivation: As pathogen genomic surveillance scales, the bottleneck has shifted from data generation to analysis. There is a need to assess whether AI agents can be trusted to autonomously select and configure appropriate bioinformatics pipelines for genomic surveillance, particularly in outbreak scenarios where timely and accurate analysis is critical.
AI.method: The authors created BioSecBench-Surveillance, a benchmark comprising 100 evaluations across seven task categories (taxonomic classification, genetic-engineering detection, etc.) spanning diverse sample types and sequencing technologies. Each evaluation provides an AI agent with only the raw sequencing data and surveillance context that a human analyst would receive. Answers are graded deterministically against a structured answer format. Sixteen model-harness pairs were tested across 3,962 gradable attempts.
AI.result: The strongest configurations achieved only about 50% accuracy: Opus 4.8 with PI and GPT-5.5 with Codex both scored 50.2% (with overlapping confidence intervals), followed by Opus 4.7 with PI (49.6%) and Sonnet 4.6 with PI (48.6%). Even when agents correctly identified the appropriate workflows, they made errors in surrounding parameter choices such as reference selection, thresholds, filters, and normalization strategies.
AI.conclusion: BioSecBench-Surveillance establishes a standardized framework for evaluating whether AI agents can reliably perform genomic surveillance analysis.
