Current state-of-the-art models fall short of trustworthy autonomous operation, highlighting the need for improved agent capabilities in workflow parameterization before they can be deployed in outbreak response settings.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for AI-Driven Crash Simulation Surrogates: A Comparative Study of Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensemble on Open-Source Bumper Beam Benchmark
summary: Machine learning surrogate models are increasingly being explored in engineering product development to augment simulation-driven design, offering near-instantaneous predictions that complement computationally expensive high-fidelity analyses. However, a critical gap limits their adoption in safety-critical workflows: a point prediction without an accompanying uncertainty estimate cannot tell an engineer when the model should not be trusted. This work presents a systematic, head-to-head comparison of two widely used uncertainty quantification approaches -- Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles -- applied to an open-source surrogate pipeline built on NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. A key contribution is the use of concrete dropout, a built-in PhysicsNeMo capability that eliminates the dropout rate as a manual hyperparameter by learning it end-to-end during training, directly addressing the most common criticism of Monte Carlo Dropout-based uncertainty quantification. Automotive crash simulation is used as the application domain, with a steel bumper beam impact problem serving as the benchmark. Both methods are evaluated on identical held-out simulations and compared on point accuracy, uncertainty band calibration, and computational cost. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration that challenges the common assumption that deep ensembles are the default gold standard for surrogate uncertainty quantification. The findings demonstrate that well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates are achievable within a fully open-source engineering workflow at a fraction of the computational cost of ensemble approaches.

AI.tldr: Head-to-head comparison of Monte Carlo Dropout (with concrete dropout) vs. Deep Ensembles for uncertainty quantification in ML surrogate models for automotive crash simulation. Concrete dropout eliminates manual hyperparameter tuning; results reveal a trade-off between accuracy and calibration, challenging the assumption that Deep Ensembles are always superior.
AI.motivation: ML surrogate models offer fast predictions for engineering design but lack reliable uncertainty estimates, which is critical for safety-critical applications. The gap is that engineers cannot know when to trust a point prediction. There is also a need to address the criticism that Monte Carlo Dropout requires manual tuning of the dropout rate, and to test whether Deep Ensembles truly represent the gold standard for surrogate UQ.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of two UQ methods — Monte Carlo Dropout (using concrete dropout via NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, which learns dropout rate during training) and Deep Ensembles — on an open-source surrogate pipeline. Benchmark: steel bumper beam impact in automotive crash simulation. Evaluation on held-out data across three dimensions: point prediction accuracy, uncertainty band calibration, and computational cost.
AI.result: A fundamental trade-off between accuracy and calibration was found. Deep Ensembles are not always the gold standard; concrete dropout provides well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free uncertainty estimates at significantly lower computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Well-calibrated, hyperparameter-free UQ is achievable in an open-source engineering workflow using concrete dropout, offering a computationally cheaper alternative to Deep Ensembles without sacrificing calibration quality.

title: LLM Detection as an Intervention: Downstream Impact under Strategic User Behavior
summary: As LLM adoption becomes more widespread, there is a growing interest in detecting LLM-generated content, for example through LLM detection tools and through heuristics based on language patterns. Detectors operate as an intervention that steers not only the detected attribute itself, but also downstream metrics such as LLM usage and output quality. In this work, we demonstrate how imperfect LLM detectors lead to counterintuitive impacts on these downstream metrics, by distorting how users are incentivized to use LLMs in their workflow. We develop a stylized model which captures how users strategically choose how much to use the LLM and how to post-process content to reduce the detected attribute. Using this model, we show that LLM detection can counterintuitively lead humans to increase their LLM usage. Moreover, even when reducing the detected attribute improves output quality, we find that introducing an LLM detector can lead users to produce lower quality outputs. In contrast, we show that detectors result in a clean "rise-then-fall" pattern for the detected attribute, which we empirically reproduce for word frequencies on arXiv abstracts. Altogether, our work illustrates how LLM detection can distort LLM usage and output quality, uncovering failure modes when LLM detectors operate as an intervention on these downstream metrics.

AI.tldr: Imperfect LLM detectors can backfire: they may perversely increase LLM usage and degrade output quality, even when users strategically post-process content to evade detection. Only the detected attribute itself shows a predictable "rise-then-fall" pattern.
AI.motivation: As LLM adoption grows, detection tools are deployed to identify LLM-generated content. However, these detectors act as interventions that alter user incentives, potentially distorting not just detection rates but also downstream metrics like LLM usage and output quality in unexpected ways.
AI.method: The authors develop a stylized theoretical model where users strategically choose (1) how much LLM assistance to use and (2) how much post-processing effort to exert to evade detection. The model captures the interplay between imperfect detector accuracy, user optimization, and resulting equilibrium outcomes across three metrics: detected attribute levels, LLM usage intensity, and output quality.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) LLM detection can paradoxically increase LLM usage; (2) even when evasion improves output quality, introducing a detector can reduce overall output quality; (3) the detected attribute follows a clean "rise-then-fall" curve as detection stringency increases, a pattern empirically validated using word frequency analysis on arXiv abstracts.
AI.conclusion: LLM detectors can produce counterproductive effects on the very metrics they aim to improve, revealing critical failure modes when detectors function as interventions. Policymakers and platforms should account for strategic user responses when designing detection-based governance mechanisms.

title: On the Limits of Support-Preserving Alignment and Bounded Filtering
summary: We study whether alignment schemes that reshape a base model's output distribution, combined with bounded safety filters, can drive the probability of harmful behavior to zero in modern large language models. Recent research suggests that harmful behaviors can persist under preference-based alignment and that external filtering can be computationally hard in the worst case, but it remains unclear whether practical alignment pipelines that largely preserve internal representations can eliminate harmful behavior entirely rather than merely suppressing its most visible forms. We formalize this setting using support-preserving alignment operators together with bounded filtering algorithms under black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access, and analyze their ability to approximate an ideal eliminator that removes all harmful mass. Building on this framework, we provide computational and information-theoretic arguments indicating that, under these constraints, bounded filtering may fail to eliminate all harmful outputs supported by the base model's distribution. To evaluate these limits empirically, we analyze a range of state-of-the-art open-weight and hosted LLMs accessed via OpenRouter under bounded black-box, white-box, and statistical-query filters on adversarial prompts drawn from curated cybersecurity scenarios and PKU-SafeRLHF. Across models, filter classes, and query budgets, the estimated harmful-output rate decreases with additional filtering compute but consistently plateaus above zero, suggesting a persistent empirical harm floor.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether alignment methods combined with bounded safety filters can fully eliminate harmful outputs from LLMs. Through both theoretical analysis and empirical testing across multiple models and filter types, the authors find a persistent "harm floor" — harmful outputs cannot be entirely removed under practical constraints.
AI.motivation: Recent work shows harmful behaviors persist under preference-based alignment, and external filtering can be computationally hard. However, it remains unclear whether practical alignment pipelines that largely preserve internal representations can truly eliminate harmful behavior rather than just suppress its most visible forms. The authors aim to formally characterize this gap.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem using support-preserving alignment operators and bounded filtering algorithms under three access models: black-box, white-box, and statistical-query access. They provide computational and information-theoretic arguments about the limits of bounded filtering. Empirically, they evaluate open-weight and hosted LLMs (via OpenRouter) using adversarial prompts from curated cybersecurity scenarios and the PKU-SafeRLHF benchmark, measuring harmful-output rates under varying filter classes and query budgets.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis suggests bounded filtering cannot eliminate all harmful outputs supported by the base model's distribution. Empirically, across all models, filter classes, and query budgets, the estimated harmful-output rate decreases with additional filtering compute but consistently plateaus above zero, revealing a persistent empirical harm floor.
AI.conclusion: Under the studied constraints of support-preserving alignment and bounded filtering, fully eliminating harmful behavior from LLMs appears infeasible. The consistent nonzero harm floor across diverse empirical settings corroborates the theoretical limits, suggesting that current safety mechanisms can only suppress — not eradicate — harmful capabilities.

title: A Better Start for Language Models: Domain-Conditional Position Offsets
summary: Autoregressive language models are least accurate at the beginning of a sequence, where little context forces reliance on a generic pretraining prior. We show that this cold-start penalty is domain dependent and reduce it with a domain-conditional position offset: a single learned vector added to the embedding activation at the first sequence positions while all model weights remain frozen. The offset trains in minutes on roughly one hundred documents, switches between domains without added sequence state, and has no measurable latency overhead. Across eight Mamba, GPT-NeoX, and Llama models spanning 410M to 8B parameters, it reduces held-out in-domain perplexity by up to 27%; the effect persists at 70B, and one position captures most of the benefit. A matched, converged direct logit-bias correction reaches at most only 7.9% and leaves later-token loss unchanged, showing that the offset propagates through model state rather than merely recalibrating the output prior. A tuned LoRA reaches lower perplexity but uses two to three orders of magnitude more parameters and an active low-rank weight path, while soft prompts add sequence positions. With wrong-domain controls, offsets improve retrieval reranking and domain classification when decisions depend on early in-domain tokens, For the few-shot reasoning whose signal occurs later, the results maintains unchanged. Position-aware prefill application also help generation tasks, whereas naive application at every cached decoding step causes repetition. The offset is therefore not the strongest adapter, but a lightweight, hot switchable tool for short in-domain scoring and calibration.

AI.tldr: Language models suffer a "cold-start" penalty at the beginning of sequences due to insufficient context. This paper proposes a domain-conditional position offset—a single learned vector added to early-position embeddings with frozen model weights—that trains in minutes, switches domains seamlessly, and reduces in-domain perplexity by up to 27% across various model architectures and scales, outperforming logit-bias corrections while being far more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LMs are least accurate at sequence beginnings because they must rely on generic pretraining priors rather than domain-specific context. The authors aim to characterize this "cold-start" penalty as domain-dependent and provide a lightweight, rapidly trainable, and easily switchable correction mechanism that addresses this early-token degradation without modifying model weights or adding inference latency.
AI.method: The proposed method is a domain-conditional position offset: for each domain, a single learned vector is added to the embedding activation at the first few sequence positions. All model weights remain frozen. The offset is trained in minutes on ~100 documents per domain. It switches between domains without additional sequence state. Comparisons are made against: (1) direct logit-bias correction, (2) LoRA fine-tuning, (3) soft prompts. Evaluations span eight models (Mamba, GPT-NeoX, Llama) from 410M to 8B parameters, with additional verification at 70B. Tasks include perplexity, retrieval reranking, domain classification, few-shot reasoning, and text generation.
AI.result: The position offset reduces held-out in-domain perplexity by up to 27% across all tested models. At 70B scale, the effect persists with a single position capturing most of the benefit. A matched logit-bias correction achieves at most 7.9% improvement and leaves later-token loss unchanged, indicating the offset propagates through model state rather than merely recalibrating the output prior. LoRA reaches lower perplexity but uses 2–3 orders of magnitude more parameters and an active low-rank weight path. Soft prompts add sequence positions. On retrieval reranking and domain classification (decisions depending on early in-domain tokens), offsets improve performance; on few-shot reasoning (signal occurs later), results remain unchanged. For generation, position-aware prefill application helps, but naive application at every decoding step causes repetition.
AI.conclusion: The domain-conditional position offset is not the strongest adapter available, but it is a uniquely lightweight, hot-switchable tool optimized for short in-domain scoring and calibration tasks where early-token accuracy matters. It offers a compelling trade-off between efficacy and efficiency for domain adaptation of frozen language models.

title: HindsightBench: A Black-Box Behavioral Audit Protocol for Parametric Hindsight in Time-Indexed LLM Decision Tasks
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code, panel, and per-model audit rows: https://github.com/Khaozhe/hindsightbench (v1.0 release archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21453191)
summary: Large language models leak parametric knowledge of realized outcomes into historical financial decision tasks. Existence is settled; what users lack is a cheap way to audit a given model for it. We present HindsightBench, a black-box behavioral audit protocol that profiles parametric hindsight in any time-indexed LLM decision task at probe-level cost (no backtests, no logprobs, no corpus access). The protocol chains a four-arm date-manipulation matrix (revealed/date-only/masked/transplanted), dual memory probes (date recovery; outcome recall), and six per-model metrics -- trigger strength, transplant effect, post-cutoff placebo, recoverability, behaviorally effective knowledge cutoff, and a recall-accuracy dissociation coefficient -- with explicit gates where identifiability is data-dependent. Applying it to 15 models from seven vendors on a 258-node vintage-correct macro panel yields three headline patterns: (i) the date-trigger reflex tracks training generation, not scale -- absent across the 2024 open-weight generation from 1B to 70B, present in every tested 2026-generation model, and switching on within one vendor lineage (Qwen3 -> Qwen3.6) at fixed MoE architecture and 3B active parameters; (ii) effective cutoffs span 22 months across vendors and precede vendor-reported dates by up to eight months, invalidating calendar-window placebo designs; (iii) audit results are not invariant to serving -- BF16 serving of an FP8-referenced model breaks the trigger estimate's stability while AWQ-INT4 preserves it, and a provider-locked reasoning regime makes one probe non-convergent -- so the protocol ships with operational requirements (pin quantization and thinking regime; disclose parser and sampling policy). We release the panel, frozen preregistrations, per-model audit rows with measured dollar costs, transcripts, and one-command regeneration.

AI.tldr: HindsightBench is a lightweight black-box auditing protocol that detects parametric hindsight bias in LLMs by manipulating date information in historical financial tasks, tested across 15 models revealing that date-trigger reflexes track training generation rather than model scale.
AI.motivation: LLMs leak parametric knowledge of realized outcomes into historical financial decision tasks, but no cheap, accessible method exists to audit models for this hindsight bias. Existing approaches require backtests, logprobs, or corpus access — all impractical for most users. A probe-level black-box audit is needed.
AI.method: HindsightBench employs a four-arm date-manipulation matrix (revealed, date-only, masked, transplanted), dual memory probes (date recovery and outcome recall), and six per-model metrics (trigger strength, transplant effect, post-cutoff placebo, recoverability, behaviorally effective knowledge cutoff, and recall-accuracy dissociation coefficient) with explicit identifiability gates. Tested on a 258-node vintage-correct macro panel across 15 models from seven vendors.
AI.result: Three headline findings: (i) the date-trigger reflex tracks training generation, not scale — absent in 2024 open-weight models (1B–70B), present in all 2026-generation models, and switches on within Qwen3→Qwen3.6 at fixed MoE architecture; (ii) effective cutoffs span 22 months across vendors and precede vendor-reported dates by up to 8 months, invalidating calendar-window placebo designs; (iii) audit results are not invariant to serving — BF16 serving of an FP8-referenced model breaks trigger estimate stability while AWQ-INT4 preserves it, and provider-locked reasoning regimes cause probe non-convergence.
AI.conclusion: HindsightBench provides a practical, low-cost audit protocol for detecting parametric hindsight in LLMs, with findings that carry immediate methodological implications for financial LLM evaluation. The authors release the panel, preregistrations, audit rows with costs, transcripts, and reproducible tooling, alongside operational requirements for deployment.

title: Associative Emotional Learning in Convolutional Neural Networks
comment: The article has been accepted for publication in Neural Computation
summary: Associative emotional learning enables organisms to adaptively link pleasant or unpleasant outcomes to the presence of predictive stimuli. Whereas computational models such as the Rescorla-Wagner model have shed light on this important function, the limitations of these models are also known, especially when they are applied to neural data. The advent of deep neural networks has opened another avenue for modeling associative emotional learning. In this work we proposed a deep neural network model of visual valence processing, consisting of a visual module that encodes complex natural scenes and a module that recognizes their emotional significance in terms of valence, a key dimension of emotion, and tested a novel Pavlovian learning paradigm on the model. The results showed that with learning, the model reproduced several observations from human associative learning studies, including association formation and generalization, and that the neural representations of the conditioned and the unconditioned stimuli became increasingly aligned both at the single unit and at the neural population level. Comparison between the model and human experimental data provided further validation of our approach. This study thus suggests that deep neural network models, when combined with appropriate learning algorithms, can be used to model behavioral and neural signatures of associative emotion/valence learning.

AI.tldr: A deep neural network model combining visual scene encoding with valence recognition successfully reproduces human associative emotional learning phenomena, including association formation, generalization, and neural alignment between conditioned and unconditioned stimuli.
AI.motivation: Traditional computational models like Rescorla-Wagner have known limitations when applied to neural data. The authors aim to leverage deep neural networks as an alternative modeling framework for associative emotional/valence learning.
AI.method: A two-module deep neural network: (1) a visual module that encodes complex natural scenes, and (2) a valence recognition module that learns the emotional significance of stimuli. The model was tested using a novel Pavlovian learning paradigm and compared against human experimental data.
AI.result: The model reproduced key human associative learning phenomena — association formation and generalization. Neural representations of conditioned and unconditioned stimuli became increasingly aligned at both the single-unit and population levels after learning. Human experimental data further validated the model.
AI.conclusion: Deep neural networks combined with appropriate learning algorithms can effectively model both behavioral and neural signatures of associative emotion/valence learning, offering a promising alternative to classical computational models.

title: TD-DPO: Difference-Aware Preference Optimization for Mitigating Sycophancy in Clinical Autism Intervention Dialogue
summary: The sycophancy of large language models can increase the safety risk in intervention dialogue for autistic children. Supervised fine-tuning can somewhat reduce sycophancy, but relying solely on positive examples is often insufficient to identify and correct failure patterns. We observe that sycophancy behaviors can often be localized to a limited span within the model response. In this regime, sequence-level preference optimization can over-update preference-irrelevant tokens and degrade intervention ability. To address this, we propose the \textbf{M}inimal \textbf{E}dit \textbf{D}ata \textbf{A}ugmentation (MEDA) strategy to construct controlled, stable, minimal edit preference pairs and \textbf{T}oken-level \textbf{D}ifference \textbf{D}irect \textbf{P}reference \textbf{O}ptimization (TD-DPO), which upweights difference tokens between chosen and rejected responses while downweighting shared tokens to suppress background drift. Extensive experiments across multiple backbones and evaluators show that TD-DPO achieves a better trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and intervention ability retention in our offline settings, highlighting its potential as a practical alignment approach for autism intervention.

AI.tldr: To mitigate sycophancy in LLMs for autism intervention dialogues without degrading intervention quality, the authors propose MEDA for constructing minimal-edit preference pairs and TD-DPO, a token-level optimization that upweights differences between chosen/rejected responses while downweighting shared tokens to prevent background drift.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy in LLMs poses safety risks in intervention dialogues for autistic children. Supervised fine-tuning alone is insufficient to correct failure patterns, and standard sequence-level preference optimization (e.g., DPO) over-updates preference-irrelevant tokens, degrading the model's intervention ability. A more targeted optimization approach is needed.
AI.method: (1) MEDA (Minimal Edit Data Augmentation): constructs controlled preference pairs by making minimal, localized edits to model responses, ensuring preference-relevant changes are confined to limited spans. (2) TD-DPO (Token-level Difference Direct Preference Optimization): extends DPO by upweighting tokens that differ between chosen and rejected responses and downweighting shared tokens, suppressing gradient updates on irrelevant positions and mitigating background drift.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple backbones and evaluators demonstrate that TD-DPO achieves a superior trade-off between sycophancy mitigation and retention of intervention ability compared to baselines in offline settings.
AI.conclusion: TD-DPO, combined with the MEDA strategy, offers a practical alignment approach for autism intervention dialogue systems by effectively reducing sycophancy while preserving task-critical intervention capabilities.

title: H$^2$SD: Hybrid Hindsight Self-Distillation
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models on tasks such as mathematical reasoning and code generation. However, most RLVR methods assign a scalar outcome reward to an entire trajectory, resulting in sparse supervision and limited token-level credit assignment. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides denser supervision by distilling token-level distributions from a stronger teacher model, but requires an additional teacher and typically assumes a shared vocabulary. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes this dependency by conditioning the same model on privileged information to construct a teacher policy. However, directly matching the teacher distribution may cause information leakage and unstable optimization. RLSD avoids direct matching by using the teacher signal only to modulate update magnitudes, but it cannot provide an explicit correction direction when the sampled reasoning fails. To address this tradeoff, we introduce $\mathrm{H}^{2}\mathrm{SD}$, a hybrid hindsight self distillation framework that uses the teacher differently according to trajectory correctness. For successful trajectories, the teacher receives the student response confirmed as correct together with a rephrasing instruction, and its probabilities on the original response tokens are used to modulate update magnitudes without changing the direction determined by the reward. For failed trajectories, we condition the teacher on a reference hint containing key reasoning steps and a verified answer, and minimize the reverse KL divergence from the student to the teacher. Experiments on multiple challenging reasoning benchmarks show that H$^2$SD consistently outperforms representative RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD baselines while maintaining stable optimization and favorable generation efficiency.

AI.tldr: H²SD is a hybrid self-distillation framework for RLVR that applies different teacher supervision strategies based on trajectory correctness: magnitude modulation for successful trajectories and reverse KL minimization for failed ones, outperforming RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR methods suffer from sparse scalar rewards and poor token-level credit assignment. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers denser supervision but risks information leakage and instability via direct distribution matching. RLSD avoids direct matching but lacks explicit correction direction for failed reasoning. H²SD addresses this tradeoff by using the teacher signal differently depending on trajectory correctness.
AI.method: H²SD employs a hybrid approach: (1) For successful trajectories, the teacher (same model conditioned on the correct student response plus a rephrasing instruction) provides probability signals to modulate update magnitudes without altering the reward-determined gradient direction. (2) For failed trajectories, the teacher is conditioned on a reference hint containing key reasoning steps and a verified answer, and the student is optimized via minimizing reverse KL divergence from student to teacher, providing explicit correction.
AI.result: H²SD consistently outperforms representative RLVR, OPSD, and RLSD baselines across multiple challenging reasoning benchmarks while maintaining stable optimization and favorable generation efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid strategy of using teacher signals adaptively — modulation for success, correction for failure — effectively balances the tradeoff between dense supervision and optimization stability in RLVR for reasoning tasks.

title: Agents in the Wild: Where Research Meets Deployment
summary: Agentic systems large language model (LLM) based architectures capable of reasoning, planning, acting, and coordinating with tools and other agents are rapidly transitioning from research prototypes to production scale deployments across domains such as software engineering, scientific discovery, and finance. While academic work has emphasized benchmarks and algorithmic innovation, deployment raises new challenges around robustness, safety, and reliability. This tutorial brings together researchers and practitioners to explore advances in reasoning and planning, multi agent coordination, and evaluation, highlighting open challenges arising from deployment experience. Through applied case studies in pharmaceutical discovery and financial systems, we analyze common design patterns that make agentic systems successful, and discuss practical mitigation strategies for failure modes, such as verification pipelines, fallback mechanisms, and human in the loop supervision. Attendees will gain a comprehensive view of the field along with concrete design patterns, evaluation checklists, and templates for safe and reliable deployment across industries.

AI.tldr: A tutorial overview of deploying LLM-based agentic systems in production, covering reasoning, multi-agent coordination, and evaluation, with case studies in pharma and finance, and practical strategies for robustness, safety, and reliability.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems are moving rapidly from research to production, but deployment introduces challenges around robustness, safety, and reliability that academic benchmarks and algorithmic innovation alone do not address. There is a gap between research emphasis and practical deployment needs.
AI.method: The tutorial synthesizes advances in reasoning and planning, multi-agent coordination, and evaluation. It uses applied case studies in pharmaceutical discovery and financial systems to analyze common design patterns and discusses practical mitigation strategies including verification pipelines, fallback mechanisms, and human-in-the-loop supervision. It also provides evaluation checklists and deployment templates.
AI.result: Key findings include identification of common design patterns for successful agentic systems, catalogued failure modes, and corresponding mitigation strategies (verification pipelines, fallback mechanisms, human-in-the-loop supervision) validated through case studies in pharmaceutical discovery and finance.
AI.conclusion: Successful production deployment of agentic systems requires going beyond algorithmic performance to incorporate robust safety and reliability mechanisms. The tutorial equips practitioners with design patterns, evaluation checklists, and templates for safe cross-industry deployment.

title: The Information Shadow: Measuring Structural Limits on What Language Models Can Learn
summary: Some limits on what language models know are not gaps in data coverage but structural properties of learning from text. We introduce the information shadow: the region of phenomena that a text-trained learner cannot acquire regardless of scale, comprising (I) structures language cannot express, (II) functions that are statistically non-identifiable from the training distribution, and (III) functions that are representable but unreachable by gradient-based training. We give each type a probe that is decisive because the premise of the shadow is, in that setting, provable. For Type I, Language Compression Residuals compare a text learner, which sees only a lossy text-like encoding of the signal, against a full-signal learner, which sees the underlying signal directly. The text learner sits at a computable expressibility ceiling while the full-signal learner pulls away by a gap that stays flat across 300x more data, so the deficit is a property of the channel, not of training. For Type II, the Counterfactual Distinction Test trains models on data exactly consistent with two incompatible rules. Across a provable string task and a language-like agreement task, behavior on counterfactuals is set by the model's inductive bias, while 5% disambiguating data steers the learned rule bidirectionally to either target (r = +/-1.0, p < 1e-10). For Type III, Basin Escape Mapping exhibits a function that is representable at 100% (by hand construction) yet reached 0% of the time by standard training and instantly from a nearby initialization, with width scaling providing no help (p = 1.6 x 10^-14). Each effect is isolated by a control that rules out a capacity or modality artifact. We release the probe suite and discuss implications for benchmark design, capability auditing, and shadow-aware uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "information shadow" — a taxonomy of three structural limitations on what language models can learn from text, regardless of scale. These are: (I) phenomena language cannot encode, (II) functions statistically non-identifiable from training data, and (III) functions representable but unreachable via gradient-based training. Each type is demonstrated with a decisive, provable probe.
AI.motivation: To distinguish between knowledge gaps caused by insufficient data coverage and those caused by fundamental structural constraints inherent to learning from text. The authors argue that some limitations are not solvable by scaling alone, and that understanding these shadows is critical for benchmark design, capability auditing, and model uncertainty estimation.
AI.method: Three probe types are constructed, each isolating one category of the information shadow: (I) Language Compression Residuals — compares a text-trained learner (lossy encoding) against a full-signal learner (direct signal access), showing a persistent, flat gap across 300x data scaling; (II) Counterfactual Distinction Test — trains on data consistent with two incompatible rules and measures whether disambiguating data (5%) can steer learned behavior bidirectionally; (III) Basin Escape Mapping — identifies a function that is 100% hand-constructible yet never reached by standard training (0% rate), but instantly reachable from a nearby initialization, with width scaling providing no help.
AI.result: Type I: The text learner hits a computable expressibility ceiling; the gap to the full-signal learner remains flat across 300x more data. Type II: Counterfactual behavior is governed by inductive bias, but 5% disambiguating data steers the learned rule to either target with r = ±1.0 (p < 1e-10). Type III: The target function is reached 0% of the time by standard training vs. instantly from nearby initialization; width scaling does not help (p = 1.6×10⁻¹⁴). Controls rule out capacity or modality artifacts for all types.
AI.conclusion: The information shadow imposes hard, provable limits on text-based learners that cannot be overcome by scale alone. These findings carry concrete implications for benchmark construction, capability auditing, and developing shadow-aware uncertainty estimates in language models.

title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents increasingly operate in executable environments where a failed attempt produces actionable feedback rather than merely an incorrect answer. Existing cost-aware systems typically treat such failures as cascade decisions: try a cheap model first, then escalate hard cases to a stronger and more expensive model. In coding, however, execution feedback can also make further cheap-model recovery worthwhile, raising a budgeted deployment question: when should an agent spend more cheap compute, and when should it escalate? We formulate this post-failure decision as recovery routing over heterogeneous actions and train a supervised router from execution rollouts. To make the same router usable under changing budgets, we add a Conformal Risk Control (CRC) layer that selects a deployment-time cost penalty without retraining and provides marginal expected-cost control under exchangeability. Across held-out failures from five coding benchmarks, cheap recovery and escalation exhibit complementary success patterns. The calibrated frontier improves over fixed actions, prompt-only routers, and a binary cascade baseline; in the main GPT-5.4-nano/GPT-5.4 setting, one CRC-calibrated frontier point exceeds always-escalate solve rate while using 35% of its mean recovery cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Qijia-He/agent-budget-control.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses budget-efficient deployment of coding agents by formulating post-failure recovery as a routing problem between cheap retries and expensive model escalation. The authors introduce a supervised router trained on execution rollouts, augmented with a Conformal Risk Control layer that enables budget-adjustable deployment-time cost penalties without retraining, achieving strong cost-recovery trade-offs across five coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing cost-aware systems treat failures as binary cascade decisions (cheap-then-expensive). In coding domains, execution feedback (e.g., error messages, stack traces) makes further cheap-model recovery attempts viable, creating a nuanced budgeted deployment question: when should an agent spend more cheap compute on recovery versus escalating to a stronger model? No existing framework addresses this post-failure recovery routing with adjustable cost constraints.
AI.method: The authors formulate post-failure recovery as "recovery routing" over heterogeneous actions (cheap recovery attempts vs. expensive escalation). They train a supervised router using execution rollouts to decide which action to take given failure state. To enable deployment-time budget flexibility without retraining, they add a Conformal Risk Control (CRC) layer that selects a cost penalty parameter, providing marginal expected-cost control guarantees under the exchangeability assumption. The router is evaluated across held-out failures from five coding benchmarks.
AI.result: Cheap recovery and escalation exhibit complementary success patterns on held-out failures. The CRC-calibrated frontier improves over fixed-action baselines, prompt-only routers, and a binary cascade baseline. In the GPT-5.4-nano/GPT-5.4 setting, one calibrated frontier point matches or exceeds the always-escalate solve rate while consuming only 35% of its mean recovery cost.
AI.conclusion: Post-failure recovery routing with CRC calibration enables cost-effective deployment of coding agents under varying budgets. The approach unifies cheap recovery and expensive escalation into a single adaptive routing framework with formal cost-control guarantees, demonstrating that intelligent failure recovery can dramatically reduce costs without sacrificing solve rates.

title: Gradient-Energy Guided Block-Wise Perturbations for Sharpness-Aware Minimization
summary: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) improves generalization by minimizing the worst-case loss in a local parameter neighborhood. Standard SAM implicitly allocates its global perturbation budget across parameter blocks according to instantaneous minibatch gradient norms. Such an allocation can be noisy and may not reflect the sensitivity that blocks accumulate throughout training. We propose Gradient-Energy Adaptive Radius SAM (GEAR-SAM), which maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of squared block gradients as a lightweight, curvature-related sensitivity signal and allocates the fixed SAM budget through a closed-form constrained optimization. GEAR-SAM preserves the global SAM radius, requires no Hessian-vector products or explicit Fisher estimation, and adds only scalar state beyond SAM. Experiments on image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition studies demonstrate improved generalization and robustness across architectures and tasks. More broadly, GEAR-SAM provides a dynamic view of sharpness-aware optimization: a fixed perturbation budget should be redistributed as the sensitivity of functional network blocks evolves during training.

AI.tldr: GEAR-SAM replaces SAM's noisy, minibatch-based perturbation allocation with an EMA of squared block gradients, redistributing the fixed global budget via closed-form constrained optimization for improved generalization.
AI.motivation: Standard SAM allocates its global perturbation budget across parameter blocks based on instantaneous minibatch gradient norms, which is noisy and fails to capture the evolving sensitivity of network blocks throughout training. The authors aim to replace this with a more principled, stability-aware allocation.
AI.method: GEAR-SAM maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of squared block gradients as a lightweight curvature-related sensitivity signal. It then solves a closed-form constrained optimization problem to allocate the fixed global SAM perturbation budget across blocks proportionally to these accumulated sensitivity estimates, preserving the global radius without requiring Hessian-vector products or explicit Fisher estimation.
AI.result: Experiments across image classification, transfer learning, noisy-label learning, and partition studies show improved generalization and robustness over standard SAM across multiple architectures and tasks.
AI.conclusion: A fixed perturbation budget in sharpness-aware optimization should be dynamically redistributed according to how the sensitivity of functional network blocks evolves during training, rather than relying on instantaneous gradient norms.

title: Agentic Calibration of Grey-Box Simulation Models: An LLM-Driven Alternative
comment: Manuscript: 19 pages, 2 figures. Appendix: 11 pages, 1 figure
summary: Calibration of grey-box simulation models is a constrained optimization problem in which model evaluations are expensive, the parameter space can be high-dimensional, and the search must respect plausibility constraints. Although the simulation code is fully available to the analyst, the joint effect of multiple parameters remains difficult to predict analytically. Classical optimizers such as Nelder--Mead (NM) are simple to deploy but sample-inefficient, particularly under constraints. Modern Bayesian Optimization methods achieve competitive solutions with far fewer evaluations but require non-trivial modeling machinery for constraint handling. We introduce an agentic calibration method in which a large language model acts as the optimizer, with constraints incorporated as a plain-language section of the system prompt. We evaluate the agentic method, NM, and Bayesian Optimization (BO) on an anal cancer simulation model under both unconstrained and clinically constrained calibration. Under unconstrained calibration, the agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than BO and NM, while requiring fewer model evaluations. Under constrained calibration, the agentic method reaches comparable error levels and both outperform NM. These results are obtained at the cost of increased inference time per iteration. Agentic calibration achieves competitive performance with substantially fewer model evaluations, and constraint handling is essentially free at the modeller-facing interface through simple textual specifications rather than additional modelling machinery. The main trade-off lies in increased per-iteration inference cost, making the approach particularly suitable when simulation time dominates. Beyond performance, the per-iteration rationale makes the search auditable and explainable, so its decisions can be scrutinised and justified to third parties.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a large language model as the optimizer for grey-box simulation model calibration, with constraints specified in plain language. Compared to Nelder-Mead and Bayesian Optimization, the agentic method achieves lower error with fewer model evaluations, at the cost of higher per-iteration inference time. Constraint handling is simplified to textual specification.
AI.motivation: Grey-box simulation model calibration is challenging: model evaluations are expensive, parameter spaces are high-dimensional, and plausibility constraints must be respected. Classical optimizers like Nelder-Mead are simple but sample-inefficient, especially under constraints. Bayesian Optimization requires complex modeling machinery for constraint handling. The authors seek a method that is both sample-efficient and simple to deploy, particularly for constraint management.
AI.method: The authors introduce an agentic calibration method where a large language model (LLM) serves as the optimizer. Constraints are incorporated directly as plain-language instructions within the system prompt, eliminating the need for additional modeling machinery. The method is benchmarked against Nelder-Mead (NM) and Bayesian Optimization (BO) on an anal cancer simulation model under both unconstrained and clinically constrained calibration scenarios.
AI.result: Under unconstrained calibration, the agentic method achieves substantially lower best error than both BO and NM while requiring fewer model evaluations. Under constrained calibration, the agentic method and BO reach comparable error levels, and both outperform NM. The trade-off is increased per-iteration inference time, making the approach most suitable when simulation time dominates.
AI.conclusion: Agentic calibration delivers competitive optimization performance with significantly fewer model evaluations. Constraint handling becomes essentially free at the modeler-facing level through textual specifications. The per-iteration rationale produced by the LLM also makes the search process auditable and explainable. The approach is particularly well-suited when simulation runtime dominates inference cost.

title: AdaFlash: Adaptive Speculative Decoding via On-Policy Distilled Diffusion Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding, in which a lightweight draft model first generates a draft sequence that is then verified in parallel by the target model, has become a prevalent paradigm for accelerating large language model inference. Recent work such as DFlash further boosts drafting efficiency by leveraging diffusion drafters, whose parallel denoising mechanism enables draft generation in a single forward pass. In this work, we uncover a central pitfall of diffusion drafters: bidirectional attention is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it endows the model with parallel generation and global contextual modeling capabilities; on the other hand, this inherent global dependency introduces high variance at both the domain-level and the token-level: acceptance rates fluctuate substantially across different domains, and draft token quality also varies heterogeneously at different token positions. To tackle this issue, we propose AdaFlash framework, comprising two components: (i) an on-policy distillation (OPD) algorithm with reverse-KL divergence tailored for diffusion drafters, bringing stable convergence and effectively reducing domain-level variance; and (ii) an adaptive length head that dynamically adjusts the candidate sequence length on the fly, substantially lowering the verification cost of the target model and handling token-level variance. Experiments demonstrate that AdaFlash consistently improves speedup rate during deployment, with especially significant gains in high-concurrency scenarios, achieving up to approximately 66% higher throughput than previous state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: AdaFlash addresses a key weakness in diffusion-based speculative decoding: bidirectional attention causes high variance in draft quality across domains and token positions. It proposes on-policy distillation with reverse-KL divergence and an adaptive length head to mitigate this, achieving up to ~66% throughput improvement over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Diffusion drafters (e.g., DFlash) use bidirectional attention for efficient single-pass draft generation, but this same mechanism introduces a "double-edged sword" problem: global dependency leads to high domain-level variance (fluctuating acceptance rates across domains) and token-level variance (heterogeneous draft quality across positions). Existing methods lack mechanisms to handle this dual variance, limiting practical deployment gains.
AI.method: AdaFlash consists of two components: (1) On-Policy Distillation (OPD) — a distillation algorithm using reverse-KL divergence specifically designed for diffusion drafters, which stabilizes training convergence and reduces domain-level acceptance rate variance. (2) An adaptive length head — a dynamic mechanism that adjusts candidate sequence length on-the-fly during inference, reducing unnecessary target model verification cost and handling token-level quality variance.
AI.result: AdaFlash consistently improves speedup rates during deployment. Gains are especially pronounced in high-concurrency scenarios, achieving up to approximately 66% higher throughput compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The bidirectional attention mechanism in diffusion drafters, while enabling efficient parallel generation, inherently causes domain-level and token-level variance that hurts speculative decoding performance. AdaFlash effectively mitigates both sources of variance through OPD and adaptive length prediction, leading to substantial and consistent throughput improvements in real-world deployment settings.

title: Spatio-Temporal Prediction of Unsteady Airfoil Aerodynamics Using Augmented Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with Exogenous Controls
comment: 27 pages, 18 figures, submitted to Computers & Fluids
summary: Unsteady aerodynamic phenomena, such as gusts, turbulence, and fluid-structure interactions affect an aircraft during flight. For design, optimisation and certification, it is indispensable to quantify such unsteady aerodynamic effects. Industry-standard computational fluid dynamics methods, such as solving the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations or the linearized frequency domain method, are either computationally expensive or restricted by assumptions like linearity. Once trained, machine learning methods are capable of computing non-linear relationships very fast, making them suitable as surrogate models. By autoregressively applying graph neural networks (GNNs), operating on a discretised spatial domain, spatio-temporal predictions can be made. However, autoregressive GNNs suffer from error accumulation leading to unstable rollouts over time. Here we show that combining GNNs with augmented Neural Ordinary Differential Equations yields temporally stable predictions of the surface forces on a pitching airfoil. We found that our approach, called GNODE, based on Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, provides temporally more stable, spatially smoother, and overall more accurate results than an autoregressive GNN baseline. Tests are conducted on a dataset consisting of a simulations of a pitching airfoil, including transonic shocks, transient behaviour and dynamic non-linearities. Augmenting GNODEs with additional latent dimensions improves the expressivity and accuracy by capturing underlying history effects. The developed method demonstrates an approach that is suitable to model non-linear spatio-temporal systems with exogenous inputs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GNODE (Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations), combining graph neural networks with Neural ODEs to predict unsteady aerodynamic forces on a pitching airfoil. GNODE outperforms autoregressive GNN baselines by providing temporally stable, spatially smooth, and accurate predictions while mitigating error accumulation.
AI.motivation: Traditional CFD methods (URANS, linearized frequency domain) for unsteady aerodynamic analysis are either computationally expensive or limited by linearity assumptions. While machine learning surrogates like autoregressive GNNs can model nonlinear spatio-temporal dynamics efficiently, they suffer from error accumulation and unstable rollouts over time. A method is needed that combines the speed of ML surrogates with temporal stability for practical aerodynamic predictions.
AI.method: The authors propose GNODE, which integrates Graph Neural Networks with Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) and augments them with additional latent dimensions. The GNN component operates on a discretized spatial mesh to handle the irregular geometry. Instead of discrete autoregressive prediction, GNODE models the temporal dynamics as a continuous ODE, which is solved numerically, yielding inherently more stable rollouts. Latent augmentation improves expressivity by capturing underlying history effects (e.g., flow memory).
AI.result: GNODE produces temporally more stable, spatially smoother, and overall more accurate predictions of surface forces on a pitching airfoil compared to an autoregressive GNN baseline. Tests on a dataset involving transonic shocks, transient behavior, and dynamic nonlinearities confirm the method's effectiveness. Augmenting with latent dimensions further improves accuracy by capturing history-dependent flow physics.
AI.conclusion: GNODE demonstrates a viable approach for modeling nonlinear spatio-temporal systems with exogenous inputs, offering a fast and stable surrogate for unsteady aerodynamic predictions. It addresses the key limitation of error accumulation in autoregressive GNNs, making it suitable for aircraft design, optimization, and certification workflows.

title: CircuitKIT : Circuit Discovery, Evaluation, and Application Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Circuit analysis can support not only model explanation but also downstream interventions such as pruning, editing, steering, and selective fine-tuning. However, conducting such analyses currently requires stitching together separate implementations for discovery, evaluation, and intervention, as well as hand-authoring the contrastive prompts required by many discovery methods. This fragmentation makes methods difficult to compare and limits their application beyond canonical tasks. We introduce CircuitKIT, a source-available library that connects the circuit-analysis workflow through a typed, serializable representation. CircuitKIT provides a suite of discovery algorithms, declarative interfaces for mapping structured data into discovery tasks, complementary circuit diagnostics, and downstream application modules. Together, these components provide common infrastructure for conducting and comparing circuit analyses. The library, examples, notebooks, and documentation are released at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/CircuitKIT .

AI.tldr: CircuitKIT is a unified library that streamlines the entire mechanistic interpretability workflow—discovery, evaluation, and intervention—by providing a typed, serializable circuit representation, multiple discovery algorithms, declarative task mapping, diagnostics, and downstream modules, replacing the current fragmented tooling landscape.
AI.motivation: Current circuit analysis workflows are fragmented: researchers must cobble together separate implementations for circuit discovery, evaluation, and downstream interventions (pruning, editing, steering, fine-tuning), and manually craft contrastive prompts required by many discovery methods. This fragmentation hinders method comparison and restricts analyses to narrow, canonical tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce CircuitKIT, a source-available Python library built around a typed, serializable circuit representation that unifies the full analysis pipeline. It provides (1) a suite of circuit discovery algorithms, (2) declarative interfaces for mapping structured data into discovery tasks (eliminating manual prompt authoring), (3) complementary circuit diagnostics for evaluation, and (4) downstream application modules for interventions like pruning, editing, steering, and selective fine-tuning.
AI.result: CircuitKIT provides common infrastructure that enables reproducible, comparable circuit analyses across diverse tasks beyond canonical settings. The library is publicly released with examples, notebooks, and documentation at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: By consolidating discovery, evaluation, and intervention into a single interoperable framework with a shared circuit representation, CircuitKIT lowers the barrier to circuit analysis, facilitates fair method comparison, and broadens the applicability of mechanistic interpretability techniques.

title: Interactive Training 2: Auditable Control Plane for Live Model Training
summary: Experiment trackers show how training is progressing, but changing a live run still usually requires trainer-specific code. We present Interactive Training 2, an open-source control plane for steering training through a shared protocol. Training applications declare which settings and actions they expose, humans and automated controllers submit requests through the same interface, and the training loop validates and applies them at safe control points. A customized Aim workspace combines live metrics and controls with a chronological record of requests and outcomes. We demonstrate the system across five NLP and reinforcement-learning workflows. The released code and traces provide a reusable foundation for auditable human- and agent-guided training.

AI.tldr: Interactive Training 2 is an open-source control plane that enables steering of live ML training runs through a shared protocol, allowing both humans and automated agents to modify training settings via a unified interface with a customized Aim dashboard.
AI.motivation: Existing experiment trackers can monitor training progress but lack a standardized mechanism for modifying running experiments without trainer-specific code. There is a need for a universal, auditable interface for both human operators and automated controllers to intervene in live training runs.
AI.method: The authors propose a control plane architecture where training applications declare exposed settings and actions via a shared protocol. Requests from humans or automated controllers are submitted through a unified interface, validated, and applied at safe control points within the training loop. A customized Aim workspace integrates live metrics, controls, and a chronological audit trail of all requests and outcomes.
AI.result: The system was demonstrated across five diverse workflows spanning NLP and reinforcement learning, showing the feasibility of protocol-based training steering. Code and execution traces are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Interactive Training 2 provides a reusable, open-source foundation for auditable human- and agent-guided training, decoupling control logic from trainer-specific implementations through a shared protocol and unified dashboard.

title: Cost Accounting for Reactive Computational Graphs: Exhaustive Sweeps, Sequential Mutation, and the Backward-Locality Gap
comment: Companion paper: "Exact Network Surgery: Functional Invariance and Gradient Plasticity in Reactive Computational Graphs" (submitted concurrently)
summary: Exhaustive site-by-site interventions on a neural network's computational graph -- activation-patching sweeps, circuit-discovery searches, systematic ablation studies -- mutate the graph at every candidate site, and their cost is dominated by recomputation after each mutation. On a reactive graph engine whose invalidation provably touches exactly the downstream cone of a mutated node, we give a complete cost accounting for such workloads. First, the aggregate speedup of an exhaustive sweep over independent full recomputations is not a universal constant: if per-layer weight varies regularly with depth at Karamata index q, the ratio converges to (q+2)/(q+1) when weight concentrates near the output and to q+2 near the input, recovering 2 only in the depth-uniform case; a wall-clock corollary predicts a ceiling of about 1.79, below 2, until interpreter overhead is compiled away. Second, we prove the exact cost of a sequence of persistent mutations, never undone between insertions: the interleaved cost exceeds the isolated sum by an exact overcount summed over comparable site pairs, with closed-form extremes over insertion orders, while batched application is order-independent and sub-additive, costing exactly the union of the sites' cones plus the fresh nodes. Third, we prove the exact mirror of forward locality for the backward pass, showing it collapses the aggregate speedup to 1 under backpropagation on architectures without long skip connections. Every identity is validated on NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia: measured sweep ratios converge to the predicted limits under four cost profiles; the training-mode ratio collapses to 1 at the predicted rate; and all 18 per-graft sequential costs and the batched total match the closed forms at zero tolerance across three insertion orders.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a rigorous cost accounting framework for exhaustive mutation-based analyses (activation patching, circuit discovery, ablation) on neural network computational graphs using a reactive graph engine. It proves three key results: (1) aggregate speedup over independent recomputation converges to a Karamata-index-dependent ratio (not universal 2×), with a wall-clock ceiling of ~1.79; (2) exact cost formulas for persistent mutation sequences, showing interleaved costs exceed isolated sums by a provable overcount, while batched application is sub-additive; (3) the backward pass collapses aggregate speedup to 1 on architectures without long skip connections. All results are validated on NeuroDSL in Julia.
AI.motivation: Exhaustive intervention studies (activation patching, circuit discovery, ablation) on neural networks require mutating the computational graph at every candidate site and recomputing after each mutation. The dominant cost is recomputation, but no rigorous accounting exists for the aggregate cost structure of such workloads on reactive graph engines.
AI.method: The authors model the cost on a reactive graph engine whose invalidation provably touches exactly the downstream cone of a mutated node. They analyze: (1) aggregate speedup of exhaustive sweeps using Karamata index theory for per-layer weight distributions; (2) persistent mutation sequences with exact overcount formulas over comparable site pairs, including closed-form extremes over insertion orders; (3) the backward pass mirror of forward locality showing speedup collapse.
AI.result: (1) Speedup ratio converges to (q+2)/(q+1) for output-concentrated weight and q+2 for input-concentrated, recovering 2× only in the depth-uniform case; wall-clock ceiling ~1.79. (2) Interleaved persistent mutation cost exceeds isolated sum by an exact overcount; batched application is order-independent and sub-additive. (3) Backpropagation collapses aggregate speedup to 1 without long skip connections. All 18 per-graft sequential costs and batched totals match closed forms at zero tolerance across three insertion orders on NeuroDSL.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that the cost structure of exhaustive neural network intervention workloads on reactive graphs is not governed by universal constants but depends on architectural weight distribution and mutation ordering. Practical speedups are bounded below naive expectations (~1.79× ceiling), and training-mode backpropagation eliminates the advantage entirely absent long skip connections. The closed-form identities provide a principled basis for optimizing such workflows.

title: Dynamic Loss Balancing for Joint SOH and RUL Prediction of Lithium-Ion Batteries via a Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer
summary: The deployment of reliable lithium-ion battery management systems is crucial for accelerating electrification, yet the joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) remains severely hindered by task heteroscedasticity. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance the bounded, low-variance noise of SOH estimation with the unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty of long-term RUL predictions. Here, we present the Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer (RoSIP-Batt), a unified co-estimation framework that resolves these optimization conflicts. By formulating joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective, RoSIP-Batt introduces a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise levels. The architecture leverages decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism, secured by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from corrupting the stable SOH representation space. To capture electrochemical degradation patterns without relying on absolute cycle steps, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is incorporated into a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles. Crucially, the intermediate SOH estimate is directly injected into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior. Evaluations across the NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets show that RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing SOH estimation error to 1.994% MAE on NASA and restricting RUL prediction error to 62.85 cycles on Stanford. These findings establish RoSIP-Batt as a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

AI.tldr: RoSIP-Batt is a unified battery management framework that jointly estimates State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) by resolving task heteroscedasticity through Bayesian multi-task learning with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-task learning approaches fail to jointly predict SOH and RUL because these two tasks exhibit fundamentally different noise characteristics: SOH estimation has bounded, low-variance noise while RUL prediction suffers from unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty. This task heteroscedasticity creates optimization conflicts that degrade performance on both tasks.
AI.method: RoSIP-Batt formulates joint SOH-RUL prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting that dynamically scales task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise. Architecturally, it uses: (1) decoupled dual classification tokens with a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism and gradient-detachment operator to prevent RUL's high-variance updates from corrupting SOH representations; (2) Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) in a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal degradation patterns without absolute cycle steps; and (3) direct injection of intermediate SOH estimates into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior.
AI.result: On the NASA dataset, RoSIP-Batt achieved 1.994% MAE for SOH estimation. On the MIT-Stanford dataset, RUL prediction error was reduced to 62.85 cycles. The framework significantly outperformed state-of-the-art baselines across NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets.
AI.conclusion: RoSIP-Batt is a highly generalizable and computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded battery management system deployment, effectively resolving the task heteroscedasticity problem in joint SOH-RUL prognosis.

title: Physics-Guided Masked Multi-Task Network for Edge-Friendly Battery Health Diagnostics from Sto-chastically Fragmented Charging Profiles
summary: The deployment of reliable lithium-ion battery management systems is crucial for accelerating electrification, yet the joint prognosis of State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) remains severely hindered by task heteroscedasticity. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance the bounded, low-variance noise of SOH estimation with the unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty of long-term RUL predictions. Here, we present the Rotary SOH-Injected Prior Battery Transformer (RoSIP-Batt), a unified co-estimation framework that resolves these optimization conflicts. By formulating joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective, RoSIP-Batt introduces a homoscedastic uncertainty weighting mechanism to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise levels. The architecture leverages decoupled dual classification tokens and a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism, secured by a gradient-detachment operator to prevent high-variance RUL updates from corrupting the stable SOH representation space. To capture electrochemical degradation patterns without relying on absolute cycle steps, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is incorporated into a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles. Crucially, the intermediate SOH estimate is directly injected into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior. Evaluations across the NASA, MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets show that RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing SOH estimation error to 1.994% MAE on NASA and restricting RUL prediction error to 62.85 cycles on Stanford. These findings establish RoSIP-Batt as a highly generalizable, computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded BMS deployment.

AI.tldr: RoSIP-Batt is a unified battery management framework that jointly predicts State of Health (SOH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) by resolving task heteroscedasticity through homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), and SOH-injected RUL regression, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on NASA (1.994% MAE), MIT-Stanford, and HUST datasets.
AI.motivation: Joint SOH and RUL prognosis is hampered by task heteroscedasticity — SOH estimation involves bounded, low-variance noise, while long-term RUL prediction suffers from unbounded, nonlinearly expanding uncertainty. Conventional multi-task learning frameworks fail to balance these conflicting optimization objectives, and RUL predictions often rely on absolute cycle steps that generalize poorly.
AI.method: RoSIP-Batt formulates joint prediction as a Bayesian multi-task objective with homoscedastic uncertainty weighting to dynamically scale task-specific gradients based on learned residual noise. The architecture features: (1) decoupled dual classification tokens with a per-dimension gated fusion mechanism; (2) a gradient-detachment operator preventing high-variance RUL gradients from corrupting the SOH representation space; (3) Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) in a shared Transformer backbone to model translation-invariant relative temporal profiles without absolute cycle steps; and (4) direct injection of intermediate SOH estimates into the RUL regression head as a physical degradation prior.
AI.result: RoSIP-Batt significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets: SOH estimation error reduced to 1.994% MAE on NASA dataset; RUL prediction error restricted to 62.85 cycles on the MIT-Stanford dataset.
AI.conclusion: RoSIP-Batt is established as a highly generalizable and computationally efficient solution suitable for real-time embedded Battery Management System (BMS) deployment, offering a principled resolution to the task heteroscedasticity problem in joint battery health prognosis.

title: ChemHyperMag: Physics-informed magnetic hypergraph learning improves molecular ADMET prediction
comment: Accepted by Proceedings of the AI4Physics Workshop at the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning (AI4Physics@ICML 2026)
summary: Accurate prediction of ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) is important for drug discovery. Most predictors use undirected molecular graphs and pairwise edges. This choice misses asymmetric interactions, nonreversible dynamics, and motif level effects from functional groups and ring systems. We propose ChemHyperMag for multitask ADMET prediction under missing labels. ChemHyperMag builds a functional group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds. It also defines a potential driven nonreversible flow guided by electronegativity and Gasteiger partial charges. The resulting circulation is encoded by a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian and processed with a magnetic Chebyshev encoder. We perturb magnetic phases to form stochastic views and train with an InfoNCE objective. Experiments on multiple ADMET benchmarks show improvements over recent methods with fewer labeled samples and no conformers. ChemHyperMag is scalable and provides interpretable directional signals through its magnetic phases.

AI.tldr: ChemHyperMag proposes a magnetic Laplacian-based hypergraph neural network that captures asymmetric molecular interactions and functional group motifs for multitask ADMET prediction, achieving superior performance with fewer labels and no conformer information.
AI.motivation: Existing ADMET predictors rely on undirected molecular graphs with pairwise edges, which fail to capture asymmetric interactions (e.g., electronegativity-driven effects), nonreversible dynamics, and higher-order motif-level information from functional groups and ring systems that are critical for pharmacological property prediction.
AI.method: ChemHyperMag constructs a functional group hypergraph from rings, BRICS fragments, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and bonds. It introduces a potential-driven nonreversible flow informed by electronegativity and Gasteiger partial charges, encoded via a Hermitian magnetic Laplacian. A magnetic Chebyshev encoder processes this representation. The model perturbs magnetic phases to generate stochastic views and trains with an InfoNCE contrastive objective, supporting multitask learning with missing labels.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple ADMET benchmarks demonstrate that ChemHyperMag outperforms recent methods, particularly in low-label regimes and without requiring conformer generation. The model is scalable and provides interpretable directional signals via its magnetic phase parameters.
AI.conclusion: ChemHyperMag effectively addresses the limitations of undirected graph-based ADMET predictors by incorporating directionality and higher-order motifs through magnetic hypergraph representations, offering both improved predictive accuracy and mechanistic interpretability for drug discovery applications.

title: Federated Lightweight Fine-Tuning
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables. Extended preprint with appendix. Under review at ACCV 2026
summary: Federated fine-tuning is bottlenecked by communication: FedAvg and pseudo-gradient schemes transmit a payload that scales with the model, and gradient compression shrinks it by only a constant factor. We take a different lever. Mapping networks generate a network's weights from a small trainable latent through a frozen affine projection; because the map is shared and affine, averaging latents is exactly averaging the generated weights. We turn this into a practical low-bandwidth federated channel with two changes: a low-rank, seed-regenerable factorisation of the projection (cutting generator memory from ~80 GB to ~10 MB), and a delta formulation $θ= θ^{\mathrm{pre}} + U V^{\top} z$ that learns an additive correction around a shared centrally-pretrained base -- federated fine-tuning, which is what makes the method work at scale. A frozen orthogonal classifier head further removes the head from the payload while improving accuracy. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm, our method (FLITE, Federated Low-rank Iterative Training Engine) communicates 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client per round -- an 8718x reduction -- and reaches 74.67%, within ~0.5 pp of full-weight FedAvg. The averaging identity holds to floating-point precision ($6 \times 10^{-8}$); the method sits one to two orders of magnitude below PowerSGD and top-k on the bandwidth-accuracy Pareto; it matches or exceeds full-weight FedAvg under strong non-IID skew. int4 latents reach 648 bytes per round at unchanged accuracy, whereas int4 full-weight FedAvg collapses to chance.

AI.tldr: FLITE introduces a federated fine-tuning method that communicates only a small latent vector (~5 KB) per round by using a frozen affine weight generator with a low-rank factorized projection, achieving near-FedAvg accuracy with 8718× communication reduction.
AI.motivation: Federated fine-tuning suffers from high communication costs because standard methods like FedAvg transmit payloads proportional to model size, and gradient compression offers only constant-factor reduction. The authors seek a structural solution that decouples communication from model scale.
AI.method: FLITE uses a frozen affine mapping network that generates weights from a small trainable latent vector z via θ = θ^{pre} + UV^⊤ z, where UV^⊤ is a low-rank, seed-regenerable factorization of the projection (reducing generator memory from ~80 GB to ~10 MB). Because the map is shared and affine, averaging latents exactly equals averaging generated weights. A frozen orthogonal classifier head is also used to keep the head out of the payload while improving accuracy. The method operates as federated fine-tuning around a centrally pre-trained base model.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18+GroupNorm, FLITE communicates 1,280 floats (~5 KB) per client per round (8,718× reduction vs. full-weight FedAvg), achieving 74.67% accuracy (within ~0.5 pp of FedAvg). The latent averaging identity holds to floating-point precision (6×10⁻⁸). FLITE sits 1–2 orders of magnitude below PowerSGD and top-k on the bandwidth-accuracy Pareto frontier. It matches or exceeds full-weight FedAvg under strong non-IID skew. With int4 latents, payload drops to 648 bytes at unchanged accuracy, while int4 full-weight FedAvg collapses to chance.
AI.conclusion: FLITE demonstrates that structural weight reparameterization via a shared, frozen affine generator enables ultra-low-bandwidth federated fine-tuning that rivals full-weight FedAvg in accuracy, even under challenging non-IID conditions and extreme quantization.

title: An Analysis of Residual-Stream Geometry Across Transformer Depth
summary: We propose a transition-centred geometric analysis of transformer residual streams. Relative displacement measures how \emph{far} representations move between consecutive layers, and orthogonal Procrustes analysis separates each transition into a rigid rotation and a non-rigid residual.
