Across six instruction-tuned models, on code generation and cross-lingual translation, these measurements reveal reproducible depth regularities. Relative displacement is strongly layer-dependent; typically larger early and late, with a quieter middle third; and nearly invariant across conditions within each model. Rotation magnitude is nearly constant across depth, while Procrustes residual and angle concentration remain depth-modulated, with residual peaking at the final transition. During generation, non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement and residual than English targets. We present these as descriptive geometric regularities, not as measures of computational effort or causal explanations. The contribution is a measurement framework for residual-stream transitions and evidence that, in the settings studied here, depth curves are model-dependent and largely condition-stable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric framework to analyze transformer residual streams by measuring relative displacement between layers and decomposing transitions into rigid rotation and non-rigid residual components via orthogonal Procrustes analysis. Across six instruction-tuned models on code generation and translation tasks, they find consistent depth regularities: displacement peaks early and late with a quiet middle, rotation is nearly constant, and Procrustes residual peaks at the final layer, with cross-lingual differences in final-layer behavior.
AI.motivation: To provide a descriptive, measurement-based geometric framework for analyzing how representations evolve across transformer layers, moving beyond scalar metrics to richer structural characterizations of residual stream transitions.
AI.method: Two geometric measures applied to residual stream representations between consecutive layers: (1) relative displacement — the distance representations move between layers; (2) orthogonal Procrustes analysis — decomposing each transition into a rigid rotation (orthogonal transformation) and a non-rigid residual component, with angle concentration metrics. Applied across six instruction-tuned models on code generation and cross-lingual translation tasks.
AI.result: Relative displacement is strongly layer-dependent (larger early/late, quieter middle third) and nearly invariant across input conditions within each model. Rotation magnitude is nearly constant across depth. Procrustes residual and angle concentration remain depth-modulated, with residual peaking at the final transition. Non-English targets show larger final-layer displacement and residual than English targets. Depth curves are model-dependent but condition-stable.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measurement framework reveals reproducible geometric regularities in residual stream transitions. Depth curves are model-specific yet largely condition-stable, and the work emphasizes these as descriptive regularities rather than causal or computational claims, providing a foundation for future interpretability research.

title: MambaLSTM: A Spatio-Temporal Framework for Enhanced Traffic Accident Risk Prediction
summary: In traffic accident risk prediction, most studies overlook the extra noise that could be incorporated when fusing temporal features into spatial features, and some models struggle to capture global correlations among spatial regions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel traffic accident risk prediction framework named MambaLSTM. First, we develop a squeeze-and-excitation temporal feature fusion module to integrate temporal information without compromising spatio-temporal integrity. Second, we introduce a new patch embedding module for effectively capturing semantic relationships among spatially adjacent regions. Additionally, we introduce a Mamba block based on state-space models to model global spatial semantics in urban regions. Finally, we propose a MambaLSTM unit to efficiently capture long- and short-term temporal dependencies for identifying dynamic risk patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed model's superiority over state-of-the-art methods. The code is released at https://github.com/Zhenzovo/MambaLSTM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MambaLSTM, a traffic accident risk prediction framework that addresses noise from spatio-temporal fusion and weak global spatial modeling by combining squeeze-and-excitation fusion, patch embedding, state-space Mamba blocks, and a dedicated LSTM unit for capturing long/short-term temporal dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing traffic accident risk prediction methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) they incorporate extra noise when fusing temporal features into spatial features, and (2) many models fail to capture global correlations among spatial regions effectively.
AI.method: The proposed MambaLSTM framework comprises four main components: (1) a squeeze-and-excitation temporal feature fusion module that integrates temporal information while preserving spatio-temporal integrity; (2) a patch embedding module for capturing semantic relationships among spatially adjacent regions; (3) a Mamba block based on state-space models to model global spatial semantics across urban regions; and (4) a MambaLSTM unit designed to efficiently capture both long- and short-term temporal dependencies for dynamic risk pattern identification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that MambaLSTM achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: MambaLSTM effectively mitigates spatio-temporal fusion noise and captures global spatial dependencies, establishing a new strong baseline for traffic accident risk prediction. The code is publicly available.

title: Multi-layer MIMO Relay as Deep Physical Neural Networks: Power Amplifiers as Activation Functions
summary: Wireless physical neural networks (WPNNs) embed neural computation directly into analog hardware, offering lower energy consumption and latency than conventional digital implementations. In this paper, we propose a deep WPNN in which nonlinear activations are realized by a multi-hop multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) relay network, in which each relay implements a trainable complex linear gain and bias, followed by the power amplifier's intrinsic nonlinearity acting as an activation function. The cascade of multiple relays therefore realizes an over-the-air fully connected network whose parameters can be trained end-to-end. We develop two transceiver designs for different channel state information (CSI) availability scenarios: a least squares (LS)-based scheme requiring only receiver-side CSI, and a singular-value-decomposition (SVD)-based scheme requiring both transmitter-side and receiver-side CSI. Simulation results show that the proposed architecture enables accurate over-the-air inference for image classification. In particular, the results highlight the advantage of exploiting hardware nonlinearity for enhanced inference capability.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deep Wireless Physical Neural Network (WPNN) that uses a multi-hop MIMO relay network to perform over-the-air neural computation, where each relay's power amplifier nonlinearity serves as the activation function, with parameters trained end-to-end.
AI.motivation: To leverage analog hardware for neural computation, achieving lower energy consumption and latency compared to digital implementations, while exploiting intrinsic hardware nonlinearities as a feature rather than a limitation.
AI.method: The authors design a multi-hop MIMO relay network where each relay applies a trainable complex linear gain and bias, followed by the power amplifier's intrinsic nonlinearity as activation. The cascade forms an over-the-air fully connected network trained end-to-end. Two transceiver designs are developed: an LS-based scheme requiring only receiver-side CSI, and an SVD-based scheme requiring both transmitter- and receiver-side CSI.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate accurate over-the-air inference for image classification tasks, with the hardware nonlinearity significantly enhancing inference capability.
AI.conclusion: Deep WPNNs with multi-hop MIMO relays are a viable approach for over-the-air neural inference, and harnessing hardware nonlinearity actively improves performance rather than degrading it.

title: Physical Self-Supervised Learning: IMU Sensing without Manual Labels
comment: 15 pages, 20 figures. Published in ACM MobiSys 2026
summary: Deep neural networks have become a promising approach for IMU-based sensing, but their scalability is fundamentally limited by costly labeled data and poor robustness to heterogeneous devices, placements, and users. Existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods reduce but do not remove this dependence, still requiring labeled data for domain adaptation and largely ignoring known physical structure. We propose physical self-supervised learning, an autoencoder-style paradigm for label-free IMU sensing. We replace the conventional neural decoder with an auto-adaptive physics decoder, a learnable family of kinematic equations that enforces explicit physical structure while adapting across environments, and adopt a hybrid two-stage IMU encoder with reconstruction in a structured latent space to mitigate sensor noise. Our framework further introduces probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor and object motion, a multi-view kinematic tree to exploit sparse physical self-supervised signals, and an uncertainty-aware formulation to handle the inherent ambiguity of IMU inference. Evaluated on inertial tracking and full-body motion capture over public datasets and realistic deployments, physical self-supervised learning reduces errors by up to 5x for tracking and 4x for motion capture in challenging generalization scenarios, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without any labels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "physical self-supervised learning," a label-free autoencoder framework for IMU sensing that replaces neural decoders with learnable physics-based kinematic equations. It introduces probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints, a multi-view kinematic tree, and uncertainty-aware formulation to disentangle sensor/object motion. The method achieves up to 5x error reduction in tracking and 4x in motion capture over supervised/self-supervised baselines without any labeled data.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks for IMU-based sensing face two critical bottlenecks: (1) reliance on costly labeled data for training, and (2) poor generalization across heterogeneous devices, sensor placements, and users. Existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods still require labeled data for domain adaptation and fail to exploit known physical priors (e.g., kinematic constraints). The authors aim to eliminate labeling entirely while leveraging physical structure to improve robustness.
AI.method: The framework is built on an autoencoder-style paradigm: (1) an auto-adaptive physics decoder replaces the neural decoder — it uses a learnable family of kinematic equations that enforce explicit physical structure while adapting across environments; (2) a hybrid two-stage IMU encoder with reconstruction in a structured latent space to mitigate sensor noise; (3) probabilistic frequency-spatial constraints to disentangle sensor motion from object motion; (4) a multi-view kinematic tree to exploit sparse physical self-supervised signals; (5) an uncertainty-aware formulation to address inherent ambiguity in IMU inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on inertial tracking and full-body motion capture across public datasets and realistic deployments, physical self-supervised learning reduces errors by up to 5x for tracking and 4x for motion capture in challenging generalization scenarios, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised baselines without using any labels.
AI.conclusion: Physical self-supervised learning demonstrates that encoding explicit physical priors into the learning architecture can eliminate the need for labeled IMU data while achieving superior generalization. The approach bridges data-driven learning with classical kinematics, offering a scalable and robust solution for IMU-based sensing applications.

title: Scalable and Efficient Joint Spiking Embedding Predictive Architecture for Large-Scale Dynamic Graphs
summary: Dynamic graph learning aims to capture evolving structural and semantic patterns in real-world systems, such as fraud detection and recommender systems. Due to the scarcity of labeled data in real-world dynamic graphs, recent studies have introduced generative or contrastive paradigms (e.g., masked graph autoencoders or graph contrastive learning) to generate task-agnostic graph embeddings. However, these methods typically rely on complex edge-level reconstruction objectives and tailored graph augmentation strategies. This incurs substantial computational overhead when scaling to large-scale dynamic graphs. In this paper, we propose SG-JEPA, a joint spiking embedding predictive architecture for large-scale dynamic graphs. In contrast to existing self-supervised methods, SG-JEPA partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension to learn embeddings that are predictive of each other via additional spatial-temporal information. Furthermore, through encoding sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings, spiking neurons enable SG-JEPA to adapt to the varying computational constraints of downstream tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SG-JEPA achieves competitive or even superior performance over discriminative baselines on node classification, while effectively scaling to the dynamic graph with 13 million edges. SG-JEPA avoids the complex machinery (negative sampling, graph augmentations, edge-level reconstruction, etc.), resulting in superior training efficiency and memory scalability compared with prior self-supervised dynamic graph baselines.

AI.tldr: SG-JEPA proposes a self-supervised learning method for large-scale dynamic graphs that uses spiking neural networks and a joint embedding predictive architecture, avoiding complex edge reconstruction and augmentations while achieving competitive performance and superior scalability.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised dynamic graph learning methods rely on computationally expensive edge-level reconstruction objectives and tailored graph augmentations, which hinder scalability to large-scale dynamic graphs with millions of edges.
AI.method: SG-JEPA partitions nodes into context and target sets along the temporal dimension, learning predictive embeddings via spatial-temporal information. It encodes sequential inputs into coarse-to-fine spike count embeddings using spiking neurons, enabling adaptation to varying downstream computational constraints.
AI.result: SG-JEPA achieves competitive or superior performance over discriminative baselines on node classification and scales effectively to a dynamic graph with 13 million edges, while offering superior training efficiency and memory scalability compared to prior self-supervised methods.
AI.conclusion: By eliminating complex machinery like negative sampling, graph augmentations, and edge-level reconstruction, SG-JEPA provides an efficient and scalable self-supervised framework for dynamic graph learning without sacrificing performance.

title: PAC--Bayes Bounds on Quotient Parameter Spaces: Geometry-induced Implicit-Bias Priors
summary:
Overparameterized models often have continuous parameter symmetries, so different parameters define the same predictor. We show that PAC--Bayesian analysis should be performed on the quotient predictor space: pushing a prior and posterior to the quotient preserves the empirical and population Gibbs risks while removing the nonnegative KL contribution caused solely by how the two distributions differ among parameterizations of the same predictor.
  Quotienting alone does not determine which prior to use. We construct a canonical choice of one parameterization for each predictor and account for the geometric volume of its equivalent parameterizations. This transforms a neutral reference prior into a data-independent prior that reflects the model's implicit bias. It approximates the ideal but inadmissible posterior-matched prior, which would minimize the KL term by depending on the training data. The resulting certificate is tighter exactly when this geometry-induced prior has smaller KL divergence from the learned quotient posterior than the neutral prior.
  We test this prediction in Fourier regression with a Hadamard parameterization and in Query-Key attention, using ordinary SGD without an explicit regularizer. The implicit-bias prior reduces the mean quotient-space KL by \(40.69\%\) and the mean PAC--Bayes certificate by \(21.40\%\) in the Fourier-Hadamard experiment. The smaller, prior-scale-dependent improvement in Query-Key attention confirms the predicted conditional nature of the effect.

AI.tldr: Overparameterized models have parameter symmetries (different parameters = same predictor). The authors propose performing PAC-Bayesian analysis on the quotient predictor space rather than raw parameter space. They construct a canonical, geometry-aware prior that reflects implicit bias, yielding tighter PAC-Bayes bounds. Empirically, KL divergence drops ~40% and certificate tightness improves ~21% in Fourier regression; smaller gains in attention confirm the effect is conditional on geometry.
AI.motivation: Standard PAC-Bayesian bounds are inflated by a KL divergence penalty that includes contributions from merely reparameterizing the same predictor function. This wastes statistical capacity. The authors aim to eliminate this redundancy by quotienting out parameter symmetries, yielding tighter generalization certificates that better reflect a model's true implicit bias.
AI.method: The authors (1) reformulate PAC-Bayes on the quotient space of predictors rather than parameters, showing the Gibbs risks are preserved while the KL term is reduced. (2) They construct a canonical parameterization per predictor class and incorporate the geometric volume (Haar measure) of equivalent parameterizations into a data-independent prior. This geometry-induced prior approximates the ideal but inadmissible posterior-matched prior. (3) They validate via Fourier regression with Hadamard parameterization and Query-Key attention, using ordinary SGD without explicit regularization.
AI.result: In the Fourier-Hadamard experiment, the implicit-bias prior reduces mean quotient-space KL divergence by 40.69% and mean PAC-Bayes certificate by 21.40%. In Query-Key attention, improvements are smaller and scale-dependent, confirming that the benefit is conditional on the geometry-induced prior having genuinely smaller KL divergence from the learned quotient posterior than a neutral prior.
AI.conclusion: PAC-Bayesian analysis benefits significantly from quotienting out parameter symmetries. A geometry-aware, data-independent prior that accounts for the volume of equivalent parameterizations yields tighter generalization bounds than neutral priors, with the improvement magnitude dependent on how well the geometry aligns with the learned posterior. This provides a principled way to incorporate implicit bias into PAC-Bayes certificates.

title: Intelligence from Learnable Novelty
summary: Intelligence appears under different names in different fields: as data compression in statistics and machine learning, as universal computation in dynamical systems, and as adaptive behavior in agents. Each field carries its own objective, and the two most influential drives often fail in mirror image: novelty search, which seeks surprise, is transfixed by a noisy television screen, while the free-energy principle, which avoids surprise, is most content in a dark room. Both failures have a single cause: each objective treats as one quantity the surprise a learner can convert into knowledge and the surprise it never can. Here we show that the learnable part of that information, which we call learnable novelty, yields the seemingly disparate projections of intelligence, and we give a closed-form estimator of it built on a cheap and differentiable reservoir computer. Used as a measure, with no supervision of any kind, the estimator recovers decades of complexity classification, ranking the Turing-complete rule~110 highest among the elementary cellular automata. Used as an objective, its gradient carries a neural cellular automaton from simple dynamics into a regime of solitons, the traveling, colliding structures by which rule~110 computes, as well as organizes the representation of an image encoder around the ten digit classes of MNIST, fully unsupervised: no label ever enters training. Handed to a reinforcement-learning agent as an intrinsic reward, it supplies the exploration that task rewards lack, improving on the task baseline in nine of ten environments and collapsing in none. Complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration, ordinarily pursued with unrelated objectives in separate fields, thus emerge from ascent on one differentiable quantity, and the projections of intelligence gain a common quantitative footing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "learnable novelty" — the portion of surprise that can be converted into knowledge — as a unified differentiable quantity. A closed-form estimator based on reservoir computing recovers complexity rankings, drives emergent computation in neural cellular automata, organizes unsupervised representations of MNIST, and improves exploration in RL agents, unifying complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration across fields.
AI.motivation: Two dominant drives in intelligence research — novelty search (seeking surprise) and the free-energy principle (avoiding surprise) — suffer from mirror-image failures: the former is captivated by pure noise (e.g., a TV screen), the latter by complete predictability (a dark room). Both fail because they treat all surprise uniformly, conflating learnable structure with irreducible randomness. The motivation is to isolate and operationalize the learnable component of surprise as a principled unifying objective for intelligence across disciplines.
AI.method: The authors define "learnable novelty" as the learnable portion of information in observations and derive a closed-form estimator using a cheap, differentiable reservoir computer (echo state network). This estimator requires no supervision. They deploy it in three domains: (1) as a measure to rank elementary cellular automata by complexity, (2) as an objective gradient to evolve neural cellular automata toward soliton dynamics (characteristic of rule 110) and to organize unsupervised MNIST representations, and (3) as an intrinsic reward for reinforcement learning agents across ten environments.
AI.result: The estimator recovers established complexity classifications, correctly ranking rule 110 highest among elementary CAs. As an objective, it drives a neural CA from simple dynamics into soliton regimes. It organizes an image encoder's representation around MNIST digit classes without labels. In RL, it improves on task baselines in 9/10 environments with no catastrophic collapse.
AI.conclusion: Complexity generation, abstraction, and exploration — traditionally pursued with unrelated objectives in separate fields — all emerge from ascent on a single differentiable quantity: learnable novelty. This provides a common quantitative foundation for the disparate projections of intelligence across statistics, dynamical systems, and agent-based AI.

title: Estimating Rare Events in Language Models with Proper Evaluation
summary: Quantifying the risk of rare failures in language models, such as those triggered by adversarial distribution shifts or very large-scale deployments, requires estimating probabilities far too small for random sampling. While recent work has formalized Low Probability Estimation, existing pipelines remain fragile in the rarest regimes: estimators can suffer zero-estimate collapse or systematic bias, and standard evaluation losses can become unstable or poorly matched to asymmetric safety costs. In this work, we introduce Gradient Activation Adaptive Multi-Level Splitting (GA-AMLS), which adapts rare-event Monte Carlo methods to the continuous activation space of language models. Specifically, GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to navigate activation space, eliminating the zero-estimate collapse of input-space search and replacing the independence assumptions of prior activation-space estimators with conditional sampling under an explicit, heavier-tailed activation prior. We also propose the Shifted-Power Bregman (SPB) Loss, a proper scoring rule that remains finite for zero-estimates and offers tunable asymmetry between underestimation and overestimation penalties. Experiments on small transformer models reveal a bias-variance tradeoff: GA-AMLS achieves the lowest loss under symmetric evaluation, reducing average log-space squared error relative to the strongest baseline across model sizes, while methods with overestimation bias prevail under asymmetric penalties. Our findings highlight that estimator choice should be matched to deployment context. More broadly, our work establishes activation space as a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in language models, circumventing the brittleness of discrete input-space search.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GA-AMLS, a gradient-based rare-event estimation method operating in language model activation space to avoid zero-estimate collapse, paired with a Shifted-Power Bregman Loss that handles asymmetric safety costs. Experiments show a bias-variance tradeoff where GA-AMLS excels under symmetric evaluation while overestimation-biased methods win under asymmetric penalties.
AI.motivation: Estimating the probability of rare catastrophic failures in language models (e.g., from adversarial shifts or massive deployments) is critical for safety but fundamentally hard: naive Monte Carlo requires infeasible sample sizes. Existing low-probability estimators suffer from zero-estimate collapse, systematic bias, and evaluation losses poorly matched to real-world asymmetric safety costs where underestimation is far worse than overestimation.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) GA-AMLS adapts multi-level splitting rare-event Monte Carlo to the continuous activation space of LMs, using a gradient-based MCMC kernel with an explicit heavier-tailed activation prior and conditional sampling, eliminating the zero-estimate collapse of discrete input-space search and the independence assumptions of prior activation-space work. (2) The Shifted-Power Bregman (SPB) Loss is a proper scoring rule that remains finite under zero-estimates and provides tunable asymmetry between underestimation and overestimation penalties via a power parameter.
AI.result: On small transformer models, GA-AMLS achieves the lowest average log-space squared error (symmetric evaluation) compared to the strongest baseline across model sizes. However, under asymmetric SPB loss penalizing underestimation more heavily, methods with inherent overestimation bias outperform GA-AMLS, revealing a bias-variance tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: Estimator choice must align with deployment context and cost asymmetry. Activation space is established as a tractable, less brittle domain for rare-event estimation in language models compared to discrete input-space search.

title: AHEAD: Advancing Multi-Class Label Aggregation with Interpretable Cross-Annotator Modeling
summary: Crowdsourced labeling provides valuable labeled data for domains across natural language processing, computer vision, and video. Label aggregation aims to infer latent true labels from noisy and biased annotations, with the key lying in annotator reliability estimation. Despite promising progress, existing approaches struggle with one real-world bottleneck: most individual annotators label only a small subset of tasks, making accurate annotator estimation highly intractable. In this paper, we focus on the considerably more challenging multi-class label aggregation and propose AHEAD (cross-Annotator learning and High-confidEnce Annotator-guideD label aggregation), a cross-annotator learning framework that advances annotator reliability estimation by leveraging the population-level data. Specifically, AHEAD first learns high-dimensional cross-annotator contexts via a graph neural network, deriving multi-view, complementary annotator embeddings by aggregating individual-level annotator features with contextual information. These embeddings are then decoded into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices to fit the observed labels. We formulate a composite objective incorporating high-confidence annotators to alleviate the unsupervised training issues faced by prior models. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, CV, Video, and Audio show that AHEAD substantially improves label accuracy, increasing average accuracy from 68.75% to 73.23%, with gains of up to 14.9% in the best case. Meanwhile, scalability experiments on the largest dataset further demonstrate the overall superiority of our method.

AI.tldr: AHEAD is a cross-annotator learning framework for multi-class label aggregation that uses graph neural networks to learn annotator embeddings from population-level context, decodes them into confusion matrices, and leverages high-confidence annotators to improve unsupervised training, achieving substantial accuracy gains across NLP, CV, Video, and Audio datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing label aggregation methods struggle with a critical real-world bottleneck: most individual annotators label only a small subset of tasks, making accurate annotator reliability estimation highly intractable. This sparsity problem is exacerbated in multi-class settings.
AI.method: AHEAD is a cross-annotator learning framework with three key components: (1) a graph neural network that learns high-dimensional cross-annotator contexts by aggregating individual-level annotator features with contextual information from the population, producing multi-view complementary annotator embeddings; (2) a decoding mechanism that transforms these embeddings into interpretable annotator-specific confusion matrices to fit observed labels; and (3) a composite objective function that incorporates high-confidence annotators to alleviate unsupervised training issues.
AI.result: On 10 real-world datasets spanning NLP, CV, Video, and Audio domains, AHEAD improved average accuracy from 68.75% to 73.23%, with best-case gains of up to 14.9%. Scalability experiments on the largest dataset further demonstrated the method's overall superiority.
AI.conclusion: AHEAD effectively addresses the sparse annotation bottleneck in multi-class label aggregation by exploiting population-level cross-annotator context via GNNs and high-confidence annotator guidance, yielding significant and consistent accuracy improvements across diverse domains.

title: Weak-to-Strong Learning in Decision Making
summary: Many operational decisions rely on predictive models that estimate uncertain outcomes conditional on observable contexts. Training such models, however, often faces a fundamental data asymmetry: labeled outcomes are scarce or costly to obtain, while contextual covariates are abundant. Motivated by this data asymmetry, we develop a decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve contextual stochastic optimization. Specifically, we first train a weak model using limited labeled data and then use it to generate predicted outcome distributions on unlabeled contexts. These distributions provide soft supervision for training a strong model. We establish a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess decision risk of W2S and a complementary lower bound for a strong-only benchmark. Their comparison yields explicit sufficient conditions under which W2S improves downstream decision performance. The key quantity is the correlation dimension between the weak and strong feature representations: when it is small, abundant unlabeled data reduce the effect of teacher errors along non-overlapping directions. A synthetic newsvendor experiment and a comment moderation experiment based on real-world data provide empirical evidence consistent with the theory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decision-aware weak-to-strong (W2S) framework that uses a weak model trained on limited labeled data to generate pseudo-labels for abundant unlabeled contexts, training a strong model to improve contextual stochastic optimization. Theoretical analysis shows W2S improves decision performance when the correlation dimension between weak and strong feature representations is small, with empirical validation on newsvendor and comment moderation tasks.
AI.motivation: Many real-world operational decisions require predictive models trained on context-outcome pairs, but labeled outcomes are scarce or expensive while contextual covariates are plentiful. Existing approaches either use only the limited labeled data (underutilizing unlabeled data) or apply standard semi-supervised learning that targets prediction accuracy rather than downstream decision quality. The key gap is a principled framework that leverages unlabeled data specifically to improve decision-making performance in contextual stochastic optimization.
AI.method: The W2S framework proceeds in two stages: (1) Train a "weak" model on limited labeled data to estimate outcome distributions given contexts. (2) Use this weak model to generate predicted outcome distributions for abundant unlabeled contexts, then train a "strong" model using these soft pseudo-labels. The theoretical analysis derives a non-asymptotic upper bound on the excess decision risk of W2S and a lower bound for a strong-only baseline trained solely on labeled data. The comparison identifies sufficient conditions for W2S to improve decisions, centered on the "correlation dimension" — a measure of overlap between weak and strong feature representations. When this dimension is small, unlabeled data help mitigate teacher errors along non-overlapping directions.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis establishes that W2S improves downstream decision performance when the correlation dimension between weak and strong feature spaces is small, as abundant unlabeled data reduce the impact of weak model errors along directions where the two models' representations diverge. Empirical results from a synthetic newsvendor problem and a real-world comment moderation experiment confirm these theoretical predictions, showing that W2S consistently outperforms the strong-only baseline and standard semi-supervised approaches in terms of decision quality.
AI.conclusion: W2S provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated approach for improving contextual stochastic optimization under data asymmetry. The key insight is that decision-aware weak-to-strong learning is particularly effective when the weak and strong models have complementary feature representations (low correlation dimension), enabling unlabeled data to compensate for limited labels. The framework bridges semi-supervised learning and data-driven decision-making with formal guarantees on excess decision risk.

title: RRPO: Reference-Relative Policy Optimization with Stratified Conditional Rollouts
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has shown strong effectiveness in reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback, where sampled rollouts can be compared within a group using task-provided correctness signals. However, extending group-relative optimization beyond verifiable settings is challenging because success in many tasks is not captured by a single correctness criterion. We propose \textbf{Reference-Relative Policy Optimization (RRPO)}, which generalizes GRPO by replacing direct correctness-based advantage construction with reference-relative contrastive comparisons. RRPO first uses \emph{stratified conditional rollouts} to construct positive and negative anchor sets, and then trains a metric projection head with a set-contrastive objective to compare candidate rollouts against these anchors. The resulting alignment scores directly define contrastive advantages: during policy optimization, the projection head is frozen, and the scores are centered within each rollout group in a standard group-relative objective. We evaluate RRPO using anchor-based contrastive advantages throughout policy optimization, without relying on task ground-truth verifiers. Across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings, RRPO remains competitive with verifier-based optimization, improves over weakly supervised baselines, and provides additional gains after supervised fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: RRPO generalizes GRPO beyond verifiable settings by replacing correctness-based advantage with reference-relative contrastive comparisons. It uses stratified conditional rollouts to construct anchor sets and trains a frozen metric projection head to produce alignment scores as contrastive advantages within group-relative optimization.
AI.motivation: GRPO relies on task-provided correctness signals (verifiable feedback) to compute advantages within rollout groups. This limits its applicability, since many tasks lack a single binary or scalar correctness criterion. The authors aim to extend group-relative policy optimization to non-verifiable settings where success is more nuanced.
AI.method: RRPO introduces two key components: (1) Stratified conditional rollouts construct positive and negative anchor sets. (2) A metric projection head is trained with a set-contrastive objective to compare candidate rollouts against these anchors. The resulting alignment scores define contrastive advantages. During policy optimization, the projection head is frozen and scores are centered within each rollout group in a standard group-relative objective, eliminating dependence on ground-truth verifiers.
AI.result: RRPO remains competitive with verifier-based optimization across verifiable reasoning, open-ended generation, and post-SFT settings. It improves over weakly supervised baselines and provides additional gains after supervised fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: RRPO successfully extends group-relative optimization beyond verifiable feedback by leveraging reference-relative contrastive comparisons. It matches verifier-based methods without requiring task ground-truth signals and offers complementary benefits when combined with SFT.

title: Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF) for Cyber Anomaly Detection
summary: Malicious anomalous activity detection is a fundamental challenge for cyber security systems. Both tensor decomposition under statistical framework with CANDECOMP-PARAFAC alternating Poisson regression (CP-APR) and normalizing flows have proven to be powerful unsupervised machine learning methods that model multi-dimensional data and capture complex and multi-faceted details of behavior profiles in cyber security applications. In this study, we propose Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework integrating CP-APR structural anomaly scores with latent-space density scores derived from normalizing flows. In our experiments, we show that the HLSF framework improves anomaly detection performance on a dataset of real-world compromised user credentials collected from the large enterprise network of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) during a red-teaming exercise, compared with using CP-APR or normalizing flows alone.

AI.tldr: HLSF combines tensor decomposition (CP-APR) with normalizing flows to improve malicious activity detection in enterprise networks, demonstrated on LANL red-teaming data.
AI.motivation: Cyber security systems require robust unsupervised anomaly detection. Existing methods — CP-APR (structural) and normalizing flows (density-based) — each capture complementary but incomplete aspects of malicious behavior profiles. A fusion approach can leverage both to improve detection performance.
AI.method: The authors propose Hybrid Latent-Structural Fusion (HLSF), a weighted anomaly fusion framework that integrates: (1) CP-APR structural anomaly scores derived from tensor decomposition under a statistical Poisson regression framework, and (2) latent-space density scores from normalizing flows. The two scores are combined into a unified anomaly score.
AI.result: HLSF outperforms using CP-APR or normalizing flows independently on real-world compromised credential data from LANL's enterprise network during a red-teaming exercise.
AI.conclusion: Fusing structural (tensor-based) and latent (density-based) anomaly signals yields superior malicious activity detection compared to either method alone, validating the complementary nature of the two approaches for cyber security applications.

title: Attractor Geometry Determines the Identifiability Limits of System Discovery
summary: Symbolic discovery of governing equations from data is limited not only by algorithm design and data volume, but by the geometry of the attractor: what the long-run dynamics allow to be recovered. Using a within-system design on Lorenz-84, where one forcing parameter drives fixed-point, limit-cycle, and chaotic regimes while the governing equations and library stay fixed, we show that a single number, $λ_{\min}(M)$, the smallest eigenvalue of the invariant-measure moment matrix, sets the identifiability ceiling for both sparse regression (SINDy) and evolutionary symbolic regression (PySR). Derived from the Birkhoff ergodic theorem and obtained from a short reference trajectory before any run, $λ_{\min}(M)$ measures how fully the attractor covers function space: where it vanishes, recovery is impossible for any algorithm, sparse or combinatorial alike; as it grows, both algorithms improve. Chaos raises $λ_{\min}(M)$ by spreading the attractor, but also enlarges it and amplifies noise; because noise enters SINDy's regression bottleneck linearly and PySR's discrimination channel superlinearly, the same transition can push the two methods in opposite directions, so deeper chaos is not uniformly better. Parameter-free mechanistic scores from this framework transfer without refitting to a held-out Lorenz-96 system, confirming mechanism rather than curve-fitting; a criterion read from the equations predicts when added chaos will not improve conditioning. We also introduce Soft F1, a coefficient-weighted structural metric that resolves performance differences invisible to binary-success and predictive scores. The first question of discovery is then not which algorithm, but what the attractor permits.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the geometry of a dynamical system's attractor fundamentally limits symbolic equation discovery, with a single metric λmin(M) — the smallest eigenvalue of the invariant-measure moment matrix — setting a hard identifiability ceiling for both sparse regression (SINDy) and evolutionary symbolic regression (PySR), outperforming algorithm choice as the primary determinant of recovery success.
AI.motivation: Existing research on symbolic discovery of governing equations focuses heavily on algorithm design and data quantity, but neglects a more fundamental limiting factor: whether the attractor geometry of the dynamical system itself makes the underlying equations identifiable in the first place. The authors seek to formalize and quantify this intrinsic limit.
AI.method: Using a within-system design on the Lorenz-84 model, the authors vary a single forcing parameter to traverse fixed-point, limit-cycle, and chaotic regimes while holding the governing equations and basis library constant. They derive λmin(M) from the Birkhoff ergodic theorem, computed from a short reference trajectory, which quantifies how thoroughly the attractor samples function space. They then evaluate both SINDy and PySR across these regimes, introducing also a new structural metric called Soft F1 (coefficient-weighted) to capture performance differences invisible to binary-success scores. The framework is validated on a held-out Lorenz-96 system without refitting.
AI.result: λmin(M) sets a strict identifiability ceiling: where it vanishes, no algorithm can recover the equations; as it grows, both SINDy and PySR improve. Chaos raises λmin(M) by spreading the attractor but also enlarges it and amplifies noise. Because noise enters SINDy's regression linearly and PySR's discrimination channel superlinearly, the transition to chaos can push the two methods in opposite directions — deeper chaos is not uniformly beneficial. Soft F1 reveals performance differences invisible to binary-success and predictive error metrics. The mechanistic scores transfer without refitting to Lorenz-96, confirming the framework captures genuine mechanism rather than overfitting.
AI.conclusion: The first question of governing-equation discovery should not be "which algorithm?" but "what does the attractor permit?" The λmin(M) criterion, computable before any discovery run, provides a principled, parameter-free diagnostic of whether recovery is even possible. The authors also provide a criterion read from the equations to predict when added chaos will not improve conditioning, offering practical guidance for experimental design.

title: Now We Know? A Systematic Comparison of TerraMind and THOR
summary: Benchmarks for Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) increasingly rank models by aggregate score, but such rankings obscure why models differ: how much of the gap is architecture, how much is decoder capacity, and how much is a use-case-specific artefact? This study addresses that gap through a controlled comparison of two GFMs developed under European Space Agency's $Φ$-lab with contrasting design philosophies: THOR, which introduces a compute-adaptive architecture supporting variable patch sizes and unifies Sentinel-1, -2, and -3 data at their native resolutions; and TerraMind, a multimodal generative GFM pretrained with a dual-scale token/pixel objective that enables any-to-any cross-modal generation (Thinking-in-Modalities) to infer missing sensors at inference time. Rather than reporting a single leaderboard, we investigate the axes along which the two architectures actually differ - patch size, decoder complexity, finetuning regime, input modality, and model scale - across ten use cases spanning segmentation and regression in diverse domains, including climate disaster response, methane leak detection, snow monitoring, or sea ice mapping. We find that architectural design choices - patch size and decoder type in particular - explain more performance variance than model identity itself, that the two models embody complementary investment strategies (pretraining-time scale for TerraMind versus inference-time tokenisation for THOR), and that correctly interpreting results requires dataset-level characterisation. The resulting picture is not a single winner but a set of hypotheses and a diagnostic ablation methodology that we expect to generalise to future GFMs beyond THOR and TerraMind.

AI.tldr: Rather than ranking geospatial foundation models by aggregate scores, this paper performs a controlled comparison of two ESA Φ-lab models (THOR and TerraMind) to isolate how architectural choices—particularly patch size and decoder type—explain performance variance across ten diverse use cases, revealing complementary investment strategies and a diagnostic ablation methodology generalizable to future GFMs.
AI.motivation: Current GFM benchmarks rank models by aggregate scores, obscuring the sources of performance differences. It is unclear whether gaps stem from architecture, decoder capacity, or use-case-specific artifacts. A systematic, controlled comparison is needed to disentangle these factors.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of two architecturally distinct GFMs (THOR: compute-adaptive, variable patch sizes, unified multi-sensor native-resolution data; TerraMind: multimodal generative, dual-scale token/pixel objective, any-to-any cross-modal generation) across ten use cases (segmentation and regression tasks including climate disaster response, methane leak detection, snow monitoring, sea ice mapping). Ablated along five axes: patch size, decoder complexity, finetuning regime, input modality, and model scale.
AI.result: Architectural design choices—particularly patch size and decoder type—explain more performance variance than model identity. The two models embody complementary strategies: TerraMind invests in pretraining-time scale, while THOR invests in inference-time tokenization. Dataset-level characterization is essential for correctly interpreting results.
AI.conclusion: There is no single "winner" between THOR and TerraMind. Instead, the study yields a set of hypotheses and a diagnostic ablation methodology expected to generalize to future GFMs, advocating for use-case-driven model selection over leaderboard rankings.

title: Automated Data Engineering and Feature Selection for the Case Study of Warpage Detection in Fused Deposition Modeling
summary: This study contributes toward development of an Automated Data Processing (ADP) framework designed to evaluate and reinforce optimal machine learning model-feature combinations for predictive tasks in fused deposition modeling (FDM) process datasets. The methodology is centered around a reinforcement learning-inspired policy updating mechanism, where multiple machine learning models are trained on both full feature sets and feature subsets selected through Shapley-based Explainable AI (SHAP XAI) across 217 datasets. At each episode, the framework assesses the predictive accuracy and F1-scores of each model-feature pair, computes a scalar reward, and updates $Q$ values to guide future model selection. SHAP XAI feature importance was employed to generate reduced yet informative feature subsets to enable the framework to explore performance with dimensionality. The policy was shown to evolve over multiple episodes, with reward distributions used to visualize performance stability. Overall, results indicate that leveraging the ADP framework through XAI algorithms successfully converges toward optimal model-feature configurations with improved accuracy and stability. Specifically, the proposed framework improves the test-set AUC from 0.9248 to 0.9731 and increases the mean reward value by more than fifty percent compared with the baseline full-feature configuration.

AI.tldr: An Automated Data Processing (ADP) framework using reinforcement learning-inspired policy updating and SHAP-based feature selection is proposed to optimize machine learning model-feature combinations for FDM process datasets, achieving test-set AUC improvement from 0.9248 to 0.9731.
AI.motivation: The need to automatically and optimally pair machine learning models with the most informative feature subsets in FDM additive manufacturing processes, where manual model selection and full-feature approaches are suboptimal, motivating a data-driven framework that self-improves through iterative reward-based learning.
AI.method: An ADP framework combining reinforcement learning-inspired policy updating with SHAP XAI for feature subset selection. Multiple ML models are trained on both full and SHAP-reduced feature sets across 217 datasets. At each episode, predictive accuracy and F1-scores are evaluated, scalar rewards computed, and Q-values updated to guide future model-feature pair selection. Reward distributions visualize performance stability over episodes.
AI.result: The framework successfully converges toward optimal model-feature configurations. Test-set AUC improved from 0.9248 (baseline full-feature) to 0.9731, and mean reward increased by over 50% compared to baseline.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging the ADP framework with XAI algorithms enables convergence toward optimal model-feature combinations with superior accuracy and stability, demonstrating the efficacy of reinforcement learning-guided automated feature and model selection for FDM predictive tasks.

title: Signed Rectified Flow: Negativity-Controlled Generation
summary: We introduce Signed Rectified Flow (Signed RF), a generalization of Rectified Flow that targets the signed measure $π^{sign} = (1+α)π^+ - απ^-$, where $α>0$, $π^+$ is the distribution to promote, and $π^-$ is the distribution to suppress. Although direct sampling from a signed measure is not well-defined, Signed RF induces a valid generative process that concentrates probability in regions where the signed measure is positive while provably excluding regions dominated by its negative component. It therefore provides a principled framework for incorporating negative information and exclusion constraints into generative modeling. We analyze the signed continuity equation underlying Signed RF and use a charged-particle interpretation to explain how negative mass forms exclusion barriers. This theory further motivates practical adaptive guidance algorithms. Across several applications, Signed RF improves the fidelity-diversity trade-off on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization experiments, and reduces nudity induced by adversarial prompts in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP and aesthetic scores.

AI.tldr: Signed Rectified Flow extends Rectified Flow to signed measures, enabling generative models to incorporate negative information by promoting desired distributions and suppressing undesired ones, with theoretical guarantees and practical applications in fidelity-diversity trade-offs, anti-memorization, and safety alignment.
AI.motivation: Standard generative models only model positive probability distributions, making it impossible to directly encode exclusion constraints or negative examples. The authors aim to provide a principled framework for incorporating "what not to generate" into flow-based generative modeling.
AI.method: Signed RF generalizes the continuity equation to signed measures of the form π^{sign} = (1+α)π^+ - απ^-, deriving a valid generative process that concentrates probability where the signed measure is positive. A charged-particle interpretation shows how negative mass creates exclusion barriers. Practical adaptive guidance algorithms are developed based on this theory.
AI.result: Signed RF improves the fidelity-diversity trade-off on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization experiments, and reduces adversarial-prompt-induced nudity in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP and aesthetic scores.
AI.conclusion: Signed RF offers a principled, theoretically grounded approach for integrating negative information into generative models, with broad practical utility across fidelity-diversity control, memorization suppression, and safety alignment.

title: Adaptive Two-Stage Online Learning for Service-Affecting Failure Detection in Mobile Core Networks
summary: Mobile network operators monitor aggregated traffic volumes to assess the operational health of core network infrastructure. Reliable failure detection is challenging due to strong temporal structure, non-stationarity, measurement artefacts, and extreme class imbalance, which limit static threshold-based monitoring. This paper proposes a two-stage online learning framework for traffic-based failure detection in mobile core networks. Stage I incrementally models normal traffic dynamics using lightweight regression with time-aware features. Stage II analyses prediction residuals together with contextual indicators to detect genuine service-affecting network failures. The framework operates fully online under a prequential evaluation protocol, enabling continuous adaptation with low computational overhead. Across linear and non-linear models, the proposed two-stage architecture achieves the best precision-recall trade-off, attaining the highest recall, F1-score, and AUC at acceptable false positive rates. These results demonstrate the importance of explicit residual decomposition for reliable failure detection in streaming mobile core network data.

AI.tldr: A two-stage online learning framework for detecting network failures in mobile core networks, using lightweight regression to model normal traffic and residual analysis with contextual indicators to identify anomalies, achieving superior precision-recall trade-offs under streaming conditions.
AI.motivation: Static threshold-based monitoring fails due to strong temporal structure, non-stationarity, measurement artefacts, and extreme class imbalance in aggregated mobile network traffic data, motivating the need for an adaptive, online failure detection approach.
AI.method: A two-stage online learning framework under prequential evaluation: Stage I uses lightweight regression with time-aware features to incrementally model normal traffic dynamics; Stage II analyzes prediction residuals combined with contextual indicators to detect genuine service-affecting failures.
AI.result: The two-stage architecture achieved the best precision-recall trade-off across both linear and non-linear models, attaining highest recall, F1-score, and AUC at acceptable false positive rates compared to alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Explicit residual decomposition is crucial for reliable failure detection in streaming mobile core network data, and the proposed framework enables continuous adaptation with low computational overhead.

title: Censoring-Aware In-Context Learning for Generalized Supplier Lead Time Estimation in Supply Chain Planning
summary: Supplier lead time forecasting is a central input to material requirements planning, inventory optimization, and supply chain risk management. However, many industrial lead time datasets are naturally right-censored: at the time forecasts are required, some orders have not yet arrived. Standard regression and classification approaches discard this information, while conventional survival models require task-specific modeling. We propose LeadTime-ICL (LT-ICL), a censoring-aware in-context learning model for probabilistic lead time forecasting. LT-ICL combines a transformer backbone with a conditional normalizing-flow head, producing a full predictive distribution over lead times. The model is pretrained on synthetic right-censored lead time tasks, enabling in-context adaptation to new industrial datasets without task-specific parameter updates. We provide theoretical support for this formulation by showing that excess CRPS is bounded by prior misspecification and amortized approximation errors, providing clear direction for improving forecasting performance. We evaluate LT-ICL on 24 proprietary supply-chain datasets spanning seven industries. LT-ICL achieves the lowest point-forecasting error on 15 of the 24 datasets, and the lowest probabilistic forecasting error on 14 datasets, yielding the best average rank across both. These results support right-censored probabilistic forecasting as a practical formulation for supplier lead time prediction and demonstrate that pretrained in-context models can provide accurate, low-adaptation-cost forecasting for industrial planning systems.

AI.tldr: LT-ICL is a censoring-aware in-context learning model for probabilistic supplier lead time forecasting that uses a transformer with a normalizing-flow head, pretrained on synthetic right-censored tasks, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on 24 industrial datasets across seven industries without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Industrial lead time data is naturally right-censored (some orders haven't arrived at forecast time), but standard regression/classification methods discard this censoring information, and conventional survival models require burdensome task-specific modeling. A method is needed that handles censoring natively while offering low-adaptation-cost deployment across diverse industrial settings.
AI.method: LT-ICL combines a transformer backbone with a conditional normalizing-flow head to produce full predictive distributions over lead times. The model is pretrained on synthetic right-censored lead time tasks, enabling in-context adaptation to new datasets without parameter updates. Theoretical analysis bounds excess CRPS by prior misspecification and amortized approximation errors.
AI.result: Evaluated on 24 proprietary supply-chain datasets across seven industries, LT-ICL achieved the lowest point-forecasting error on 15/24 datasets and the lowest probabilistic forecasting error on 14/24 datasets, yielding the best average rank on both metrics.
AI.conclusion: Right-censored probabilistic forecasting is a practical formulation for supplier lead time prediction. Pretrained in-context models like LT-ICL can deliver accurate, low-adaptation-cost forecasting suitable for real industrial planning systems.

title: Operational Proto-Introspection in Looped Language Models: Process-Quality Taps, Executable Branching, and the Readout-Control Boundary
comment: 49 pages, 8 figures. Paper 1 of a two-paper series; companion methodology paper submitted separately
summary:
Can a language model read the quality of ongoing computation, and can an external intervention turn that readout into better outcomes? We test both questions in a frozen 2.6B looped transformer, Ouro-RLTT. On GSM8K, a strict pre-answer probe excludes the answer region and gold value yet predicts eventual success: hidden states plus length and log-probability shortcuts reach AUROC 0.797, versus 0.731 for the shortcuts alone (incremental +0.066; task-clustered 95% CI [+0.021, +0.112]; 170 tasks, 680 candidates). Low-capacity taps also read role-specialized properties: task-disjoint branch survival reaches 0.9697 oracle retention, content ranking reaches 0.6310 macro top-1, and generated-branch correctness reaches AUROC 0.7755. A non-looped control replicates a candidate-quality readout, so recurrence is not required for every signal.
  We build branch/carry/prune machinery over Ouro's 192-slot recurrent cache, including branch-specific cache lineage and a bit-exact residual-capture splice that recomputes only the affected suffix and saves up to 88% of per-branch layer passes. No frozen intervention produces a validated capability gain. Directional steering is an established negative; a four-task matched-sampling comparison removes evidence for a frozen-fork gain but cannot estimate a general deficit; terminal selection remains unresolved and underpowered; and bounded LoRA changes surface behavior without improving net reachability. A two-null audit does not support the simplest span-misalignment explanation.
  We call this readable-but-not-yet-usable property operational proto-introspection. The model is not consulting our probes: we read its hidden trajectories, and our interventions fail to convert those readouts into validated capability. The pre-answer result is limited to one domain. Load-bearing values use source-item-disjoint splits and antisymmetrized evaluation where applicable.

AI.tldr: A frozen 2.6B looped transformer exhibits hidden-state readouts that predict task success, branch survival, and answer correctness without accessing the answer region, but no external intervention successfully converts these readouts into validated capability gains — a property termed "operational proto-introspection."
AI.motivation: The authors investigate whether a language model's internal hidden states contain decodable signals about ongoing computation quality, and crucially, whether those readouts can be leveraged through external interventions to improve task outcomes. This probes the gap between interpretability (reading) and steerability (writing) in frozen models.
AI.method: Using a frozen 2.6B looped transformer (Ouro-RLTT) on GSM8K and 170 tasks, the authors: (1) train linear probes on hidden states — strictly excluding the answer region — to predict eventual correctness; (2) extend probing to role-specialized properties (branch survival, content ranking, generated-branch correctness); (3) build branch/carry/prune machinery over the model's 192-slot recurrent cache with cache lineage and residual-capture splicing (saving up to 88% of layer passes); and (4) test interventions including directional steering, frozen-fork matched sampling, terminal selection, and bounded LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.result: The pre-answer probe achieves AUROC 0.797 (vs. 0.731 for length/log-probability shortcuts alone; +0.066, CI [+0.021, +0.112]). Task-disjoint branch survival oracle retention hits 0.9697, content ranking macro top-1 reaches 0.6310, and generated-branch correctness AUROC is 0.7755. A non-looped control replicates candidate-quality readout, so recurrence is not necessary. However, no frozen intervention yields validated capability gain: directional steering is negative, frozen-fork shows no gain, terminal selection is underpowered, and LoRA changes surface behavior without improving net reachability.
AI.conclusion: The model exhibits "operational proto-introspection": hidden states are readable and predictive of downstream outcomes, but the authors' intervention machinery cannot yet convert these readouts into validated capability improvements. The pre-answer result is limited to one domain (GSM8K), and all key values use source-item-disjoint splits with antisymmetrized evaluation where applicable.

title: Robust Multi-View Classification under Noisy Supervision via Global Anchor Consensus
summary: In recent years, multi-view learning has attracted increasing attention, as it integrates the complementary information of heterogeneous views. Most existing multi-view classification methods rely on accurate annotations to guarantee performance. However, noisy labels are ubiquitous in practice due to imperfect annotation, and the refinement signals that existing methods derive from models trained on such noisy supervision can gradually lose their reliability. To deal with this problem, we propose a novel Global Anchor-based Label Auditing method (GALA) for multi-view classification to resist the negative impact of noisy labels. Specifically, we construct a global anchor for each class in every view, which aggregates the samples of the whole class and thus offers a stable reference insensitive to individual predictions. Then, each view measures how close an instance is to the anchor of its observed label relative to the nearest competing anchor, and the per-view evaluations are fused with the classifier confidence into a cross-view audit score. Based on the audit scores, suspicious samples are assigned small weights, and an adaptive correction strategy rewrites a label only when the anchor-based candidate agrees with the classifier prediction. Finally, the corrected labels in turn refine the anchors and supervise noise-robust representation learning. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that GALA outperforms eight state-of-the-art methods, especially under high noise rates.

AI.tldr: GALA is a multi-view classification method that resists label noise by constructing stable per-class global anchors in each view, computing cross-view audit scores to identify suspicious samples, and adaptively correcting labels through agreement between anchor-based candidates and classifier predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view classification methods rely on clean annotations, but real-world labels are often noisy. Current noise-handling approaches derive refinement signals from models trained on noisy supervision, causing reliability to degrade over time. A stable, noise-resistant reference mechanism is needed.
AI.method: GALA operates iteratively: (1) Constructs a global anchor per class per view by aggregating all samples of that class, providing a stable reference. (2) Computes per-view closeness of each instance to its observed label's anchor versus the nearest competing anchor. (3) Fuses per-view evaluations with classifier confidence into a cross-view audit score. (4) Assigns small weights to suspicious samples and applies adaptive correction — rewriting a label only when the anchor-based candidate agrees with the classifier prediction. (5) Refined labels update anchors and supervise noise-robust representation learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six datasets show GALA outperforms eight state-of-the-art methods, with particularly significant gains under high noise rates.
AI.conclusion: Global anchors provide a stable, noise-insensitive reference that, combined with cross-view auditing and conservative label correction, effectively mitigates the impact of noisy labels in multi-view classification.

title: AMICA-Python: Adaptive Mixture Independent Component Analysis with Anderson Acceleration
summary: Adaptive Mixture Independent Component Analysis (AMICA) is widely used in EEG research and has long been associated with strong empirical performance for blind source separation. Despite its impact, practical use has historically depended on a single Fortran implementation, accessed via the EEGLAB toolbox for MATLAB, limiting its accessibility for analytical pipelines not designed within the MATLAB ecosystem. Here we present AMICA-Python, a Python implementation of the AMICA algorithm, with a scikit-learn-conformant API designed for integration with existing scientific Python pipelines. The implementation follows the reference algorithm closely while adopting modern software engineering practices and an interface familiar to Python users. Additionally, we introduce an optional Anderson acceleration scheme that can dramatically reduce the time to convergence for this relatively slow algorithm. To evaluate numerical agreement and practical performance, we benchmarked AMICA-Python against the reference Fortran implementation on 14 open EEG recordings. After averaging 3 runs of each implementation on all 14 recordings, AMICA-Python closely matched the reference, with a median final normalized log-likelihoods of 11.572 for both the Fortran and Python implementations, and a negligible median relative absolute difference of only $1.07\times10^{-8}$ when normalized by the absolute Fortran value. Runtime was also competitive. Relative to the reference implementation, AMICA-Python was 17.7\% faster, while the Anderson-accelerated variant was 34.1\% faster. AMICA-Python reproduces the reference implementation to high numerical precision with competitive runtime, while making AMICA available through a more accessible and extensible Python interface.

AI.tldr: AMICA-Python is a Python reimplementation of the AMICA blind source separation algorithm for EEG data, featuring a scikit-learn-conformant API. It reproduces the reference Fortran implementation to high numerical precision (median relative absolute difference ~10⁻⁸), runs 17.7% faster, and an Anderson-accelerated variant achieves 34.1% speedup.
AI.motivation: The widely-used AMICA algorithm for EEG blind source separation has historically been available only through a single Fortran implementation in MATLAB's EEGLAB, restricting its use to MATLAB-dependent pipelines. There is a need for a Python-native implementation with a modern, standardized API to broaden accessibility and enable integration with scientific Python ecosystems.
AI.method: The authors developed AMICA-Python, faithfully reproducing the reference AMICA algorithm while adopting modern software engineering practices and a scikit-learn-conformant API. They also introduced an optional Anderson acceleration scheme to speed up convergence. Benchmarking was performed on 14 open EEG recordings, comparing normalized log-likelihoods and runtime against the Fortran reference across 3 runs per recording per implementation.
AI.result: AMICA-Python achieved a median final normalized log-likelihood of 11.572, identical to the Fortran reference, with a median relative absolute difference of only 1.07×10⁻⁸. Runtime was 17.7% faster than the reference, and the Anderson-accelerated variant was 34.1% faster.
AI.conclusion: AMICA-Python successfully reproduces the reference Fortran implementation with high numerical fidelity and competitive-to-superior runtime, while providing a more accessible, extensible, and Python-ecosystem-friendly interface for EEG blind source separation.

title: Conditioned Direct Feedback Alignment via Activity and Error Geometry
summary: Direct feedback alignment (DFA) trains hidden layers with fixed random projections of the output error, avoiding the transposed-weight backward pass of backpropagation (BP). We study a failure mode of DFA training that is distinct from feedback quality: the local weight update is calculated by an outer product, so anisotropy can enter through either its presynaptic-activity factor or its local-error factor. Our analyses with controlled synthetic regimes isolate the first failure mode and show an approximately 40-percentage-point activity-conditioning gain when high-variance directions contain task-irrelevant nuisance. Three clean confirmations isolate a different regime: error conditioning improves raw DFA by 1.77--7.53 percentage points, and combining independently selected activity and error factors adds 0.40--0.90 points over activity conditioning. The signs hold for tanh/one-vs-rest MNIST and preregistered Fashion-MNIST, and replicate on eight fresh seeds in a ReLU/softmax MNIST model. This factorization yields a symmetric block-local family of normalized DFA (nDFA): activity nDFA right-preconditions by an inverse activity second moment, error nDFA left-preconditions by an inverse local-error second moment, and K-nDFA applies both factors with separately tuned damping. A linearized post-alignment calculation gives an exact input-side spectral identity and a Kronecker-factor motivation for the two-sided rule, whereas norm matching rules out a scalar step-size explanation. The error factor is fragile when under-damped, BatchNorm is a strong activity-side alternative, and convnet gains remain partial. We therefore frame conditioned DFA as a factor-level study of when local outer-product rules fail, not as a general replacement for BP or a solution to all-layer convolutional credit assignment.

AI.tldr: DFA training can fail due to anisotropy in either the presynaptic-activity factor or the local-error factor of the outer-product weight update. The authors factorize this problem, propose a family of normalized DFA (nDFA) methods with activity and error conditioning, and demonstrate consistent gains across multiple datasets and architectures, while clarifying this is a factor-level study, not a general BP replacement.
AI.motivation: To isolate and analyze a distinct failure mode of Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA) beyond feedback quality: anisotropy in the outer-product local weight update, which can enter through either the presynaptic-activity or local-error factor, and to develop conditioning strategies that mitigate this failure.
AI.method: The authors propose a factorized analysis of the DFA outer-product update, yielding a symmetric block-local family called normalized DFA (nDFA): activity nDFA (right-preconditions by inverse activity second moment), error nDFA (left-preconditions by inverse local-error second moment), and K-nDFA (both factors with separately tuned damping). They validate using controlled synthetic regimes, tanh/one-vs-rest MNIST, preregistered Fashion-MNIST, and ReLU/softmax MNIST with fresh seeds. A linearized post-alignment calculation provides a spectral identity and Kronecker-factor motivation.
AI.result: Activity conditioning yields approximately 40 percentage points gain when high-variance directions contain task-irrelevant nuisance in synthetic regimes. Error conditioning improves raw DFA by 1.77–7.53 percentage points on clean tasks, and combining both factors adds 0.40–0.90 points over activity conditioning alone. Results hold across multiple architectures/datasets. The error factor is fragile when under-damped; BatchNorm serves as a strong activity-side alternative; convnet gains remain partial.
AI.conclusion: Conditioned DFA is framed as a factor-level study of when local outer-product rules fail — not as a general replacement for BP or a solution to all-layer convolutional credit assignment. The factorization into activity and error conditioning provides a principled lens for diagnosing and partially remedying DFA training failures.

title: On the Diverse Dynamical Behaviors Arising in Deep Linear Transformers
summary: We study the inference-time behavior of deep linear encoder-only transformers through the lens of interacting particle systems. In this perspective, tokens are modeled as particles that interact dynamically through successive linear self-attention layers. We show that in embedding dimension two, for any key, query, and value matrices, the dynamics can be reformulated as a generalized Kuramoto-type model with pure second-harmonic coupling. This formulation is amenable to Watanabe--Strogatz theory which reveals the dynamics are intrinsically low-dimensional regardless of the parameter matrices. For a class of token initializations associated with the Ott--Antonsen (OA) manifold, we show that the parameter matrices induce a diverse variety of long-time behaviors in linear transformers, including clustering, oscillations, and bifurcations. The oscillations and bifurcations are characterized by uncovering a hidden Hamiltonian structure in the dynamics. By establishing a structural stability result, we further show that dynamics initialized near the OA manifold exhibit the same long-time behavior as those initialized exactly on the manifold. Motivated by our theory in dimension two, we conduct numerical experiments for analogous parameter regimes in higher-dimensional transformers. Our numerical experiments suggest that the long-time behaviors characterized in our theoretical results persist in higher dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes deep linear encoder-only transformers as interacting particle systems, showing that in 2D embedding space the dynamics reduce to a generalized Kuramoto model with second-harmonic coupling. Using Watanabe–Strogatz theory and the Ott–Antonsen manifold, the authors characterize clustering, oscillations, bifurcations, and a hidden Hamiltonian structure, with structural stability ensuring robustness near the OA manifold. Numerical experiments suggest these behaviors persist in higher dimensions.
AI.motivation: To understand the inference-time dynamical behavior of deep linear encoder-only transformers by reformulating token interactions as a particle system, thereby revealing low-dimensional structure and long-time behaviors that are otherwise obscured in the standard attention framework.
AI.method: The authors model tokens as interacting particles under successive linear self-attention layers. In embedding dimension two, they reformulate the dynamics as a generalized Kuramoto-type model with pure second-harmonic coupling, then apply Watanabe–Strogatz theory to prove low-dimensionality. They identify the Ott–Antonsen (OA) manifold as a reduced description, characterize parameter-induced clustering, oscillations, and bifurcations via a hidden Hamiltonian structure, prove structural stability near the OA manifold, and conduct numerical experiments in higher dimensions.
AI.result: In 2D, the dynamics are intrinsically low-dimensional regardless of parameter matrices. On the OA manifold, parameter matrices produce clustering, oscillatory regimes, and bifurcations governed by a hidden Hamiltonian.
